note: Project-authored construction observations distilled from shipped Roblox UI. No image, asset or third-party source is reproduced here.

genres.label: Anime fighting / battlegrounds — move bar with cooldowns, combo counter, quest list, boss bar, ability gacha
demonstrates: the request that defines the genre's HUD is literally 'a hotbar UI that displays four moves' — four is the default slot count, not an arbitrary pick
the slot is not Roblox's default backpack; the thread's whole premise is that battlegrounds games replace the backpack with a fixed custom bar
cooldown is described as a 'sliding cooldown' — a moving wipe across the slot rather than a number alone
cooldown truth lives on the server: remaining time is computed from workspace:GetServerTimeNow() timestamps, so the slot's visual state is a render of a server number, not a client timer
the poster ended up on HotbarPlus and asked it for auto-use, i.e. a slot that fires its ability the moment the keybind is pressed rather than selecting a tool first
the cooldown state is a coloured overlay ON the slot ('the red thing on the tool'), tweened, and the slot becomes usable at the moment the overlay completes
the answer given is always 'build a custom bar' — the default backpack is treated as disqualifying for this genre
no slot is ever removed while on cooldown; it stays in place and changes appearance, so the bar's geometry is constant across the whole fight
the radial cooldown is built from frames plus a ROTATING UIGradient, not from rotating the frame

the reason is a concrete engine fact stated in the post: ClipsDescendants stops working when you rotate a UI element, but rotating a UIGradient does not break it — so the gradient carries the rotation and the frame carries the clip
this is what makes a TRANSPARENT radial possible; the older technique needs an opaque backing to hide its halves
the API is one call against the slot's own indicator: module.RadialStart(CooldownIndicatorUI, duration) — the radial is a child of the slot, not a separate screen element
the fill is driven by a transparency NumberSequence with keypoints at 0, i/101, i/101 + 0.001, and 1 — a hard edge one thousandth wide is what reads as the sweep line
rotation advances 1.8 degrees per one percent (100 steps x 1.8 = 180), i.e. the gradient's half-turn spans the full cooldown
a constant +90 degree offset is what pins the 0% point; without it the start of the sweep drifts, which the poster reports as the visible bug
so the sweep's origin is a deliberate constant, not a default — a radial whose 0% sits somewhere other than the top is the signature of skipping this offset

a commercial pack built for this exact problem separates THREE layers per slot: the ability FRAME (120 PNGs), the cooldown RING around it (264 PNGs), and a cooldown SWEEP overlay (22 PNGs) — the ring and the sweep are not the same object
the hotkey badge is its own art layer (28 badge PNGs), separate from both frame and icon — the keybind is decoration on the slot, never the slot's label

slot state is enumerated as art, not as a tint: alongside elemental styles the list names 'Locked', 'Cooldown Slate' and 'Overcharge' as first-class styles, so locked and charged are distinct frames rather than a dimmed ready frame
rings ship as discrete progress frames at 10% steps (…_000 through …_100), which is the granularity the pack considers legible
everything exports at both 64px and 128px — the slot is a small square icon, at icon sizes, not a card
six slots, on E R T Z X C — so the bar is not always the number row, and 4–6 is the real range rather than 4 being universal
the in-fight display is described as showing 'the skills and the keys they are assigned' — icon plus key, together, on the same element
rebinding is a SECOND screen, not the bar: a UIGridLayout of every owned skill plus a set of key buttons, where you click a skill and then click a key
the binding is stored as a key→ability map (for example ["E"] = "FireJab") and persisted, so the bar's contents are player data and the generator must not hard-code slot order
the combo counter is a number with a TIMER bar behind it, built from two stacked frames: a static dark backing frame and a coloured fill frame over it
the fill starts at UDim2.new(1, 0, 1, 0) and is tweened to zero width — it drains, it does not fill
the fill's AnchorPoint is Vector2.new(0, 0.5), so it collapses toward one edge rather than shrinking about its centre
the tween is Linear easing for the whole combo window — an eased decay would misreport how much time is left
every new hit CANCELS the running tween and replays it from full; the element hides itself and the count resets only when the bar reaches zero
the combat HUD carries SEVERAL separate meters rather than one composite bar: health, a green ultimate meter, a blue energy meter, and an orange percentage mechanic
each meter has its own hue, and the hue is the only thing distinguishing them — they are the same shape repeated
the ultimate meter is a first-class HUD element in its own right, not a fill inside the health bar
the shipped surfaces around the fight are a main menu with an animated logo and a skins menu — cosmetics get their own screen, separate from abilities
the one substantive critique was of motion, not layout: the logo's expand/contract read as 'choppy' and needed a smoother transition
the set a designer builds for this genre is Battle Pass + Summons + Upgrades + a button sheet — progression, gacha and stat upgrade are the three panels, and they are designed as one family
the first correction reviewers gave was structural: the experience bars needed 'a little bit of a stronger outline' — a progress bar in this style fails by having too LITTLE outline, not too much
the second was redundancy: the Battle Pass's secondary progression bar was questioned as duplicating the primary one — one track per panel
the third was the genre's characteristic failure: 'way too bright and colorful… make it either a bit darker', with shading suggested — saturation is the trap, and shading is the fix reviewers name
horizontal wins outright; the argument given against vertical is that it 'would produce clutter' at the screen edge

rules.note: Distilled from the references above; each rule names the reference ids it rests on so it can be checked or overturned. IMPORTANT: unlike simulator.json, NO stroke weight or corner radius in this file is measured. Those references were screenshots the owner supplied and read proportionally; these are text pages, and a page that says 'stronger outline' does not say 3px. Every rule here is about SHAPE, LAYER, STATE and PLACEMENT, which is what the text actually supports. Where a number appears it is a number the source states.

moveBar.shape: square icon slot, repeated, equal size
moveBar.layout: one horizontal row, constant — slots never reflow or disappear mid-fight
moveBar.why: four moves is the stated default and six is the observed upper end; both sources build a fixed custom bar specifically because the default backpack is wrong for this genre. A slot that vanishes while unusable destroys the muscle memory the whole genre runs on.

slotKeybindBadge.rule: the keybind is a small separate badge layered on the slot, alongside the icon
slotKeybindBadge.never: the keybind as the slot's main text, or the slot rendered as a labelled button
slotKeybindBadge.why: the cooldown pack ships 28 hotkey badges as their own layer, and the six-slot system shows 'the skills and the keys they are assigned' together. Keys are E R T Z X C in one reference and the number row in another, and they are stored as a persisted key→ability map, so the generator must render whatever binding it is given rather than hard-coding 1 2 3 4.

slotLayers.rule: the cooldown indicator is a CHILD of the slot, not a separate HUD element
slotLayers.why: the pack separates frame, ring and sweep into three sets of art; the radial module's entry point takes the slot's own indicator (RadialStart(CooldownIndicatorUI, duration)); and the TSB thread describes the cooldown as the coloured thing ON the tool. A cooldown drawn anywhere but on the slot loses the association the player is reading for.

accepted: radial sweep around or over the slot
cooldownForm.rule: the slot is always present and changes appearance; the indicator drains rather than fills
cooldownForm.remainingTime: the move's NAME belongs with the cooldown readout, not only its icon
cooldownForm.authority: remaining time is derived from a server timestamp (workspace:GetServerTimeNow()), and the indicator renders a state it does not own
cooldownForm.why: 'sliding cooldown' and the tweened overlay are the two shapes described; the cooldown module's entire configurable surface is text colour, bar speed and the move name, which is how the name earns its place.

radialConstruction.quantization: 10% steps are enough to read; 1% is smooth
radialConstruction.why: this is the one place the genre has a hard engine fact: ClipsDescendants stops working on a rotated UI element but survives a rotated gradient, which is why the transparent radial is built this way and why the naive 'rotate the frame' version fails. The +90 offset is what pins 0% to the top — the source reports the drift as a bug when it is missing — and 1.8 degrees per percent is the half-turn the transparency sweep spans. A generator that invents this from scratch gets a radial whose start point wanders.

resourceMeters.rule: health, ultimate and energy/stamina are SEPARATE bars of the same shape, distinguished only by hue
resourceMeters.never: one composite bar with the ultimate as a fill inside health
resourceMeters.why: the shipped HUD reviewed on the forum carries four of them at once. Repeating one bar shape and changing only the hue is what lets a player read four numbers without four legends.

barOutline.rule: progress and resource bars carry an outline HEAVIER than the surrounding UI's default, and the fill is shaded rather than flat
barOutline.never: a flat fully-saturated fill with a hairline or no outline
barOutline.why: the first correction reviewers gave an anime-styled set was that the experience bars needed a stronger outline, and the second was that the whole thing was too bright and needed shading. This genre's bars fail by being under-outlined and over-saturated. NO thickness is recorded because none was stated — inventing one here would be the exact failure this library exists to stop.

oneTrackPerPanel.rule: a progression panel shows one progress track; a second bar measuring a related thing reads as redundant
oneTrackPerPanel.why: the Battle Pass's secondary progression bar was the thing reviewers questioned. Two tracks make the player ask which one matters.

comboCounter.structure: a large number with a two-frame timer bar behind it — a static dark backing frame and a coloured fill over it
comboCounter.onHit: cancel the running tween and replay it from full
comboCounter.onEmpty: hide the whole element and reset the count
comboCounter.why: every one of these is stated in the source. Linear matters: an eased decay misreports how much combo window is left, which is the only thing the bar exists to say. The anchor at the left edge matters: shrinking about the centre reads as a meter shrinking, not as time running out.

bossHealthBar.placement: front and centre — the top-centre band of the screen, never an edge rail
bossHealthBar.justified: only when the pool is large enough to read as progress; a three-hit boss gets no bar
bossHealthBar.why: the vertical option was rejected for producing clutter, and the placement argument was explicitly about status — a boss pushed to the left reads 'like a side character'. The no-bar case is recorded because it is the rule a generator will otherwise never apply.

hudIsChromeless.rule: HUD elements float directly on the screen with no shared panel, plaque header or frame behind them; panels (shop, quests, summon, battle pass) are a separate surface that opens OVER the fight
hudIsChromeless.contrastWith: simulator.json, where nearly every element lives inside a plaque-headed stroked panel
hudIsChromeless.why: the combat HUD is described as loose meters plus a bar; the menus are named as separate screens. Wrapping a move bar in a simulator-style panel is the most likely way a shared UI kit gets this genre wrong.

screenAnchors.ultimateMeter: with the other resource meters, as its own bar
screenAnchors.comboCounter: floating over the play area, not docked to a panel
screenAnchors.why: only the boss bar's placement is stated outright by a source. The move bar's bottom-centre position is the near-universal convention these threads assume without stating, and it is flagged as inferred rather than dressed up as an observation. The ultimate meter's position relative to the move bar is NOT recorded here — see unverifiedLeads.

abilityStates.rule: each state is a different frame treatment, not a tint or an opacity on the ready frame
abilityStates.why: the cooldown pack enumerates Locked and Overcharge as their own art styles alongside the elemental ones. And the one defect reviewers actually caught in a quest panel was a state glyph that did not move with the state — every row drawn with the same unlocked padlock. A state glyph that is decoration is worse than none.

questList.structure: vertical rows; each row carries objective text, its progress, and a state glyph
questList.rule: the state glyph is bound to the state — locked rows draw a locked glyph
questList.motion: the list is expected to animate; a static list reads as unfinished
questList.why: taken directly from the defect and the request reviewers raised on a shipped-quality quest panel.

gachaBanner.oddsSplit: centre 50%, sides 20% each (within the featured rarity)
gachaBanner.ratesVisibility: an index/rates view hangs off the banner itself, one tap from the pull button
gachaBanner.pullButtons: separate x1 and x10 buttons, each with its own cost on the button
gachaBanner.pity: a displayed count toward a guarantee, per rarity, with thresholds that differ by rarity and can be SHARED between banners
gachaBanner.bannerSwitching: tabs over one screen, not separate screens
gachaBanner.why: all of the numbers here are stated on the Anime Vanguards summon page. The three-up with the featured unit in the centre is the genre's single most recognisable screen, and the centre slot carrying more than double either side's odds is why the layout is asymmetric in meaning while symmetric in shape. Pity as a visible count is what makes the screen a progress surface rather than a slot machine.

cosmeticsAreTheirOwnScreen.rule: skins/cosmetics get a dedicated screen, separate from the ability and upgrade screens
cosmeticsAreTheirOwnScreen.why: observed as a named separate menu in the shipped HUD set, and the anime panel family (Battle Pass, Summons, Upgrades) keeps progression, gacha and stats apart too. One merged 'customise' panel is a tell.

saturationDiscipline.rule: shade the fills; restrain the saturation. The genre's failure mode is everything at full chroma and flat.
saturationDiscipline.why: the strongest critique an anime-styled set received was that it was 'way too bright and colorful' and needed to be darker with shading added. This is the one colour-adjacent rule in the file and it is here because it was stated as a defect, not because colour is construction.

motionQuality.rule: scale and reveal transitions must be eased and smooth; a choppy expand/contract is read as a defect even when the static layout is praised
motionQuality.why: the only substantive critique of a shipped fighting HUD was that its logo animation was choppy. The counterweight is the combo bar, which is deliberately LINEAR — ease the decorative motion, never ease a bar that reports time.

genres.label: Arena shooter / round-based FPS (team deathmatch, objective modes, 1v1 duels)
demonstrates: A control row is a key AND THE STATE IT LEAVES THE PLAYER IN, not a keybind. The table's Notes column carries the transitions and they are the real content: 'Use when crouched/prone to stand up' on Jump, 'Press again while crouching to stand. Press while prone to crouch' on Crouch, 'Sprinting never expires, and forces standing up' on Sprint. A keybind list without those notes is not a controls screen, it is a legend.
Keyboard/mouse and controller are COLUMNS OF ONE TABLE, never two screens. Every function has both bindings on the same row, so a player switching input never has to learn a second layout.
One function can have two bindings with different feel: Sprint is 'Double-tap W' OR 'Hold Shift'. A tap and a hold are offered for the same verb rather than one being declared correct.
The page states its own freshness in its opening sentence — "up-to-date (as of 12 October 2019)". A controls reference that cannot say when it was last true is a controls reference nobody can trust.

A vote popup with THREE keys, not two: y votes yes, n votes no, and j dismisses the popup and abstains. Abstaining is a first-class action with its own control rather than a thing you do by ignoring the modal — which means the interface can tell an abstention from a player who was mid-fight.
The vote runs 40 seconds and resolves the instant the required yes count is reached, rather than always running the clock down. A timer is an upper bound, not a ceremony.

THE TALLY WAS DELIBERATELY MADE LESS INFORMATIVE. Before version 7.0.0 the popup showed how many voted yes and how many voted no; it was changed to show only how many people voted at all. Showing the split let a server see who was winning and apply pressure. This is the rare recorded case of a shipped UI REMOVING a number on purpose, and it is the most transferable thing in this file.
Capability is split INSIDE one feature by progression: a player below Rank 25 cannot initiate a votekick but can still vote in one. The control is visible to everyone and actionable by some.
Failure has consequences the UI must express: a failed vote starts a server-wide cooldown, and the player who initiated it cannot start the next one until somebody else does.

The votekick is explicitly NOT a report — reporting is a separate command entirely. Two actions that look adjacent to a player are kept apart, and the wiki says so in as many words: votekicking 'does not submit a report'.
Settings are reached from a navigation tab in the MAIN MENU, not from a gear icon floating over the HUD. The in-match surface stays free of configuration.

Options that cost frames were labelled 'Expensive' in the list — Viewport Character and Particle Physics — to warn a player before enabling them. The label was attached to the option itself rather than buried in a performance section.

Settings were RENAMED toward plain language in a design revamp: Announcer Voice Overs became Announcers, Death/Pain Noises became Character Vocal Damage Noises, Haptic Feedback became Gamepad Vibration, Subtitles became VO Subtitles. The direction is not uniformly toward shorter — it is toward saying exactly what the switch does.

The developers shipped a note at the bottom of their own settings menu admitting the design was still 'a mess' after an overhaul, and removed it at the next revamp. A settings screen is a surface teams knowingly ship half-finished.

A recorded defect worth designing against: the information panel for Victory Themes displayed the title 'Kill Hitsound'. A reused panel that does not re-read its own title is how a settings list lies about what it is configuring.

INPUT MODES ARE EXCLUSIVE, NOT ADDITIVE. Connecting a controller to a PC makes the WASD keys inactive and switches the layout to the console one. The interface picks a mode rather than accepting both at once, so the on-screen prompts can never show the wrong glyphs.

A control can exist on one platform and not another: crouching is available to PC players and is listed as a PC advantage. The control list is therefore per-platform, and a shared list would promise a key that does nothing.
Movement keys carry alternates on the same row — W or the Up arrow, S or Down — rather than a second remapping screen.

Platform imbalance is compensated in the ECONOMY rather than in aim: mobile and console players earn more Credits per hit and need one fewer tag to activate an ability. The fairness adjustment is a number in the reward path, which is legible, instead of a hidden assist in the aiming code, which is not.

The backpack sits along the bottom of the screen and displays ONLY items that can be opened. It is a container filtered by what is actionable right now, not a complete inventory — the cosmetics you already own live elsewhere.

Matchmaking is a PHYSICAL OBJECT in the lobby: players step onto a duel pad to enter a match, and a countdown from 3 begins once the pad is ready. There is no queue dialog; standing somewhere is the queue.

The pad encodes the gamemode: a 1v1 pad needs one player per side, a 2v2 needs two, and private servers can enable pads that accept unlimited players. The rule of the match is expressed by the object you stand on.

Try-before-buy is reachable FROM THE LOCKED ITEM ITSELF — clicking a locked weapon offers 'Try out for free!', or Q on PC, which sends the player to the shooting range with it. The path from wanting a thing to holding it is one click, not a separate demo mode.
Party size CONSTRAINS the gamemode list: with two people in a party, 1v1 becomes unavailable. A social choice made in one screen removes options in another, so the mode list cannot be a static menu.
Practice targets carry different health on purpose — red bots have 150 health, purple and yellow have infinite — so a range can teach both time-to-kill and sustained tracking without a mode switch.

The shop is divided into seven sections, and the Home section is an OVERVIEW OF THE OTHER SIX rather than a seventh category. The landing tab shows a sample of everything, so nothing is discoverable only by tabbing.

TWO CURRENCIES SIT SIDE BY SIDE and each item is priced in the one that applies to it: Robux for cases and bundles, Keys for wraps, charms and finisher packs. A single price field per item, not a converted dual display.

A price is shown WITH ITS CAVEAT: the article states plainly that listed Robux prices are the standard global ones and that Roblox regional pricing may make an item cost differently. A number the product does not fully control is displayed as such.
The shop home carries banners for the Season Pass and for a rewarded-advertisement offer, so a promotional surface and a purchase surface share one screen and must be visually separable.

Bundle contents are itemised line by line — crate, weapon, skin, wrap, charm, finisher — rather than summarised as a count. A bundle that says "6 items" cannot be compared against another bundle; a list can.

EVERY MODE STATES BOTH WIN CONDITIONS AT ONCE — a score target and a time limit. Team Deathmatch ends at 150 kills or 15 minutes; Free for All ends at 30 kills or 10 minutes. A scoreboard showing only one of the two cannot tell a player how close the round is.

A capture point has THREE states, not two. The hill captures faster the more players stand on it, and when both teams are present it becomes "contested" — progress FREEZES rather than reversing. Contested is a distinct state the bar must render, and freezing is a different promise from decay.
Holding the objective pays continuously — one point per second while controlled — so the score display changes between kills and the round reads as ongoing rather than turn-based.

A mode variant can change one rule and keep everything else: SWAT TDM is Team Deathmatch with headshots dealing double damage even on weapons that normally have no headshot multiplier, and the same 150-kill, 15-minute ending. Variants are a diff, not a new mode screen.

Only a SUBSET of modes can be assigned as daily challenges — TDM, KOTH, Domination, Patrol and Hardpoint. The challenge system draws from a narrower list than the mode picker, so the two lists are not interchangeable in code.

0.rule: Write a control row as a key plus the state it leaves the player in.
0.why: Phantom Forces' controls table carries its meaning in the Notes column — jump stands you up from prone, crouch toggles differently depending on whether you are already crouched. A table of key-to-verb pairs omits exactly the part a player needs.

1.rule: Put keyboard and controller bindings on the same row, and pick ONE input mode at a time.
1.why: Phantom Forces columns them in one table; BIG Paintball 2 deactivates WASD the moment a controller is connected. Together: show both, run one — which is what lets on-screen prompts show the right glyphs without guessing.

2.rule: Show both win conditions at once — the target and the clock.
2.why: Every Bad Business mode is defined by a score AND a time limit. A round display carrying one of the two cannot answer "how close is this?", which is the only question a scoreboard exists to answer.

3.rule: A contested objective is a THIRD state, and it freezes rather than reverses.
3.why: Bad Business KOTH: capture rate scales with attackers, and with both teams present the progress stops changing. A two-state bar has to choose between lying and decaying, and decaying is a different game.

4.why: Phantom Forces' votekick binds j to dismiss and abstain, alongside y and n. Without it, a player who was mid-fight and a player who declined to judge are the same row in the tally.

5.rule: Remove a number when showing it invites pressure on a person.
5.why: Phantom Forces showed the yes/no split on votekicks and changed it in 7.0.0 to show only the number who voted. This is a shipped UI deliberately becoming less informative because the information was being used against players, and it is the clearest precedent in this library for that trade.

6.rule: Gate capability inside a feature by progression, and leave the feature visible.
6.why: Below Rank 25 a Phantom Forces player votes but cannot initiate. Hiding the whole feature would teach nothing; showing it with one action unavailable teaches what the rank is for.

7.rule: Label an option that costs performance, on the option itself.
7.why: Arsenal marked Viewport Character and Particle Physics 'Expensive' in the settings list. A player who cannot see the cost until frames drop blames the game, not the switch.

8.rule: Name a setting after what it does, not after its subsystem.
8.why: Arsenal renamed Haptic Feedback to Gamepad Vibration and Subtitles to VO Subtitles in a revamp. The rewrite went toward precision about the effect, sometimes at the cost of brevity.

9.rule: Offer the trial from the locked item, not from a separate demo mode.
9.why: Rivals puts 'Try out for free!' on the locked weapon and sends the player to the range holding it. Wanting the thing and holding the thing are one click apart.

10.rule: Let the queue be a place, not a dialog, when the game already has a lobby.
10.why: Rivals duel pads: step on the pad, a countdown from 3 begins, and the pad itself encodes how many players the mode needs. A lobby that exists and also shows a queue modal is two matchmaking interfaces.

11.rule: Price each item in the one currency that applies to it, and state the caveat on prices you do not control.
11.why: Rivals quotes Robux for cases and Keys for wraps, never both, and says outright that regional pricing may change the Robux figure. A converted dual price implies an exchange rate the product cannot honour.

12.rule: Itemise a bundle; never summarise it as a count.
12.why: Rivals lists every bundle line — crate, weapon, skin, wrap, charm, finisher. "6 items" is not comparable against another bundle, and comparison is the entire decision a shop asks for.

genres.label: Horror / survival-horror — vitals and sanity meters, flashlight budgets, objective trackers, jumpscare overlays, lobby vote screens
demonstrates: the bar caps at six UNIQUE non-essential items, and run-critical items (keys, fuses) bypass the cap instead of competing for it — the bar holds two classes of thing at once

each slot carries four pieces of information simultaneously: the item icon, the keyboard number that equips it, a stack count when the item stacks, and a meter of remaining uses or usage time drawn INSIDE the slot
the two classes are distinguished inside the same row rather than by a second container: run-critical items get smaller icons with striped lines under them
slot count is a mode parameter, not a constant — 5 in PARTY MODE, 6 in Battle Mode, 10 in SUPER HARD MODE — so the bar must lay out for a variable count
the wiki names a 'Bar' element separately from the slot variants (normal slot, item-skin slot, buddy slot), so the bar is a frame the slots sit in, not merely the slots side by side
death is a three-phase SEQUENCE, not a panel: the entity jumpscare (eyes filling the screen with sound), then a narrated interstitial, then the run overview

the interstitial is a dark flooded field with one speaker's symbol emitting coloured light at the top — blue for Moonlight, yellow for Starlight — and the text is click-to-advance so the player can skip it
a third speaker (Glitch, in Visions) renders as white uppercase text on black with glitch treatment: speaker identity is carried by type treatment and light colour, never by a name plate
the tone of the interstitial changes with repeat failure — Starlight becomes 'more frustrated' on repeated deaths to the same entity — so the copy slot is stateful
the overview is sectioned rows: run info (doors escaped, whether the run succeeded, which entity killed you, or 'Unknown'), then currency, then up to seven further statistic rows

the currency section shows its ARITHMETIC as separate itemised lines — 1 per room survived, 50 per floor escaped, 1 per 20 gold, a 500% boost multiplier, 10% per friend, modifiers — rather than one total
a penalty is stated as a rule in the same block: dying in the first five rooms cancels all currency gain
the buttons are Return to Lobby and Play Again, and Play Again carries a 30-second countdown on the button itself
a hide-menu control is present so the death screen can be dismissed to spectate without leaving the run
the tension minigame is ONE ICON, not a bar: a heart splits into two halves and the player times each half flying back into it
failure is signalled by recolouring that same icon — the heart turns red on a missed beat — rather than by a separate error message or a shake
the minigame accelerates as the failure window closes, so pacing IS the difficulty curve and no numeric timer is drawn
the same minigame is re-laid out for touch rather than being shown with keyboard prompts a phone cannot press
a single miss is terminal, so the widget has no partial-progress state to draw
approaching a hiding spot raises a small icon prompt keyed to the device (E on PC, a hiding button on touch, a face button on console)
while hidden the state is communicated by a FULL-SCREEN treatment — a black vignette image over the whole view — not by a panel, badge or corner icon
exiting is a movement input (walk forward) on PC with an explicit exit button only on touch, so the overlay must not itself capture the whole screen as a button on desktop
the vitals cluster lives at the BOTTOM-LEFT of the screen, with the oxygen meter sitting beside the health indicator — not centred, not along the top
health is icon-led rather than numeric: it becomes 'increasingly redder in color' as damage accumulates and a skull becomes progressively more visible inside it
a regenerating state RECOLOURS the same meter yellow rather than adding a second indicator, at 1 HP every 8 seconds
temporary/artificial health (AHP) draws as a layer ON TOP of real health and is consumed first, so the meter is layered rather than duplicated
an empty oxygen meter does not kill: it opens a named coughing state that drains 1 HP rapidly, so zero on a survival meter is a new state with its own feedback rather than an end

low-health feedback is spread beyond the bar into the avatar and the world — bleeding at 60 HP, larger blood at 20, altered idle and walk animation at 28, and the diving mask visibly cracking in proportion to damage taken
the light source is budgeted in SECONDS and stated as a number in the item's stats: 127 seconds of charge, with a single battery adding 50% for roughly 63 more seconds
the page documents unequipping as turning the light off faster than the normal toggle, so the charge is spent by equip state as much as by the on/off control

the page documents NO on-screen battery bar, percentage or flicker warning anywhere in its text — recorded here as an absence in the source, not as a claim that the game has no indicator; it is evidence that a seconds-budgeted light can be documented purely as a stat
the battery readout is owned by the TOOL, not by the persistent HUD: the ScreenGui is enabled on equip (BatteryGui.Enabled = true) and hidden otherwise
the value is presented as a numeric TextLabel inside a small named frame (BatteryFrame containing BatteryText), so the baseline form is a number rather than a bar
the display refreshes on the drain tick rather than every frame — the poster's rate is 1.5 seconds per step, so the number visibly steps down instead of animating smoothly
a BRIGHT OUTLINE on the HUD was the single thing that made the interface read as a mobile game rather than a horror game — reviewers said it 'looks a bit out of place'
the fix asked for repeatedly was transparency — 'make it a bit more transparent' — not a different palette
green was rejected for a stamina bar specifically because 'green is commonly used for health': hue carries a fixed meaning and a second meter must take another
the bar in question was a vertical bar pinned to the left side, and solid fills with minimal transparency were named as part of the mobile-game read
reviewers pointed at Amnesia as the construction reference for atmosphere rather than at any Roblox game
concrete values a reviewer asked for on a horror menu: black semi-transparent backgrounds at 0.5 transparency and a slight UICorner bevel around 0.15 scale

rules.note: Distilled from the references above. Units are Roblox UI units: px for stroke and radius, seconds for holds, unitless scale where a source gave a scale. Values marked approximate are read from descriptions rather than sampled. This genre inverts most of simulator.json: where the simulator kit says thick stroke, big radius and saturated fills, horror says hairline or none, small radius and translucent black. Do not inherit the simulator rules here.

panelFill.why: the one numeric value a reviewer actually handed a horror developer was black backgrounds at 0.5 transparency, and a separate thread's whole critique of a horror HUD resolved to 'make it a bit more transparent' — translucency is what lets the scene stay the subject

panelStroke.never: a bright outline, and never the simulator's thick near-black stroke
panelStroke.why: a bright outline on the HUD was named as the single thing that made a horror interface read as a mobile game; separation in this genre comes from the translucent dark fill, not from an edge, which is the exact opposite of the simulator rule

cornerRadius.why: a reviewer's concrete suggestion was a slight UICorner bevel around 0.15 scale, which on a standard button height lands near 4-6px; the same threads show developers questioning whether rounding belongs in horror at all, so this is recorded as a small value that is a live decision rather than as a house default

vitalsCluster.pairing: the second meter sits BESIDE the first, further meters stack above
vitalsCluster.never: centred along the bottom, and never along the top
vitalsCluster.why: Pressure documents health at the bottom left with the oxygen meter beside it; the corner keeps the centre of the screen clear for the thing the player is afraid of, which is the whole point of the genre

meterState.mechanism: the meter changes its own appearance instead of gaining a number
meterState.damaged: progressively redder as the value falls
meterState.regenerating: the same meter recolours (yellow), no second indicator is added
meterState.overlayIcon: a skull fades up inside the meter as it empties
meterState.never: a percentage label bolted beside the bar
meterState.why: Pressure's health readout reddens and reveals a skull as HP drops and turns yellow while regenerating — one element carrying three states, which is why a horror meter can be read at a glance in the dark where a number cannot

temporaryHealth.rule: a shield or temporary value draws as a LAYER on top of the real meter and depletes first
temporaryHealth.never: a second separate bar next to the real one
temporaryHealth.why: Pressure's artificial HP displays on top of actual health and is consumed before it, so the player reads one meter with a cap that moved rather than two competing quantities

emptyMeterIsAState.rule: zero on a survival meter opens a NAMED state with its own feedback rather than ending the run
emptyMeterIsAState.example: empty oxygen starts a coughing state draining roughly 1 HP rapidly, which the player can still escape
emptyMeterIsAState.why: Pressure's oxygen at zero begins suffocation rather than death, so the last few seconds of a meter are playable; a meter that kills at zero removes the only moment it was built to create

vitalsFeedbackLeavesTheHUD.rule: low vitals also change the avatar and the view, not only the bar
vitalsFeedbackLeavesTheHUD.examples: bleeding thresholds, altered idle and walk animation, a cracked visor over the camera
vitalsFeedbackLeavesTheHUD.why: Pressure ties bleeding to 60 HP, larger blood to 20, changed animation to 28 and progressive mask cracking to cumulative damage — the bar is a confirmation of something the player already feels, which is why horror vitals do not need to be large

slotContents: the keyboard number that equips it
stack count when the item stacks
a remaining-uses or remaining-time meter drawn INSIDE the slot
hotbar.criticalItemTreatment: smaller icon with striped hatching under it, and exempt from the slot cap
hotbar.variableCount: lay out for a count that changes by mode (5, 6 and 10 all ship in the same game)
hotbar.why: the DOORS inventory packs four values into every slot and distinguishes run-critical items inside the same bar by icon size plus hatching, which is how one row carries two classes of item without a second container

batteryDisplay.ownedBy: the tool, not the persistent HUD
batteryDisplay.visibility: enabled on equip, hidden on unequip
batteryDisplay.form: numeric text in a small frame
batteryDisplay.refresh: on the drain tick, not per frame
batteryDisplay.alsoValid: no indicator at all, with the budget stated in seconds and the pressure carried by the light itself
batteryDisplay.why: a working DevForum system enables the battery ScreenGui on equip and steps a TextLabel once per 1.5s drain tick, while Pressure documents a 127-second flashlight charge as a stat with no on-screen meter described — so the meter is optional but the tool-scoped visibility is not

objectiveTracker.rule: one active objective at a time with a 'New Task' announcement label above it
objectiveTracker.never: a full checklist of the chapter
objectiveTracker.emptyState: reserve the panel's height and keep the text anchored when there are zero tasks
objectiveTracker.why: the entire reported defect in a shipped horror task system was the zero case — the announcement label vanishes, the remaining text goes oversized and off-centre and the panel reads broken — and the zero case is what players stare at between beats

jumpscare.container: its own ScreenGui above everything else
jumpscare.content: a single full-bleed ImageLabel, held Visible false and toggled on
jumpscare.audio: fires on the same frame as Visible becomes true, with no offset
jumpscare.why: the canonical construction is a static full-screen image toggled on with its sound on the same frame and hidden after a fixed short hold — the impact is the cut and the audio, so animating the image or letting the player click it away removes the only thing it does

deathScreen.interstitial: a dark field with one speaker, that speaker's symbol emitting coloured light at the top, click-to-advance text, and copy that changes with repeat failure
deathScreen.speakerIdentity: carried by type treatment and light colour, never by a name plate
deathScreen.overview: sectioned rows — run info, then the reward arithmetic ITEMISED line by line, then up to seven further statistic rows
deathScreen.spectate: a hide-menu control that dismisses the screen without leaving the run
deathScreen.never: a single panel reading You Died with one button
deathScreen.why: the DOORS death screen spends three screens on a failure and shows its currency as per-room, per-floor, conversion, multiplier and per-friend lines rather than a total — the run summary is the reward, which is why players replay, and a one-panel death screen throws that away

fullScreenState.rule: a player state that changes the camera's relationship to the world — hiding, suffocating, losing sanity — is drawn as a FULL-SCREEN overlay, typically a black vignette, not as a panel, badge or corner icon
fullScreenState.prompt: entering the state is offered by a small device-keyed icon prompt near the interactable, not by a panel
fullScreenState.exit: a movement input on desktop, with an explicit exit button only on touch
fullScreenState.why: DOORS communicates hiding with a black vignette over the entire view while the entry prompt stays a small icon — the state is something the player is inside, and a panel would make it a thing they are looking at instead

tensionMinigame.form: a single icon that splits and re-converges
tensionMinigame.failureSignal: the same icon recolours red on a miss
tensionMinigame.difficulty: the widget accelerates as the window closes; no numeric timer is drawn
tensionMinigame.partialProgress: none — a single miss is terminal, so there is no progress state to render
tensionMinigame.touch: re-lay the same widget out for touch rather than showing key prompts a phone cannot press
tensionMinigame.never: a progress bar with a moving marker and a target zone
tensionMinigame.why: the DOORS heartbeat minigame is one heart splitting into halves that fly back in, turning red on a miss and speeding up as the failure window closes — a bar with a target zone would turn a felt rhythm into a read task

lobbyVote.noVoteFallback: the previous map repeats, so the panel can never produce an empty result
lobbyVote.confirmButton: outside the card frame, so it stands out from the cards it acts on
lobbyVote.entranceTiming: every element animates in on the same beat as the backdrop — staggered arrival was reported as a defect
lobbyVote.pagingIcons: custom, never the default arrow glyphs
lobbyVote.cardImage: the card is carried by its map image; a poor capture sinks the card
lobbyVote.diegeticAlternative: physical voting plates in the lobby instead of a panel
lobbyVote.why: Flee the Facility votes four maps over a 30-second intermission on world plates with a leftmost tie-break and a previous-map fallback, and a DevForum voting panel's whole critique was the confirm button sitting inside the frame, default arrows, and elements arriving off the backdrop's beat

colorSemantics.rule: a second meter must take another hue — stamina and sanity do not get green
colorSemantics.accent: small areas of deep red rather than large areas of bright red
colorSemantics.contrast: never red ink on a red field; check contrast, because horror palettes collapse into themselves
colorSemantics.readabilityFloor: there is a darkness below which the UI stops being readable, and reviewers report it as black boxes
colorSemantics.why: a stamina bar was rejected for being green specifically because green already means health, and a separate thread called out red on red directly while recommending smaller deep reds — in a genre with one narrow palette, hue is the only semantic channel left

typography.rule: the title is authored as an image asset and placed as an ImageLabel, not set in a built-in font
typography.bodyText: plain text is acceptable in the HUD; it is titles and buttons that must be authored
typography.hierarchy: the game title is the most prominent element on the menu
typography.why: default Roblox fonts were the most-cited tell across two independent threads — 'it just screams default to me' — and both landed on generating the lettering as an image instead, which makes this a convention rather than one reviewer's taste

controlsAreImages.rule: buttons are ImageButtons on authored plates, not TextButtons with a flat fill
controlsAreImages.minimum: if a control must stay text, it still gets its own backing plate — bare text on a background does not read as a button
controlsAreImages.why: reviewers pushed a horror developer off TextLabel and TextButton onto ImageLabel and ImageButton explicitly to escape the blocky studio-produced look, and a separate thread's complaint was that the buttons lacked visual button-like qualities

backdrop.rule: a flat black field is not a horror background
options: static or film grain behind the content
a dark scene rendered live behind the menu by camera manipulation
backdrop.motif: one strong focal motif, alive — blinking, drifting or slowly rotating — rather than scattered decoration
backdrop.why: a plain black menu background was judged insufficient by every reviewer on the thread, who asked for static behind the title and for the single approved motif to move, while another thread's named strength was a dark room rendered behind the menu by a camera

motion.hoverScale: subtle — a strong zoom on hover was the specific complaint
motion.sound: the hover sound is a pitched-down version of the click sound, one family
motion.why: all three were concrete critiques on one horror menu — the gradient loading wheel did not fit the style, the hover zoom was too strong, and the hover and click sounds did not belong together, which is the difference between a menu that feels authored and one that feels assembled

genres.label: Obby / parkour — stage counters, checkpoints, skip-stage, progress bars, round timers
demonstrates: the bar is a single Frame sitting slightly below the top edge, horizontally centred, and is extremely wide and thin — the author's own capture of it is 1702 by 178, roughly 9.6:1

UICorner is set to CornerRadius 0.2 in SCALE, not in offset — the radius is a fraction of the bar's height, so the ends stay a proportional lozenge at any screen size instead of a fixed px radius that goes square on a phone
UIStroke Thickness is 3 and the colour is black — the same near-black outline convention the simulator references use, at a thinner weight because the element is thin

a horizontal UIGradient runs the length of the bar through seven stops, dark red at 0 through red, orange, amber and olive to green at 1 — progress is read by WHERE you are along a heat ramp, not by a fill that grows

every player in the server rides the bar: one ImageLabel per player, its Image set to that player's HeadShot thumbnail, cloned from a hidden 'playersample' template and positioned by UDim2.fromScale(progress, 0.5) so the heads straddle the bar's centre line

the template ImageLabel is parented into the LocalScript so it is never visible itself, and there is a hard-coded fallback image for when the thumbnail request fails — the bar must still read with a missing avatar
progress is computed geometrically, by projecting the character's position onto a Start→End vector in the world and clamping to 0..1, not by counting stages
the selector is exactly three children: a TextButton named 'Left', a TextBox named 'Input', a TextButton named 'Right' — the stage NUMBER IS THE INPUT FIELD, not a label with arrows beside it

the field's text is seeded from leaderstats.Stage.Value on spawn and re-seeded on every Stage.Changed, so the widget's resting state is always the player's current stage rather than a remembered selection
typing is committed on FocusLost with enterPressed — the field is a jump-to-stage box as well as a readout
Left refuses to go below 0 and Right refuses to exceed leaderstats.Stage.Value; the refusal is silent, the number simply does not move
checkpoints are Parts named with bare sequential integers ('1', '2', '3'…) and the initial SpawnLocation is named '0', so the UI's number and the world object's name are the same string
the stat is an IntValue named exactly 'Stage' inside a Folder named 'leaderstats' — this is the name every other obby widget reads

the stage selector carries two named shortcut buttons alongside the numeric control: 'Lobby' (teleports to stage 1) and 'Last Checkpoint' (returns to the furthest stage reached) — the two destinations a player actually wants are buttons, not values to dial to

a separate 'stage teleport from input text' control exists and the author notes it is optional and can be removed because it confuses some players — the typed field is the advanced path, the arrows are the default one
skip stage is wired to a Developer Product ID, not a Game Pass ID — it is consumable and repeatable, so the button is a purchase surface that stays live after the first buy
the spectate system is bound to Q and E to change the viewed player, so the obby HUD has a camera mode that must not be occluded by the persistent strips
a permanent small on-screen watermark is part of the shipped system (noted as a con on the Obby Wiki) — free obby systems put a persistent credit line somewhere on the HUD

the complete HUD surface of a shipped obby system is: stage selector, progress bar, stage indicator arrow, settings, skip stage and a coil/easy-mode shop — six things, and none of them is a large panel
'Reached checkpoint colour' is a first-class configurable: the checkpoint PART recolours when you have passed it, so the map itself is the progress display and the HUD only summarises it
'Checkpoint animation' is chosen from presets, so arriving at a checkpoint is an event with motion, not a silent state write
settings offered free are exactly Shadow, Blur and Hide UI — 'Hide UI' being a shipped toggle means an obby HUD is expected to be dismissable for clean runs and recording

the mobile shiftlock button is DRAGGABLE (hold 0.7s, then drag) rather than fixed — added touch controls are moved by the player because the bottom corners are already contested by Roblox's own jump and joystick

the system's version 0.8.6 update exists only to make its icons work with TopbarPlus 3.x and Roblox's new experience controls — the launcher buttons for this genre live in the TOP bar, not on a bottom-left circular rail
'Checkpoint Reached' is its own named GUI, separate from the stage counter — arrival is announced by a transient element, and the counter merely settles at the new number
the progress bar is described as being at the TOP of the screen and carrying a percent-completed readout, so the bar and the number are one component and not two
the kit ships a Gamepass shop GUI and a separate 'Troll shop' GUI — obby monetisation is split into two storefronts with different tones, and the second one sells effects rather than advantages
friend-invite and favourite-the-game prompts fire automatically as part of the HUD, so the genre's modal layer includes social nags the core loop never asked for
the kit's pitch word for the GUI is 'fully animated' — motion on the HUD is the differentiator being sold, not layout

the remaining-skip count lives INSIDE the button's own label, in parentheses: the text is set to 'Skip Stage (' .. Limits .. ')' and is rewritten on every use — there is no separate badge or counter beside the button
one control, two behaviours: while the count is above zero the button skips; at zero the same button calls PromptGamePassPurchase instead — it is never disabled and never greyed

the skip itself increments leaderstats.Stage by one and then moves the character to the Part whose NAME equals the new stage number, so the button's effect is expressed in the same integer the counter shows
the author's design gives three free skips before the purchase prompt appears at all, so the paywall is reached by use rather than shown up front

skips are sold as a ladder of Developer Products at quantities 5, 25, 50, 100 and 1000 — five rising tiers of the SAME good, which is a very different shop shape from a simulator's grid of unrelated items
a separate Game Pass sits above the ladder and makes skips unlimited, so the storefront is 'five quantities plus one pass', and the pass is the row that ends the ladder
the author states the infinite-skip UI should be visible only to owners of the pass — ownership hides a control here rather than restyling it, which is the opposite of the simulator OWNED convention

the middle element is a TextBox and the author disabled typing in it after players used it to reach stages they had not earned — shipped selectors often degrade the field to a read-only number, so the number must look the same whether or not it is editable
the step-by-ten control is added as an EXTRA pair of buttons on the same strip rather than as a mode on the existing arrows, which is why the strip reads as five cells: ±10, ±1, number, ±1, ±10

moving the selector moves the character immediately with PivotTo to the checkpoint's CFrame plus about 5 studs of vertical clearance — there is no confirm step, so the widget is a teleporter and not a form

both threads show the clamp being got wrong (values going negative) — the clamp at 0 and at the player's best stage is the part of this widget that is actually hard, and math.clamp is the accepted fix

Weakest source in this file: it is instructional prose about a template rather than an observation of a shipped screen, and it is recorded only for the two screens no stronger source here covers.

rules.note: Distilled from the references above. Units are Roblox UI units: px for stroke and offset radius, scale (0..1) where a reference explicitly used scale, unitless for ratios. Values marked approximate were read from a single source or from a stated capture size and are not measured across the genre. The overriding structural fact: an obby HUD is made of thin persistent strips and small transient toasts, NOT of the plaque-headed modal panels that define simulator.json. Applying the simulator's panel construction to an obby's core loop is the failure this file exists to prevent.

surfaceShape.why: every persistent element observed is a wide thin horizontal bar — the progress bar capture is about 9.6:1 and two independent stage selectors are about 7.4:1 and 3.3:1 — and not one reference shows a bordered panel with a title in the always-on HUD; panels appear only in the shop and settings modals

stageStat.name: Stage
stageStat.worldKey: checkpoint Parts are named with the same bare integer, in a Workspace Folder named Checkpoints
stageStat.why: five independent references read and write exactly leaderstats.Stage and index checkpoints by the stringified number; the selector, the skip button, the progress bar, the world indicator and the global leaderboard all agree on this one value, so inventing a different stat name silently breaks every other widget

stageCounter.default: Roblox's own player list, with the column labelled Stage
stageCounter.customHud: an addition, not a replacement: a short 'Stage: N' or 'N / total' strip near the top edge
stageCounter.pairsWith: difficulty band name and colour in a difficulty chart obby
stageCounter.why: Checkpoint+ exposes LeaderstatsEnabled as its only display setting, and the DevForum threads that build a custom counter all describe disabling the player list first — so the counter is the one HUD element whose default is Roblox's own chrome, and a generator that omits leaderstats leaves the player with no readout at all

progressBar.position: top-centre, inset slightly from the top edge
progressBar.fillStyle: static left-to-right heat gradient, dark-red through orange and amber to green, about seven stops
progressBar.marker: one circular head-shot image per player in the server, positioned along the bar by scale, vertically centred on the bar
progressBar.why: measured from the one tutorial that states engine values; the two decisions that matter are that the radius is expressed in SCALE so a thin bar keeps lozenge ends on every device, and that the bar does not fill — it is a fixed rainbow track that markers travel along, which is what lets every player in the server appear on the same bar at once

progressIsSocial.rule: the progress bar shows EVERY player in the server, each as their own avatar head, not just the local player
progressIsSocial.handlesMissingThumbnail: fall back to a placeholder image; the bar must still read
progressIsSocial.why: the reference clones one marker per player from a hidden template, keys the cache by player name and destroys the marker on PlayerRemoving; the comparison against other players is the point of the element, and it is the single clearest difference from a simulator's private progress meter

stageSelector.layout: one horizontal strip of five cells: -10, -1, number, +1, +10
stageSelector.numberCell: a TextBox, not a TextLabel — the number is the input
stageSelector.seededFrom: leaderstats.Stage, re-seeded on every Stage.Changed and on respawn
stageSelector.commit: arrows act immediately; the typed field commits on FocusLost with enterPressed
stageSelector.why: three independent selectors agree on the arrows-around-an-editable-number shape and two of them carry the step-of-ten pair as extra cells rather than as a mode; the named Lobby and Last Checkpoint buttons exist because those are the two destinations players actually want, and dialling to them one arrow-press at a time is the thing the shortcuts remove

selectorClamp.upper: the player's own leaderstats.Stage — never higher
selectorClamp.feedback: silent — the number simply does not move
selectorClamp.why: going back is free and going forward past your best is refused, and that asymmetry is the entire reason the widget exists; three references show the clamp being got wrong and players reaching unearned stages, so it is the part a generator must get right rather than the part it can omit

teleportOnSelect.rule: selecting a stage moves the character immediately to that checkpoint's CFrame plus about 5 studs of vertical clearance
teleportOnSelect.why: both shipped selectors PivotTo on the button press with no intermediate step — the widget is a teleporter, and wrapping it in a confirmation turns a two-second traversal into a four-click form

skipButton.labelCarriesCount: Skip Stage (3) — the remaining count is written into the button's own text and rewritten on every use
skipButton.never: a separate count badge beside the button, or a disabled button
skipButton.atZero: the same button prompts the purchase instead of skipping
skipButton.why: observed verbatim in a live game's script; one control with two behaviours keeps the paywall in the place the player already looks, and a greyed-out button would hide the offer at exactly the moment the player wants it

skipShop.shape: a single column ladder of the same good at rising quantities
skipShop.terminalRow: one Game Pass that makes skips unlimited, closing the ladder
skipShop.productKind: Developer Products for the quantities (consumable, repeatable), a Game Pass for the unlimited row
skipShop.why: taken from a live game's Products table; because every row sells the same thing, the shop is read by comparing one number down a column, which is why a simulator's four-across grid of unrelated tiles is the wrong container for it

ownedState.rule: owning the pass HIDES the purchase control and reveals the unlimited one
ownedState.never: leave the price visible with an OWNED tag, as the simulator genre does
ownedState.why: two references state the owner-only control is shown only to pass holders; obby monetisation is a live consumable rather than a collection, so there is no cabinet of owned items to display and a persistent OWNED tag would just be clutter on a HUD strip

checkpointFeedback.screen: a transient 'Checkpoint Reached' toast, separate from the counter
checkpointFeedback.world: particles at the checkpoint and a permanent colour change on the checkpoint Part itself
checkpointFeedback.counterRole: the counter does not announce; it settles at the new number
checkpointFeedback.why: the world object carries the durable state and the screen carries only the announcement — that split is why passing a checkpoint in a shipped obby never interrupts the run, and why a modal here would be wrong

nextStageIndicator.form: a floating marker Model above the next checkpoint
nextStageIndicator.why: two references place a star or arrow in Workspace at checkpoint (stage + 1) and reposition it as the stat changes; no reference in this file shows a minimap or a screen-edge compass, so direction in this genre is given in the world and the HUD is left to carry numbers

difficultyBand.rule: in a difficulty chart obby the stage number is always shown against a named, coloured band; bands run in groups of roughly twenty stages
difficultyBand.colourSource: the band, not the theme — the band colour overrides the palette wherever the two meet
difficultyBand.drift: Effortless was originally dark green and is now usually grey; past Hard the wiki states there is no standard at all
difficultyBand.why: the band ladder is the whole information architecture of the sub-genre — counter, selector sections and level geometry are partitioned identically — so a stage label that is only a number throws away the one piece of context the player navigates by

roundTimer.appliesTo: round-based tower obbies, which have no checkpoints and therefore no stage counter
roundTimer.form: one mm:ss countdown, reset at the start of every round
roundTimer.observedRound: 8 minutes, with the tower regenerated from 8 sections
roundTimer.multiplier: part of the same readout: it doubles (1x to 2x) once a player wins, and the clock visibly runs at that rate for everyone still climbing
roundTimer.why: in this branch the clock is the only progress signal the HUD carries, and the multiplier is the only thing on screen that reports another player's success — putting it anywhere but beside the digits loses the causal link between someone winning and the clock speeding up

winScreen.content: a congratulation plus an exit — celebration art, particles, and a return to the lobby
winScreen.never: a score summary or a stats table
winScreen.trigger: touching a specific world object (a victory platform, or a glowing door at the top of a tower)
winScreen.confidence: low — one instructional source; the round-based reference confirms only that the trigger is a place
winScreen.why: the run's whole record is already the stage counter, which persists, so an end screen that re-states it would be reporting a number the player has been watching for an hour; what the screen adds is the moment and a way out

launcherPlacement.mechanism: TopbarPlus icons beside Roblox's own experience controls
launcherPlacement.never: the bottom-left circular rail that simulator.json records
launcherPlacement.why: the one shipped system whose icon layer is documented spent a whole release migrating its icons onto TopbarPlus, and the bottom of an obby screen is already taken by the jump button, the joystick and the persistent selector strip — this is the sharpest layout divergence between the two genres and the easiest one to get wrong by reflex

touchSafety.reservedRegion: the bottom-right quadrant belongs to Roblox's jump button on touch devices
touchSafety.addedControlsAreDraggable: a shipped system ships its extra mobile control as draggable (hold 0.7s, then drag) rather than fixed
touchSafety.why: an obby is played with both thumbs on the movement controls for its entire duration, so any HUD element parked over them costs the player the run; the referenced system solved it by letting the player move the control rather than by picking a position

hideUi.rule: ship a Hide UI toggle in settings
hideUi.why: the three free settings in the most-installed obby system are exactly Shadow, Blur and Hide UI — players record and speedrun these games, so a HUD that cannot be dismissed is a HUD that gets cropped out in software instead

cornerRadius.thinStrips: express as SCALE (about 0.2 of the element's height), not as a px offset
cornerRadius.modalsAndButtons: px offset is fine, in the same large-radius family the simulator references use
cornerRadius.why: measured from the one source that states the property; a fixed px radius on an element whose height changes with the viewport goes square on a phone and pill-shaped on a monitor, and the persistent obby elements are exactly the thin ones where that shows

stroke.why: the one measured HUD element uses UIStroke thickness 3 in black; the near-black outline convention carries over from the simulator references, at a lighter weight because a 4px stroke on a bar 30px tall eats a quarter of it

genres.label: Pet simulator / collection — pet inventory grids, rarity borders, egg-hatching screens, index books, equip slots
demonstrates: the pets menu is opened from a button on the BOTTOM edge of the HUD, not from a side rail — the pet screen is the game's primary screen and gets the primary slot
the open menu carries exactly three controls along its TOP: a padlock, a pet face, and a four-windows icon — lock, auto-select, and grid density
equipping is AUTOMATIC by default; tapping a pet raises a prompt offering 'Edit Mode', and manual selection only exists inside that mode
the pet-face icon is the way back OUT of manual mode to automatic — the manual/auto switch is a persistent toggle in the toolbar, not a one-shot action
the equip capacity is a number the player owns (the guide works an eight-slot example), so the screen must render a capacity it is told, not a fixed row
the redesigned inventory sorts pets greatest-to-lowest by strength and auto-equips the top eight
additional equip slots are unlocked by rank progression, so the slot strip grows over a player's lifetime
variants (Golden 1.5x, Rainbow 3x, Shiny 5x) are a SECOND axis on top of rarity — a tile has to show both a rarity and a variant without them fighting
the equip strip starts at FOUR slots and tops out at ELEVEN — a small opening row that roughly triples, never a grid
extra slots arrive from three different sources (mastery levels, quests, a gamepass), so the strip has to render partially-filled and locked states side by side
the pet screens are reached as TABS ('Quests tab', 'Mastery menu') off one menu rather than as separate windows
the assembly is: side navigation rail, header with an X at its right, and a ScrollingFrame of square slots in fixed columns
each slot carries the unit image, a level/amount badge and a rarity mark — three pieces of information on one square, no more

UIStroke is the framing device on every element, and the top critique was that 'the UIStroke color is different between the X button and the frame' — one stroke colour across frame, close button and tile or the screen falls apart
second critique: 'the content cant fully fit in the scrolling frame horizontally. adjust your cell size to make it fit!' — the grid cell is derived from the container width, never a fixed pixel size
third critique: the 'Lvl 1' / 'Lvl 50' badges drifted left because the label was not centre-anchored inside its badge
the thread's praise was for keeping 'that classic simulator feel' while staying clean — the genre's chunky construction is the goal, not something to modernise away
ViewportFrame is the WRONG renderer for an inventory tile: it 'do[es] not support particles' and 'can cause lag if too many of them are used with models specially with a lot of parts'
the shipped answer is a flat pre-rendered ImageLabel per pet, produced offline against a greenscreen and keyed out
consequence for layout: a tile is an image slot of a known aspect, so the grid can be packed tightly and scrolled without a per-tile render budget
the polished look 'looks much more like an image than a viewport frame' — a fixed camera angle and fixed lighting per pet is what reads as finished
the pet art carries its own stroke/outline baked into the render, so the icon stays readable on any tile tint
tiles are produced by cloning one template UI element into a scrolling container and filling it from data — the template is the unit of design, not the screen

walking up to an egg opens a PurchaseMenu anchored to the egg via worldToScreenPoint and SCALED by camera distance — it is a screen-space panel tracking a world object, not a BillboardGui and not a centred modal
the panel is three stacked bands: NameBackground (egg name), SlotBackground (the odds), AmountBackground (a 'Cost' label)
the odds band is FOUR preview slots, each one a pet preview plus a 'Chance' line plus a colour-coded 'Rarity' line — four is the readable count for an odds strip

hatch sequence, in order: egg tweens UP over 0.65s on Quad easing; oscillates left/right for TEN cycles with the delay starting at 0.11s and shrinking by 0.007s each cycle so the shake accelerates; snaps back to neutral; a flash ImageLabel grows and fades over 0.2s; camera blur steps down over ten steps as the pet appears; the hatch frame tweens DOWNWARD off-screen to dismiss
the revealed pet's name and rarity are held on screen briefly and then cleared as the blur finishes — the reveal has a hold, it does not cut
the hatched pet in PSX is a real 3D model placed in world space in front of the camera, aligned to where its UI element sits — 'that's also how PSX do'

the stated reason is that ViewportFrame 'render[s] 3D model in a very bad quality and didn't rendering particle effects and graphic changes' — the reveal needs particles, so it cannot live inside the UI
the model is positioned by a camera-relative CFrame, not fixed world coordinates, because fixed positions that line up at 766x754 break at 1280x720
so the hatch screen is TWO layers: a UI layer holding the name, rarity and frame, and a world layer holding the pet — and the two are locked together by projection
the detail panel is: pet art in a central box, pet name and stat labels, EQUIP and DELETE as the two bottom actions — equip and delete are a PAIR and they live at the bottom
progress readouts render as fraction bars ('0/3', '0/50') rather than percentages — a pet screen counts things, it does not measure them
a middle bar is reserved for modes such as multi-delete, i.e. bulk operations are a MODE strip between content and actions, not a button on every tile
critique: the name should sit ABOVE the image so the stats block below has room — art in the middle, identity above, numbers below

critique: saturated blue at full strength made reviewers 'want to keep looking away from it'; pure red text (255,0,0) with a (170,0,0) stroke read 'very bright and chunky'. Rarity colour has to be pulled off the primaries or the grid becomes unreadable at tile size
critique: setting the Rotation property made elements 'pixelated and cheap' — an angled badge or ribbon must be a pre-rotated image

'rarity colours are the source of truth. Set a rarity's colours once and every surface follows: the card in the Pets menu, the hatch toast, the egg billboard' — one rarity token, three surfaces, no per-screen colour decisions
the shipped ladder is five rarities: Common green, Uncommon blue, Rare purple, Epic red, Legendary yellow — twenty-eight pets spread across five tiers, roughly five or six pets per tier
