rules.note: Distilled from the references above. Units are Roblox UI units: px for stroke and radius, seconds for timing, unitless for counts. This genre sits ON TOP of simulator.json — panel stroke, plaque header, overhanging red circular close, price pills and text stroke are inherited from there and are not repeated. What follows is only what a PET screen adds.

screenSet.rule: ship three separate screens, not one screen with filters: the bag (what is held now), the index (what has ever been obtained), and the egg panel (what can be obtained)
screenSet.never: a single Pets window with an Owned/All toggle
screenSet.why: the published GUI pack lists Pet Index, Pet Inventory and Egg Display as three separate GUIs, and the devforum enumeration of an expected pet system names index, inventory and hatching as three things

petTile.why: ViewportFrame 'do[es] not support particles' and lags 'if too many of them are used with models specially with a lot of parts'; the shipped look is a fixed-angle, fixed-light pre-render that 'looks much more like an image than a viewport frame'. The PS99-derived tile carried exactly image + level + rarity and no more.

detailPreview.rule: the one-pet detail pane MAY use a live 3D render; the grid may not
detailPreview.why: a shipped system pairs a Module3D preview in the detail pane with flat tiles in the grid — the cost is per visible model, so one is affordable and forty are not

grid.cellSizeRule: derive CellSize from the ScrollingFrame's inner width minus padding, then round DOWN to a whole number of columns
grid.why: the single loudest critique on the PS99-styled inventory was 'the content cant fully fit in the scrolling frame horizontally. adjust your cell size to make it fit!' — a fixed cell clips the right-hand column at the first resolution that is not the author's. Five columns rather than the shop grid's four because a pet bag holds hundreds of stacks where a shop holds a dozen offers.

rarityColour.rule: one colour per rarity, defined once, applied to the tile backing/stroke, the hatch reveal label and the egg odds line
rarityColour.never: a different rarity palette per screen, and never a fully saturated primary
rarityColour.why: 'rarity colours are the source of truth. Set a rarity's colours once and every surface follows: the card in the Pets menu, the hatch toast, the egg billboard.' The counter-example is the hatch panel whose pure (255,0,0) label read 'very bright and chunky' and whose full-strength blue made reviewers 'want to keep looking away from it' — at tile size a grid of full primaries is unreadable.

rarityLadder.pacing: roughly five to six pets per tier
rarityLadder.extendTo: up to nine tiers by appending above Legendary (Mythic, Secret), never by inserting below Common
rarityLadder.why: five is the ladder in both the shipped plug-and-play system (28 pets / 5 rarities) and in Adopt Me's classification (Common, Uncommon, Rare, Ultra-Rare, Legendary); larger games extend upward (Bubble Gum Simulator INFINITY runs nine with Secret at the top). Common is always the bottom and always the quiet colour.

rarityBorder.carrier: the tile's own stroke plus a tint on its backing
rarityBorder.never: a separate decorative frame image per rarity
rarityBorder.why: the rarity token has to survive being restated on the hatch reveal and the egg odds line, which have no tile to put a frame on; and the PS99-styled inventory failed review precisely because 'the UIStroke color is different between the X button and the frame' — one stroke system, recoloured per rarity, is the only version that stays coherent

variantAxis.rule: a variant (Gold / Rainbow / Shiny) is a SECOND mark on the tile, placed in a corner, and must not recolour the rarity backing
variantAxis.why: PS99 pets carry a rarity and independently a Golden 1.5x / Rainbow 3x / Shiny 5x variant; collapsing the two axes into one colour makes a Common Rainbow indistinguishable from a Legendary

stacking.rule: identical pets stack into one tile with an xN counter
stacking.why: a shipped system stacks duplicates with a counter and backs the bag with a 'Unique Pet ID system (UID) — prevents duplicates', so lock, delete and equip address an instance while the grid shows a stack

equipStrip.placement: a separate horizontal strip outside the grid
equipStrip.why: Bubble Gum Simulator INFINITY opens at four slots and caps at eleven from three different unlock sources, so the strip must render filled, empty and still-locked slots together; PS99 unlocks further slots by rank. The devforum recommendation for equipped items is 'a separated section for the equipped item ... as well as potentially the player's character with the equipped item' — equipped state is a place, not only a badge on a tile.

autoEquip.default: automatic — the top n pets by the sort stat are equipped without the player acting
autoEquip.why: PS99 equips the best eight by default and only offers manual selection behind an explicit 'Edit Mode' prompt; 'Equip Best' is named as a first-class button in two independent sources. A pet screen that opens in manual mode with empty slots is the wrong default for this genre.

toolbar.why: PS99's open pets menu carries exactly three icons across its top — a padlock, a pet face and a four-windows icon — and the pet-face icon is also the route back out of manual mode

bulkActions.rule: lock and mass-delete are MODES entered from a strip between the grid and the action row, not buttons repeated on every tile
bulkActions.why: the reviewed hatch/inventory panel reserved a middle bar for options such as multi-delete, and a shipped pet system exposes 'Merge All' as one labelled button; per-tile delete buttons on a grid of hundreds is the failure this avoids

detailPane.why: the reviewed panel put the name beside the art and was told to move it above so the stats had room; equip and delete sit together at the bottom as a pair

counters.rule: progress on a pet screen renders as a fraction (3/8, 0/50), not a percentage and not a bare number
counters.why: the reviewed panel used '0/3' and '0/50' bars; a pet game counts discrete things — slots, hatches, index entries — so the denominator is the information

eggPanel.anchoring: screen-space panel positioned by worldToScreenPoint on the egg and scaled by camera distance
eggPanel.neverAnchoring: a centred modal, or a raw BillboardGui
eggPanel.why: the hatch framework builds exactly NameBackground / SlotBackground / AmountBackground with four chance+rarity slots and tracks the egg by projection; single and triple hatch ship together in a published pet system

hatchReveal.renderer: a real 3D model positioned in front of the camera by a camera-relative CFrame
layers: world layer: the pet model and its particles
UI layer: name, rarity label, frame
sequence: shake: 10 left/right cycles, first delay 0.11s, each cycle 0.007s shorter, so the shake accelerates
flash: an ImageLabel grows and fades over 0.2s
blur steps down over 10 steps while the pet appears
dismiss: the frame tweens DOWNWARD off-screen
hatchReveal.why: the sequence and its numbers are the hatch framework's; the renderer choice is PSX's, whose stated reason is that ViewportFrame 'render[s] 3D model in a very bad quality and didn't rendering particle effects'. A reveal without particles is the tell that a generated pet game is fake, and a camera-relative CFrame is required because fixed world positions that line up at 766x754 break at 1280x720.

index.rule: an index entry stays filled after the pet is deleted, sold or traded away
index.why: the index is described as saving 'the pets you have already hatched' — keying it on current holdings would empty a player's collection every time they merge, and that is the single most common way this screen is built wrong
index.unownedTreatment: NOT OBSERVED — no fetched source described how an undiscovered entry is drawn, so the silhouette/question-mark convention is deliberately not asserted here

rotation.rule: never set the Rotation property on an angled badge, ribbon or label — ship a pre-rotated image
rotation.why: on the reviewed hatch UI, rotated elements read 'pixelated and cheap'. simulator.json's daily-reward banner sits at a deliberate angle, so this rule is how that angle gets built.

genres.label: Arcade racing / driving / car game
demonstrates: the ScreenGui sets ScreenInsets to DeviceSafeInsets and a UIPadding of 16px on all four edges — a HUD is built inside an inset frame, never flush to the raw screen
the meter anchors to a screen corner by matching AnchorPoint to that corner: Position {1,0},{0,0} with AnchorPoint 1,0 pins the bar to the top-right and keeps it there at every aspect ratio
the bar is sized in SCALE, 0.35 wide by 0.05 tall, and its height is then capped by a UISizeConstraint MaxSize of (inf, 20) so a tablet does not render a fat slab

the track is a dark translucent frame (black at 0.75 transparency) with a UIStroke of 3px at 0.25 transparency — the HUD reads over a moving world because of the scrim plus stroke, not because of its fill colour
both track and fill take UICorner with CornerRadius 0.5 in SCALE, which is what produces a true capsule at any height instead of a rounded rectangle
the fill is a child frame at AnchorPoint 0,0.5 anchored to the track's left edge, resized by scale, and tweened over 0.5s with exponential easing rather than snapped
the value is coloured by a five-stop gradient red 225,50,0 → orange 255,100,0 → yellow 255,200,0 → lime 150,225,0 → green 0,225,50, so the bar's colour carries the reading independently of its length
the icon is an ImageLabel at 200% of the bar's height with a UIAspectRatioConstraint and ZIndex 2, centred ON the bar's left end so it overhangs the capsule rather than sitting beside it
size and position in scale, not offset: a frame at {0,100},{0,100} is a different object on a phone and on a 1080p monitor, and a racing HUD is the surface where that difference is worst
UICorner radius should also be expressed in scale (e.g. 0.2); an offset radius of 20 reads completely differently between devices
UIStroke supports OFFSET ONLY — there is no scale stroke — so a single stroke thickness has to be chosen that survives phone-to-desktop, and that is why stroke is the one constant across a kit
centring requires AnchorPoint 0.5,0.5 with Position {0.5,0},{0.5,0}; the countdown overlay and the race-state banner are the two racing elements that depend on this
the Roblox top bar occupies a fixed offset band at the top of the screen (36px in the post, reported as 58px in the current client) and pushes UI down in play mode
mobile virtual controls occupy the bottom-left and bottom-right of the screen, so HUD elements must be designed away from those zones
design mobile-first: mobile has the least room, and scaling a HUD up is easier than scaling one down

the HUD started at the BOTTOM of the screen (gen 1), moved to the SIDE (gen 2), and settled as a corner cluster — the bottom strip was abandoned, which is evidence against centring a driving HUD along the bottom edge
speed was a BAR before it was a dial, and the bar TINTS TOWARD RED as the vehicle approaches its own top speed (gens 6 and 7) — the colour carries 'near the limit', which a bare number cannot
the speed limiter / cruise setting is drawn as a marker ON the speed bar rather than as a separate field, so the target and the current value are read in one glance
gen 5 pairs an analogue gauge with the EXACT numeric speed — the dial and the digits coexist; neither replaces the other
the fuel bar was turned VERTICAL (gen 5 v3) so it reads as a tank beside the round gauge instead of competing with the horizontal speed bar
gen 6 enlarged the speedometer and moved every auxiliary function (vehicle functions, radio) OFF the main cluster onto a sidebar and a strip beneath it — the driving HUD shrank to the driving values
gen 7 adds a boost meter that shows remaining charge and REFILLS while unused, so the meter needs a recharging state distinct from empty
gen 8 adds a tachometer reading engine RPM up to 10,000 with a per-vehicle REDLINE marked on it, plus a three-letter transmission token showing AUTO or MNL
gen 8 also adds a control-bar legend along the GUI listing which key performs which function, because the functions had just been moved from on-screen buttons to the keyboard
a metric/imperial toggle in settings changes the units on this HUD and on the weather HUD together — the unit is a setting the HUD reads, not a hard-coded suffix

the menu splits at the top level into exactly two sections, APPEARANCE (cosmetic, does not change stats) and PERFORMANCE (changes stats, costs cash) — the split is by what the change does, not by part of the car
every option inside a section has its own icon and opens a SECOND-LEVEL sub-tab row rather than a new window; Rims, for example, opens into 'Paint Rims' and 'Rim Type'

a colour option is a compound control, not a swatch grid alone: a preset swatch list, a colour wheel with a brightness slider to its LEFT, a reflectance slider running 0 to 1 in 0.05 increments, and a numeric RGB entry
a performance option is a named LADDER of four tiers — Engine reads Stock / Street / Race / Drag, Brakes reads Stock / Street / Sport / Race, Tires reads Slippery / Stock / Grippier / Insane Grip
each tier row states the signed DELTA it grants against stock (+4% / +8% / +12% top speed; +17% / +39% / +62% brake power) and its price, so the player compares effect against cost inside one row
prices are shown as a MINIMUM and MAXIMUM because the cost scales with how far the vehicle already is from stock — a single price would be a lie for most cars
options unavailable to the current vehicle are simply absent (a boat has no Rims section) rather than shown disabled
suspension exposes ride height, camber and wheel offset as continuous settings whose price scales with how far they are moved — the same panel therefore has to host ladders AND sliders
the same two-family split as Driving Empire, named Appearance and Modifications, with the wiki stating outright that Appearance changes the look and not the specifications

the tuning panel needs only THREE control types across its whole option set: a tier list (Brakes 3, Engine 4, Horn 4, Nitrous 5, Transmission 4, Turbocharger 3), an on/off toggle (Turbo Jump, Air Thrusters, Manual, Welded Differential), and a slide-bar (Window Tint, and two slide-bars for Camber)
the tier COUNT differs per option — 2, 3, 4 and 5 all appear — so the ladder cannot be drawn as a fixed five pips; it has to size itself to the option

every modification row carries a one-line EFFECT string ('Increase Acceleration and Max Speed', 'Changes the braking power') beside its name — the panel explains each stat rather than assuming the name is self-evident

appearance controls come in triplets per surface — colour, reflectance and material for primary, secondary and rims — which is what makes the cosmetic tab a repeating three-control row rather than a list of one-offs
garage layout: the car-select strip runs along the BOTTOM of the screen, the action column (UPGRADE / MODIFY / SELL) sits to one side, and modification slots are a grid of equal squares
an unfilled modification slot is the SAME square at higher transparency, not a missing tile — the grid stays legible when the car is stock

rules.note: Distilled from the references above. Units are Roblox UI units. Values taken from the Roblox HUD-meters documentation and the carousel thread are EXACT (they are quoted property values). Everything else is a convention read off prose describing a screen, and is stated as approximate. Where only one reference supports a rule, the why says so.

hudIsNotAPanel.rule: The in-race HUD is a set of corner-anchored clusters over the world. It is never a bordered panel, never centred, and never grows a second row of buttons.
hudIsNotAPanel.why: The single loudest finding: a developer's speedometer was rejected as looking 'more like a menu rather than a speedometer', and Ultimate Driving's sixth-generation GUI solved the same problem by moving every auxiliary function off the cluster onto a sidebar. Two independent sources, one shipped, arriving at the same fix.

screenRegions.gaugeCluster: bottom-right, raised clear of the mobile jump button
screenRegions.minimap: bottom-right when present, in which case the gauge cluster moves to bottom-left
screenRegions.standings: top-right or left edge, as a truncated list
screenRegions.insets: ScreenInsets = DeviceSafeInsets, plus a 16px UIPadding on the root frame
screenRegions.why: Roblox's own HUD tutorial sets DeviceSafeInsets with 16px padding and anchors by matching AnchorPoint to the corner; the Staff best-practices post states that mobile virtual controls own the bottom-left and bottom-right and that the top bar eats a fixed band at the top; the CorporateChaos devlog puts the minimap bottom-right, which is what forces the gauges to the other side.

cornerAnchoring.rule: Every HUD cluster sets AnchorPoint to the corner it lives in (top-right 1,0; bottom-left 0,1; bottom-right 1,1) and positions at that corner in scale.
cornerAnchoring.why: Taken directly from Roblox's HUD tutorial, where Position {1,0},{0,0} with AnchorPoint 1,0 is what keeps a meter pinned to the top-right across aspect ratios. Positioning a corner element from the top-left is the defect this prevents.

scaleNotOffset.stroke: offset, one value for the whole kit
scaleNotOffset.why: The Roblox Staff post states that offset sizing produces a different object on a phone and a 1080p monitor, that UICorner should be scale, and that UIStroke supports offset only so one thickness must serve every device. The HUD tutorial adds the MaxSize cap so a scale-sized bar does not become a slab on a tablet.

speedReadout.rule: The speed is shown TWICE — as a swept gauge or a fill bar, and as an exact numeral with a unit label beside it. Neither replaces the other.
speedReadout.why: Ultimate Driving's fifth generation pairs an analogue speedometer with the exact speed, and its metric/imperial toggle changes the suffix on the HUD from settings — so the unit is data the HUD reads, not a baked string. A gauge alone cannot be read precisely and a numeral alone cannot be read at a glance.

dialGeometry.structure: background circle → face → centred pivot frame → needle as a child of the pivot
dialGeometry.circleFrom: UICorner CornerRadius 1 in scale, not an image
dialGeometry.why: All of it is stated explicitly in the DevForum speedometer-wheel thread, including the failure it prevents: rotating the needle itself puts the pivot in the wrong place, and the 270° arc with the gap at the bottom is what makes a frame read as a gauge rather than as a circle with a line in it.

speedBar.structure: static outer track frame + inner fill resized by scale
speedBar.cornerRadius: 0.5 in scale on BOTH track and fill
speedBar.trackFill: black at ~0.75 transparency with a 3px UIStroke at ~0.25
speedBar.rampDirectionForSpeed: reversed — the bar tints TOWARD RED as it approaches the vehicle's top speed
speedBar.why: Structure, radius, scrim, stroke, tween and the five-stop ramp are exact values from Roblox's HUD-meters tutorial; the reversal is from Ultimate Driving, whose sixth and seventh generation bars turn red near the vehicle's limit. A health meter and a speed meter share a mechanism and run their ramp in opposite directions, which is exactly the kind of thing a generator gets backwards.

limiterMarker.rule: A cruise or limiter setting is a marker drawn ON the speed track at its target position, not a separate numeric field.
limiterMarker.why: Ultimate Driving drew the speed limiter as a bar on the speedometer from its sixth generation onwards, so the target and the current value are compared in one glance instead of two.

tachometer.present: only when the vehicle has gears
tachometer.redline: a marked zone on the arc, per-vehicle rather than fixed
tachometer.placement: second gauge beside the speedometer, smaller
tachometer.why: Ultimate Driving's eighth generation added exactly this — RPM to 10,000 with a redline that depends on the vehicle being driven — at the same moment it added manual transmission. A tachometer in a game with no gears is decoration.

gearAndMode.gear: one large glyph at the centre of the dial — a number, R or N
gearAndMode.transmissionMode: a three-letter token, AUTO or MNL, small, adjacent to the gear
gearAndMode.neverDuplicate: if the speed already appears twice, the second instance becomes the gear
gearAndMode.why: The AUTO/MNL token is Ultimate Driving's own wording from its eighth generation. The no-duplicate rule is the one concrete critique on a posted vehicle speedometer: a reviewer told the author to replace the second MPH readout with a gear indicator because two displays of one number is wasted space.

secondaryMeters.fuel: vertical bar beside the round gauge
secondaryMeters.boostOrNitrous: shows remaining charge and needs a distinct RECHARGING state, because it refills while unused
secondaryMeters.throttleAndBrake: two thin bars, not numerals or icons
secondaryMeters.why: Ultimate Driving turned the fuel bar vertical so it stops competing with the horizontal speed bar, and its boost meter refills when not in use; the throttle/brake bars are what the critiqued speedometer added in its revision, and the published racing HUD kit lists pedals as a first-class element.

controlLegend.rule: When functions are on the keyboard, a small key-legend strip sits along the bottom of the cluster. On touch, the same functions become tappable buttons and the legend disappears.
controlLegend.why: Ultimate Driving added a control-bar legend in its eighth generation precisely because functions had just moved from on-screen buttons to keys, and restored the click buttons for emergency vehicles later. The legend and the buttons are the same information for two input methods, so a build must pick one by platform.

raceState.layout: two rows in one strip at the top-left
raceState.emphasis: the player's own ordinal is the largest glyph in the strip; the denominator is set noticeably smaller
raceState.sizing: size these larger than instinct suggests
raceState.why: Position and lap counter were the two elements the CorporateChaos polish pass had to ENLARGE, which is the single recorded correction to a race HUD's sizing. The ordinal/denominator split follows from both values being fractions where only the numerator changes.

standingsBoard.rows: top 5, plus the local player's own row pinned when outside the top 5
standingsBoard.scrim: a translucent dark plate behind the list — never pure transparency over the world
standingsBoard.rowIdentity: each row keyed to a player so rows animate between places rather than re-rendering
standingsBoard.why: The top-five-plus-self shape is the stated requirement in the race-leaderboard thread. The scrim is the concrete critique of Downhill Rush's in-race list, which a reviewer called too transparent to read. Row identity follows from placement being recomputed continuously from checkpoint progress.

countdown.sequence: a 'GET READY' line, then one numeral at a time, then GO
countdown.hudDuringCountdown: SUPPRESSED — the driving HUD is hidden or dimmed while the overlay is up, and is handed the screen on GO
countdown.why: The mutual exclusion is not a preference: 'the main ui overlaps the race start screen every time' is the bug a reviewer reported against a shipped Roblox racing game, and the CorporateChaos devlog describes the opposite — a countdown that hands over to the HUD as the icons fade into the minimap. Two sources, one showing the failure and one showing the pass.

minimap.playerIcon: rotates so the icon's bottom faces the player's heading; the map itself does not rotate
minimap.offscreenMarkers: pinned to the border rather than removed, with a second visual state distinguishing groups
minimap.constraint: the rendered region must be square and axis-aligned or every icon drifts
minimap.why: All from the published Roblox minimap renderer, which pre-renders square tiles at a fixed pixels-per-stud, rotates icons rather than the map, and pins out-of-region markers to the border. The square-and-axis-aligned constraint is the documented failure mode, and it is the sort of thing a generator silently gets wrong.

wrongWayWarning.rule: A centred warning icon appears when the player is travelling against the course direction.
wrongWayWarning.why: Recorded from one reference only, and a non-Roblox one — the CorporateChaos devlog. It is listed because no Roblox source described this element at all, and a rule with one source that says so is better than a gap nobody notices.

carSelectCarousel.interpolation: smoothstep t*t*(3-2*t) by distance from screen centre
carSelectCarousel.why: Every number is the author's own from the carousel code-review thread. The two that matter most are the scale ratio — the centre item is two to three times its neighbours, which is what makes the centre READ as the selection without a highlight — and the 15px threshold, without which every attempted drag also selects a card.

carPreview.rule: The car is a live ViewportFrame of the actual model, rotating, never a flat image.
carPreview.selectionFeedback: a border highlight on the entry, strong enough to read at a glance
carPreview.why: The dealership prototype already used viewports and was told to rotate the models so the player sees front and back before buying; the same thread's author was told their existing selection highlight was too faint. A decal of a car is the shortcut that makes a dealership look like a catalogue.

statBars.rule: Car stats are a fixed, ordered list of labelled horizontal bars, identical rows in identical order on every car.
statBars.structure: static outer track always at full width + inner fill sized by scale
statBars.fill: UDim2.fromScale(value / max, 1), value expressed as a fraction of the best in the game
statBars.why: From the vehicle-stats thread: a stat is a percentage of best, so a full bar means best in the game rather than some number, and the outer track stays visible so the unfilled remainder is part of the reading. Fixed order is what makes two cars comparable — reordering rows per car destroys the only thing the bars are for.

garageLayout.carSelect: a horizontally scrolling strip of cards along the BOTTOM edge
garageLayout.subject: the selected car large, centre screen, in a viewport
garageLayout.actions: a column to one side: UPGRADE / MODIFY / SELL
garageLayout.modificationSlots: a grid of equal squares; an empty slot is the same square at higher transparency, never a missing tile
garageLayout.cardOverlap: cards in the strip overlap identically or not at all
garageLayout.selectionLabel: the selected car's name animates on change
garageLayout.why: The bottom card strip with the car above it appears in two independent Roblox garage threads. The transparent-not-absent empty slot and the identical-overlap rule are both specific defects that were caught in review, and the animated name label is the fix for a strip where a static label leaves the selection ambiguous.

actionHierarchy.secondary: MODIFY — same size family, quieter fill
actionHierarchy.destructive: SELL — the QUIETEST of the group
actionHierarchy.accent: one accent value, never two shades of the same hue in one panel
actionHierarchy.why: This is the whole accepted fix list from the Fantasy Racing garage critique: a white SELL button was pulling the eye away from the two buttons that matter, and two different yellows read as a mistake. The instinct to make the destructive action loud is exactly backwards for a garage, where selling is rare and upgrading is the loop.

tuningLadder.shape: a named ladder of tiers per option, sized to the option rather than to a fixed pip count
tuningLadder.rowContents: tier name + the signed delta it grants against stock (+8% Top Speed, +39% Brake Power) + its price
tuningLadder.priceRange: show a minimum and a maximum when cost scales with distance from stock
tuningLadder.ownedAndNext: mark the owned tier; the next tier up is the purchasable one
tuningLadder.otherControls: only two others are needed — an on/off toggle and a slider
tuningLadder.effectLine: every option carries a one-line plain-language effect string beside its name
tuningLadder.why: Driving Empire's performance tables are literally this: Stock / Street / Race / Drag with percentage deltas and a min/max price per tier. Vehicle Simulator's option list proves the tier count varies (2, 3, 4 and 5 all appear) and that the whole tuning surface needs only a ladder, a toggle and a slider. The effect line is Vehicle Simulator's — the panel explains each stat rather than assuming the name is self-evident.

customizationTabs.secondLevel: each option opens a sub-tab row in place, never a new window
customizationTabs.colorControl: preset swatch row + colour wheel with a brightness slider to its left + reflectance slider 0–1 in 0.05 steps + numeric RGB entry
customizationTabs.surfaceTriplet: colour, reflectance and material per surface (primary, secondary, rims)
customizationTabs.why: Driving Empire and Vehicle Simulator independently split their garage menus by what the change DOES rather than by part of the car, which is the decision a generator would not make on its own. The compound colour control and the 0.05 reflectance step are Driving Empire's exact published values; the colour/reflectance/material triplet is Vehicle Simulator's, and it is what turns the cosmetic tab into one repeating row instead of a list of one-offs.

typographyWeight.rule: No thin weights anywhere in a driving HUD or a garage panel — labels, numerals and icon strokes all carry weight.
typographyWeight.why: Thin fonts and thin icon strokes were the first thing named in the Fantasy Racing critique as the reason the panel read as unfinished; a plus icon had to be thickened before it read as a control at all. Over a moving world this is legibility, not taste.

mobileSizing.rule: Size the HUD and the car-select text for a phone first, keep clusters out of the bottom-left and bottom-right control zones, and allow for the top bar's fixed band.
mobileSizing.why: The Staff post states mobile has the least room and that virtual controls own the bottom corners; the garage critique caught car-select text sized for desktop as a mobile failure, and controller glyphs drawn small as unreadable. A racing HUD is the surface where this is worst, because the player is also steering.

resultsBoard.rows: finishing order with each racer's final time and the reward
resultsBoard.why: Recorded from a commissioning thread's feature list rather than from an observed screen, and flagged as such. It is kept because an end-of-race board is unavoidable in the genre and a rule that says how thin its evidence is beats an invented reference.

modeDegradation.rule: The HUD must degrade: a drag race has no lap counter and no field of eight, so lap and position rows are omitted rather than shown as 1/1.
modeDegradation.why: The same racing system is expected to serve circuit races, drag races and highway races. A HUD that always renders every row shows LAP 1/1 in a drag race, which is the tell that the layout was built for one mode and reused.

genres.label: Roleplay / town-and-city (job pickers, phone hubs, house and furniture placement, avatar and outfit editors, money HUD)
demonstrates: the game's front door is a four-button menu — Play, Neighborhoods, Store, What's New — with the logo at the TOP LEFT and an options gear at the BOTTOM RIGHT; four buttons, not a grid

every one of those four destinations is ALSO reachable from an in-world cellphone: 'the Neighborhoods icon in the cellphone', 'the Updates app in the cellphone menu', 'the Settings icon in the cellphone menu'
the cellphone button itself sits at the LOWER RIGHT corner of the screen once the player is loaded onto their plot
the Store has a second entry point at the BOTTOM LEFT corner — money-spending lives on the opposite corner from the hub
the same feature therefore has two doors (a full-screen menu and a phone app) and they are not allowed to look like two different features

entry is a single hammer button at the BOTTOM RIGHT of the screen (or a mailbox interaction in the world); exit is 'the large X button on the bottom right of the screen' — one corner owns both the way in and the way out

the catalog is a TWO-LEVEL tree with exactly two top-level sections, titled 'Build!' and 'Decorate!'; Build! lists 18 categories (Basements, Basic Shapes, Chimneys, Doors, Fence Gates, Fences, Fireplaces, Floor, Garden, Hatches, Mailboxes, Paths, Pillars, Pools, Roof, Stairs, Structural, Trash, Vehicles, Walls, Wall Trim, Windows) and Decorate! lists 19 (Appliances, Baby & Kids, Beds, Cabinets, Carpets, Chairs, Comfort, Curtains, Counters, Decorations, Electronics, Instruments, Household, Lighting, Plumbing, Pool Items, Storage, Tables, Training)
each category is presented as a tile carrying ONE representative item as its face — the category is illustrated by a product, never by an abstract icon
the player's own bought/earned items live in a separate 'Inventory' reached from the BOTTOM LEFT of the build screen, opposite the exit — purchasable catalog and owned stock are different doors
the search inside a build section has a defined empty state, documented as its own screen ('when a player types something in a build mode section and nothing is found')

the tools are a named verb set, each on a single-key hotkey: Transform (T), Paint (F), Clone (C), Scale (V), Sell/Delete (G), grid on/off (H), grid size cycle (J), collision on/off (K), hide-above-floor (U), floor up/down (Page Up / Page Down), undo/redo (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y), overhead view (hold Space)
linear and area items carry PLACEMENT MODES — 'Default, Box, Chain, and Auto for floors and roofs' when placing walls, roofs, floors and fences — cycled with the same key that selects the tool
Backspace is bound to 'go back to the previous menu', so the catalog is explicitly a navigable stack with a back step, not a flat list
the editor is reached from the Avatar app in the cellphone menu OR by interacting with a wardrobe, dresser or clothing rack in the world — a diegetic object opens the same panel as the menu entry
a life-stage control sits at the TOP of the menu as a slider with six named stops: Baby, Toddler, Kid, Teen, Adult, Elderly — a continuous-looking control quantised to named states

skin tone is also a slider rather than a swatch grid, and the wiki records a real defect of that choice: one tone 'is extremely hard to see against the menu's white' because the slider's own background is white
outfits are SLOTS, bought one at a time (60 Blockbux each), with a dedicated 'Buy new outfit slot' pop-up and a distinct error state for insufficient slots
there is a dedicated field for entering item codes from the Roblox catalog, sitting alongside the browsable categories rather than replacing them
the editor has named, illustrated error states for rule violations that are not about money — too young for a task, too old for a task
four needs meters (Fun, Energy, Hunger, Hygiene) live in a Moods MENU at the bottom right, not on the HUD

the always-visible HUD carries a single aggregated token instead: 'the mood emoticon is in the shape of a notch displaying a single word', colour-coded (Great/Marvelous blue, Energized pink, Happy green, Clean teal, Fine grey)
the wiki states the reason outright — the notch 'serves as a simple method of determining mood without looking at the Moods menu'
that notch has MOVED twice across versions (top of screen pre-0.7.2, top notch, then bottom left as of 0.16.0) while remaining one word and one colour — the summary format survived every relayout
the fix action lives inside the menu next to the meters ('Boost Mood'), and is hidden entirely unless at least one gauge is below 50% — the remedy button only exists when it applies
the hub is a vertical SIDEBAR of ten icon entries, each an icon plus a name: Avatar Editor, Inventory, Animations, Vehicles, Houses, Character Bio, Jobs, Map Themes, Pets & Kids, Store
the Store is one entry in the same rail as everything else — monetisation is not given its own chrome
a second, smaller group of interfaces sits outside the rail: Home Cams, a Time readout, Settings, Family and Quick Chat

the page opens by defining the whole surface functionally — 'the buttons on the screen… essentials in games for making the game playable such as getting houses, editing the players avatar or shop' — i.e. the rail IS the game's feature list
strict two-level navigation: five top-level categories (Animations, Body, Clothes, Pre-Outfits, Accessories) each opening a list of subcategories
Body 'is the default category that opens when accessing the Avatar Editor' — the editor never opens on an empty or neutral screen
Accessories is subdivided by ATTACHMENT POINT, eight of them: Hats, Hair, Face, Back, Waist, Front, Neck, Shoulders — the taxonomy is anatomical, not stylistic
Animations is subdivided by MOVEMENT STATE: All, Idle, Walk, Run, Jump, Fall, Climb, Swim
opening Accessories first offers a 'Search All Categories' option — a cross-category search above the subcategory list

every catalog-backed subcategory carries the same control set: search by keyword / ID / creator / group, six sorts (Relevance, Best selling, Most favorited, Price low→high, Price high→low, Recently published), and a six-step time filter (All time, Past month, Past week, Past 3 days, Past day, Past 12 hours) that appears ONLY for the two popularity sorts
character scale is a ten-stop discrete control from 0.50 to 1.00, not a free slider

the Animations subcategories 'have the name of the animation unlike other categories that don't' — icon-only tiles are the default and names are the exception, reserved for items a picture cannot distinguish
over 80 jobs, grouped into five named categories chosen by roleplay fiction rather than by reward: Service, Family, Shop, Arts, Outside
each job is a tile with a job icon and a name, plus a requirement column that reads 'Free' or names a game pass — the requirement occupies the slot a price would occupy in a shop
selection is immediate and unconfirmed: 'Once a job is selected, it is immediately assigned to the player' — no confirm dialog, no cost step
the picker is NOT where a job is ended: 'After a player equips a job, a new menu labeled Job appears under the Home Cams button', containing exactly Take a Break, End Break and Quit

rules.note: Distilled from the references above. Units are Roblox UI units: offset px for stroke, scale for radius and size unless stated. Counts and positions are quoted from the sources; anything not stated by a source is in openQuestions rather than guessed. The simulator rules (thick stroke, plaque header, overhanging red circle close, price pills) are a DIFFERENT genre's construction and are not assumed here.

oneHub.rule: Every non-diegetic feature opens inside ONE persistent hub. Do not give jobs, avatar, houses and vehicles four separate floating windows.
oneHub.openedFrom: a single button in a screen corner, present at all times
oneHub.why: Berry Avenue's phone is 'the hub for almost everything… picking a job, customizing your avatar, choosing a house, and grabbing a vehicle'; Brookhaven routes ten features through one sidebar; Bloxburg routes Neighborhoods, Updates, Settings and Avatar through one cellphone. Three independent games, one container each.

hubForm.rule: Pick exactly one hub form and commit: (a) a PHONE — a portrait body with a visible frame, a status strip, a home screen of app icons, and a back/home affordance at the bottom; or (b) a RAIL — a vertical stack of icon-plus-name entries down one screen edge whose selection swaps the adjacent panel. Never ship both.
hubForm.phoneSeen: ERLC (8 apps), Bloxburg (cellphone menu), Berry Avenue
hubForm.why: Both forms are shipped and successful, but they are different navigation models — a phone has a home screen you return to, a rail has a persistent selection. Mixing them produces a rail of icons that each open a modal, which is the shape that reads as a developer tool.

phoneFrame.rule: If the hub is a phone, the BORDER is what makes it read as a phone. Give the body a visible bezel and a rounded rectangle silhouette before adding any content.
phoneFrame.cornerRadius: scale, not offset — Roblox's own HUD tutorial uses a scale radius so the shape survives every screen size; UIStroke stays in offset px because it cannot scale
phoneFrame.why: The single concrete piece of construction feedback on the DevForum City RP hub was to add a border so the panel would read as a smartphone. The same thread records the author's warning that curved corners fight an open/close animation — so the radius has to be decided before the animation, not after.

railContents.rule: The rail is the game's feature list, one entry per feature, icon plus name. Monetisation is ONE entry in the same rail with the same treatment — it does not get its own chrome.
railContents.observedLength: 10 entries in Brookhaven (Avatar Editor, Inventory, Animations, Vehicles, Houses, Character Bio, Jobs, Map Themes, Pets & Kids, Store)
railContents.why: Brookhaven's Store sits between Pets & Kids and nothing special, styled like its neighbours. A store rendered louder than the features around it is the tell that the interface was designed by its revenue model rather than by its player.

flattenNestedTabs.rule: When a hub entry grows a second level of tabs, SPLIT it into sibling entries in the rail rather than nesting.
flattenNestedTabs.why: Brookhaven did exactly this in spring 2026: one Character Bio menu holding Character Bio / Jobs / Map Themes / Kids became four separate sidebar buttons, leaving Character Bio with only name and bio. The observed direction of travel in this genre is nested tabs → a longer flat rail.

appIconGrid.rule: A phone home screen is a grid of rounded-square app icons identified by SHAPE AND COLOUR. Each app gets a silhouette distinct enough to be named without reading a label.
appIconGrid.why: The ERLC wiki navigates entirely by icon description — 'the messaging app (speech bubble icon)', 'the yellow taxi app right next to the Emergency Services app'. A grid of same-coloured glyphs cannot be described that way, and a player who cannot describe a button cannot be told where it is.

statusStrip.rule: The phone's top strip carries TIME and ambient world state. It does NOT carry currency.
statusStrip.why: The concrete review note on the DevForum City RP hub was to take money out of the top-left status position, put in-game time there, and give money its own widget under a bank icon. Brookhaven likewise keeps a separate Time readout outside the feature rail. Currency in a status bar reads as a phone battery indicator — ignorable.

homeScreenSummary.rule: Surface live state on the home screen so an app need not be opened for a glance — and give every distinct state its own glyph.
homeScreenSummary.why: ERLC shows the weather on the phone's home screen 'without the need to open the Weather app', and the same wiki records the defect that follows from cutting corners on it: 'the home screen shows the same icon for Rain and Thunderstorm conditions'. A summary that collapses two states into one glyph is worse than no summary, because it is confidently wrong.

contextualHudDocking.rule: A HUD affordance that appears because of player STATE docks onto an existing anchor button, extending it into a short stack. It does not claim a fresh corner.
contextualHudDocking.examples: Brookhaven's Job menu appears under the Home Cams button; a quick-access garage button appears near the Home Cameras button when driving a small vehicle
contextualHudDocking.why: Two independent Brookhaven features attach to the same anchor. This is what keeps a roleplay HUD from accumulating one orphan button per system until all four corners are full — which is the failure mode of every city-RP screenshot in the DevForum thread.

moneyHud.rule: Currency is its own always-on HUD widget: a capsule with the currency icon overhanging its leading end and the number inside, hugging one screen corner.
moneyHud.geometry: 16px padding from the screen edges; width in scale; height in scale with a hard pixel maximum (20px in Roblox's own tutorial) so it cannot balloon on a large screen; corner radius 0.5 in SCALE so it stays a true capsule; 3px UIStroke in offset px because stroke cannot scale; icon at 200% of the bar height, locked 1:1, centred on the leading end so it overhangs both edges
moneyHud.topAnchorCaution: a top-anchored row must start below the Roblox top bar, cited as 36 offset px and reported nearer 58 in replies; use ScreenInsets so it clears notches
moneyHud.why: These are Roblox's own published numbers for a corner HUD readout, and they answer the two things a generator gets wrong: the icon is NOT inside the bar, and the radius is scale rather than pixels, which is why hand-built money pills look right on desktop and wrong on a phone.

needsMeters.rule: N needs meters live in a PANEL. The always-visible HUD carries one aggregated token — a single word plus a colour — not N bars.
needsMeters.observed: Bloxburg: four moods (Fun, Energy, Hunger, Hygiene) in a bottom-right menu; the HUD carries a one-word colour-coded notch (blue Great, pink Energized, green Happy, teal Clean, grey Fine)
needsMeters.why: The wiki states the purpose of the notch directly — determining mood 'without looking at the Moods menu' — and the notch kept that one-word form across three different screen positions in three versions. Four bars on the HUD is the thing this game replaced.

remedyButtonIsConditional.rule: A button that fixes a bad state is rendered only while the bad state exists. Do not ship it disabled.
remedyButtonIsConditional.why: Bloxburg's 'Boost Mood' button lives beside the meters and is available only when at least one gauge is below 50%. This is the roleplay counterpart of the simulator's ownedState rule: change what occupies the slot rather than greying out what is in it.

jobPicker.rule: Jobs are a grid of icon-plus-name tiles, grouped under FICTION headings, not reward tiers.
jobPicker.observedGroups: Brookhaven: Service, Family, Shop, Arts, Outside (80+ jobs); ERLC: 19 civilian jobs listed by name, location, items, clothing options, vehicles and tasks
jobPicker.why: Both games sort by what the role IS, and Brookhaven's own page says why — jobs 'contribute to character identity and interaction rather than progression-based mechanics'. Sorting a roleplay job list by pay turns an identity picker into a grind ladder.

jobTileLockSlot.rule: The slot a shop tile uses for price is used here for a REQUIREMENT, and the requirement reads 'Free' when there isn't one. Lock reasons are not all money: a game pass and an in-game counter must render in the same slot.
jobTileLockSlot.observed: Brookhaven job rows read Free or name a game pass; ERLC gates La Mesa on 50 job points and Judge on a game pass
jobTileLockSlot.why: The simulator rules put a price pill in that slot. A roleplay job has no price, and a tile that leaves the slot empty loses its alignment and its scannability — the requirement is the thing the player is checking.

jobEquipIsImmediate.rule: Selecting a job from a MENU applies it instantly with no confirm dialog. Selecting one from a WORLD POINT gets an acknowledge step.
jobEquipIsImmediate.observed: Brookhaven: 'Once a job is selected, it is immediately assigned to the player'; Berry Avenue: 'no test or application'; ERLC: stand in the glowing yellow circle, acknowledge the terms, press 'Start Job'
jobEquipIsImmediate.why: Two shipped conventions, split cleanly by where the choice happens. The menu costs nothing and is reversible, so a confirm step is friction; the world point is a commitment that changes the player's equipment and wanted-status eligibility, so it earns one.

activeJobControl.rule: An active job produces a small persistent HUD control whose ONLY contents are pause and quit. Quitting is never in the picker.
activeJobControl.observed: ERLC: a briefcase icon at the top right holding 'Quit Job'; Brookhaven: a Job menu under Home Cams holding Take a Break / End Break / Quit
activeJobControl.why: Two unrelated games arrived at the same split. A player who wants to stop working is not shopping for a job, and making them reopen a grid of 80 tiles to find the one they already have is the single most common failure in generated job UIs.

jobsAreExclusive.rule: One job at a time. Joining a second requires quitting the first, and the UI states that rather than silently swapping.
jobsAreExclusive.why: ERLC: 'A player must quit the job they are in to be able to join another job.' Silent replacement destroys the HUD control above — the player loses the affordance for a job they did not know they had ended.

overheadIdentity.rule: Every identity choice in these menus is PUBLISHED above the avatar — job icon, RP name, bio. The editor must show a live preview of the overhead nameplate, not only the body.
overheadIdentity.why: Brookhaven renders RP Name and Bio above the character and puts the job icon over the head; ERLC's jobs come with visible clothing options. In this genre the menu is not configuring a private loadout, it is composing what strangers read, and an editor that previews only the avatar hides the actual output.

identityEditor.rule: An RP-name screen is two text fields plus a two-step colour control: a large palette for hue, then a shade strip docked directly beside the field it recolours.
identityEditor.why: Brookhaven does exactly this — 'selecting a color from the large color palette and then choosing a final shade next to the name input bar'. The shade strip has to touch the field because hue and shade are one decision made in two moves, and separating them across a panel breaks the loop.

premiumIsATreatment.rule: Express premium as extra TREATMENTS of an existing control, not as extra controls.
premiumIsATreatment.observed: Brookhaven VIP adds Flash and Gradient (Slow/Fast) name effects to the same name field; premium map themes and premium children appear in the same lists as the free ones
premiumIsATreatment.why: It keeps one layout for paying and non-paying players, so the free player sees a complete screen rather than a screen with holes in it — and the upsell sits on a control the player is already using.

avatarEditorNav.rule: Two levels, never three: a category row, then a subcategory list, then items. Open on a real category — never on an empty chooser.
avatarEditorNav.observed: Brookhaven: Animations / Body / Clothes / Pre-Outfits / Accessories, with Body 'the default category that opens'
avatarEditorNav.why: The default-open rule is explicit in the source, and it is what prevents the first frame of the editor from being a menu about a menu. Every additional level multiplies the taps between a player and a hat.

accessoryTaxonomy.rule: Subdivide accessories by ATTACHMENT POINT and animations by MOVEMENT STATE, not by style.
accessoryTaxonomy.attachments: Hats, Hair, Face, Back, Waist, Front, Neck, Shoulders (8)
accessoryTaxonomy.animationStates: All, Idle, Walk, Run, Jump, Fall, Climb, Swim (8)
accessoryTaxonomy.why: Brookhaven uses both taxonomies, and they map one-to-one onto what the engine can actually equip. A style-based taxonomy ('cute', 'cool') cannot be generated correctly because nothing in the data says which bucket an item belongs to.

catalogControls.rule: Any browsable item list carries the same control set: a search field, a sort menu, and a time filter that appears only for popularity sorts. A cross-category 'search all' sits above the subcategory list.
catalogControls.sorts: Relevance, Best selling, Most favorited, Price low→high, Price high→low, Recently published
catalogControls.timeFilter: All time, Past month, Past week, Past 3 days, Past day, Past 12 hours — shown only for Best selling and Most favorited
catalogControls.why: Brookhaven repeats this identical control set on every catalog-backed subcategory, which is what lets a player learn it once. The conditional time filter is the detail generators drop; it is what makes 'best selling' mean anything.

importIdField.rule: An avatar editor must include a direct 'enter an item ID' field beside the browsable categories. It is not an advanced escape hatch; it is a primary path.
importIdField.observed: Bloxburg's code field, Brookhaven's Size & ID subcategory, Berry Avenue's Menu → Equipped → Import ID → paste → Add
importIdField.why: Three of three roleplay games ship it, because the genre's players get outfit IDs from outside the game. An editor with only a browser is unusable for the way this audience actually shops.

iconOnlyTilesByDefault.rule: Item tiles are icon-only. Add a name only where the picture cannot distinguish the items.
iconOnlyTilesByDefault.why: Brookhaven's Animations subcategories 'have the name of the animation unlike other categories that don't' — a walk cycle and a run cycle look identical as a thumbnail, a hat does not. Labelling every tile costs the grid its density; labelling none costs the animations their meaning.

quantisedSliders.rule: Continuous-looking avatar controls are quantised to named or numbered stops, and the current stop is displayed.
quantisedSliders.observed: Bloxburg age slider with six named stops (Baby, Toddler, Kid, Teen, Adult, Elderly); Brookhaven scale in ten steps from 0.50 to 1.00
quantisedSliders.why: Both games ship stops rather than a free range because each value changes animations and abilities, not just size. Also record Bloxburg's own documented defect: the skin-tone slider has a tone that 'is extremely hard to see against the menu's white' — a swatch control must never share a value with its own background.

outfitSlots.rule: Saved looks are numbered SLOTS in a row, each one either filled or an explicit empty slot, with buying another slot as its own action and its own pop-up.
outfitSlots.why: Bloxburg sells outfit slots at 60 Blockbux each with a dedicated 'Buy new outfit slot' pop-up and a separate error state for insufficient slots. Slots are the unit players count and compare; an unbounded list of saved outfits removes the thing being sold.

buildModeTakeover.rule: Placement is a MODE, not a panel. Entering replaces the normal HUD with build chrome; one button enters and one large X exits, and both sit in the same screen corner.
buildModeTakeover.observed: Bloxburg: hammer at the bottom right, 'the large X button on the bottom right of the screen' to exit; Adopt Me: a purple Edit button at the top of the screen
buildModeTakeover.why: The entry corner differs per game; the single-button, single-exit, same-corner structure does not. A build mode reachable from a submenu and exited through a different control strands players inside it, which is why both games put the door where the player last touched.

catalogDock.rule: The item catalog is DOCKED to one screen edge for the whole session. It is never a centred modal.
catalogDock.observed: Adopt Me: 'the menu on the right side of their screen'; Bloxburg: sections along the bottom with Inventory at the bottom left
catalogDock.why: The thing being decorated has to stay visible while the catalog is open — a centred sheet hides the exact 3D space the player is judging. This is the clearest single difference from the simulator genre, where the shop IS a centred modal.

catalogStaysOpen.rule: The catalog does not close after a placement, and there is an explicit control to pin it.
catalogStaysOpen.observed: Adopt Me shipped a 'Lock mode to keep the furniture menu in place' specifically for 'placing large amounts of items'
catalogStaysOpen.why: A studio added this after shipping, which is the strongest possible evidence that close-on-place was a real defect. Furnishing a room is tens of placements from the same category; one-shot modal behaviour multiplies that by two taps each.

catalogTree.rule: Two levels above the items: a small number of top-level SECTIONS, then roughly 15-20 categories inside each, each category faced by one representative product image rather than an abstract icon.
catalogTree.observed: Bloxburg: two sections, 'Build!' (~18 categories) and 'Decorate!' (~19); Adopt Me groups by themed collection instead of object type
catalogTree.why: Bloxburg splits structure from decoration at the top because the tools and placement modes differ between them. The representative-product face matters because a player scanning for 'a sofa' recognises a sofa, not a chair glyph.

ownedStockIsSeparate.rule: The player's owned/earned items get their own door, at the opposite end of the build chrome from the buy catalog, plus a Storage concept that survives moving house.
ownedStockIsSeparate.observed: Bloxburg 'Inventory' at the bottom left, opposite the exit; Adopt Me Storage holds any placed item for use 'even in a different house'
ownedStockIsSeparate.why: Mixing bought stock into a priced catalog makes every tile ambiguous — the player cannot tell what will cost money. Two doors is the cheaper answer than a badge on every tile.

placementTools.rule: A persistent tool strip with one button per verb and a visible active state, every verb on a single-key hotkey, plus undo and redo.
placementTools.verbs: Transform (move/rotate) T, Paint F, Clone C, Scale V, Sell/Delete G; grid on/off H, grid size cycle J, collision toggle K, hide-above-floor U, floor up/down, undo Ctrl+Z, redo Ctrl+Y, overhead view on hold
placementTools.why: This is Bloxburg's actual bound set, and the verbs are what the generator has to emit as buttons. Hiding any of them in a right-click menu makes them unreachable on touch, which is most of this genre's players.

placementModes.rule: Linear and area items (walls, fences, floors, roofs) get placement MODES cycled from the same control that selects the tool.
placementModes.why: Placing a room's worth of wall one segment at a time is the difference between a build system and a prop spawner, and the modes live on the tool key because the player is already holding the tool.

gridControl.rule: Grid is two controls, not one: an on/off toggle and a coarse step-size control with about three named steps. Offer per-axis handles for fine work.
gridControl.observed: Bloxburg: grid on/off (H) and grid size cycle (J); Adopt Me: Large / Medium / Small plus red, green and blue axis arrows
gridControl.why: Both games shipped a small number of named sizes rather than a continuous slider, because the useful sizes are the ones that tile. Colour-coded per-axis arrows are how Adopt Me exposes the third dimension without a numeric field.

placementBudget.rule: State the placement budget against the house, and make the over-limit case non-punitive: refuse the placement and charge nothing.
placementBudget.observed: Adopt Me: 4,000 items default, +500 per upgrade to a maximum of 8,000; over the limit 'the item will not be placed and the player will not be charged'
placementBudget.why: The limit is a number the player plans around, so it has to be visible. The refund-nothing rule is the part a generator forgets, and it is the difference between a limit and a trap.

propertyTileState.rule: A property tile's primary state is AVAILABILITY, not price: unclaimed reads green and the action is Claim. The property list doubles as the fast-travel list.
propertyTileState.observed: Brookhaven: unclaimed homes 'shown in green', tab does claim + teleport + enter build mode; Berry Avenue houses are claim-or-premium with no currency at all
propertyTileState.why: Houses in this genre are a contested shared resource rather than stock — someone else can hold the one you want, which is a state a shop tile has no slot for. Berry Avenue proves the pattern survives with no economy behind it.

houseControlPanel.rule: House controls are a grouped toggle list that shows only the rows this property actually has. Omit inapplicable rows entirely rather than greying them out. Keep the one bulk destructive action inside the same panel as the per-item permissions.
houseControlPanel.observed: Brookhaven's panel is dynamic per property type, groups locks/windows/cameras/garage, music/disasters, colour/sign/props/pool, and holds 'remove all placed props in the house at once'
houseControlPanel.why: The source says the panel displays only relevant features, and a greyed row in a house panel is indistinguishable from a broken one. Keeping the bulk delete beside the permission that caused the mess is where a player looks for it.

diegeticDuplicate.rule: A world object may open the same panel as a menu entry. If the two versions differ, the difference must be deliberate and the in-world one is the superset.
diegeticDuplicate.observed: Brookhaven's wall panel carries House Fire, which 'only appears on the manual wall panel, not the main GUI'; Bloxburg's wardrobes, dressers and clothing racks open the Avatar Editor; ERLC's jobs are joined from a glowing circle in the world
diegeticDuplicate.why: Diegetic entry points are half of how this genre is navigated, and an object that opens a different-looking panel from the menu teaches the player there are two systems. Where they differ, the physical one earns the riskier action because standing at it is itself the confirmation.

formLayout.rule: A form inside a hub is a short vertical stack with the required field first and optional fields below it, submitted by one icon button pinned to the bottom edge of the container.
formLayout.observed: ERLC's 911 app: a top box for the emergency, a bottom box for location that 'may remain blank', and 'the blue paper plane button on the bottom of the phone'
formLayout.why: The submit button belongs to the phone body, not to the form, so it stays in the same place across every app. Required-first is what lets the player send without reading to the bottom.

stepperNotTabs.rule: Two or three mutually exclusive options inside a small panel use a left/right stepper with the current value between the arrows, not a tab row.
stepperNotTabs.observed: ERLC: Police / Fire / DOT chosen 'using the 2 arrows at the top of the screen'
stepperNotTabs.why: Tabs need width this genre's phone body does not have, and a stepper keeps the label at full size. Reach for tabs only when the container is a full-screen rail panel.

unreadBadge.rule: Unread state is a red bubble carrying a COUNT, placed against the row it belongs to inside the list — plus a separate arrival notification outside the hub.
unreadBadge.why: ERLC puts 'a red bubble with the amount of message they received from a player next to the player's name', and notifies separately when the phone is closed. A badge only on the app icon tells a player something arrived but not from whom, which is the whole question in a roleplay game.

hardwareIsCosmetic.rule: If the hub is a phone, the phone body itself is a legitimate cosmetic slot — a small number of models, each with a small number of colourways.
hardwareIsCosmetic.why: It monetises the chrome instead of the content, which is why every app can stay free. Note the trap the wiki records: switching model loses the previous one, so the slot must be presented as a swap and not a collection.

hubCanBeRevoked.rule: Game state can take the hub away. Design the absent case — a jailed, wanted or restricted player must see why the control is gone, not a dead button.
hubCanBeRevoked.observed: ERLC: every player has the phone 'except currently jailed players'; wanted players cannot join a job; equipping a job unequips a weapon
hubCanBeRevoked.why: Roleplay games have adversarial states that simulators do not, and the HUD is where those states are enforced. A generator that assumes the hub is always available produces a button that does nothing at the exact moment the player most wants an explanation.

genres.label: Cartoony simulator / pet-sim / clicker
demonstrates: banner title 'Store!' sits ABOVE the panel body and overhangs it, with a small icon tucked against the word
tab row directly under the banner: pill buttons, the active one filled, inactive ones outlined
gamepass tiles are a 4-across grid of square cards, each with icon, name, and either a price pill or the word OWNED
owned state replaces the price entirely rather than greying the button — the card still reads as a card
bottom action row is four equal chunky buttons in a single colour (PLAY / BACK / SETTINGS / QUIT)
currency readouts run along the very top as separate pills, each with its own icon
one visual language across every panel: same corner radius, same stroke, same header treatment
header is a narrower bar centred on top of the panel, reading as a plaque rather than a title bar
the side rail is a vertical stack of square icon buttons, each labelled underneath in small text
inner content areas are a LIGHTER tint of the panel colour, never white, and inset with visible padding
item slots are empty rounded squares in that lighter tint — the grid reads even with no content
destructive and confirming actions are colour-coded (green Accept, red Cancel) and sit at the top of the trade panel, not the bottom
modal is a tall near-white sheet with a red header bar and a red circular X overhanging the top-right corner
featured offer is a full-width band at the top with its own background tint, larger art and a price pill
below it, a 3-across row of small square offers, then full-width currency rows
every price is a pill containing a currency icon then the number, never bare text
section bands alternate background tint so the list reads as groups without drawing separator lines
left edge of the screen carries a vertical icon rail; bottom centre carries the level bar and cash readout
three-column layout: narrow category list, wide item grid, narrow detail pane
category buttons are stacked pills, the selected one a different hue
item grid is 4-across rounded squares with the name on a small bar across the top of each tile
detail pane shows the item large, then a description block, then a single green Equip button at the bottom
the whole assembly sits on one rounded panel with a single outer stroke, not three separate windows
close is a red circle at the top-right of the OUTER panel, overhanging it
the wheel is segmented in saturated primaries with white dividing lines and a white pointer
each segment carries an icon and a short all-caps label, rotated to the segment
the launcher rail is circular icon buttons with the label directly beneath in small bold text
circular buttons get the same thick dark stroke as rectangular panels — the stroke is the constant, not the shape
small single-purpose modal: banner title, one line of instruction, one text field, one confirm button
the text field is white with a dark stroke and rounded ends, with placeholder text in grey
the confirm button is green, chunky, and noticeably smaller than the field above it
modal width is roughly a third of the screen — a one-field dialog does not become a full sheet
clearest reading of the construction: panel stroke is very thick and near-black, corner radius is large
the title plaque is a separate rounded bar overlapping the panel's top edge, with its own stroke
content area is split into two equal rounded sub-panels with a diagonal stripe texture at low contrast
the red X is a circle with the same near-black stroke, sitting proud of the top-right corner
tab pills sit on the panel body just below the plaque, not inside the content area
seven-day strip of equal tiles, each with the day label on top, the reward icon centred, the amount beneath
the claimable day is highlighted with a brighter tile and a green Claim! button directly under it
the banner title is set at a slight angle and overhangs the left edge — the angle is deliberate and is part of the style

rules.note: Distilled from the references above. Units are Roblox UI units: px for stroke and radius, unitless for scale. Values are read proportionally from screenshots, not sampled, and are stated as approximations.

panelStroke.why: every reference outlines every panel, card and button in the same near-black; it is the single most identifying feature and the simulator theme shipped with stroke 3 applied inconsistently

cornerRadius.why: large and consistent; a small radius immediately reads as a developer tool

header.why: in eight of ten references the title is a separate rounded bar overlapping the panel's top edge, not text inside the panel

buttonBevel.why: chunky buttons read as pressable because the top half is lighter and a darker band sits along the bottom

textStroke.why: white text over saturated fills is illegible without it, and every reference uses it

closeButton.why: a red circle proud of the corner in six references; a square X inside the header reads as a dialog, not a game

contentTint.rule: inner areas are a lighter tint of the panel, or a near-white sheet — never the panel colour itself
contentTint.why: flat panels lose their grid; every reference separates frame from content

priceDisplay.rule: icon then number inside a pill

ownedState.rule: replace the price pill with the word OWNED
ownedState.never: disable the button and leave the price
ownedState.why: seen in the gamepass grid; keeps the card readable

launcherRail.why: appears in three independent references, so it is a convention rather than one game's choice

grid.why: four-across square tiles in five references; the shipped kit used tall 240px cards which is why it reads as a list rather than a shop

genres.label: Neutral / default — a restrained Roblox UI built to core-platform convention
demonstrates: icons are 44 pixels, and the post states the size was chosen to meet WCAG 2.1 target-size guidance at the AAA rating — the platform's own control row is built to an accessibility number, not to a look
the controls are left-aligned and the announcement says the right side is deliberately left for creators, so a well-behaved custom HUD puts its own chrome on the right

two parts only: a hamburger that absorbs everything secondary (report, self view, capture, leaderboard, emotes, inventory, respawn) and a persistent row of live communication toggles (text chat, microphone)
the bar's width is dynamic — it changes as features enable and disable, and on portrait mobile it can span the entire width, so no custom element may assume a fixed gap beside it
two APIs are given for adapting: TopbarSafeInsets to find the reserved space and a signal to react when its width changes
stated intent is consistency and immediate access across every experience, which is what makes this row the neutral baseline other genres decorate around

the top bar is described as an offset height of 36; a community reply in the same thread updates this to 58 in current clients, so the number is disputed and must be read from the API rather than hardcoded
size and position are to be authored in scale, not offset, with a worked conversion: a 100x100 pixel frame becomes 0.257 scale on both axes

corner radius is to be set in scale (example 0.2) because an offset radius 'appears drastically different between devices' — this is the single construction habit that separates a platform-native panel from a pasted-in one
UIStroke is called out as supporting offset only, never scale, which is why stroke cannot be the load-bearing device in a responsive neutral theme
AnchorPoint conventions are stated plainly: (0,0) top-left, (0.5,0.5) centre, (1,1) bottom-right
ScreenGui.ScreenInsets is given as the mechanism for staying clear of notches, Dynamic Island and core UI
mobile virtual controls occupy the bottom-left and bottom-right corners, and the post's instruction is to design for mobile first and let desktop follow

a transparency ladder rather than a palette does the work: layout containers sit at BackgroundTransparency 1 and hold no fill at all, subtle backing sits at 0.15, overlays at 0.3–0.5, and a de-emphasised control at 0.65
corner radius is authored in scale throughout — roughly 0.05 to 0.2 for buttons, 0.075 for a modal container — and some elements deliberately carry no UICorner
UIListLayout padding is expressed in scale as well, 0.025 to 0.035 between horizontal items, with 2–3% margins from the screen edge
one type family across every screen (Montserrat) with weight carrying the hierarchy: Medium for standard, Bold for emphasis, Black reserved for critical alerts
text is pure white on dark surfaces with TextScaled enabled, and no text outline is used anywhere
LayoutOrder is used as z-order intent: headers at -1 so they resolve first, interactive buttons at 2
square elements (crosshair, blast button, icons) hold their shape with UIAspectRatioConstraint rather than with matched width/height values
HUD parts are sized as percentages of the screen — objective frame 50% x 13%, blaster selector 80% x 25%, player display 23% x 8% — so the layout survives any aspect ratio
a pressed state is a swapped PressedImage and a disabled state is a transparency change, not a colour change
screen regions are assigned by category and stay assigned: objective and global state at the top, the action focal point at centre, player state at the sides and periphery

the bottom-left and bottom-right are reserved because the thumbstick and jump button live there; the instruction is to put interactive elements 'near the natural resting position for thumbs' and that reaching away from those corners is 'either uncomfortable or impossible'
one adaptive design is produced for all devices rather than separate mobile and desktop layouts, and the wireframe accounts for Roblox core UI, touch controls and custom elements in the same drawing
balance and symmetry are sought between the custom UI and the system UI — the core UI is treated as part of the composition, not as an obstacle
layouts are tested against a variety of possible backgrounds for legibility, because a translucent neutral UI sits on top of whatever the world is doing
the opener is an icon-only gear at top-centre, sized 0.1 in scale but clamped by a UISizeConstraint MaxSize of (inf, 44) — the same 44 the shipped experience controls use, reached independently
the panel is 0.75 x 0.75 in scale, constrained to AspectRatio 2.5, MaxSize 800 wide and MinSize 350 — a neutral panel is a proportion with a pixel ceiling and floor, never a fixed rectangle
the panel is translucent: a dark navy fill at BackgroundTransparency 0.25, so the world stays visible behind it
UICorner on the panel is 0.1 in scale; the slider track and its handle both use 0.5, which UICorner turns into a pill and a circle regardless of dimensions
the slider track carries a UIStroke of thickness 3, black, at transparency 0.25 — the stroke is a soft separation from whatever is behind, not a cartoon outline
close is an icon glyph anchored (1,0) at position (1,-10,0,10) — inset ten pixels INSIDE the panel's top-right corner — at ImageTransparency 0.25, sized 0.15 of the panel with a 1:1 aspect constraint
the accent colour appears exactly twice per control: the handle's stroke and the filled portion of the track; everything else is neutral
opening tweens over 0.5s and closing is instant (0s) with Visible flipped — the exit is not a mirror of the entrance
the gear rotates 45 degrees to signal the open state, so the opener is also the state indicator
prominence is bought with size, negative space, proximity and movement before colour: 'Elements encircled by ample negative space or padding are eye-catching'

'Housing buttons in a container, such as a color surrounding the text or icon, distinguishes them from the background, making them appear interactive' — a bare label is not a button even in a restrained theme
three button states are named as the requirement: hover, depressed, and released (selected)
'Headers and titles containing significant high-level information should be larger and bolder than body text' — the header is a type-scale step, not a separate plaque object
