A second pass on a game page (/p/<game>) read every button on the action bar, which is where the full variant set is visible at once.

0.rule: One weight. Set every heading and every paragraph at 400 and let size, colour and space carry hierarchy.
0.why: Measured across every text node on the bar: there is no bold anywhere. Reaching for 600 is the reflex that makes a page look like a template, and it is the first thing to go.

1.rule: Warm neutrals only. The page, every surface step and the text all sit on the same warm axis; no blue-grey.
1.why: rgb(20,19,18) against rgb(244,243,242) — red highest, blue lowest, by one or two points at every step. It is barely perceptible per colour and unmistakable across a page.

2.rule: Separate with a 1px hairline, not with a shadow.
2.why: One border colour on the bar and effectively no shadows. Elevation is implied by the surface step, not by a blur.

3.rule: Tighten tracking as type grows; loosen it below 12px.
3.why: -0.02em at 56px and 96px, -0.01em at body, +0.018em on uppercase micro labels. Uniform tracking is what makes large type look rented.

4.rule: A section is a 32px title, a 14–16px muted line, and then the thing itself.
4.why: Repeated at every section on the bar without variation. The consistency is the effect.

5.rule: Never ship a section whose content we cannot fill truthfully.
5.why: Not a rule from the bar — a rule against it. Half its structure is social proof, and an empty or invented version of that is worse than omitting the section.

6.rule: Spend the motion budget on RESPONSE first and scenery last.
6.why: Measured across all four sites the owner named as the bar: ChatGPT has 138 keyframes and zero ambient animation; Grok has 18 keyframes and no canvas or video at all. Not one of the four treats a moving background as the thing that makes a page feel alive, and two of them do not have one.

7.rule: One house transition duration, applied widely, beats several tuned ones applied narrowly.
7.why: Cloudflare runs 0.2s on 147 elements; Gemini runs 0.2s on 74 and 0.3s on 54. The consistency is what reads as craft. A page with six durations on twenty elements reads as unfinished even when every individual choice is defensible.

8.rule: Two bands only: 0.1-0.16s for anything under the finger, 0.2-0.3s for anything that moves on its own. Nothing in between.
8.why: Every one of the four references separates these cleanly, and none of them uses a mid-range duration for a hover state.

9.rule: Fade an expensive layer IN after it is ready; never let first paint depend on it.
9.why: Cloudflare declares a canvas-fade-in keyframe for exactly this. Our own hero shipped a canvas that never ran at all, and because the CSS atmosphere underneath it was independent, the page still rendered a composition instead of a blank panel.

10.rule: A long page whose every section shows the product working beats a short page with an effect on top of it.
10.why: Gemini carries 29 videos and 10 keyframes. It is the least animated page of the five by authored motion and among the most alive to look at, because the motion is the product rather than the decoration.

11.rule: Tint every surface step toward the accent hue instead of using neutral grey.
11.why: Measured on the bar: rgb(21,18,26), rgb(10,8,12), rgb(34,29,46) — red and blue above green at every step, on a purple-accented page. A pure-grey ramp under a saturated accent is what makes a dark interface read as a default theme rather than a designed one.

12.rule: Carry three tints of the accent: a fill, a lighter one for borders, a darker one for the primary button.
12.why: rgb(203,82,251) fills and focuses, rgb(236,146,251) borders, rgb(143,0,200) is the primary button. One accent doing all three jobs is why an accented button looks flat.

13.rule: Elevate with a glow, and keep the one real shadow inset.
13.why: The only box-shadows on the bar are an accent halo on the chip and, on the primary button alone, `0 0 0 1px inset` plus a 2px lift. Everything else separates with a hairline.

14.rule: Two radii: 8px for panels, 6px for controls. No pills.
14.why: 23 elements at 8px, 11 at 6px, and nothing rounder anywhere on the page.

15.rule: Four control heights — 28, 32, 36, 50 — and padding that tracks the height.
15.why: Every button on the bar lands on one of those four. A fifth height is how a control bar stops looking machined.

16.rule: Nothing takes longer than 0.26s, and colour-only changes use a hard ease-out.
16.why: cubic-bezier(0.32,0.72,0,1) at 0.26s for colour, 0.15s ease-out for everything else. Measured across every interactive element on the page.

17.rule: Buy the atmosphere with one piece of art direction, not with a stack of layers.
17.why: The entire background is a single fixed webp at z-index -1, on a page with zero keyframes and zero canvases. Ours was an SVG mesh, a light column, a dust layer, an aurora and a flow field — five mechanisms to do one job, and the owner still called the result static.

18.rule: Synthesise interaction sound; never ship an audio file for a click.
18.why: The bar fetches no audio asset at all and its keypress sound is generated through AudioContext. A synthesised click costs no bytes, has no load state, and cannot be the reason a button feels late.

19.rule: Turn an unavailable control DOWN; never grey it out into a different object.
19.why: Measured on the bar: their unavailable action keeps the same height, radius, padding and tracking as the live one beside it, and differs only by border alpha 0.38 -> 0.12 and label 100% -> 38%. Our composer currently carries two controls that read as broken rather than as not-yet, and this is the shape that fixes them without hiding a roadmap.

20.rule: Differentiate buttons by border and text colour, not by fill.
20.why: Four of the bar's five variants have no fill at all; only the single primary button per screen is filled. A page where every button is a filled rectangle has no hierarchy left to spend.

screens.label: Code redemption — the one-field screen: where it hides, the text box, the confirm button, and what the game says back
demonstrates: the whole screen is five instances and no more: a Frame named 'Background' holding a Title TextLabel, a Description TextLabel, one TextBox and one TextButton, plus a UICorner — a codes screen that grows a sixth element has stopped being a codes screen

the opener is a SEPARATE TextButton ('CodesButton') living on the HUD, outside the panel, and it TOGGLES the panel rather than opening it: `background.Visible = not background.Visible`, so the same button closes it again
there is a line of instruction text between the title and the field — the field is not left to explain itself
sizes are authored in Scale with Offset pinned at zero ('0.1, 0, 0.1, 0', and the reader is told 'don't edit the 2nd and 4th values'), so the panel rescales rather than staying a fixed pixel box
three distinct replies, not two: 'Valid code', 'Already redeemed', 'Incorrect code' — 'already redeemed' is broken out from 'incorrect' at the very first tutorial level
codes are one-time-use PER PLAYER, checked against a per-player folder, so the already-redeemed reply is a normal outcome and not an error

the single most transferable construction decision in this whole file: the RESULT IS WRITTEN INTO THE FIELD'S OWN PlaceholderText, not into a separate status label — the TextBox clears on submit and its placeholder becomes the answer, so the player's eye never has to move off the box it was already on
the placeholder is recoloured per outcome: success green (Color3 0.333333, 1, 0.498039), failure red (Color3 1, 0.313725, 0.313725), resting grey (Color3 0.698039, 0.698039, 0.698039)
exact strings used: resting 'Type Here', success 'Code Redeemed', failure 'Invalid Code', third state 'Code Already Redeemed' — all title case, two or three words, no punctuation, no apology

the recoloured message is TRANSIENT: it displays for a beat and then resets to the default grey placeholder, so the screen returns to a resting state ready for the next code instead of holding an accusation on screen
the panel carries the player's currency readouts (Coins, Gems) live inside it, so the reward lands visibly in the same frame the player is looking at
three separate sounds are wired: a button click, an error sound for invalid/already-redeemed, and a distinct redeem sound for success — the audio carries the same three-way split as the colour
the panel has BOTH a close button of its own and the external toggle button; either dismisses it

the critique that repeats three times in one thread is about the close control, not the layout: 'make the X more thick so that it is more visible', 'make the X to close the UI a little bit thicker', 'the X is kinda small' — on a one-field modal the X is the second most-used control and gets built too small by default

'add a border to the "Redeem" button, so It will cover up the distortion against the background' — the confirm button needs its own stroke, because a green fill sitting directly on a coloured panel has no edge
'make everything bigger (buttons and text)' — a codes panel authored at desktop-cursor scale is too small the moment it is touched
'blur it a little bit, so the text is more visible' — the world behind the modal is blurred or dimmed rather than left sharp

a replier draws the genre line explicitly: a flat minimal treatment is 'too simple' for a cartoony game and 'simple is better for more realistic games and horror games' — the codes screen inherits the game's construction language, it does not have one of its own
the panel is built as a frame inside a frame: an outermost coloured border frame with a grey body frame inset within it, rather than a single frame carrying a UIStroke

the concrete geometry rule for that construction: 'The cornering on the outermost blue border does not go with the cornering of the gray background' — the fix given is to measure the gap between the two frames and ADD it to the inner radius to get the outer radius, otherwise the two curves diverge at the corners

'The text in the TextBox and "Redeem" button are noticeable closer to the top in each box' — centred text rides high in several Roblox fonts and needs a UIPadding correction; a codes screen is two boxes of centred text, so the defect shows twice
the same two elements are named as the whole screen again: the TextBox and the Redeem button

the codes UI is NOT a panel here: it is a SECTION inside the settings menu — 'Tap the Settings button (the cog) in the top-left corner', then 'Scroll down the settings menu until you see the "Redeem Codes" section'
in that inline form the field and the button share one ROW: the field on the left, 'the green Claim button on the right'
the placeholder is a lowercase invitation with an ellipsis: 'Type code here…' — not a label, not all-caps, and it sits inside the field
the confirm word is 'Claim', not 'Redeem' — the verb varies by game while the colour (green) does not
the codes affordance is reached in two taps from the HUD, and the HUD icon it hides behind is a gear in the top-left corner
the codes entry point is buried inside the SHOP, at the very bottom of it: open the store from the shopping cart icon, scroll to the bottom, and find 'a banner with a Redeem button in the corner'
so the affordance is a full-width BANNER row with the action button tucked into its corner — the same band construction the shop uses for a featured offer, reused for codes
tapping that banner's Redeem opens the actual entry surface, where the code is typed 'into the box' — two stages: an advertisement row, then the field
the confirm control is described by size and colour before it is described by label: 'the big green "Redeem!" button' — big, green, exclamation mark
the word 'Redeem' is used for BOTH the banner's opener and the confirm inside; the repetition is the shipped behaviour
the opener is a standalone HUD icon with no menu around it: 'Click the Present icon near the compass' — one tap from play to the field
the icon is a GIFT/PRESENT, and it is placed next to an unrelated HUD element (the compass) rather than in a tidy rail — codes affordances colonise whatever HUD corner is free
the confirm control is labelled 'Redeem'
this game previously used the Twitter-bird icon for the same job; the bird has been replaced by a present, so a generator that hard-codes a bird is reproducing a retired convention
the opener is a generic overflow button — 'the "Extra" button in the top-left corner' — and Codes is one item inside it, alongside whatever else did not earn its own HUD slot
the confirm control carries NO WORD AT ALL: 'Click the green check mark' — an icon-only green tick sitting beside the field
that is the floor of the convention: the confirm may lose its label, but it does not lose its green
codes is a SUB-SCREEN of an unrelated screen: 'Click the Profile button' on the right side of the screen, then 'Click the Codes button' in the top-left corner of the profile screen

rules.note: Distilled from the references above. Sources are TEXT, so these rules state placement, order, proportion, state and copy. Stroke weights and corner radii are NOT stated here — the codes screen inherits those from the game's genre file (see simulator.json rules.panelStroke, rules.cornerRadius). Where a value is reasoned rather than read, it says so.

entryPoint.rule: codes is always behind ONE affordance; it is never a field sitting open on the HUD
observedForms: own icon on the HUD launcher rail (present/gift, legacy Twitter-or-X bird)
a section inside the Settings panel, reached from the gear
a banner at the bottom of the Shop panel, with its Redeem button in the banner's corner
a tab inside a multi-panel menu
a corner button inside an unrelated big screen (Profile)
an item inside a generic overflow button ('Extra')
entryPoint.defaultForGeneration: own circular icon on the same launcher rail as shop and settings, top-left or left edge
entryPoint.why: five shipped games in this file put it in five different places, but never on the right-hand thumb side and never loose on the HUD; find-the-needle-codes-tab states the class as 'a shop, gift, or Twitter-style button' on 'the left or top'

existenceCondition.rule: only generate this screen when the game actually has a code source; do not ship a Codes button with nothing behind it
existenceCondition.why: 'if no Codes tab exists, a public wave has not shipped yet' — the absence is the signal, and a dead Codes button trains players to distrust the menu

panelExclusivity.rule: opening codes closes any other open panel
panelExclusivity.why: stated as the framework-level contract in the General UI Kit thread; two stacked panels over a one-field form is never the shipped behaviour

forbidden: tabs inside the codes panel itself
elementCount.why: every reference that enumerates the screen enumerates the same handful; the tutorial, the kit listing and both critique threads independently name only the field and the button

panelProportion.why: simulator.json's codes-modal reference reads the width as 'roughly a third of the screen — a one-field dialog does not become a full sheet'; the height follows from the five-element cap

verticalPlacement.rule: the field's centre sits ABOVE the vertical midline of the viewport — target 0.38-0.45 of screen height, never below 0.5
verticalPlacement.why: 'TextBoxes on iOS will be covered by the on screen keyboard', and the engine's OnScreenKeyboardSize was reported not to work as expected, so the field cannot be repositioned reactively and must be placed clear by construction. Separately, 'the code box is easy to miss behind the jump button' rules out the bottom of the screen on touch even before the keyboard opens.

stackOrder.rule: feedback occupies the field's own placeholder or a line immediately under the confirm — it is never above the title and never off-panel
stackOrder.why: the tutorial builds Title, Description, TextBox, TextButton in that order; the redeem-code-system puts the answer in the field itself

inlineRowVariant.whenEmbedded: inside Settings or Shop rather than as its own modal
inlineRowVariant.layout: field left, confirm right, one row, button width roughly a quarter of the row
inlineRowVariant.why: 'the green Claim button on the right' in Grow a Garden; the modal stacks, the embedded row does not

field.textAlign: centre, with UIPadding correcting the vertical rise
field.placeholderColor: grey, visibly quieter than entered text
field.why: ClearTextOnFocus must be false because every shipped guide tells players to paste rather than type ('copy and paste the code directly'), and a field that wipes on a mis-tap destroys the paste. Centred text 'noticeable closer to the top in each box' is the named defect and UIPadding is the named fix.

submitPaths.why: the TextBox reference exposes all three; a screen wired only to the button ignores how desktop and touch players actually finish typing

inputNormalisation.rule: trim, case-fold and strip internal spaces before matching
inputNormalisation.why: the shipped kit states 'Case and spaces do not matter'; every guide that documents case sensitivity documents it as a warning to the player, which is a defect being worked around, not a feature

confirmButton.position: directly under the field in the modal form; to the RIGHT of the field in the embedded row form
confirmButton.widthRelativeToField: noticeably narrower than the field — roughly 0.4-0.55 of its width in the modal form
confirmButton.why: green is the only element of this screen that never varies across the references — the label may vanish entirely down to a bare check mark and the colour stays. 'add a border to the "Redeem" button, so It will cover up the distortion against the background' is why it carries its own stroke. simulator.json's codes-modal independently reads the confirm as 'green, chunky, and noticeably smaller than the field above it'.

feedback.primaryForm: rewrite the field's own PlaceholderText and recolour it
never: a chat system message as the only response
a toast in a screen corner away from the panel
a second modal confirming the first
feedback.why: the strongest single finding in this file. The shipped redeem system writes 'Code Redeemed' green / 'Invalid Code' red / 'Code Already Redeemed' red straight into the placeholder the player is already staring at, clears the entry, then reverts to grey 'Type Here'. The chat-message form is recorded in bloxcreators-chat-feedback and is the weaker convention: it answers where the player is not looking.

resultCopy.register: flat and factual, title case or sentence case
never: 'Something went wrong, please try again later'
resultCopy.why: unanimous across the tutorial, the shipped system and the kit; nothing on this screen is longer than three words

refusalStates.rule: each state gets its OWN message; 'already redeemed' must never be collapsed into 'invalid'
refusalStates.why: the published kit ships eight named refusals and the beginner tutorial already splits three. 'Already redeemed' is the one that changes what the player does next — it tells them to stop retyping — and it is the one a generator writing a single failure string destroys. 'TooFast' (rate limit) and 'GrantFailed' (reward side failed after a valid code) are states a generator will never invent unprompted.

successDetail.rule: name what was granted, not just that it worked
successDetail.why: the kit lists custom rewards so they 'appear by name in the menu'; the shipped redeem system keeps live Coins and Gems readouts inside the codes panel so the increment is visible where the code was typed

closeButton.strokeWeightRelativeToPanel: not thinner than the panel's own stroke
closeButton.why: shape and position inherit from the library convention (simulator.json rules.closeButton). The size and weight floor is here because one critique thread said it three separate times — 'make the X more thick', 'a little bit thicker', 'the X is kinda small' — on a panel where the X is the second most-used control.

nestedFrameRadius.rule: when the panel is an outer border frame containing an inset body frame, outerRadius = innerRadius + gapBetweenFrames
nestedFrameRadius.why: 'The cornering on the outermost blue border does not go with the cornering of the gray background' — the named fix is exactly this arithmetic, and a generator that gives both frames the same radius produces visibly diverging curves at all four corners

backdrop.rule: blur or dim the world behind the modal
backdrop.why: 'blur it a little bit, so the text is more visible' — a one-field form over a moving game world loses its text otherwise

touchSizing.rule: author in Scale with Offset at zero, and size buttons and text for a thumb before a cursor
touchSizing.why: 'make everything bigger (buttons and text)' as a critique, and the tutorial's insistence on Scale sizing with the Offset values left alone

audio.rule: success and failure get DIFFERENT sounds, matching the colour split
audio.why: three distinct sounds wired in the shipped redeem system; it is the same three-way state machine expressed a second way

inheritsFromGenre.rule: stroke weight, corner radius, header/plaque treatment, button bevel and text stroke are NOT decided by this screen — take them from the game's genre file
inheritsFromGenre.why: 'simple is better for more realistic games and horror games' and 'too simple' for a cartoony one, said about the same panel in one thread: the codes screen has a fixed skeleton and a borrowed skin

screens.label: The CRAFTING screen, across genres — recipe lists, ingredient rows read against inventory, quantity and craft-all, timed queues, station tiers, and upgrade trees with prerequisites
demonstrates: A RECIPE HAS THREE INDEPENDENT REQUIREMENT AXES AND TWO OF THEM CAN BE ZERO: a level gate, a currency price, and a material list. The page renders them as three fixed headings — 'Requirements' carrying Level and Price, then 'Needed Materials'. The Vineweaver Rod is Level 0 and 150,000 C$; the Rod of the Eternal King is Level 400 and 0 C$. THE MATERIAL LIST IS NEVER EMPTY: every rod tabbed on this page carries at least one ingredient, so the 'each can be zero' this row claimed until 2026-09-20 is false of the third axis. A requirement block that only renders the axes in play still changes shape between two rows of the same list, on the two axes that do reach zero.

AN INGREDIENT SLOT IS AN ITEM PLUS ITS VARIANT, NOT AN ITEM ID. Rod recipes on this page call for Mythical, Lunar, Frozen, Atlantean, Poisoned and Vined Driftwood as SIX different ingredients, and for Spirit Sea Mine and Spirit Speed Core. The page's ingredient index lists nine Driftwood rows in all — plain Driftwood plus eight mutations — of which Festive and Shrouded appear in no rod recipe here; the Shrouded variant that a recipe does call for is a Golden Sea Pearl. The crafting screen's match against inventory has to compare the modifier as well as the base item, and the ingredient chip has to show which variant.

AN INGREDIENT CAN BE UNOBTAINABLE BY GATHERING. The Evil Pitchfork needs one Evil Sigil, and the page's sub-bullet under that ingredient is 'Completing Crimson King's quest'. So the 'how do I get this' affordance on an ingredient chip is sometimes a quest, not a location.

THE WHOLE STATION IS GATED BEHIND A WORLD ACTION, NOT A LEVEL: the Notes say the player must have completed the Ancient Isle puzzle with the totems to access the area at all. The recipe-level gates are a second, finer gate inside a screen that some players cannot reach.

THE STRONGEST ROW IN THIS FILE'S INVENTORY-COUPLING: the page's own Notes warn 'Make sure to unfavorite the materials before crafting. Otherwise, it will appear as the player doesn't own the materials.' A protection flag set in the INVENTORY screen silently changes the CRAFTING screen's availability readout — the recipe reports the ingredient as missing rather than as protected. The two screens share one item list and disagree about it.

Quantities are written on both sides of the item in the same list — '1x Magic Thread' on some rows and 'Lunar Thread ×3' on others — which is what an ingredient line looks like when nobody owns the format.

THE STATION'S OWN UPGRADE IS A ROW IN ITS OWN RECIPE LIST. The starter workbench has exactly two recipes: Wooden Pickaxe, and Workbench Tier 1 for 5 Oak Wood and 2 Iron Ore. The upgrade is not a separate button or a separate screen; it is the last recipe in the list, priced like any other.

UPGRADING REPLACES THE STATION IN PLACE. Stated on every tier page in the same words: 'Upgrading the crafting station will replace the workbench with a workbench tier 1.' The node becomes the next node; there is no moment where both exist.

AN UPGRADED STATION IS A SUPERSET AND NEVER LOSES A RECIPE. Tier 2's own description: 'It contains all of the recipes in the workbench tier 1 and other recipes too.' Tier 4 still lists the Wooden Pickaxe at 3 Oak Wood, the very first recipe of the game. Counted from the wiki tables on 2026-09-20, the recipe rows run roughly 55 at tier 1, 139 at tier 2 and 185 at tier 3 — those counts are a measurement of the wiki's tables, not a figure the game states.

THE CATEGORY LIST COUNTS THE UNFILTERED VIEW AS ONE OF ITS CATEGORIES. Tier 4: 'The workbench tier 4’s recipes are sorted into 7 categories: All, tools, blocks, workbenches, utility, factory, and fun.' Tier 3 names the same seven with a weaker verb — 'can be sorted into 7 categories' — which may be the wiki describing its own taxonomy rather than the game's filter; this row quoted both pages as 'are sorted' until 2026-09-20. Seven names, one of which is the unfiltered view. WHAT THE PAGES DO NOT SAY, and what this row asserted anyway: where the filter sits relative to the list, and that it appears because the list got long. The tier 1 and tier 2 pages are simply silent about categories, and a wiki's silence is not the game's absence.

A RECIPE ROW CARRIES A PREREQUISITE COLUMN THAT IS MOSTLY EMPTY. The tables run Image, Name, Recipe, Required skill — and Required skill reads 'None' on the large majority of rows, 'Level 3 Farming' on the Watering Can, 'Level 2 Animal Care' on the Net. The column exists for the minority; deleting it when most rows are None is how a skill-gated recipe becomes a mystery.

A BLOCK CAN BE CRAFTABLE AT SEVERAL STATIONS AT ONCE: the Workbench Tier 1 page notes it is 'the only block that is able to be crafted in 4 different crafting stations', and its own infobox lists five stations under 'crafted with'. A recipe belongs to a SET of stations, not to one.

ONE LEVEL NUMBER GATES THREE DIFFERENT SCREENS. Levelling a skill gives 'access to new villager trades or crafting recipes, and islands' — the same progression value is read by the trade screen, the crafting screen and the world. A crafting screen that owns its own unlock table will disagree with the other two.

SKILL GROUPS ARE ENCODED BY COLOUR, NOT BY TAB: 'Skills are divided into 3 groups organised by type and differentiated by color: brown, green and red. Brown skills are related to gathering resources/coins. Green skills are aimed at the production of goods... Red skills are related to combat.' Three colours over a longer list of skills, which is a legend a crafting screen can reuse when it shows why a recipe is locked.
THE PROGRESSION SCREEN HAS A KEYBOARD ROUTE AND A TOUCH ROUTE AND THE PAGE STATES BOTH: 'tap on the three bars icon on the left, or tap the J key for PC players.'

THE FIRST CRAFTING SCREEN A NEW PLAYER SEES IS DELIBERATELY REDUCED. The Tutorial page: instead of giving a Workbench Tier 1, the tutorial 'now gives you a Workbench, a type of workbench with only 2 recipes'. Those two are the tool the next tutorial step needs and the upgrade out of the tutorial — a tutorial station is the same screen with a shorter list, not a different screen.

THE TUTORIAL STEP NAMES THE SCREEN AND THE ROW: 'Open your Starter Workbench and craft the Wooden Pickaxe.' The instruction is addressable because the list is two rows long; the same sentence against 185 rows would need a highlight.

THE QUEUE IS ONE RECIPE DEEP AND N ITEMS WIDE: 'the player is only able to craft one type of item at a time', with a quantity selected before starting. There is no multi-recipe queue; there is a selected recipe and a count.

ENDING A QUEUE EARLY SETTLES PARTIALLY, AND THAT IS THE DESIGN. 'The player can end the crafting process at any time by clicking on the End Crafting button. This will give the player all finished items, and all unfinished items will be turned back into their ingredients and given back to the player.' Cancelling is never a loss — finished output is delivered and unfinished input is refunded. Most crafting screens make the player choose between waiting and losing the batch; this one removes the choice.

THE SAME BUTTON'S COLOUR IS THE COMPLETION STATE: 'If the button is green, then everything has been blended. If not (red button), then the Blender has not finished blending.' One control, two colours, and the colour tells you which of the two settlements you are about to take before you take it.

THE TIMER'S MEANING CHANGES WITH AN OWNED ENTITLEMENT, AND THE SCREEN SAYS SO IN WORDS. Each item takes 5 minutes and 'the timer only counts down when the player is in-game, unless they have an Offline Voucher'. The wiki records the exact string: with the voucher redeemed, the message above the buttons reads "You've redeemed the offline voucher! The blender will continue running for up to 24 hours while you are offline." A status line above the controls, whose text is selected by an entitlement.

THE SPEED-UP PRICE IS A PER-RECIPE RATE, NOT A GLOBAL ONE: 'For every 1 item being crafted, the Blender requires 1 more ticket to speed up. Except for Moon Charm and Gumdrops, for which each ticket serves for speeding up whole 10 items.' Two recipes out of twenty are priced ten times cheaper to rush, so the rush control cannot render a constant.

THE QUANTITY SELECTOR IS NOT CLAMPED TO AFFORDABILITY; THE CONFIRM IS. From the page's own Trivia: leaving and reopening the Blender 'would show that you would select the number of red extracts you want to craft, even if the amount displayed is above the amount you would be able to craft with your resources, though you won't be able to select the Confirm option.' Selecting an impossible amount is allowed and the commit is refused.

THE INGREDIENT LINE IS WRITTEN AS WHAT WILL BE SUBTRACTED, AND THE PLURAL IS BUILT BY APPENDING A LETTER. Trivia records two live spelling defects: a recipe needing two or more strawberries renders as '[-n Strawberrys]', and anything needing enzymes renders as '[-n Enzymess]' — but crafting the enzymes themselves spells it correctly, because that path formats the OUTPUT rather than the ingredient. A shipped game's ingredient label is name-plus-s, and the bracketed minus prefix is the format.
THE WHOLE TREE IS GATED AS ONE FEATURE, AT Level 15, before any node is. A screen that does not exist yet is a different problem from a node that is not affordable yet, and this game separates them.

FOUR CATEGORIES, SEVENTEEN NODES: Offensive (4), Economy (4), Strategy (4) and Defense (5). Counted from the page on 2026-09-20 the named skills are Enhanced Optics, Improved Gunpowder, Fight Dirty, Precision, Resourcefulness, Bigger Budget, Stonks, Scavenger, Accelerator, Scholar, Expanded Barracks, Re-enforcements, Fortify, Over-Heal, Bandages, Extreme Conditioning and Beefed Up Minions.

A NODE IS A METER WITH ITS OWN CAP, NOT A BINARY UNLOCK. The caps read 10, 15, 20, 25 and 40 across the seventeen skills — Re-enforcements caps at 10, Precision at 15, Fortify at 40 — and the page states the spread in its own prose: 'Each Skill has its own level cap, some being as low as 10 and others having up to 40 levels.' No single progress geometry fits the whole tree, so the cap has to be per node.

THE PREREQUISITE IS A CONSTANT THRESHOLD ON THE PARENT, NOT A FRACTION OF THE PARENT'S CAP. Thirteen of the seventeen skills carry the sentence 'There is a requirement of reaching Level 10 in <named skill> before it is unlocked', and it is Level 10 whether the parent caps at 20, 25 or 40. The tree is therefore a set of short chains inside each category, all with the same unlock depth.

A LEVEL ROW SHOWS THREE THINGS — the price of that level, the cumulative total, and the resulting value — except the first row of a skill, which carries only the price and the value because there is nothing yet to accumulate. Enhanced Optics opens '20 coins • 0.5% total increase' and its second row reads '75 coins • 95 total cost • 1% total increase'. Where the stat counts down rather than up, the third column follows: Precision, the critical-hit skill whose own prerequisite is Level 10 in Fight Dirty, lists '29 shots required' and then 28, 27, 26 as the levels rise.

THE PRICE CURVE IS EXPONENTIAL AND THE PAGE PUBLISHES THE FORMULA — base cost times level, raised to an exponential value, floored and then rounded to the nearest multiple of 5. Prices in a shipped upgrade tree land on round numbers on purpose.

THE RESPEC REFUNDS INTO A CURRENCY THAT CANNOT LEAVE THE TREE. A reset returns 95% of what was spent as Skill Credit, 'a unique currency only usable for Skills'; the reset itself costs 200 Coins and 'each reset will become more expensive by 200'; and after resetting, skills 'are unable to be upgraded using Coins, they are restricted to only Skill Credit' until the credits run out. So the tree has two spend currencies, one of which is a refund that must be spent back into the same screen before the ordinary one is accepted again.

THE TREE'S STATE IS MIRRORED OUTSIDE THE TREE: 'After the player unlocks a Skill from a specific path, a modifier for that path will appear... The description of the modifier will list every single Skill owned and how much it boosts specific statistics.' One chip per category, whose tooltip enumerates every owned node.

THE TREE CAN BE TURNED OFF: Skills have their own toggle in Settings, and certain modes disable them outright. A purchased upgrade that is not in effect this match is a state the match HUD has to be able to say.

THE PROGRESS LIVES ON THE INVENTORY TILE, NOT IN A SEPARATE SCREEN: 'the tower will have a orange progress bar in the inventory, indicating the current level of the tower.' The upgrade state is a bar on the item you already see.

ONLY THE LAST STEP OF THAT BAR MEANS ANYTHING for an unevolved tower — 'the only level that actually matters is the last one, as all others have no impact' — so the bar is progress toward ONE gate, and labelling its intermediate stops as upgrades would be a lie.

THE PLAYER DOES NOT CHOOSE WHICH NODE UNLOCKS: 'The player does not get to pick which upgrades they unlock as each one has a determined level it is unlocked on.' This is the other kind of upgrade tree — a fixed ladder revealed by level — and it needs no affordability state at all, only a reached/not-reached one.

AN EVOLVED TOWER STARTS PARTIALLY UNLOCKED: it 'starts out with only some of its upgrades unlocked', and every upgrade past that set requires levelling. So the same panel renders owned, not-yet-reached and never-available side by side.
THE LADDER HAS A PAID SKIP: the player 'can also skip getting experience with Robux', on both the unevolved and the evolved tower. A level gate with a purchasable bypass is two controls on one node.

LEVEL COUNTS ARE PER TOWER and the page states the observed ceiling as 20 'outside of development screenshots', with experience per level computed from a base value and a growth rate raised to level minus one, rounded down.

THE UPGRADE SCREEN IS A PLACE AND A PERSON: the menu 'can be accessed by interacting with Fulco, who can be found in each team's base'. Like a shop keeper, the tree is reached by walking to it rather than by a button on the HUD.

0.rule: Build the requirement block from three axes — materials, a level or skill gate, and a currency price — and keep the gate and the price on screen even when they read zero.
0.why: Fisch's recipes vary independently: the Vineweaver Rod is Level 0 at 150,000 C$, the Rod of the Eternal King is Level 400 at 0 C$. Islands' recipe tables carry a 'Required skill' column that reads None on most rows and 'Level 3 Farming' on one. A block that only draws the axes in play changes shape between two rows of the same list. The zero case is demonstrated for the level gate and for the price and NOT for materials — no recipe on the Fisch page has an empty material list — so nothing here says what a recipe that costs no materials should look like.

1.rule: Treat an ingredient as an item PLUS its variant, and show the variant on the chip.
1.why: Fisch's rod recipes call for six different Driftwoods as six different ingredients — Mythical, Lunar, Frozen, Atlantean, Poisoned, Vined — and separately Spirit Sea Mine and Spirit Speed Core; the page's ingredient index carries nine Driftwood rows in all. A crafting screen that matches inventory by base item will tell a player they have an ingredient they do not have.

2.rule: Write the ingredient line as what will be SUBTRACTED, and never build its plural by appending a letter to the item name.
2.why: Bee Swarm's Blender renders ingredient cost as a bracketed negative, and its own wiki records two live defects from naive pluralisation — '[-n Strawberrys]' and '[-n Enzymess]' — while the same item spells correctly when it is the OUTPUT, because that path formats a different string. The minus prefix is worth copying; the plural is worth fixing.

3.rule: Put the station's own upgrade in the station's recipe list, priced like any other recipe.
3.why: Islands' starter workbench has exactly two recipes and one of them is Workbench Tier 1 at 5 Oak Wood and 2 Iron Ore; 99 Nights in the Forest does the same at all four steps, Crafting Bench 2 inside tier 1 and so on up to tier 5. Two unrelated shipped games reached the same convention, and it means the upgrade needs no second surface.

4.rule: An upgraded station is a superset. Never remove a recipe on the way up.
4.why: Islands states it outright — tier 2 'contains all of the recipes in the workbench tier 1 and other recipes too' — and tier 4 still lists the Wooden Pickaxe at 3 Oak Wood. A player who upgraded and lost a recipe has been punished for progressing.

5.rule: Make the upgrade replace the station in place, so there is never a moment when both exist.
5.why: Every Islands tier page repeats the same sentence: 'Upgrading the crafting station will replace the workbench with a workbench tier 1.' Leaving the old station standing beside the new one turns a linear ladder into an inventory problem.

6.rule: Ship the first crafting screen with a short list, not a filtered long one.
6.why: Islands' tutorial hands out a starter workbench 'with only 2 recipes' — the tool the next tutorial step needs and the upgrade out of the tutorial — where the same station at tier 3 carries a list long enough to need seven categories. Same screen, shorter list, and the tutorial line 'Open your Starter Workbench and craft the Wooden Pickaxe' is addressable because of it.

7.rule: When a recipe list carries a category filter, count the unfiltered view as one of the categories.
7.why: Islands' workbench tier 4 page states that its 'recipes are sorted into 7 categories: All, tools, blocks, workbenches, utility, factory, and fun', and the tier 3 page names the same seven with 'can be sorted'. 'All' is one of the seven rather than a control beside them, which is the whole of what the source supports. Two things this reason claimed until 2026-09-20 are gone: where the filter is drawn, which no page states, and that the row arrives with list length, which was read off the tier 1 and tier 2 pages saying nothing about categories at all.

8.rule: Give a scrolling recipe list a search field.
8.why: In one DevForum feedback thread on an unreleased survival game, a search field was the only thing two different repliers both asked for, and one of them gave the reason: the hand-crafting UI 'could be a bit complicated for people who are trying to look for specific recipes'. The second reply opens 'Adding on to the person above me' and names no reason, so this rule rests on one stated reason from one reviewer looking at one screenshot — not on two independent ones.

9.rule: Label every region of the crafting screen in the UI itself, and give the screen a title that says it is a crafting screen.
9.why: The 2024 crafting-menu thread opened with the author posting a SECOND annotated image to explain his regions, and the first reply's point was that without those annotations 'players are required to learn alone for a few seconds'. A later reviewer went further, in his own spelling: 'Or at least add a title telling peole that this is infacet a crafting menue and not a shop or somthing.' A crafting grid and a shop grid look alike.

10.rule: Order the screen ingredients-then-output, left to right.
10.why: One reviewer argued it from reading order — 'Im used to the output being on the right... because you also read left to right' — and the next reply asked for the same reorder while crediting earlier posts rather than giving a reason. The author posted a revision saying he had taken the advice; what it looks like is a screenshot, so the reorder is reported rather than seen, and the same reviewer was still asking for a swap of the name and the materials line two posts later. It is the only layout question in the file settled by an argument rather than by taste, but the argument was made once and seconded, not made twice.

11.rule: Render the ingredient requirement as a layout of chips, not one scaled text line.
11.why: The author who used TextScaled on a single label hit the wall himself — 'the ingredients can sometimes be a list of items, and having that text on the same text box might look weird if it ends up on multiple lines' — and said he would 'adapt it to work for a grid layout' when a reviewer pointed out a list can grow, then reported it working — the result is a screenshot, so the rebuild is reported rather than seen. Fisch's recipes run up to four ingredients and Bee Swarm's up to four, so the list does grow.

12.rule: On selecting a recipe, ghost its ingredients into the slots — and when a slot accepts a CLASS of item, make the ghost show the class.
12.why: A reviewer asked for 'transparent hints inside the crafting spaces', and the author's own caption on the revision that added them is the important half: 'The multi-colored log in the hint just represents any kind of log.' A ghost showing one specific item would misstate what the slot accepts.

13.rule: One craft button for the screen, driven by a stored selected-recipe value — not one button per recipe row.
13.why: A Scripting Support thread exists because its author connected the single craft button inside the loop over recipe rows, and crafting one item handed out every item. The accepted fix is literally the missing state: a variable holding the current selected recipe. This is where a crafting screen diverges from a shop grid, in which every tile legitimately owns its own buy button.

14.rule: Let the quantity stepper go above what the player can afford, and refuse at the commit instead of clamping.
14.why: Bee Swarm's Blender does exactly this, and its own wiki records the consequence: reopening the machine shows a selected count 'above the amount you would be able to craft with your resources, though you won't be able to select the Confirm option'. Clamping the stepper hides how short you are; refusing the commit shows it.

15.rule: A timed crafting queue holds ONE recipe and a count, and ending it early settles partially — finished output delivered, unfinished input refunded.
15.why: Bee Swarm's Blender: 'the player is only able to craft one type of item at a time', and End Crafting 'will give the player all finished items, and all unfinished items will be turned back into their ingredients and given back to the player'. This is the strongest crafting decision found: most queues make the player choose between waiting and losing the batch, and this one deletes the choice, which is why the cancel control can sit in the open instead of behind a confirm.

16.rule: Put the queue's completion state in the colour of the control that ends it.
16.why: Bee Swarm again: 'If the button is green, then everything has been blended. If not (red button), then the Blender has not finished blending.' One control, two colours, and the colour tells the player which of the two settlements they are about to take before they take it.

17.rule: When an entitlement changes what the timer MEANS, say so in a status line above the controls.
17.why: The Blender's timer only counts down while the player is in-game unless an Offline Voucher is redeemed, and the wiki records the exact replacement string shown above the buttons in that case. A countdown whose rules changed silently is a countdown the player will misread once and stop trusting.

18.rule: Price a speed-up per recipe, not per screen.
18.why: The Blender charges one ticket per item rushed, 'except for Moon Charm and Gumdrops, for which each ticket serves for speeding up whole 10 items' — two of twenty recipes at a tenth the rate. A rush control that renders a constant will be wrong on those two.

19.rule: Show a per-run or per-save craft cap as a badge on the recipe, and support three cases: a finite number, unlimited, and one-off.
19.why: 99 Nights in the Forest describes the badge as 'a white circle with a certain number inside, indicating how many of a certain item can be crafted during a run', and its own list uses all three cases — 20 Farm Plots, 8 Bear Traps, 10 Torches, 'an infinite amount' of Shelves and Log Walls. A card that only knows affordable and unaffordable cannot say any of this.

20.rule: If a count is shown as repeated icons rather than a number, say what the icons mean.
20.why: 99 Nights shows material yield as repeated bolt glyphs and states plainly that 'the number of symbols doesn't match the quantity you get' — one glyph is 1 scrap, two is 3, three is 5, four is 8. A shipped game chose an ordinal rank over a number and then published the mapping, which is the only thing that makes the rank usable.

21.rule: Give every resource counter its own maximum, and never assume one cap fits the row.
21.why: Dead Rails caps Components at 15 and the other five resources at 30, and caps deposits at 5 items per session on top of that. A shared 'x / 30' chip would be wrong for one of the six, and the one it is wrong about is the scarcest.

22.rule: Do not render the rarest result last and below the fold of its own summary.
22.why: Dead Rails' own wiki records it as a problem: special resources 'display in yellow text below the basic resources obtained from depositing. Players may have to scroll down to see what they have obtained.' The result the player most wants to see is the one the panel hides.

23.rule: List recipes the player cannot yet make, and name the missing precondition on the row.
23.why: Dead Rails annotates the Skeleton Grenade row '(requires Blueprint)' and links the dungeon it drops from; Fisch's material list points at a quest for the Evil Sigil. A recipe hidden until its precondition is met teaches nothing; a recipe shown with its precondition named is a goal.

24.rule: Let one recipe row cover a family of outputs at one price when the cost is identical.
24.why: Dead Rails prices Light Ammo, Medium Ammo and Shotgun Shells as one row at 6 Wood, and Revolver, Rifle and Shotgun as one row at 4 Wood, 1 Component and 10 Metal. Three rows carrying the same numbers is three chances to disagree.

25.rule: Gate the whole tree as one feature before gating any node inside it.
25.why: Tower Defense Simulator unlocks Skills at player Level 15, and Fisch's crafting altar sits behind a world puzzle before any recipe's level gate applies. A screen that does not exist yet is a different message from a node you cannot afford yet, and collapsing the two produces a tree full of locks with no explanation.

26.rule: Make a node a meter with its own cap, not a binary unlock, and put its prerequisite at a constant depth on the parent.
26.why: In TDS, seventeen skills cap at 10, 15, 20, 25 or 40 levels, and thirteen of them carry the same sentence — 'There is a requirement of reaching Level 10 in <named skill> before it is unlocked' — regardless of whether that parent caps at 20, 25 or 40. The unlock depth is a constant, which is what keeps the chains inside each category comparable.

27.rule: On a levelled node, show three numbers per step: this step's price, the cumulative total, and the resulting value.
27.why: TDS publishes exactly that per level — '75 coins, 95 total cost, 1% total increase' — and where the stat counts down, the third column follows it down ('29 shots required', then 28, 27). Without the cumulative figure the player cannot compare a node against a node; without the resulting value they cannot compare a node against nothing.

28.rule: Refund a respec into a currency that can only be spent back into the same tree, and escalate the price of resetting.
28.why: TDS returns 95% as Skill Credit, 'a unique currency only usable for Skills', charges 200 Coins to reset and states the escalation in its own sentence — 'Each reset will become more expensive by 200.', and refuses ordinary Coins in the tree until the credits are exhausted. The refund cannot leak into the rest of the economy and the escalation prices the optionality — this is the clearest worked respec in the file, and the part worth arguing with is the forced ordering, not the percentage.

29.rule: Mirror the tree's purchases into ONE summary outside the tree.
29.why: In TDS, unlocking any skill on a path makes a modifier for that path appear, and 'The description of the modifier will list every single Skill owned and how much it boosts specific statistics'. One chip per category, enumerating the nodes — so a player in a match can check what they bought without reopening the tree.

30.rule: State how many nodes are affordable right now.
30.why: BedWars' Forge 'displays how many upgrades are currently available based on the player's current forge point count'. It is the only affordability readout any source read here describes, and it answers the question a tree screen is actually opened to answer — is there anything I can do — without making the player scan for it.

31.rule: If buying a node closes other doors, write that into the node's own description.
31.why: BedWars' first sword upgrade reads '+5% Sword Damage + Locks in Sword class + Unlocks Iron Sword', and the page confirms 'once a tool is picked, it cannot be changed'. The irreversibility is on the node, where it is read before the click, rather than in a confirm dialog after it.

32.rule: Support tiered nodes and one-shot nodes in the same list, and let the tier column read None.
32.why: BedWars' team upgrade list runs Team Generator at tiers 1-3 (4, 8, 16 diamonds) beside Armory, Healing Fountain and Enchant Table with no tier at all. A tree that assumes every node has a next step cannot render half of this list. Of the five untiered rows only Enchant Table has no removal date: Armory is dated June 23, 2023 and Healing Fountain, Iron Arrows and Charging Gloops April 5, 2024. One current untiered node beside five current tiered ones still makes the shape real, and the list that shows it off best is the one BedWars has since cut down.

33.rule: Model prerequisites as expressions, not as a parent pointer: AND across clauses, OR inside one.
33.why: BedWars' Season 9 tree — since removed, which is stated in the reference — published prerequisites like 'Diamond Era + Destruction I' and 'Emerald Era + Magic I': a spine tier AND the previous step of the same branch. Deepwoken writes a talent's prerequisites as '[15 Fortitude OR 15 Willpower, 30 intelligence, Other]'. A single-parent model cannot express either, and a node with a disjunctive prerequisite belongs under more than one branch.

34.rule: Re-render the inventory after an upgrade purchase, because a node can change items already held.
34.why: BedWars' Iron Arrows upgrade 'unlocks iron arrows and upgrades any arrows already in the inventory', and Charging Gloops does the same. The purchase happens in one screen and the mutation lands in another. BOTH ROWS ARE DATED REMOVED April 5, 2024 in the Team Upgrades table's own 'Date Of Removal' column, and nothing else read for this file shows the behaviour, so the rule rests entirely on a system BedWars no longer runs. The mechanism is worth copying; the evidence for it is historical, which this reason did not say until 2026-09-20.

35.rule: Accept that a node's payload may be rows in a DIFFERENT screen, and put the locked state there.
35.why: BedWars' Armory upgrade 'unlocks several combat items inside of the Item Shop'. The tree records that the node is bought; the shop is where the items stop being locked. A tree that tries to show the items itself duplicates the shop. The Armory row is dated removed June 23, 2023, and the only other example read here — a Brewing Stand row unlocking 5 Unique Potions in the Item Shop — is inside the Season 9 table the page files under 'Removed'. Both sources for this rule are historical.

36.rule: A fixed level ladder needs a reached/not-reached state, not an affordability state — and it should say the player does not choose.
36.why: TDS tower evolution: 'the player does not get to pick which upgrades they unlock as each one has a determined level it is unlocked on', the progress shows as an orange bar on the inventory tile, and for an unevolved tower 'the only level that actually matters is the last one'. That bar is progress toward ONE gate, and drawing its intermediate stops as purchasable nodes would be a lie.

37.rule: Reach the crafting or upgrade screen from a place or a person when the game has a world to put it in.
37.why: BedWars' team upgrades are bought by 'interacting with Fulco, who can be found in each team's base'; Fisch's crafting altar is inside the Ancient Archives; Islands' workbench is a block on the player's island that is spawned with the island. A world that already has a location for the screen and also floats a button for it has two entry points to keep in sync.

38.rule: Make crafting output a placement token rather than the finished object when the thing is placed in the world.
38.why: In 99 Nights in the Forest the bench produces a Crafting Blueprint into the inventory, and placement is a separate step with its own controls — the game's own tips include 'Press R to rotate structures before you place them.' Crafting and placing are two screens' worth of state and one of them is the world.

39.rule: Let an upgrade ladder introduce a new currency at the top rather than only scaling the old one.
39.why: 99 Nights prices bench tiers 1-3 in Wood and Scrap, tier 4 adds Cultist Gems, tier 5 adds Gem of the Forest. The price row grows a slot partway up, which is a clearer statement that the top is a different kind of goal than a larger number in the same slot.

40.rule: Keep the node graph as data, so the tree can be re-balanced by someone who cannot script.
40.why: The developer of a 750-ability tree said the hard part was 'making it able to be easily customizable and allowing the developers to create skill trees with virtually no programming knowledge'. A tree whose graph is hand-placed is a tree nobody re-balances. THE SECOND HALF OF THIS RULE WAS DELETED ON 2026-09-20. It said to expect to draw the edges with something other than a Frame, on the strength of the same author's 'isn’t a GUI but bricks using beams to connect them'. Post 15 of that same topic, two years later, is that author saying he 'ended up making a completely 2D version of this skill tree'. A ScreenGui still has no line primitive, but nothing read here settles what to draw an edge with, and the only developer who answered the question answered it twice and differently.

screens.label: The SUMMON / HATCH / REVEAL screen, across genres — banners and egg machines, odds panels, pity counters, luck modifiers, multi-pull width, the roll control, the reveal cutscene and its skip
demonstrates: THE ODDS PANEL IS NOT A FEATURE, IT IS A CONDITION OF SHIPPING. If an outcome is bought with Robux, or with a currency that Robux can buy, the creator must indicate all possible outcomes AND the actual numerical odds. A summon screen without a rate table is not an austere summon screen, it is a non-compliant one.

PITY SYSTEMS ARE NAMED IN POLICY AS A PROBABILITY MODIFIER ITEM, in the same list as luck boosts, enhanced resource drops and rate-up scrolls. The counter that looks like a mercy mechanic is classified with the things that sell you better odds, and inherits their disclosure duty.

THE ODDS AFFORDANCE MUST CARRY A WORD, NOT JUST A GLYPH. When there are too many outcomes to fit in the player's view, the itemised list may live in a clickable pop-up — but the page says outright that 'using a standalone symbol like the (i) icon without a descriptive word is not sufficient'. What the page requires is a descriptive WORD; the two labels it prints — 'Info' and 'Details' — are its examples, not an enumeration, and the announcement FAQ words it the same way ('it needs an accompanying word like “Info” or “Details”'). This is the rare case of a platform specifying that a control must be worded at all.
The odds panel must be visible and accessible PRIOR to purchase, not after the spend and not inside the result.

Odds are displayed as percentages and the percentages of all final outcomes must sum to exactly 100%. So a rate list is a closed set, and an outcome nobody bothered to enumerate is a hole in a number that has to add up.

There is a stated rounding rule and a stated disclaimer for it: round to four or more decimal places lower than the decimal place with the first non-zero number, and carry a line such as 'Probabilities are rounded; total of displayed individual probabilities may not equal 100%'. A 1-in-400,000 outcome therefore needs both a long number and a sentence about it.
A shortcut exists for flat tables: if many items share one probability, the list may be headed 'Odds for each item listed below: X%' rather than repeating the figure on every row.

THE RATE TABLE IS PER PLAYER AND LIVE, NOT A CONSTANT. Where a player can only obtain one instance of an outcome, the odds shown for the remaining outcomes must be updated to that player's up-to-date remaining odds — the list re-normalises as a collection fills.

A luck item's effect must be numerically explained before purchase, AND while it is active the displayed odds must be dynamically updated to the player's true odds. A rate panel that shows base rates while a potion is running is wrong by policy, not merely unhelpful.
Indirect purchase counts: keys, re-roll tokens and spin tickets bought with Robux drag the thing they open into scope, so a currency layer between Robux and the reveal does not remove the duty.

A free path is exempt: randomised rewards given for an action that costs no Robux and no Robux-purchasable currency need no odds disclosure. The same chest can require a rate panel or not depending on how it was opened.

PolicyService:GetPolicyInfoForPlayerAsync() returns ArePaidRandomItemsRestricted and IsPaidItemTradingAllowed, so the summon screen has a per-player restricted variant that the client must ask for before drawing.

SIX named treatments are listed for a restricted player, and the page requires the creator to apply one of them: offer an unpaid, earnable path to the same item (mystery eggs granted free at gameplay milestones); offer the outcomes in a pre-determined, non-random order disclosed before purchase (first spin always 5 gems, second always 10); offer the specific outcome for direct guaranteed purchase priced on its expected value (a 10-Robux box with 5% odds on a sword becomes a 200-Robux sword); remove or hide the generator, replacing a prize wheel with a shop offering direct purchases; block the purchase with an error message; or remove the user from the parts of the game with paid random items, by teleporting them away. Only one of the six is an error state; the other five are design choices.
The blocked-purchase treatment is given with its copy: the purchase button is replaced by 'Sorry, this item is unavailable for users in your region'. The button is REPLACED, not greyed.

When IsPaidItemTradingAllowed is false the player must not be able to reach trading for the outcome of a paid random item — so a reveal card's onward actions are gated by the same per-player policy call.

The announcement states the enforcement path in as many words: audit your game for compliance to avoid moderation, noncompliant experiences are moderated with notice through Roblox's moderation message system, and reinstatement goes through the appeals system. The odds panel is load-bearing for the experience staying up.

Paid random items are described as a highly regulated monetization mechanism that is legally prohibited for certain users — which is why the per-player PolicyService branch exists at all, and why it cannot be treated as an optional regional nicety.

The four categories are enumerated by name, and they cover more of a game than a prize wheel: Capsule (spin a wheel, hatch an egg, open a chest), Enhancement (a potion whose duration is random, an upgrade that may fail), Combination (synthesising two rare eggs for a better chance at a better result), and Probability-Adjustment (luck boosts, pity, rate-up scrolls). An upgrade machine with a failure chance is a gacha screen wearing different art.

A creator raised an unresolved edge in the replies and it is worth designing around rather than answering: a crate that TELLS you what it contains before you buy, where buying it changes what the next crate contains. Outcome disclosed, no randomness at the moment of purchase, yet the sequence is random. No staff answer to it was read in the posts fetched here.

The first substantive creator reply is 'these will be a bit of a hassle to implement for existing games', which places the cost of this screen where it actually lands: retrofitting disclosure onto a reveal that was built without it.

THE BANNER IS THREE SLOTS AND THE MIDDLE ONE IS NOT DECORATION. Three Mythics are featured; the centre has a 50% chance of being the Mythic you get, the two beside it 10% each, and any unfeatured Mythic 0.526%. Position on the banner IS the weight, so the layout is the odds table in another form.

THE PITY BAR BELONGS TO THE MIDDLE SLOT, NOT TO THE RARITY. Each summon adds 1/400 to a pity bar that guarantees the featured MIDDLE unit at 400 pulls. A player at 399 is 399 pulls into one specific character, not into a tier.

Pity has TWO reset causes and only one of them is the player's: pulling any Mythic resets it to 0, and the banner refreshing also resets it. The banner refreshes every hour with random featured units, so an hourly clock the player does not control can erase the counter.

The event banner moves its pity target by what you already own: pity is 200 summons there instead of 400, and unowned featured Mythics are PRIORITISED until all of them are obtained. The guarantee is computed against the collection, not fixed at authoring time.
The pity depth is a property of the banner, not of the game — 400 on Legacy and Special, 200 on Event — so the denominator has to be read off the banner the player is looking at.
Event pity is quoted as a total price as well as a count: 2,000 event currency for the Mythic pity. The screen states what the guarantee costs, not just how far away it is.

The published rate table is PER-RARITY, NOT PER-UNIT, and the page says so: 'Every single unit has the same chance of being obtained from a Summon according to their Rarity.' Rare 81.9%, Epic 16%, Legendary 2%, Mythic 0.25% (0.5% on Special and Event), Secret 1 in 400,000 — with a separate shiny sub-rate printed beside FOUR of the five (Rare 0.819%, Epic 0.16%, Legendary 0.02%, Mythic 0.0025%, each restated for the Shiny Hunter gamepass and Mythic restated again per banner) while Secret's shiny rate is published as '???'. A blanket shiny chance sits on the same list without being reconciled with them: 'All summoned unit has 1% chance to be Shiny version (3% if obtained Shiny Hunter gamepass)'. The page never says the list sums to anything, and it does not: the four figures given as percentages total 100.15% before the Secret rate is counted at all.

LUCK POTIONS DO NOT REDUCE PITY, and the page says so explicitly. Two systems that both look like 'help' are kept independent, which means the screen must not let a potion appear to advance the counter.

Stacked luck is published as a single resulting figure rather than as three multipliers: Luck plus Super Lucky plus Ultra Lucky sets the Mythic chance to 0.936%. The player is told the answer, not the arithmetic.

The luck potions are sold FOR ROBUX INSIDE THE BANNER WINDOW (Super Lucky 99 Robux for 2x, Ultra Lucky 149 Robux for 3x). The odds-modifier shop is a surface of the summon screen, not a trip to the main shop.
A rare enough pull leaves the screen entirely: Secret and Shiny Mythic summons are announced in Roblox chat globally, across every server. The reveal has a server-wide tier above the personal one.

BANNER TIERS GATE WHAT THE RATE TABLE EVEN CONTAINS, BY ACCOUNT LEVEL: Tier 0 (level 0+) cannot summon Secret units or shinies at all, Tier 1 (level 5+) can summon shinies but not Secret, Tier 2 (level 20+) both. The stated reason is to stop late-game players farming pulls on alt accounts. Two players looking at one banner are looking at two different outcome sets.
Secret is explicitly excluded from pity — one outcome in the table has no floor under it, and the page states that as a fact about the system rather than leaving it to be inferred.

The two banners differ in CURRENCY, not just contents: the Legacy banner spends legacy gems obtained by converting regular gems or disenchanting units, and a summon can alternatively be paid with a Summon Ticket. One roll control, three payment forms.
The price is per-player before anything else: 50 gems, or 40 with the VIP gamepass.

The odds panel has a NAME AND A HOME: 'the Index menu on the banner states the chances of being obtained for every unit on the banner'. It is a sub-menu of the banner, which is exactly the clickable details pop-up Roblox's policy permits — and it is reached from the banner rather than from a settings screen.

The summon area is a hub of three stores, not one screen: the banners themselves, a Unit Index, and a Normalize shop for transferring or removing shiny status. The reveal's downstream actions get their own counters nearby rather than living on the result card.

The same three-slot banner appears independently here — middle 50%, left and right 20% each, rotating hourly — which makes the weighted centre a convention across two unrelated games rather than one studio's habit.

THREE PITY COUNTERS RUN AT ONCE ON ONE BANNER, at wildly different depths: on the Special and Selection banners, Legendary at 50 summons, Mythic at 400, Vanguard at 25,000. The restart rule is not uniform across them and the page states the exception in the same breath — 'Their pity counts restart after you get a unit of that specific rarity. This does not apply to the Vanguard rarity.' A single progress bar cannot represent this screen.

Each pity depth is published WITH ITS PRICE IN BOTH FORMS — Legendary 2,500 gems (2,000 with VIP), Mythic 20,000 (16,000), Vanguard 1,250,000 (1,000,000). The counter and the invoice are the same fact shown twice.
