0.rule: Draw the odds panel before you draw anything else, label its opener with a WORD, and put it in reach before the spend.
0.why: Roblox's paid random items policy requires all outcomes and their numerical odds to be disclosed prior to purchase, permits the itemised list to live in a clickable pop-up, and says in as many words that a bare (i) glyph without a descriptive word is not sufficient. Anime Vanguards ships exactly this as a named Index menu on the banner. A summon screen without it is not minimal, it is moderatable.

1.rule: Make the rate list a closed set that sums to 100%, keep the zero rows, and carry the rounding disclaimer when a number is long.
1.why: The policy requires the percentages of all final outcomes to sum to exactly 100% and gives the rounding rule and the disclaimer sentence for long decimals. Adopt Me prints '0% Common' on eggs that cannot produce one, which is what makes two eggs comparable line against line instead of read twice.

2.rule: Recompute the displayed odds while a luck buff is active, and while a one-per-player outcome is already owned.
2.why: The policy requires enhanced odds to be dynamically updated to the user's true odds when a modifier is active, and requires the remaining outcomes to re-normalise once a player can no longer obtain one of them. Anime Adventures publishes the stacked result as a single figure — 0.936% — rather than three multipliers, which is the same instinct: show the answer, not the arithmetic.

3.rule: Branch the whole screen on PolicyService before drawing it, and REPLACE the purchase control rather than greying it.
3.why: GetPolicyInfoForPlayerAsync returns ArePaidRandomItemsRestricted and IsPaidItemTradingAllowed, and the policy's own blocked-purchase example replaces the button with 'Sorry, this item is unavailable for users in your region'. A greyed roll button with a tooltip is a dead end; the policy lists six treatments in all, and the other five — a free earnable path, a disclosed deterministic order, direct purchase at expected value, removing or hiding the generator, or moving the player out of the parts of the game that carry paid random items — each send the player somewhere instead of stopping them.

4.rule: Decide the outcome at the click, animate a result you already hold, and do not let the inventory show it first.
4.why: The Blox Fruits wiki states that the rolling interface is purely visual and the item is awarded at the moment the trigger is pressed — and proves it by noting that players on unusual latency see the item in their inventory before the animation starts. That leak is the shipped version of the bug a generated reveal will have: two surfaces fed by one response, with nothing holding the second back.

5.rule: Give the reveal a rarity floor. Animate the rare outcome and resolve the common one.
5.why: Sol's RNG plays opening cutscenes only for Epic and above, in a game that is nothing but pulls. Animating every outcome spends the ceremony on the outcomes that did not earn it, and it is the reason the skip has to be sold in the first place.

6.rule: Let the tier be legible before the identity is — colour and staging first, name last.
6.why: Each rarity in Sol's RNG has its own cutscene style, and the staging described per tier puts a coloured star or a coloured screen edge before the reveal of what was actually obtained. The player's question in the first half-second is how good, not what.

7.rule: Drive the reveal's colour from the same per-item token as the inventory row.
7.why: In Sol's RNG the cutscene star takes its colour from the item's title colour in the Collection, and the wiki states that changing the Collection colour changes the star and the end-of-cutscene background with it. One token, three surfaces, and no possibility of the reveal and the inventory disagreeing about what rarity something is.

8.rule: Make the skip a threshold the player sets, not a toggle, and sell the instant version separately if you sell one.
8.why: Sol's RNG's Roll Cutscene setting takes a rarity number and skips anything below it, while the 100-Robux Quick Roll gamepass removes the animation entirely — and the same threshold shape is reused for auto-equip and for swap warnings. A binary skip forces the player to choose between watching everything and watching nothing.

9.rule: Let an auto-skip or auto-sell rule name only outcomes the player has already obtained.
9.why: Sol's RNG's Aura Filter can only be applied to auras already in the Collection. That single constraint makes it impossible for a rule written on Monday to silently discard the first-ever sighting of something on Friday — the option list IS the collection, so a first reveal is always seen.

10.rule: Withhold the automation switch that can destroy the outcome the screen exists to produce, and say that you withheld it.
10.why: Anime Vanguards' auto-sell covers five rarities and the wiki states plainly 'There's no option to auto sell shiny units.', while auto-selling trait units — which is recoverable — is offered under a settings submenu. This is a shipped game refusing to ship a convenience because a forgotten toggle would delete a one-in-a-thousand pull, and it is the clearest precedent in this file for leaving a capability out on purpose.

11.rule: Scope a bulk automation to what happens AFTER it is switched on, and say so on the control.
11.why: Anime Vanguards' auto-sell acts only on summons made after the feature is toggled on and does not reach backwards into the inventory. That temporal scope is the entire reason the switch is safe to offer, so it belongs on the switch.

12.rule: A pity counter needs its target, its denominator, its price, and a consumed state.
12.why: Anime Adventures binds pity to the middle banner slot rather than to a rarity; Anime Vanguards runs Legendary, Mythic and Vanguard counters at 50, 400 and 25,000 on one banner, publishes each one's gem cost with and without VIP, and marks the Vanguard counter 'pity reached' when it is permanently spent. A single bar labelled Pity can represent none of that.

13.rule: Say what resets the counter, including the resets the player does not cause.
13.why: Anime Adventures resets pity both on a Mythic pull and when the banner refreshes on its hourly clock, and Anime Vanguards' Selection and Special banners SHARE one counter. A counter whose reset rules are invisible reads as a betrayal the first time it empties on its own.

14.rule: State the non-interactions as loudly as the interactions.
14.why: Both Anime Adventures and Anime Vanguards say outright that luck potions do NOT reduce pity, and Anime Vanguards adds that they do not raise Secret, Vanguard or shiny odds. Two systems that both look like help are independent, and the screen has to prevent the potion from appearing to move the bar.

15.rule: Position on a banner IS weight — put the heaviest outcome in the middle and let the layout carry the odds.
15.why: Two unrelated shipped games converge on a three-slot banner with the centre weighted at 50% and the flanks at 10% and 20% respectively. Once players know the convention, the arrangement communicates the rate table before the Index menu is opened.

16.rule: Treat the rate table's ROW SET as mutable, not just its percentages.
16.why: A Blox Fruits event banner made one item rollable and common items unrollable for 24 hours; a Pet Simulator 99 enchant reads 'Adds +1 RARE Active Huge to hatch'. Equipment and campaigns add and remove entries, so a rate panel built from a static list will show outcomes that cannot happen and hide ones that can.

17.rule: Assume the outcome has two axes — identity and finish — and roll both on one pull.
17.why: Pet Simulator 99 grants golden and rainbow hatch chances on the same track as the pets themselves; Anime Adventures publishes a shiny sub-rate beside four of its five rarities and prints '???' for the fifth; Anime Vanguards publishes ONE blanket shiny chance (1.5%, 3% with Shiny Hunter) and says shinies exist only for some Epic, some Legendary and all Mythic and higher. Neither publishes one per rarity — but both price the finish as a separate number from the identity, which is the part that transfers. The result card has to render a variant of a thing, not a thing, and the rate panel has to price both.

18.rule: Show remaining storage on the hatch screen, and rank the small x-of-y readouts second in the visual order, right after the buttons.
18.why: Pet Simulator X's auto-hatch 'will cease when the user can no longer afford the egg or has no more storage' — storage is one of exactly two named ways an unattended reveal loop ends, so a screen that hides it cannot explain why it stopped. Separately, and weaker: one reviewer on a hatch panel named two small fraction readouts, the 0/3 and the 0/50, as what the eye should reach after the buttons. The thread never says what either counts, so the ranking is the finding and the meaning is not.

19.rule: Do not assume a fixed number of simultaneous reveals.
19.why: Pet Simulator 99 grows the egg count through a stacking, prerequisite-gated ladder of Robux passes — the +40 pass requires the +15 pass to be owned first, so those two alone stack to +55 — AND through FOUR mastery levels that add slots (+1 at 40, +2 at 60, +3 at 90, +5 at 99, another +11). No page read here publishes the base count, so this file cannot state a maximum; what it can state is that the layout is handed a count at runtime and that the count is not small.

20.rule: Compute the price on the control from the player, and never bake it into the tile.
20.why: Blox Fruits derives the roll price from player level with a published formula and a Premium discount; both unit-collectors read here quote a VIP price beside the base price, and Anime Vanguards notes the discount does not apply on event banners. Pet Simulator 99 makes eggs 10, 20 and 30% cheaper by mastery level. Every one of these games recomputes the number on the button per player, per banner.

21.rule: Build the reveal's impact out of screen-space interface elements and give it sound.
21.why: A feedback thread's concrete advice for a working hatch was sound plus two-dimensional interface frames for confetti and shell fragments, tweened — not a world-space emitter. Sol's RNG gives the reveal two audio slots — a sound while rolling and a separate sound after rolling — although the files that fill them are reused across tiers and split per item at the top end, so the two-slot shape is the convention and not a per-tier sting. Interface particles survive a camera that is looking somewhere else; a part-attached emitter does not.

22.rule: End the reveal by leaving a durable line somewhere other than the reveal.
22.why: Sol's RNG posts the outcome and its odds to server chat after the cutscene, in a per-tier colour and with a fixed grammar that includes the 1-in-N. Anime Adventures escalates a Secret or shiny mythic to a global announcement across every server. The modal closes; the line stays, and it is what makes a rare pull a social event rather than a private one.

23.rule: Reserve the accent on the result card for the action the card exists to offer, and give the destructive action weight without giving it the accent.
23.why: On a reviewed hatch panel one reviewer said the Equip button was the only red thing on it and stood out a lot while matching nothing; a different reviewer said the delete button beside it looked too blended into the background. Both were wrong at once and in opposite directions — each named by a single reader, not by a consensus.

24.rule: Lay the result card out as name, then image, then stats — and never let a control strip read as an empty bar.
24.why: ONE reviewer on a hatch panel proposed exactly that order because the name and stats labels were too close to each other, and the same reviewer had to ask what the empty bar in the middle of the panel was; it turned out to be the options strip. A row of affordances with no visible contents is invisible to the people it is for.

25.rule: Format the number on the roll control from the value that is actually applied, and show the interval from the end the player is counting toward.
25.why: Sol's RNG's roll button displays 'x1.3 Luck Ready' for a gear that grants 1.35x, and the wiki has to explain to readers that the bonus roll is the one AFTER the number shown on the counter. Two small formatting decisions that generated a paragraph of errata on a community wiki.

26.rule: Give the roll control a cooldown state and treat it as the normal state.
26.why: The Blox Fruits gacha rolls once every two hours and shares that cooldown with sibling machines — and the shipped interface got the sibling's NAME wrong in its own cooldown string, because the line was reused and never re-read. If cooldowns are shared, the string that names the sibling is generated, not typed.

27.rule: Treat the reveal animation's duration as a resource the player spends, and give them a way to spend less of it.
27.why: Three unrelated shipped games monetise or reward exactly this: Sol's RNG sells the skip for 100 Robux, Adopt Me sells an instant hatch for 35 Robux per egg, and Pet Simulator 99 makes animation speed the level-10 reward of five separate mastery tracks. A studio that makes shortening its own ceremony the first thing progression buys has told you what the ceremony costs.

28.rule: When a paid skip fails, hand back an equivalent consumable rather than a refund or a silence.
28.why: Adopt Me states that an egg that fails to hatch after the Hatch Now gamepass is bought yields an Instant Hatch Potion instead, which does the same job. The failure is resolved inside the game's own economy, at a moment of the player's choosing, without a support ticket.

29.rule: Keep retired content in the catalogue with an availability flag instead of deleting the row.
29.why: Adopt Me's egg table carries an 'Available Right Now?' column and keeps eggs that left rotation, noting they can only be obtained by trading. The odds of something a player already owns or might be offered still have to be readable after it stops being sold.

30.rule: Put the luck shop and the collection board inside the pull surface, not a menu away.
30.why: Anime Adventures sells its Robux luck potions in the banner window itself; Anime Vanguards' summon area is three stores including the Unit Index; Adopt Me puts a board showing every pet in the game and the ones you have in the nursery where the eggs hatch. The place you pull is the place you see what is missing and what improves your odds.

31.rule: Let the world model carry the campaign state as well as the interface.
31.why: When a limited gacha is running in Blox Fruits, the vendor gains a purple aura. A player who walks past learns the banner is live without opening anything, which is the only way a limited window reaches somebody who was not already looking at the screen.

screens.label: The in-game HUD — currency pills, meters, the button rail, minimap, toasts and the quest tracker
demonstrates: the whole HUD lives in ONE ScreenGui named for the job (HUDContainer), with a UIPadding of 16px on all four edges so nothing touches the physical screen edge

ScreenInsets is set to DeviceSafeInsets, not the default CoreUISafeInsets, specifically because CoreUISafeInsets 'adds a large gap between the meter and the physical top edge' — the doc calls that gap the error and the tucked-in version the success

the meter is right-aligned at the top: AnchorPoint 1,0 and Position {1,0},{0,0}, and the doc's stated reason is that right alignment is what keeps it clear of the Roblox top bar while still hugging the physical edge
meter size is expressed as scale, 35% of screen width by 5% of screen height, never as pixels
a UISizeConstraint with MaxSize `inf, 20` caps the bar at 20 pixels tall so it does not grow fat on a tablet's taller aspect ratio

the bar frame is black at BackgroundTransparency 0.75 (25% opacity) with a UIStroke of Thickness 3 at Transparency 0.25 — the dark translucent plate plus a dark outline is what makes it readable over both a bright and a dark world
corner radius is UICorner CornerRadius `0.5, 0` — a SCALE of 50%, which yields a true pill at any height, rather than a pixel radius that changes character between devices
the inner fill is a separate child Frame anchored 0,0.5 at Position {0,0},{0.5,0} filling 100%x100%, carrying its OWN UICorner at the same 0.5 scale so the fill stays pill-shaped as it shrinks

the icon is an ImageLabel sized `2,0,2,0` — 200% of the bar — pinned with AnchorPoint 0.5,0.5 at Position {0,0},{0.5,0}, so it sits centred ON the bar's left END and OVERHANGS it on both sides, held square by a UIAspectRatioConstraint and raised with ZIndex 2

fill colour is driven through a five-stop ramp — rgb(225,50,0), (255,100,0), (255,200,0), (150,225,0), (0,225,50) — interpolated by the fraction, so the meter changes hue continuously rather than switching at thresholds

the tutorial's first instruction after building the custom meter is to call StarterGui:SetCoreGuiEnabled(Enum.CoreGuiType.Health, false), because otherwise the default Roblox meter 'will duplicate and potentially overlap the custom meter'
the headline counter sits TOP-CENTRE: AnchorPoint 0.5,0 and Position {0.5,0},{0.01,0} — one percent down from the top edge, not flush with it
size {0.25,0},{0.08,0}, i.e. a quarter of the screen wide, and the stated reason is to 'grab the player's attention' — the primary counter is deliberately the largest thing on the HUD
a UISizeConstraint with MinSize `0, 40` guarantees the counter never falls below 40 pixels tall on a small screen
the counter's internals are laid out by a UIListLayout set to FillDirection Horizontal with VerticalAlignment Center — icon and number are a LIST, not two hand-positioned children
the icon carries LayoutOrder 1 so it is always the leftmost item, and is sized `{1.25,0},{1,0}` with SizeConstraint RelativeYY so it scales off the bar's HEIGHT and keeps its aspect

the number's TextXAlignment is Left, explicitly 'to ensure the score text remains left-aligned near the crown icon regardless of whether the player's score is 0, 1,000, or 1,000,000' — the icon must not jump as digits are added
the plate is black at BackgroundTransparency 0.6, and the number is tinted toward the currency's own colour, rgb(255,200,100) for gold, at TextSize 30
the doc's stated reason for an icon at all is that it 'allows players to easily recognize what you're communicating without using text, which can clutter the screen'

Spellbound RPG is described as a single circular Items button carrying a book icon that, once selected, reveals three further buttons for skills, equipment and deck — the rail is COLLAPSED by default and fans open on press, and the doc credits this to small mobile screens

Super Striker League is described as swapping its action buttons by context: Sprint and Tackle while the player lacks the ball, Deke and Pass once they hold it, so 'the UI stays contextually useful, avoiding unnecessary distractions' — the same two slots, different contents

The Survival Game's HUD is described as health and hunger status plus quick access to map, inventory and tools — status meters and launcher buttons are the two element families, and the doc treats them as the minimum set
Winds of Fortune's player stats are described as icons sharing a colour palette and similar shapes so a family of stats is recognisable as a family

the listed close-button convention across Winds of Fortune, Dragon Adventures, BotClash Simulator and DOORS is an X on a button in the top-right; grey means unusable; a lock overlay means not yet unlocked
the consistency examples are stated as hard rules a game commits to: the Health stat is green in every text, icon and bar; a price the player cannot afford renders in red
buttons are made to read as pressable by 'housing buttons in a container' and by 'adding highlights or shadows to enhance their tactile appeal by suggesting 3D depth'
feedback the doc names as required includes 'a progress bar filling up as the player completes quest objectives' and a button that visibly changes on hover, press and release

four inset modes exist and they are not interchangeable: CoreUISafeInsets (the default, clear of top bar AND cutouts, 'recommended if the ScreenGui contains interactive UI elements'), DeviceSafeInsets (clear of cutouts only), TopbarSafeInsets (the ScreenGui flexes horizontally to fill the gap BETWEEN the top bar controls and the right edge), and None (documented as suitable 'only for non-interactive content like background images')

eight core UI elements ship enabled in every experience and each can be individually turned off through SetCoreGuiEnabled: PlayerList, Health, Backpack, Chat, EmotesMenu, SelfView, Captures, AvatarSwitcher

the Health bar only appears once the Humanoid is below full health and the Backpack only appears once a Tool exists — two core elements that are invisible at design time and appear mid-session on top of whatever was drawn there
the Captures button is documented as sitting 'along the right side of the screen', so the right edge is not free even when the player list is hidden
touch devices additionally draw a virtual thumbstick and a jump button, removable only wholesale via GuiService.TouchControlsEnabled = false

multiple ScreenGui containers are the intended way to separate interfaces, layered by DisplayOrder, and a disabled ScreenGui 'will not render, process user input, or update' — so a closed menu costs nothing
ResetOnSpawn defaults to true, which silently rebuilds the HUD on every respawn unless the ScreenGui is a DIRECT child of StarterGui with ResetOnSpawn false

'On mobile devices, the default controls occupy a portion of the bottom-left and bottom-right corners of the screen. When you design a game's UI, avoid placing important info or virtual buttons in these zones.' — both bottom corners are reserved, not just one

the thumb-zone rule is stated numerically: 'A button placed 40% below the screen's top edge is reachable on a phone but almost unreachable on a tablet' — the same scale position is not the same ergonomics across devices

the recommended fix is not a scale position at all but RELATIVE positioning against the live jump button, and the doc's own sample sizes the custom button at 80% of the jump button's pixel size and offsets it 20 pixels to the jump button's left, with AnchorPoint 1,1
the sample parents the custom button to the JUMP BUTTON'S OWN PARENT and waits on `jumpButton.IsLoaded` before reading its position, so the rail follows the control rather than guessing where it is
contextual actions are documented as belonging to a proximity prompt rather than the HUD: 'it doesn't make sense to constantly show an open button on the screen'

Roblox's own worked example of HUD placement is currency: 'the UI container holding the gem/coin counters ... is positioned at an X scale of 1 (right) and Y scale of 0 (top) with an upper-right anchor point' — currency counters belong top-right, anchored 1,0

rules.note: Distilled from the references above. Units are Roblox UI units: Scale is a 0-1 fraction of the parent, Offset is pixels, transparency is 0 opaque to 1 invisible. Figures taken verbatim from a source are exact; anything read off prose is marked approximate. This file describes a SCREEN, so the rules are about where things sit, what owns what, and how each element is assembled — a genre file supplies the palette and the chrome on top.

screenOwnership.rule: Treat the screen as already occupied. Roblox owns the top strip (top bar, 36px offset, expanding), the top-right (player list), the right edge (capture button), the bottom-left (thumbstick) and the bottom-right (jump button). The HUD may use the top-centre band, the left edge below the top bar, the mid-right, and the bottom-centre — everything else is borrowed and must survive the owner reappearing.
screenOwnership.why: Roblox's Engine UI designer gives the top bar as offset height 36 and says it expands; the docs reserve both bottom corners for touch controls and put the capture button on the right side; the player list and chat are user-toggleable so their footprint changes mid-session. A HUD generated without this map draws its best element under a control the player cannot move.

coreUiCollision.rule: Any custom element that duplicates a core one must disable the core one in the same breath: a custom health bar requires SetCoreGuiEnabled(Enum.CoreGuiType.Health, false), a custom hotbar requires Backpack false, a custom leaderboard requires PlayerList false.
coreUiCollision.why: Roblox's own HUD tutorial shows the failure first and then fixes it — the default meter 'will duplicate and potentially overlap the custom meter'. The trap is that Health and Backpack are INVISIBLE at design time and only appear once the player takes damage or picks up a tool, so the collision never shows up in Studio and always shows up in play.

screenInsets.rule: Interactive HUD goes in a ScreenGui at CoreUISafeInsets. Use DeviceSafeInsets only for an element that must hug the physical edge AND is aligned away from the top bar. Never use None for anything the player touches.
screenInsets.why: The docs recommend CoreUISafeInsets 'if the ScreenGui contains interactive UI elements' and restrict None to 'non-interactive content like background images'. The HUD meter tutorial takes the exception deliberately and states the trade: CoreUISafeInsets is correct but 'adds a large gap between the meter and the physical top edge', and the right-aligned meter can afford DeviceSafeInsets because its alignment already keeps it clear of the Roblox controls.

edgePadding.rule: Put a UIPadding of 16px on all four edges of the HUD container, once, rather than nudging each child away from the edge.
edgePadding.why: The first-party HUD tutorial applies exactly `0, 16` to all four edges of the ScreenGui so contents are pushed off the screen edge 'for a cleaner appearance and to prevent them from being clipped'. Applied on the container it survives every child being repositioned later; applied per child it is forgotten on the next one added.

slotMap.rule: Elements have assigned homes and a generator should not improvise them. Currency counters: top-right, AnchorPoint 1,0, Position {1,0},{0,0}, as a single container holding all counters. Primary score or objective count: top-centre, AnchorPoint 0.5,0, Position {0.5,0},{0.01,0}. Status meters (health, stamina, hunger): upper area opposite the currency, or grouped under it, never scattered into separate corners. Launcher rail: one edge, left or the top bar. Toasts: top-right stack unless currency already fills it, then top-centre. Touch action buttons: relative to the jump button only.
slotMap.why: Every one of these numbers is a first-party figure, not a taste: Roblox's cross-platform guide places 'the gem/coin counters' at X scale 1 and Y scale 0 with an upper-right anchor point, the score bar tutorial positions the headline counter at {0.5,0},{0.01,0} at a quarter of screen width, and the HUD meter tutorial anchors the meter 1,0 at 35% by 5%. Scattering the same information into different corners is what the 'Trying to make a HUD like this' reviewer called confusing.

meterConstruction.rule: A meter is a pill plate plus a pill fill plus an overhanging icon. Plate: black at BackgroundTransparency 0.75, UIStroke Thickness 3 at Transparency 0.25, UICorner CornerRadius {0.5,0}. Fill: a child Frame anchored 0,0.5 at {0,0},{0.5,0}, size {1,0},{1,0}, with its OWN UICorner at {0.5,0}. Icon: ImageLabel at 200% of the bar, AnchorPoint 0.5,0.5 at {0,0},{0.5,0}, UIAspectRatioConstraint, ZIndex 2. Cap the height with UISizeConstraint MaxSize inf,20.
meterConstruction.why: Read verbatim off Roblox's HUD meter tutorial, which gives every one of these values and explains each: the dark translucent plate plus dark outline is so the meter 'stands out better on both light and dark backgrounds', the 0.5 SCALE radius 'ensures a fully rounded curve no matter how tall or wide the container becomes', and the 20px cap exists because 5% height 'may look slightly too tall on tablet screens'. The overhanging oversized icon is the detail a generator invents wrongly — it is not inside the bar, it is centred on the bar's left end at twice the bar's height.

meterColourRamp.rule: A meter's fill colour interpolates continuously across five stops rather than switching at thresholds: rgb(225,50,0), rgb(255,100,0), rgb(255,200,0), rgb(150,225,0), rgb(0,225,50), indexed by the fill fraction.
meterColourRamp.why: The first-party tutorial ships exactly this five-keypoint sequence and a fraction-to-colour function rather than if/elseif thresholds. A three-step red/yellow/green switch is the common reinvention and it reads as a state machine; the continuous ramp reads as a quantity draining.

counterConstruction.rule: A counter is a horizontal UIListLayout — icon first at LayoutOrder 1, number second with TextXAlignment Left — never two hand-positioned children. Size the icon with SizeConstraint RelativeYY so it scales off the row height. Floor the row with UISizeConstraint MinSize 0,40. Tint the number toward its own currency's colour.
counterConstruction.why: Roblox's score bar tutorial gives the reason in one sentence — left-aligning the number keeps the icon still 'regardless of whether the player's score is 0, 1,000, or 1,000,000'. A centred number makes the icon jump sideways every time the player earns anything, which is precisely when the player is looking at it.

buttonRail.rule: The launcher rail is one stack of equal circular icon buttons on one declared edge. Unit 44x44, fully round (CornerRadius scale 1.0), 4px between neighbours, glyph at 50% of the button, plate near-black rgb(18,18,21) at BackgroundTransparency 0.08. If a button carries a label the widget grows horizontally with PaddingLeft 9 / PaddingRight 11 and the label is Bold at TextSize 16. Cap a vertical group at 4.5 visible icons and a horizontal one at 4.
buttonRail.why: Every figure is the shipped default theme of TopbarPlus, the library most Roblox games use for this rail, so these are the proportions players have been trained on. The 4.5 cap is the interesting one: the half-icon is deliberate, it is how a scrollable group tells the player there is more below without adding a scrollbar.

railBadge.rule: An unread or claimable count on a rail button is a fixed 20x20 badge hung off the button's TOP-RIGHT corner at Position {1,-12},{0,-1}, overlapping the button, with the count at TextSize 13. The badge does not resize with the count.
railBadge.why: Taken from the TopbarPlus default theme. Fixed size matters: a badge that grows to fit '12' changes the silhouette of the rail, and a rail whose shape changes when a quest completes is a rail that reads as broken rather than as notifying.

railSelectedState.rule: A selected rail button is marked by adding a lighter spot behind the glyph — white at BackgroundTransparency 0.7 with a 45-degree gradient — not by recolouring the button.
railSelectedState.why: TopbarPlus's default Selected state changes only IconSpot, leaving the plate colour, size and radius untouched. Recolouring the whole button is the obvious move and it breaks the rail's read as one family, which the Roblox UX guide names as the point of a consistent visual language.

touchButtonPlacement.rule: Custom touch action buttons are positioned RELATIVE to the live jump button, not by scale. Size them at 80% of the jump button's pixel size, AnchorPoint 1,1, offset to its LEFT (the docs' sample uses -20px; the community tutorial uses one button-width plus a tenth), parented to the jump button's own parent, after waiting on jumpButton.IsLoaded. Never place a button in the thumbstick zone.
touchButtonPlacement.why: The jump button moves: 'there's 2 presets of size and position for the controls. The preset changes when any of the screen dimensions reach over 500 pixels.' A scale position that lands beside it on a phone lands far from it on a tablet, and the docs give the ergonomics directly — 'a button placed 40% below the screen's top edge is reachable on a phone but almost unreachable on a tablet'. The thumbstick side is barred because the left thumb is committed to movement.

touchButtonLabelling.rule: A touch action button carries an icon, not a word. Reserve text for a caption on press or hover.
touchButtonLabelling.why: The community tutorial states the platform's own logic — 'The jump button doesn't say jump, it just has a self-explanatory up arrow' — and names text-labelled mobile buttons as the legacy pattern that 'contradicts the modern Roblox UI'. TopbarPlus reaches the same place from the other direction by defaulting every icon to label-less and growing the widget only when a label is explicitly set.

toasts.rule: Toasts are a stacked pile at one of six anchors, top-right by default: newest in front, older ones peeking behind, at most 5 per anchor, expanding to 3 on hover or tap. Default life 3000ms, timers PAUSE while the pile is hovered or tapped, every toast closable, important ones sticky. Motion is a slide from the nearest screen edge plus a fade, 0.25s per phase on Quint, with neighbours tweening to close the gap. Put them in their own ScreenGui at a DisplayOrder above the HUD.
toasts.why: All figures are the shipped defaults of the SimpleToasts library, and Roblox's own UI-pattern taxonomy puts quest progress, achievements and event notices in this bucket specifically because they 'display for a limited time, then disappear'. The pause-on-hover is the rule a generator omits and it is what makes a 3-second lifetime defensible: without it a 3-second toast is a test of reflexes.

toastSeverity.rule: Exactly five severities — success, info, warn, error, secondary — and each carries a colour PAIR plus an icon, never colour alone. The card is a very pale tint of the accent and the accent does the work: success #F0FDF4 card with #4ADE80 / #16A34A, warn #FFFBEB with #FBB024 / #D97706, error #FEF2F2 with #F87171 / #DC2626.
toastSeverity.why: The SimpleToasts theme table gives five and only five, each with colours, an icon and an optional sound. Roblox's accessibility guidance requires that nothing rely solely on colour to distinguish an outcome, which is exactly what the paired icon buys; and the pale-card/saturated-accent split is what keeps body text legible on a card that still reads as green or red at a glance.

minimap.rule: A minimap is a pre-rendered image tile grid panned under a mask, not a live ViewportFrame. Author the map bounds as two invisible anchored parts at opposite corners sharing a Y-only rotation, render at a declared pixels-per-stud so each tile is Grid x PPS, and expose exactly three runtime settings: grid, tile ids, zoom. Blips are coloured by team; a blip that leaves the view is PINNED to the border rather than deleted; place markers counter-rotate so the icon's bottom always faces the player.
minimap.why: Taken from a released open-source minimap renderer with a public showcase place. The pin-to-border rule is the one a generator would not invent and the one players feel: a teammate blip that vanishes at the edge tells you nothing, and a blip that sticks to the rim tells you which way to turn. NOT EVIDENCED by these sources: which screen corner a minimap belongs in — no source fetched stated it, so a generator should take the corner from the genre file or the request, not from this rule.

questTracker.rule: Split quests across two surfaces. Progress EVENTS are toasts ('objective complete', 'stage 2 of 4'), transient and timed. Current objective STATE is a persistent tracker that lives on a screen edge and is built from the counter and meter rules — a line of text plus a progress bar that fills, not a number alone.
questTracker.stateSurface: persistent edge panel with a fill bar
questTracker.why: Roblox's Engine UI designer lists 'quest progress messages' under alerts/toasts — the transient pattern — while the UX guide separately names 'a progress bar filling up as the player completes quest objectives' as required feedback. Those are two different elements and collapsing them into one is why trackers either nag or go unnoticed. NOT EVIDENCED: the tracker's exact edge, width or row height — no fetched source gave figures, and this rule deliberately stops short of inventing them.

contextualSlots.rule: Keep the number of visible HUD buttons fixed and change their CONTENTS with context, or collapse the secondary ones behind one button that fans open on press. Do not grow the rail to cover every case.
contextualSlots.why: Roblox documents both shapes with named shipped games: Super Striker League swaps the same two action slots between Sprint/Tackle and Deke/Pass depending on whether the player has the ball, and Spellbound RPG keeps a single circular Items button that reveals skills, equipment and deck only once pressed — which the doc attributes directly to small mobile screens getting 'overwhelmed with excessive buttons'.

scaleVersusOffset.rule: Position and size in Scale; bound the result in pixels with UISizeConstraint. Set UICorner radius in SCALE. Set UIStroke thickness in pixels, choosing a value that survives every screen, because stroke has no scale option. Add a text size constraint so HUD type cannot go illegible on a phone or absurd on a TV.
scaleVersusOffset.why: Roblox's Engine UI designer measured both: a UICorner at offset 20 'looks drastically different between devices' while the same corner at scale 0.2 'looks much more consistent', and 'UIStroke does not currently support scale, only offset'. This is the single most mechanical rule in the file and the one that silently ruins a HUD that looked right in the Studio viewport.

deviceBuckets.rule: Adapt to GuiService.ViewportDisplaySize, which has three values and only three — Small (phones, tablets, handhelds), Medium (laptops and monitors), Large (TVs and above). Do not branch on pixel width.
deviceBuckets.why: Roblox provides the categorisation precisely because 'attempting to predict screen size by pixels often leads to misinterpretation', and gives the failure case: a container at 75% width is right on a phone and enormous on a 4K TV. Designing mobile-first is the stated order — 'mobile devices have the least amount of screen space and you'll want to make sure all your UI fits there first'.

textLegibility.rule: Every HUD value drawn over the 3D world carries a dark outline, and sits on its own tinted plate rather than directly on the world. A coloured value (a bounty, a debuff, a warning) needs the outline more than a white one, not less.
textLegibility.why: The community's first two corrections on a posted HUD were exactly this — 'add a black outline around it' for the red bounty text, and round the bars to pills — and Roblox's own tutorials never place a HUD number on bare world: the score bar sits on black at transparency 0.6 and the meter on black at 0.75 with a stroke. A HUD value that is legible over grass and invisible over snow is the default outcome without both.

layering.rule: One ScreenGui per surface, layered by DisplayOrder: the HUD lowest, modals above it, toasts highest. Toggle a surface with ScreenGui.Enabled rather than hiding children. Set ResetOnSpawn false on the HUD and make it a DIRECT child of StarterGui.
layering.why: The docs state a disabled ScreenGui 'will not render, process user input, or update in response to changes', so a closed menu costs nothing, and that ResetOnSpawn only stays false for a DIRECT child of StarterGui — a HUD tucked inside a Folder silently rebuilds on every respawn, losing its animation state and any runtime wiring, which is a bug that only appears the first time the player dies.

hierarchyOfInformation.rule: Rank HUD elements before placing them: the single most decision-relevant number gets the top-centre slot and the largest size; resources the player spends get the top-right group; status the player reacts to gets a meter; everything else is a button, and anything contextual is a proximity prompt rather than a permanent button.
hierarchyOfInformation.why: Roblox's UX guide builds the whole chapter on the Hierarchy of Information and names the questions — what is the player doing, what is the most important thing to be aware of, how frequently will they make this choice. Its own tutorial follows it literally, sizing the score bar at a quarter of the screen 'to grab the player's attention', and it moves one-off actions off the HUD entirely because 'it doesn't make sense to constantly show an open button on the screen'.

consistencyContract.rule: Fix the per-stat associations once and hold them across every HUD element: a stat's colour is the same in its icon, its bar and its text; an unaffordable price renders red; grey means unusable; a lock overlay means not yet unlocked; close is an X at the top-right.
consistencyContract.why: Roblox lists these as the worked examples of UI consistency and of convention, drawn across Winds of Fortune, Dragon Adventures, BotClash Simulator, DOORS and Arcane Odyssey. They are cheap to honour and they are what lets a player read a HUD they have never seen; breaking one of them costs more than the whole visual style is worth.

screens.label: The INVENTORY screen — item grid, rarity treatment, equipped state, sort/filter row, stack counts, detail pane, delete/lock affordances
demonstrates: the inventory cell is a SQUARE of 60px with a 5px buffer between neighbours — a cell pitch of 65px — and that pitch is fixed in offset, not in scale

the grid's column count is not a constant: it is computed at layout time as the scrolling frame's width divided by the cell pitch, so the grid REFLOWS with the window instead of holding a fixed column count

the frame that width comes from is the hotbar, whose slot count is 10 on desktop, 3 on small screens under 1024px wide, and 6 in VR — so the inventory grid is as wide as the hotbar and inherits its density
the expanded inventory shows 4 rows on desktop, 2 on small screens and 3 in VR, i.e. the visible depth shrinks before the width does
a 40px header band is reserved above the grid for the title and the search field; the search field itself is 200px wide with a 5px margin
EQUIPPED is drawn as a highlight frame of four coloured EDGE borders around the slot, in a distinct blue, and it is added and removed on the equip state — the slot's own fill is not what changes
the small digit in a slot's top-left corner is the keyboard hotkey, shown for slots 1-9 plus 0 for the last one, and HIDDEN entirely when there is no keyboard — the digit is a keybind, never an index
hovering a hotbar slot raises a tooltip carrying the tool's name, 16px tall with a 6px buffer, and only when that name is non-empty

searching REFLOWS the grid: matching slots are re-parented into the grid with a new layout order and sorted by relevance while non-matches are hidden, so a filtered grid compacts rather than leaving holes
the inventory panel sits over the game at a backdrop fade of 0.50, and a slot that cannot be dragged is faded to 0.50 rather than being removed
the failure is specifically a Studio-versus-play divergence: the author reports a 'BIG difference' between the two, which means an inventory grid cannot be signed off in the editor
the diagnosis given and accepted: 'the different sizes are a mismatch between the desired frame size coming from the UIGridListLayout and the UIAspectRatioConstraint inside the frames themselves'
the accepted fix was to REMOVE the aspect-ratio constraint from the individual slot frames — 'That was my problem, the aspect ratio constraints were messing everything up, now it looks perfect'
the recommended construction is to put the aspect-ratio constraint on the PARENT frame and let 'the grid items themselves just be controlled by the UIGridLayout'
negative cell padding in the grid layout was separately called out as a defect: 'dont use a negative padding'

the stated visual recipe for the slot is three things together: 'rounded corners, a darker theme, an outline surrounding each element' — the outline is per-element, not one frame around the whole panel

slots scale DOWN near the screen edges and UP above 1080p, and the author names the default backpack's constant 60-pixel slot as the thing being corrected — a fixed-offset cell is a known defect at both ends of the resolution range
rarity is carried by a numeric attribute rendered as STARS on the tile, and the zero/absent case is a real state: the tile reverts to white with no stars rather than to a made-up bottom tier
stack quantity is written as 'xN' on the tile, and the author distinguishes that from the separate idea of counting duplicate slots
the sort control offers Name, Rarity and Quantity, with a search field beside it — three axes, not one

the search at the time required exact spelling and the author's own listed next fix was 'changing the search bar into an algorithm based one, so you don't have to write the names 100% accurately' — an exact-match filter is a shipped-and-regretted decision
number keys re-sort the inventory directly so items can be rearranged without dragging, i.e. the keyboard is a first-class reordering path, not an accelerator for the mouse path
the filter row is a HORIZONTALLY SCROLLING strip of categories along the top ('All Materials Weapons...'), not a vertical rail — the inventory screen spends its vertical space on the grid

the first and sharpest critique is that the selected filter is unreadable: 'I can not tell if this view is from which category' — an unmarked active filter is the single most reported failure on this screen

the second critique is the absence of stacking: 'if you have too much of one item it's going to be annoying scrolling through it all' — an unstacked grid is judged as a scrolling problem, not a data problem
the third is naming and separation: 'add better dividers and icons for each thing, make each item have a name', with the summary verdict 'it's really basic'
the author's slots are viewport frames parented under a scrolling frame — the tile renders the item in 3D rather than as a flat icon
the layout is three regions on one sheet: a character/equipment panel on the LEFT with its equipment slots drawn as white squares, the item grid beside it, and the bottom row acting as the hotbar

the accepted critique on destructive actions: 'Not a big fan of drop item having such a large, dedicated button, I'd move that to a drop-down, key binding or drag event' — a destructive action does not get prime real estate on this screen
rounded corners on the slots were requested and accepted as an omission the author had not considered — square-cornered slots read as unfinished even to their own author
typographic consistency was raised as a defect in its own right: the 'Inventory' title was in a different font from the rest and that was changed
the character panel was asked to be 'less transparent, and a bit brighter' — the equipped region must be more solid than the backdrop it sits on, not equally ghosted
stack counts are present as text per slot
the governing interaction, stated plainly: 'The inventory is based on a drag-and-drop system; when selecting a specific item, the slots it can be equipped to are marked with a white border'
so SELECTION is a two-sided state — it marks the source tile and simultaneously marks every legal destination; the screen teaches its own rules at the moment of pickup
the equipped-character view is rotatable by dragging left/right, i.e. the equipped region is interactive rather than a static portrait

the accepted critique was about the tile's immediate surround: 'make the black stuff right by the items a bit lighter and it'll look fine!' — the field behind an item icon must be lighter than the chrome, not the darkest thing on screen

the accepted answer is a dedicated region, not a floating tile: 'have a separated section for the equipped item (like the slot for the left hand item) as well as potentially the player's character with the equipped item in a viewport'
the reasoning is visual separation — the equipped set is a region of its own, adjacent to the grid and bounded, rather than a slot that happens to sit outside the grid
a character viewport showing the item IN CONTEXT is offered as the upgrade over a bare equipped slot

rules.note: Distilled from the references above. Units are Roblox UI units: px offset for cell geometry, unitless for ratios. Values marked 'published': true are constants Roblox or a named framework actually ships. Values marked 'derived': true are arithmetic on published constants and the arithmetic is stated. Everything else is a shape/hierarchy/state rule with no number attached, which is deliberate — the references support the shape strongly and the pixel far more weakly.

screenRegions.layout: one panel over a dimmed world, divided into a header band, a filter/sort row, the item grid, an equipped region and a detail region
screenRegions.why: TYPHOON's container pane appears only when the player is near or searching a container and the toolbar slides across to take the space back; its belt and holster slots appear only once filled. The regions of an inventory are allowed to come and go, and their neighbours must reflow rather than leave a hole.

backdrop.rule: the whole screen sits on a full-screen dimmed backdrop, not on an opaque page
backdrop.why: Roblox's own backpack uses a backdrop fade of exactly 0.50, and the 'Inventory design' author confirms the same treatment ('The background is already slightly transparent'). An opaque inventory reads as a scene change; a dimmed one reads as a pause.

gridCell.derivedNote: pitch = size + buffer = 65 is arithmetic on two published constants
gridCell.why: these are the shipped values of Roblox's default backpack. A square cell is the platform's own default and every reference that names a slot shape names a square.

gridColumns.rule: columns are COMPUTED, never authored: floor(availableWidth / cellPitch)
gridColumns.derivedNote: the column formula is published; the 10 and 3 follow because the grid inherits the hotbar frame's width and the hotbar ships 10 slots on desktop and 3 under 1024px wide
gridColumns.contrastWithShopGrid: a shop grid is 4 across because its tiles are products being compared; an inventory grid is roughly 10 across on desktop because its tiles are possessions being scanned. Reusing the shop's 4-across on an inventory is the loudest wrong answer available on this screen.
gridColumns.why: an inventory that holds its column count while the window changes will letterbox or clip; the platform's own inventory reflows.

gridRows.why: Roblox's own inventory drops from 4 visible rows to 2 on a small screen while the columns follow the hotbar. The grid gets shorter before it gets narrower.

gridSizingTrap.rule: put the UIAspectRatioConstraint on the grid's PARENT frame; never on the individual slot frames
gridSizingTrap.why: the one thread whose grid broke between Studio and play broke for exactly this reason — 'a mismatch between the desired frame size coming from the UIGridListLayout and the UIAspectRatioConstraint inside the frames themselves' — and removing the per-slot constraints fixed it outright. A generator that squares its cells with a per-cell aspect constraint ships a grid that is correct in the editor and wrong in play.

cellScaling.rule: the cell may not be a hard 60px offset at every resolution — it scales down near screen edges and up above 1080p
cellScaling.why: the author of the most complete custom backpack names the default's 'constant size of 60 pixels' as the specific thing being corrected. 60px is the right pitch RATIO to reproduce, not a literal size to freeze.

slotOutline.rule: one outline per element, applied to every tile, plus a rounded corner on the tile
slotOutline.why: the finished custom backpack's whole recipe is 'rounded corners, a darker theme, an outline surrounding each element'. Square-cornered slots were named as an omission by a reviewer and conceded by the author. Intersecting outlines were the FIRST defect a reviewer named on the TYPHOON inventory ('Belt, holster, and back borders are all intersecting'), so slot bounds must be laid out to touch or gap, never to overlap.

tileField.rule: the field directly behind an item icon is OPAQUE and lighter than the surrounding chrome
tileField.never: a visible pattern, a grid-of-squares texture, or a see-through field behind the icon
tileField.why: 'the small grid of squares behind is to distracting' was fixed by making the backgrounds more opaque, and 'make the black stuff right by the items a bit lighter' was the accepted note on another. The icon is the content; the field exists to hold it, not to decorate.

emptySlot.rule: empty slots render as the same outlined rounded square with the field and no content
emptySlot.why: the grid must read as a grid at zero items, and a hotbar with a declared Static mode keeps its empty slots visible on purpose. A grid that only exists where there are items is not a grid.

equippedState.rule: equipped is a highlight BORDER — four coloured edges drawn around the slot in a distinct hue — added and removed with the state
equippedState.never: recolouring the tile's fill, swapping the icon, or greying the tile
equippedState.hueRole: a single reserved accent used for nothing else on this screen
equippedState.why: Roblox's own backpack draws equipped as a four-edge highlight frame in one reserved blue and leaves the slot itself untouched. A fill change collides with rarity, which already owns the tile's field.

selectionMarksTargets.rule: selecting a tile marks it AND outlines every slot that item can legally be equipped into, in a second, neutral hue
selectionMarksTargets.why: stated exactly in the menu-and-inventory thread: 'when selecting a specific item, the slots it can be equipped to are marked with a white border'. The screen teaches its own rules at pickup instead of rejecting a bad drop afterwards.

equippedRegion.rule: a bounded, adjacent section of the panel — never a floating slot outside the grid
equippedRegion.solidity: more opaque than the backdrop, with outlines QUIETER than the grid's
equippedRegion.why: the accepted answer to 'where does the equipped slot go' was 'a separated section for the equipped item... as well as potentially the player's character with the equipped item in a viewport', against the author's floating slot. Separately the equipped panel was told to be 'less transparent, and a bit brighter' in one thread and to make its 'very white borders... more transparent' in another: the region must be more present than the backdrop and less insistent than the grid.

equippedCapacity.rule: when equipping is capped, the cap is shown as a used/max count near the equipped region
equippedCapacity.why: PS99's pet screen is built around it — 'if you have eight slots, you can select up to eight pets'. A cap the player cannot see becomes a rejected tap.

rarityTreatment.rule: rarity is carried by the TILE'S OWN FIELD — a subtle gradient or tint — optionally reinforced by a repeated glyph such as stars
rarityTreatment.never: a saturated badge that competes with the icon, and never the equipped hue
rarityTreatment.zeroState: an item with no rarity renders plain and un-starred rather than being forced into a bottom tier
rarityTreatment.why: the two references that describe a shipped treatment agree on restraint: TYPHOON puts a deliberately subtle gradient on the grid piece, and the finished custom backpack renders a numeric rarity as stars while reverting to plain white with no stars when the attribute is absent or zero. Nothing fetched supports a loud rarity frame, so nothing here specifies one.

rarityIsAlsoASortKey.rule: rarity must be selectable as a sort axis, not only drawn
rarityIsAlsoASortKey.why: both the custom backpack (Name / Rarity / Quantity) and the Stoway framework (None / Name / Rarity / ItemType) ship rarity as a first-class sort key. A rarity you can see but cannot order by is decoration.

stackCount.position: a corner of the tile, not its centre
stackCount.why: 'xN' is the format the finished custom backpack ships. The centre of the tile belongs to the item; the corners belong to the numbers about it.

stackingIsRequired.rule: duplicate items stack by default; an unstacked grid is a defect
stackingIsRequired.publishedNote: 5 is Stoway's published default maximum stack, offered as a starting point rather than a law
stackingIsRequired.why: the clearest complaint on the filter thread was 'if you have too much of one item it's going to be annoying scrolling through it all'. Stacking is judged as a layout obligation, not a data-model preference.

hotkeyDigit.rule: the small digit in a slot's corner is the KEYBOARD BIND, top-left, and is hidden entirely when there is no keyboard
hotkeyDigit.never: a slot index or a position number
hotkeyDigit.why: Roblox's own backpack shows it for 1-9 plus 0 on the last slot and removes it when keyboard input is unavailable. A digit that survives onto a touch screen is a promise the device cannot keep.

itemNaming.rule: every tile must be identifiable — EITHER a name on the tile OR a hover tooltip carrying it, chosen deliberately
itemNaming.why: one thread asked for permanent names ('I recommend adding the name of the item in the backpack') and the author chose hover-reveal instead because a label did not 'fit the UI theme'; another simply demanded 'make each item have a name'. Both sides were arguing against the same failure: an unnamed tile with no hover. Roblox's own tooltip ships at 16px tall with a 6px buffer and only appears when the name is non-empty.

headerBand.why: Roblox reserves a 40px header for the title and search. The one thread devoted entirely to title placement settled on the upper-left corner, which is weak evidence and is recorded as such.

filterAndSearchPair.rule: a category dropdown or pill row and a search field are a PAIR, anchored in the header, and they are per-tab
filterAndSearchPair.why: Blox Fruits ships exactly this: 'All tabs except Build have a dropdown menu and a search bar at the top of the interface (toward the top-right corner)'. The exception proves the rule — the equipped/Build tab has neither, because there is nothing there to filter.

filterRowOrientation.rule: categories run as a HORIZONTALLY scrolling strip along the top, not as a vertical rail
filterRowOrientation.why: the inventory screen spends its vertical budget on grid rows. Both fetched filter implementations are horizontal strips.

activeFilterMustBeUnmistakable.rule: the selected category is filled and the rest are outlined; the difference must survive a glance
activeFilterMustBeUnmistakable.why: 'I can not tell if this view is from which category' is the single most direct critique in the whole fetched set. An inventory whose active filter is ambiguous is showing the player a subset they cannot name.

filteringReflows.rule: filtering and searching COMPACT the grid — matches are re-ordered into the front of the layout and non-matches are removed from flow
filteringReflows.never: leaving holes where filtered-out tiles used to sit
filteringReflows.why: Roblox's own backpack re-parents matching slots with a new layout order and sorts them by relevance while hiding the rest. A grid with gaps after a search reads as a broken grid, not a filtered one.

searchMustBeForgiving.rule: match on substring and tolerate imperfect spelling; do not require an exact name
searchMustBeForgiving.why: the author of the most complete custom backpack shipped exact-match search and named replacing it as their own first fix: 'so you don't have to write the names 100% accurately'. This is a shipped-and-regretted decision, which is the most reliable kind of evidence in this file.

sortAxes.why: unanimous across the two references that ship a sort control at all.

detailPane.rule: a slot-driven region that fills in on selection and is EMPTY until something is selected
detailPane.position: beside or beneath the grid, and smaller than the grid
detailPane.why: the 'Item Information' panel in one thread fills in on selection; a centre-screen detail readout in another was told to move 'under the inventory and could be a lot smaller'. The detail region loses the argument for space to the grid every time it is raised.

primaryActionIsSingular.rule: one primary action button per selected item, at the bottom of the detail region
primaryActionIsSingular.why: Blox Fruits states that a stored fruit 'can no longer be dropped' — an item's legal actions differ item by item, so the action row is built from the selected item and not printed as a fixed footer.

destructiveActionIsDemoted.rule: delete/drop never gets a large dedicated button on the grid surface; it lives in a context menu, a keybind, or a drag gesture
destructiveActionIsDemoted.why: stated and accepted verbatim: 'Not a big fan of drop item having such a large, dedicated button, I'd move that to a drop-down, key binding or drag event'.

deleteConfirmation.rule: a destructive action is confirmed by DISTANCE, not merely by a second click
patterns: in-place: the button greys for ~1.5s, returns relabelled 'Confirm?', and deletes on the second press
modal: a separate confirm surface whose button sits somewhere else on the screen
undo: delete immediately and offer a restore for roughly 30 seconds
deleteConfirmation.why: the thread's own reasoning for the modal is spatial — 'the confirm button would be somewhere else on the screen' — and the strongest position stated is 'always add a revert system'. A second click in the same place is the weakest of the three.

lockAffordance.rule: a padlock toggle in the header icon cluster, and a locked tile is excluded from bulk delete, bulk sell and auto-equip
lockAffordance.why: PS99's pet inventory carries 'a padlock, a pet face, and four windows' as its three header icons, and the same thread that proposes 'a button that allows you to delete all selected items' is what makes the lock necessary. A bulk destructive action without a lock is an unguarded bulk destructive action.

headerIconCluster.rule: screen-level toggles — lock, layout/density, auto-equip mode — sit together as a small row of icon buttons in the header, unlabelled
headerIconCluster.why: PS99 groups exactly three of them; they are modes of the screen rather than actions on an item, which is why they sit in the header and not on a tile.

selectionMayBeModal.rule: when equipping is a multi-select with a cap, an explicit edit mode is legitimate — tiles become selectable only inside it
selectionMayBeModal.why: PS99 requires entering 'Edit Mode' before pets can be manually chosen, and the screen's default is automatic selection. A capped multi-select needs a state in which taps mean 'choose' rather than 'inspect'.

tabsCutByKind.rule: top-level tabs divide the inventory by ITEM KIND, with the equipped/loadout view as a peer tab that carries no search
tabsCutByKind.why: Blox Fruits ships Backpack / Treasure / Wardrobe / Stash / Build. Rarity is a sort axis and a tile treatment; it is not how the top level is cut.

buttonVersusLabel.rule: labels carry no border and no filled background; anything with a border and a fill must be pressable
buttonVersusLabel.why: 'Drawing a hard line between what's a button and what's a text label is one of the most important parts of UI design', written about an inventory whose title and Close button were styled identically. On a screen that is mostly bordered rectangles, this is the rule that keeps it readable.

perTileFeedbackIsMultiplied.rule: hover sound, hover scale and hover glow are applied at a fraction of the intensity used elsewhere, because they fire once per tile in a field of dozens
perTileFeedbackIsMultiplied.why: 'UI sounds are too loud, specially the hover sound. They can become annoying quickly, make them more subtle' — a note that only exists because this screen puts fifty hover targets under one cursor sweep.

tilePadding.rule: padding inside the tile and between tiles is generous enough that the grid does not read as cramped; the reference pitch gives a 5:60 gap-to-cell ratio at the platform default
tilePadding.why: 'maybe increase the padding. it's getting a little cramped in there' was the accepted note on one inventory, and the platform's own ratio is the only measured anchor available.

verifyInPlayNotInStudio.rule: an inventory grid is not signed off until it has been seen at play resolution
verifyInPlayNotInStudio.why: the one grid in the fetched set that broke, broke ONLY in play — 'a BIG difference' from Studio — and the cause was invisible in the editor. This screen has a known Studio-versus-play failure mode, so the profile records the check rather than the hope.

screens.label: The LEADERBOARD screen, across genres — in-world ranking boards, podium treatment for the top three, ranked rows, avatar thumbnails, scope/time-window switching, and the player's own standing
demonstrates: the scope switch is THREE views of ONE list, not three screens: 'Here, Friends, and Global are views of that same list'. Here = 'Session rankings for players in the current server', Friends = 'Persistent rankings among a player's friends who have played the experience', Global = 'Persistent rankings across players in the experience'. The platform's axis is WHO, not WHEN.

the two halves are fed by different machinery and therefore behave differently: 'Use leaderstats to populate Here. Use an ordered data store to populate Friends and Global.' A screen that switches between a live server list and a persisted global list is switching data sources, so the empty and loading states are not shared.

column order is an explicit, authored property with three mechanisms — insertion order, a child BoolValue named IsPrimary, or a child NumberValue named Priority where 'Higher priority values appear earlier in the leaderboard' and stats without one default to 0. 'IsPrimary takes precedence over any Priority values.' Column order is never incidental.
the stat's instance Name IS the column header: 'This is exactly how the stat will appear on the leaderboard.' There is no separate label field, so a header and its key cannot drift apart

a custom leaderboard has to actively evict the built-in one, and the documented way is a LocalScript calling StarterGui:SetCoreGuiEnabled(Enum.CoreGuiType.PlayerList, false) — the docs give this as the method 'To hide the leaderboard, such as on a menu screen or during a cutscene'

the persistent half is scoped hard: 'The initial beta supports one active persistent leaderboard per experience' and 'Only a registered, active leaderboard appears in the Friends and Global views' — so a multi-board design cannot be built on the platform surface and has to be built in-experience

one numeric score per player, keyed by user ID: 'Each player has one numeric score in that ordered data store' and 'Each key identifies one player by user ID'. Rank is derived, never stored, and ties are not addressed anywhere in the page
deactivating a board is a visibility change, not a deletion: 'Deactivating a leaderboard hides it from players but doesn't delete its ordered data store or scores'
the docs' own verification screenshot is captioned 'An in-experience persistent leaderboard showing player ranks, names, and scores' — rank, name, score is the platform's own three-field row

every avatar thumbnail the engine will hand you is SQUARE. The complete size list is 48x48, 60x60, 100x100, 150x150, 180x180, 352x352, 420x420 — seven values, all 1:1. A row's avatar slot that is not square is cropping or stretching somebody's face.

there are exactly three framings, and they are different pictures, not different crops: HeadShot is 'just the headshot (head and up)', AvatarBust is 'the bust (chest up)', AvatarThumbnail is 'the entire body of the user's avatar'

the full-body AvatarThumbnail is the only one that reads at podium scale; HeadShot is the only one that reads at row scale. Using one where the other belongs is the visible failure — a full body shrunk into a 40px row slot is a smudge, a headshot blown up onto a podium is a blurred crop

the enumerated sizes are the ONLY resolutions served, so a 40px row slot should request 48x48 and a 120px podium slot should request 150x150 — requesting an unlisted size is not an option the API offers

the ranked row is FOUR fields, and the wiki names them in order: 'Their avatar icon, username, level and total statistic are displayed next to their spot on the Leaderboard.' The rank number is the spot the other four sit next to — so the row is rank | avatar | name | secondary stat | primary value, and the secondary stat (level) is a real column, not decoration

the podium is a SEPARATE ASSEMBLY BESIDE THE LIST, not the first three rows of it: 'Top three players are displayed on podiums next to the Leaderboards.' The board still lists ranks 1 through 50, so the podium duplicates the top three rather than removing them
list depth is 50: 'These display the current month's total statistics for up to 50 players'
the time window is baked into the board and stated as part of what it is — 'the current month's total statistics' — rather than chosen by the player from a control

boards ship in PAIRS flanking a landmark: 'two boards can be found on the sides of the Elevators', one for total triumphs and one for total EXP. One board carries one stat; a second stat gets a second board

a different lobby gets a different pair with a different window: the Survival and Hardcore Intermission Lobbies each carry 'two large signs' showing 'the top triumphs for the current month and day' — month and day are two boards side by side, not two tabs on one board

the top three is a REWARD BRACKET with a persistent trophy, and the wiki treats that as the point of the podium: 'Any players in the top three of either two Leaderboards obtain the Champion Nametag through their Gift Box, which they will get to keep even after the month ends'

the same podium treatment is explicitly NOT given a reward on the intermission boards — 'no additional rewards are granted for placing in the top three' — so podium presentation and reward bracket are separable

the time window is signalled by the BOARD'S FRAME COLOUR, not by a tab: the 'Daily Leaderboard, which is indicated by the yellow-colored frame' sits beside the 'Global Leaderboard, which is indicated by the gray-colored frame'. Two physical boards, two frame colours, no switch
depth is ten: 'scoreboards that display 10 top players with their respective scores/wins'

one board cycles categories on its own instead of offering a category control — the Global board 'is an all-time leaderboard that cycles through multiple categories' covering Top 10 Wins, Top 10 High Scores, Top 10 Hardcore Wins and Most 5.0 Intensity Wins

rank is carried OUT of the board and onto the player: 'A ranked player will have special icons with a number corresponding to their ranking position above them.' The badge carries the NUMBER, so it is not a generic medal
the badge identifies WHICH board you ranked on, by icon: the daily board's ranks get a crown icon, the Top 10 Wins board's ranks get a star icon, and 'Other categories do not have special icons'

the reward bracket extends far past what the board renders: after v3.30.4, 'players within the top 100 will also have special icons above them. Though, they are still not listed on the boards' — rank standing and rank listing are two different depths
the daily board's reset is a stated wall-clock time, not a rolling window: scores 'reset back to 0 points at 4:00 AM (UTC +0) everyday'
the boards have a fixed home relative to a landmark: 'They can be found to the right of the area where players are normally teleported to the lobby'
the window/page relationship, stated exactly: 'Each leaderboard displays the ranks of the top 100 players, showing ten ranks at a time.' Ten rows are rendered; the depth behind them is 100
time windows are SEPARATE BOARDS with the window in the title — 'All-Time Top Honeymakers', 'Monthly Top Honeymakers', 'Daily Top Honeymakers' are three distinct boards, not three states of one

the boards are in the world first and in a menu second: 'Out of the 64 total leaderboards, 18 are able to be viewed at various locations around the map, and the rest are available to view in the System Page.' The world board is the primary surface; the menu is the overflow

the own-score affordance is a PROXIMITY READOUT standing outside the list, not a pinned row inside it: 'Upon standing on the white pad in front of a leaderboard, it will show a message stating the player's score for the corresponding leaderboard'
freshness is honest rather than live: 'Leaderboards are usually not in real-time but update very often'

abbreviation is a change that gets made under pressure, not a style choice: on 2022-03-17 'Onett abbreviated the amount of honey for the Daily Top Honeymakers and the All-Time Top Honeymakers leaderboard due to players having massive amounts of honey'

a board is allowed to omit the value column: 'The Top Brown Bear Helpers leaderboard is the only leaderboard that does not show the player's current amount of the stated objective' — and the wiki notes the score is then reachable only from the menu or an NPC, which is recorded as an oddity
daily boards reset on one stated clock — 'All leaderboards that reset on a daily basis reset at 12:00am GMT-5' — and boards can skip a scheduled reset during events
reward tiers are attached to the window: 'On daily and monthly leaderboards, players are able to gain rewards by placing high enough in one', while all-time boards carry none

the ten-visible / hundred-deep rule restated for one board: 'It shows 10 leaderboard positions at one time. The player can scroll down the leaderboard to see more players, all the way to the 100th place' — the list scrolls, it does not paginate with arrows

the proximity readout has a literal sentence form — the pad prints "You've made [x] Honey" — a full sentence naming the stat, not a bare number, because outside the board there is no column header to read it against
