rules.note: Distilled from the references above. This is a SCREEN, not a genre: stroke weight, corner radius, bevel and text stroke come from the genre file the leaderboard is being built in (simulator.json for a cartoony game). What is here is the leaderboard's own construction — which surface it lives on, what a row is made of, how the top three differ, how scope and time window are expressed, and what the states are. Numbers are quoted from the sources named in each rule's `why`, not sampled from pixels.

surface.primary: a board standing in the world, on a SurfaceGui attached to a part, placed at or beside the spawn/lobby landmark
surface.secondary: a screen list, which is the SERVER list and a different thing from the global board
surface.never: a centred modal over the game — no fetched source puts a global leaderboard in one
surface.why: TDS flanks the elevators, Super Bomb Survival sits right of the teleport area, CONTROL sits 'directly in front of the spawning point', Infinite Tower Tycoon puts four on the centre spawn pad, Bee Swarm has 18 around the map, and the GLeaderboard module's constructor takes a Part. Five independent games and a published module agree, so the world board is the convention and the modal is the invention.

boardSet.rule: one board renders ONE stat over ONE window; more stats and more windows mean more boards, placed as a set
boardSet.arrangement: symmetrical — a flanking pair around a landmark, or a ring on the spawn pad
boardSet.overflow: past roughly four boards, the remainder move into a menu page and only the headline boards stay in the world
boardSet.why: TDS 'two boards ... on the sides of the Elevators', Super Bomb Survival's daily+global pair, CONTROL's two, Infinite Tower Tycoon's four on the pad, and Bee Swarm's split — '18 are able to be viewed at various locations around the map, and the rest are available to view in the System Page'

timeWindow.rule: the time window (daily / monthly / all-time) belongs in the board's TITLE and is fixed for that board — it is not a tab
timeWindow.signal: give the paired boards different frame colours so the window is readable before the title is
timeWindow.pairing: the same stat over two windows ships as two boards facing or flanking each other
timeWindow.resetDisclosure: a resetting board states its reset as a wall-clock time with a zone
timeWindow.why: Super Bomb Survival's 'Daily Leaderboard, which is indicated by the yellow-colored frame' beside the grey-framed Global one; Bee Swarm ships Daily / Monthly / All-Time Top Honeymakers as three separate boards and the all-time one sits 'on the opposite side of the path ... from the Daily Top Honeymakers leaderboard'; resets stated as '4:00 AM (UTC +0)' and '12:00am GMT-5'. A daily/all-time TAB was searched for and not found in any shipped game read here.

scopeSwitch.rule: the axis that IS switched in place is WHO, not WHEN: server / friends / global, as three views of one list
scopeSwitch.perViewLoading: each view is a separate fetch and needs its own loading and empty state
scopeSwitch.reserveGeometry: the switch's geometry is fixed by the control, never derived from its contents
scopeSwitch.why: the platform's own leaderboard is exactly this — 'Here, Friends, and Global are views of that same list' — and the beta thread reports 'a lag spike when swapping between here/friends/global' plus tabs that go 'squished when no score is configured'. A game that wants both axes should switch scope in the UI and split the window across boards.

row.order: left to right, exactly that order
row.minimumViable: rank, name, value — three text fields
row.aspect: ≈11.8 : 1 (width : height); about 16 rows to a full-height list
row.columnSplit: name ≈67% of the row, each numeric stat ≈17%
row.leftInset: ≈4% of row width, as proportional padding, not a pixel offset
row.cornerRadius: 2px — a row is a strip in a stack and does NOT take the card radius the rest of the game uses
row.pressable: a row is a control: it opens the person, and it must release camera input when it does
row.why: TDS names the fields in order — 'avatar icon, username, level and total statistic ... next to their spot'; the Roact rebuild gives the numbers — PlayerChip at UDim2.fromScale(0.99, 0.061) with aspect 11.76, name 67%, two stats at 17.1% each, 4% left padding, UDim.new(0, 2) radius; the tutorial's template has exactly Rank/Name/Value; and the new-leaderboard thread reports 'you cannot move your camera after pressing on someones name'

sectionHeaderRow.rule: a grouping row (team, bracket, section) is THINNER than a player row, not thicker
sectionHeaderRow.why: TeamChip is UDim2.fromScale(0.99, 0.046) at aspect 15.474 against the player row's 11.76 — the group bar reads as a divider, and a generator's instinct to make headers bigger inverts the hierarchy

avatar.shape: square, always — every thumbnail the engine serves is 1:1
avatar.rowFraming: HeadShot, requested one step above the slot's rendered size (48x48 for a ~40px slot)
avatar.podiumFraming: AvatarThumbnail (full body) for a podium figure, or a live posed character; never a HeadShot blown up
avatar.fetch: client-side, per row, and the row must render with a placeholder before it arrives
avatar.why: Enum.ThumbnailSize has exactly seven square values and ThumbnailType has exactly three framings — HeadShot 'head and up', AvatarBust 'chest up', AvatarThumbnail 'the entire body'. The published system renders the top three as full characters: 'The first three stand on the podium wearing their real Roblox avatar, playing a looping emote.'

podium.rule: the top three are a SEPARATE ASSEMBLY BESIDE OR ABOVE THE LIST, and they are ALSO still rows 1-3 in the list — the podium duplicates them, it does not remove them
podium.figure: a full-body avatar (or a live posed character), not the row's headshot
podium.why: TDS: 'Top three players are displayed on podiums next to the Leaderboards', while the same boards still list up to 50 players; the published system's headline is 'Top-3 Avatars' as a feature distinct from the board's rows
podium.notObserved: no fetched source states the left-to-right order or the relative heights of 1st/2nd/3rd. The familiar centre-highest arrangement was NOT confirmed in any source read here, so a generator should treat the ordering as a choice it is making, not a convention it is following. Searched: TDS wiki, the Leaderboard+Podium open-source thread (no layout stated), the Improving Podium System feedback thread (the only critique in it is about sound volume).

topThreeMarking.element: the ROW BACKGROUND colour, decided at row-clone time inside the loop where the rank is in scope
topThreeMarking.bands: exactly four — gold #1, silver #2, bronze #3, one neutral for every other rank
topThreeMarking.never: a gradient fading down the list, and never a colour on the rank glyph alone
topThreeMarking.why: the accepted answer in the rank-colour thread is 'when you clone the frame, check if the player's rank is for example 1 and if yes, change the BackgroundColor'; no shared RGBs exist in any source, so what is conventional is the element and the band count, not the hues

rankBadgeOutsideTheBoard.rule: a ranked player carries their standing out of the board and onto their character, and the badge carries the NUMBER
rankBadgeOutsideTheBoard.iconIdentifiesBoard: a different icon per board (crown for the daily board, star for the wins board), and boards without a reward tier get no icon
rankBadgeOutsideTheBoard.standingDepth: the badge can be granted far deeper than the board renders
rankBadgeOutsideTheBoard.why: Super Bomb Survival: 'A ranked player will have special icons with a number corresponding to their ranking position above them', crown for the daily top 10 and star for Top 10 Wins, and after v3.30.4 'players within the top 100 will also have special icons above them. Though, they are still not listed on the boards.' TDS grants the top three a Champion Nametag they keep after the month ends.

depth.paging: vertical scroll inside the board, not arrow pagination
depth.why: Bee Swarm states it exactly — 'displays the ranks of the top 100 players, showing ten ranks at a time' and 'The player can scroll down the leaderboard to see more players, all the way to the 100th place'; Super Bomb Survival shows 10; GLeaderboard's example passes 10; TDS goes to 50; the tutorial fetches TotalEntires = 50 in pages of 5. Ten visible is unanimous across four independent sources.

listContainer.rule: a ScrollingFrame with AutomaticCanvasSize = Y and a UIListLayout; CanvasSize authored at zero
listContainer.rowPlacement: LayoutOrder = rank; never compute a Position per row
listContainer.rowLifecycle: rows are cloned from one template, keyed by rank, and DIFFED on refresh — a rank whose occupant has not changed is left untouched
listContainer.why: the tutorial: 'new.LayoutOrder = Rank', 'AutomaticCanvasSize is set to Y', CanvasSize {0,0},{0,0}; the published system: 'A rank whose player has not changed is left alone, so only a real change costs a lookup'. A hardcoded CanvasSize is the standard defect this avoids, and diffing is what makes a rank change the one place an animation belongs.

valueColumn.alignment: right, in a FIXED width reserved before any data arrives
valueColumn.widthSource: size it from the widest value the board can hold, never from the first row
valueColumn.format: one of three, chosen per board: raw, comma-separated, or abbreviated to ≤4 significant digits plus a magnitude suffix
valueColumn.abbreviateWhen: the board's values can exceed roughly six digits
valueColumn.truncation: never — a clipped number shows its least significant digits, which is worse than showing nothing
valueColumn.why: the published system offers exactly 52500 / 52,500 / 52.5K per board; Bee Swarm's Onett 'abbreviated the amount of honey ... due to players having massive amounts of honey' and its top ten reads 1.6219 Qn down to 1.0002 Qn — near-identical widths and only 1.6x between first and tenth, so the column must not be sized from the leader; CONTROL's board carries 10,137,426 at full length; and the beta thread reports a value column 'showing the tail end of the number'

nameColumn.rule: the name is the ONLY flexible column — rank, avatar and value are fixed, and the name absorbs the remainder
nameColumn.truncation: truncate at the END with an ellipsis; never let the start be clipped
nameColumn.nameKind: display name, with username as an explicit authored toggle
nameColumn.composite: if the game prefixes a rank title, the name cell is a two-part composite and needs more room than a username
nameColumn.why: Bee Swarm's real top ten runs from 'ruiream' to 'roblox_user_494351377' in one column; the beta thread reports 'names are being cropped out'; the platform list sorts and shows 'Display Names'; CONTROL renders 'Commissioner X aestheticminerald' — title then name, inline

badgeSlot.rule: reserve a slot between the avatar and the name for role/entitlement icons — developer, admin, premium, gamepass holder
badgeSlot.why: the platform player list has carried this slot through every redesign, its contents replaced each time (Builders Club hard hats, then Premium, then the game-owner ribbon 'a white hammer with a coding symbol (<>)', the administrator tilted-O, the Video Stars shooting star), and the Leaderboard+ plugin exposes it as an authorable feature: 'custom symbols for admins, premium users, and gamepass holders'

sorting.rule: descending on the FIRST column; the first column IS the sort key, so column order must be authored explicitly
sorting.mechanism: IsPrimary (a child BoolValue) beats Priority (a child NumberValue, higher first, default 0), which beats insertion order
sorting.fallback: with no leaderboard at all, the server list sorts alphabetically by display name
sorting.why: the Roblox Wiki states the platform rule outright — sorted 'from the highest value of the leaderboard's first column to the lowest value of the same column' — and the docs give the three ordering mechanisms with 'IsPrimary takes precedence over any Priority values'

ownStanding.observedForm: a SEPARATE readout outside the ranked list — a proximity message at the board, or a value shown in a menu — written as a full sentence naming the stat, because outside the list there is no column header to read the number against
ownStanding.notObserved: a pinned own-rank row inside or beneath the list was searched for and NOT found in any source read here. Searched: the platform leaderboards doc, the persistent-leaderboards beta thread and its replies, four shipped-game wikis (Bee Swarm, Super Bomb Survival, TDS, Infinite Tower Tycoon), the global-leaderboard tutorial, GLeaderboard, Leaderboard+, and two DevForum feedback threads. A generator may still build one, but it should know it is inventing, not citing.
ownStanding.why: Bee Swarm: 'Upon standing on the white pad in front of a leaderboard, it will show a message stating the player's score for the corresponding leaderboard', and the Top Brown Bear Helpers board — the one that shows no value column — pushes the player's own score into the menu or an NPC instead

refresh.disclose: show the board's staleness — a next-refresh countdown, or a stated note that updates lag
refresh.why: the tutorial's 'RefreshTime = 15 -- In Seconds'; GLeaderboard's example UPDATE_TIME of 60; the published system 'refresh on an interval you set' with next-refresh timing displayed; Bee Swarm 'usually not in real-time but update very often'; Infinite Tower Tycoon prints 'Note: There is a delay between updates' on the board

screenListPlacement.rule: if a leaderboard is drawn on screen, either disable the platform one or stay out of the top-right corner
screenListPlacement.sizeToOccupancy: the screen list's height is computed from the number of players present, not fixed
screenListPlacement.why: the docs give SetCoreGuiEnabled as the documented way to hide it; developers complained the platform list 'was covering my game UI', 'covers f3x uis', obscures 'the networkping from performance stats', and is 'wasting my screen space ... even tho im the only person in the server' with the request to shrink it when alone. The same critique was made of a custom board — 'when there's one player in a team, it's as big as if there were more players'.

serverListVsGlobalBoard.rule: they are different objects with different contents, and players name them differently
serverListVsGlobalBoard.serverList: text-only rows, no avatars, sorted by the first stat, rebuilt as players join and leave
serverListVsGlobalBoard.globalBoard: avatars, podium, rank badges, persisted, refreshed on an interval
serverListVsGlobalBoard.why: the Infinite Tower Tycoon wiki opens by disambiguating them — 'Not too be confused with the UI Leaderboard on the top right corner of the screen'; the Leaderboard+ in-screen plugin offers no thumbnails at all while every in-world global board carries them

states.loading: render the row skeleton with the rank numbers already in place — ranks are known before names are
states.empty: the columns keep their widths; an unconfigured or empty board must not collapse its tab row or its value column
states.playerLeaves: a server-list row keyed to a player is DESTROYED on PlayerRemoving
states.removedEntry: a moderated-out entry disappears and the ranks below close up — there is no struck-through or flagged state
states.why: the beta thread's 'squished when no score is configured'; Leaderboard+'s public defect 'whenever a player leaves the leaderboard stays on'; Bee Swarm's 'Only legitimate players appear on the leaderboards for lengths of time (exploiters will be removed)'

rewardBrackets.rule: if a board pays out, the payout is banded by rank and the bands are far deeper than the ten rows on screen
rewardBrackets.why: TDS grants the top three of either board a Champion Nametag; Super Bomb Survival grants icons to the top 100 who are 'still not listed on the boards'; Pet Simulator 99's Time Trials leaderboards pay out in exactly those brackets. The bands are attested in the DATA; none of the fetched sources describes how (or whether) a bracket threshold is drawn on the board itself, so this rule tells a generator the bands exist and does NOT tell it they are rendered as separators.

categoryControl.rule: when one board must cover several related stats, the category control sits at the TOP of the board as arrows and the rows scroll vertically beneath it — or the board rotates categories on its own with no control at all
categoryControl.why: Infinite Tower Tycoon's Board 2 'is scrollable using the arrows on top' across Kills/Crates/Keys/Codes; Super Bomb Survival's global board 'cycles through multiple categories' unattended. Two shipped answers, neither of which is a tab row.

themePerBoard.rule: boards in the same game are allowed to look different from each other; the row template is shared, the chrome is not
themePerBoard.why: the published system states it as a selling point — 'A cash board and a wins board can look nothing alike' — and ships three board templates each with its own podium styling; GLeaderboard exposes exactly TopBar, TopLine, Title, TitleStroke and ScrollBar as the restyleable parts, all chrome

screens.label: The LOBBY, MATCHMAKING and PARTY surfaces — queue objects and queue menus, party rosters and invites, ready gates and countdowns, rank bands and eligibility gates, private servers, and the teleport that ends the screen
demonstrates: THE QUEUE OBJECT CARRIES A FULL CARD, NOT A LABEL. Each elevator displays the map it leads to, the map name, THE MAP'S CREATOR, and the difficulty. Crediting the map author on the matchmaking surface is a decision — the creator's name is the one field on that card that has nothing to do with deciding whether to get in.

ONE COMPONENT IS BOTH THE EMPTY STATE AND THE PROGRESS. A progress bar sits at the bottom of the card and first reads 'Waiting for Players...'; it CHANGES INTO A TIMER once players have entered. The empty state is not a separate panel that gets swapped out — it is the same bar saying it has nothing to count yet.
The current number of players in the elevator is shown at the RIGHT END of that progress bar, so occupancy and time-remaining are one reading rather than two widgets.

A SECOND STATE READOUT EXISTS BESIDE THE CARD: 'On all elevators, it shows a floating label that indicates player size, which would display the timer after the server size had been set.' The source states that the label is on the elevator and says nothing about where — not above it, not how far it reads — so only its existence and its two states are recorded. Before v1.89.0 the floating label 'would only exist on Challenge Trials elevators', so it went from one elevator type to all of them: the card alone was not enough.

THE FIRST PLAYER IN CONFIGURES THE QUEUE. On entering, the elevator asks the player who entered what party size it should be for; after that choice the timer starts. On Story Mode elevators the same rule picks the MISSION — the first player to enter chooses it, and everyone who joins afterwards is taken to that mission.

Once configured, a box appears inside displaying 'nearly identical information to the map icon of the elevator' — the person standing inside is shown the same card the people outside are reading, deliberately duplicated rather than assumed.
CAPACITY IS PER MODE AND THE WAIT IS NOT: Survival elevators hold 4, Hardcore 3, Voidcore 3, Story 4, and ALL FOUR wait up to 20 seconds. The clock is a constant; the capacity is the variable.

QUEUES ARE DUPLICATED RATHER THAN SHARED. There are TWO Survival elevators for each available Survival difficulty — twelve in the Main Lobby — so arriving at a full one is not the same as being blocked.

PROGRESSION IS GATED AT THE OBJECT, NOT ON A BUTTON. There is exactly one Voidcore elevator, sited between the two Hardcore ones, and it 'can only be entered by players who have beaten Hardcore'. The lock is on entry, so an ineligible player never fills a slot they cannot use.
Hardcore elevators show a map that CHANGES EVERY MINUTE — a rotating offer on a queue object, which means the card a player is reading has a shelf life.

TEAM CHOICE WAS ONCE EXPRESSED AS WHICH OBJECT YOU STOOD IN: the removed Versus elevators were TWO SEPARATE elevators, one per team, four players each for eight per map. When Versus moved to the matchmaking menu, teams became randomly assigned instead — the physical form was the only thing that had let players pick a side.

A PAID VOTE WEIGHT SHIPPED IN A SHARED LOBBY VOTE. On the original Survival elevators the difficulty was decided by player vote, and a player holding the VIP gamepass 'would be able to place two votes on the difficulty'. This is the file's clearest case of monetisation reaching inside a group decision surface.

There is an explicit control for LEAVING the queue: the button that exits the elevator shipped before BETA v1.7 with the placeholder text 'leave elevator lol', which is how the wiki records that the button exists at all.

TWO ENTRY POINTS INTO ONE SYSTEM: the main method is a 'Play' button in the MIDDLE of the screen, and the secondary method is statues placed in the lobby, used only for limited-time events. The physical object and the centre-screen button are alternatives to each other, not different queues.

THE CURRENT FLOW IS MODE THEN PLAYER COUNT, WITH THE PAGE'S OWN HEDGE KEPT: 'in most cases a screen with multiple options will appear', and 'After getting through the mode selection, you will be asked to select a player count'. It is not the only flow the same page documents — for events up to the Ducky Revenge Event 'the old Matchmaking menu is used instead, where a small pop-up window will appear with multiple difficulty options if they exist before choosing the player count', which is three steps. An earlier draft called the flow EXACTLY two steps and said nothing else is asked; the page supports neither word.
The mode step has FIVE sections — Survival, Story, PVP, Arcade, Sandbox — and Survival itself contains eight modes. Sections group modes by what kind of session they are, not by difficulty.

THE SIZE STEP'S OPTIONS ARE CONSTRAINED BY THE MODE CHOSEN IN THE STEP BEFORE. Hardcore and Voidcore cap at trios because quads is unavailable there; PVP REPLACES the solo/duo/trio/quad vocabulary entirely with 1v1 and 2v2. The same slot in the same flow renders a different vocabulary depending on the previous answer.

AN ICON SHIPPED LYING ABOUT ITS COUNT: Sandbox and the Halloween 2025 live events add five-player 'squads' and six-player 'mega' options, and 'in both cases, the same icon for quads is used'. Two options that mean five and six are drawn with the icon for four.

A DOUBLE GATE ON ONE OPTION: the five- and six-player Sandbox options are locked unless the player BOTH owns the Sandbox Plus+ gamepass AND is in a party with other players. Purchase alone does not unlock it.

THE SEARCH STEP IS SKIPPED WHEN IT HAS NOTHING TO DO: 'If playing in solos or if the Party size is the same as selected player count, a match will be created instantly.' A queue screen that always appears would be showing a search that is not happening.

MATCHING WIDENS ON PURPOSE AND THE WIKI SAYS SO: pairing starts on similar Level (or ELO in ranked PVP) 'however, the system will not try to find players of similar Level forever. After a certain point, it will accept players of lower Level and higher Level, creating large gaps'. The quality of a match degrades with waiting, by design.

AGE GROUP IS A MATCHMAKING CONSTRAINT FOR A COMMUNICATION REASON: similar age groups are considered 'to ensure that all players in the match are able to see each other's messages'. Who can be matched is decided partly by who will be able to read each other's chat.

The match-found readout is a ROSTER WITH STATS, not a list of names: 'every single player's loadout, level, triumph count and loss count will be displayed, alongside their username and avatar'. (Recorded with its ambiguity: this sentence sits inside the article's Sandbox bullet but is phrased generally, and the article's own gallery carries a separate 'Match found' caption.)

A MODE CAN BE REACHABLE FROM A DIFFERENT SCREEN ENTIRELY: Challenge Maps have no option in the matchmaking menu and can only be accessed through the Quests menu. The mode picker is not the complete list of modes.

THE PRIMITIVE VERSION IS RECORDED AS WELL: Legacy Event Matchmaking 'had no actual options for the player' — match size was always the maximum and the game filled the remaining slots with strangers. Choice of size was added later, which dates it as a feature rather than a given.

An abandoned design is described in full: the Matchmaking Elevator, tested publicly and never shipped, moved the player out of the lobby into an elevator where 'player avatars would start appearing inside' as they were found. Representing the search as bodies arriving in a room was built, tested, and dropped in favour of a menu.

THE EMPTY STATE OF A PARTY SCREEN IS A BROWSER OF OTHER PEOPLE'S PARTIES. A player opening the menu while not in a party is shown 'a list of public Parties and a button which allows them to create a Party'. The screen does not open on an empty roster with a create button alone.

PARTY SIZE BLOCKS THE MATCH RATHER THAN RESIZING IT. Up to six people can be in a party, 'though if the Party player count is higher than the selected squad size in Matchmaking, the game will not allow the player to start a match'. The game refuses; it does not silently raise the squad size or split the party.

THE ROSTER AND THE INVITE LIST SIT TOGETHER, AND THE PAGE CONTRADICTS ITSELF ABOUT HOW: 'Once in a party, there are two screens. The first is Party member list, showing every member of it, including their username, level and profile icon. On the right, there is a list of users to invite.' Two screens and 'on the right' cannot both be literal, and the word 'left' appears nowhere on the page. Recorded as the page has it: the member row carries username, level and profile icon, the invite list is placed 'on the right', and no further layout is attested.

THE INVITE LIST IS TWO GROUPS THAT SHOW DIFFERENT FIELDS, AND THAT IS THE ARGUABLE DECISION. Friends come first and their level is NOT displayed — 'only information about them is them being online'. Players in the server are the second group and their level IS displayed. A friend is someone you invite because they are a friend; a stranger in your lobby is someone you invite after checking their level.

THE PRIVACY DEFAULT WAS FLIPPED TOWARD CLOSED: 'Party Lock is a setting which makes the Party be invite only. It is enabled by default, but it used to be disabled.' A shipped game changed its party from open-by-default to invite-only-by-default.
A SECOND DEFAULT POINTS THE SAME WAY: 'Members Can Invite' is DISABLED by default, so only the leader can invite until the leader says otherwise.

PARTY SETTINGS INCLUDE A LEVEL BAND WITH NO CEILING: Maximum Level defaults to 1,000 and Minimum Level to 0, and both are stated to have 'no limit to what it can be set to'. The host filters who may join by progression, before matchmaking ever does.

THE SETTINGS ARE STATED AS THE LEADER'S, WITHOUT AN EXCLUSION: 'There are a few settings for Parties which can be changed by the Party leader.' The page attributes the change to the leader and never says a member cannot make it; the word ONLY was an earlier draft's, and the settings pane being a leader-only surface is not attested here.

AN UNACCEPTED INVITE BECOMES A QUEUE, NOT A LOST POPUP: 'If invited in the lobby and the invite is not accepted instantly, the invite will be included in the invites section of the Party menu', where it can be accepted or denied later.

THE INVITE'S FORM DEPENDS ON WHERE THE INVITEE IS: in the same lobby it is an in-screen invite; elsewhere it is a Roblox notification 'either in-game or in their Roblox notifications, giving them an option to dismiss the invite or to join the lobby' — the far-away version's affirmative action is joining a LOBBY, not joining a party.

INVITE COPY IS A SET RATHER THAN ONE STRING, FOR TWO OF THE THREE INVITE SURFACES: 'Invites during a match or on the Roblox sites can have the text:' introduces seven variants, each naming the friend and the game ('[Friend name] is gathering a squad in Tower Defense Simulator!'). The page does not say the seven are randomised, does not say how one is chosen, and does not extend them to the in-lobby invite — which its own gallery lists as a third, separate case.

THE CREATE CONTROL IS ANCHORED TO THE HOTBAR, NOT TO A MENU BAR: players 'select the "Create Party" button above their hotbar', and this can only be done in the Lobby. The party entry point sits in the gameplay HUD's own furniture.
A PARTY IS SIXTEEN PEOPLE HERE — against Tower Defense Simulator's six — so the roster component cannot assume it fits on screen without scrolling.

THE MENU IS THREE THINGS AT ONCE: the party's current players, a list of all the players in that server, and A SEARCH BAR to search through them. Sixteen slots and a whole server's population is the size at which browsing stops working and search becomes a component.

THE WEAKEST ROW IN THIS FILE and marked as such: the original post is a video, which was NOT watched, so everything below is read from the replies of people who did watch it rather than from the artefact.

0.rule: When the game already has a lobby, make the queue a PLACE and give that place a card: destination, name, author, difficulty.
0.why: Tower Defense Simulator's elevators display the map, its name, its CREATOR and its difficulty; RIVALS' duel pads and BedWars' NPCs do the same job with no dialog at all. Roblox's own docs name Touched and ProximityPrompt.Triggered as the way to start a teleport, so the pad is the documented pattern rather than a substitute for a missing menu.

1.rule: Let the progress bar BE the empty state — one component that says 'Waiting for Players...' and turns into a timer.
1.why: That is exactly what a Tower Defense Simulator elevator does, with the occupancy count parked at the bar's right end. A separate empty panel that gets swapped for a separate timer is two components that must agree; this is one that cannot disagree with itself.

2.rule: Start the countdown on the first player, not on the queue being full, and give the last few seconds their own state.
2.why: DOORS begins a 5–30 second count when a minimum of ONE player enters, so a solo player is never held for a group that may not come. A lobby-queue showcase's reviewers named the change at five seconds as the moment that lands, and DOORS' sound set carries a separate 'Major Timer Tick' for the same reason.

3.rule: Let the first player in configure the queue, and show everyone else what was chosen.
3.why: Tower Defense Simulator asks the first entrant for the party size, and on Story elevators the first entrant picks the mission for everyone who follows. The choice is then echoed on a floating label on the elevator and in a box that appears once a player is inside, so nobody joins a queue whose terms they cannot read.

4.rule: Duplicate queue objects per option rather than queueing behind one.
4.why: Two Survival elevators per difficulty — twelve in Tower Defense Simulator's main lobby — and RIVALS' duel pads, whose stated requirement is the per-side count rather than the match total. Duplication is also how Tower Defense Simulator once assigned teams: Versus Elevators had 'two separate elevators for each team', and when Versus moved into Matchmaking 'teams would instead be randomly assigned'. The RIVALS page never says its pads decide the side, so the team evidence here is Tower Defense Simulator's alone.

5.rule: Gate progression at the entrance to the queue object, not on a greyed button inside it.
5.why: Tower Defense Simulator's single Voidcore elevator 'can only be entered by players who have beaten Hardcore'. An ineligible player never occupies a slot they cannot use, and the lock is discovered by walking rather than by clicking and being refused.

6.rule: Make the size step depend on the mode step, including its vocabulary.
6.why: Tower Defense Simulator caps Hardcore and Voidcore at trios, and in PVP it replaces solo/duo/trio/quad entirely with 1v1 and 2v2. The same slot in the same flow renders a different set of words depending on the previous answer, so the size control cannot be a constant.

7.rule: Never reuse an icon for a count it does not depict.
7.why: Tower Defense Simulator's Sandbox five- and six-player options ship using the QUAD icon, and the wiki records it plainly. An icon is the fastest read on a size picker, and one that is wrong is worse than a number alone.

8.rule: Skip the search screen when the party already fills the match.
8.why: 'If playing in solos or if the Party size is the same as selected player count, a match will be created instantly.' A searching animation that runs when no search is happening teaches players that the animation means nothing.

9.rule: Say that matching widens with time, because it does.
9.why: Tower Defense Simulator matches on Level and age group but 'will not try to find players of similar Level forever', accepting large gaps after a point; RIVALS bands parties at 800 ELO. Match quality degrades as the wait grows in every ranked system read here, and a queue screen showing only a spinner hides the one thing changing.

10.rule: Make the match-found screen a roster with stats, not a list of names.
10.why: Tower Defense Simulator's wiki says 'every single player's loadout, level, triumph count and loss count will be displayed, alongside their username and avatar' — in a sentence that sits inside the article's Sandbox bullet while being phrased generally, which is the ambiguity references[1] and limits[8] record and which this rule now carries too. The question at match-found is who these people are, and the answer is the numbers that predict how the session will go; what is certain is that one shipped mode does it, not that every mode does.

11.rule: Open the party screen on a browser of other people's parties, not on an empty roster.
11.why: Tower Defense Simulator shows 'a list of public Parties and a button which allows them to create a Party' to a player who is not in one. A create button alone assumes the player wants to lead; most of them want to join.

12.rule: Show different fields for friends than for strangers in the same invite list.
12.why: Tower Defense Simulator lists friends first with ONLY their online status, and players in the server WITH their level. A friend is invited because they are a friend; a stranger in your lobby is invited after you check what they bring. Showing level for both would imply you are meant to judge your friends by it.

13.rule: Default a party to closed, and default invite rights to the leader alone.
13.why: Tower Defense Simulator's Party Lock is 'enabled by default, but it used to be disabled', and Members Can Invite is disabled by default. A shipped game moved its own default toward closed after running the open version.

14.rule: Give the host filters over who may join — including a level band — and put them behind the leader.
14.why: Tower Defense Simulator's party settings are the ones 'which can be changed by the Party leader', and they include Minimum Level (default 0) and Maximum Level (default 1,000) with no stated ceiling. The host screens the party before matchmaking screens the match, and the two filters are different jobs. (That the leader is the only one who can change them is this file's recommendation, not something the page states.)

15.rule: Refuse a mismatched party at the moment the player asks, and name which member is the problem.
15.why: Tower Defense Simulator will not allow a match to start when the party is larger than the chosen squad size; BedWars returns an error when the leader queues an oversized party; BedWars ranked refuses to queue a party containing anyone outside the rank band; RIVALS requires party members within 800 ELO. Four shipped systems all let the player ask and then say no. The one thing none of the sources record is naming the member responsible, which is the only fact that would let the player fix it.

16.rule: Let party size prune the mode list rather than letting the player pick a mode it forbids.
16.why: RIVALS: two people in a party removes 1v1 from the list. BedWars: a full sixteen leaves only custom matches, infected and 30v30. A social choice made in one screen changes what is reachable in another, so the mode list cannot be a static menu.

17.rule: Route every queue action through the leader, and build the member's view as something other than a Play button.
17.why: 'To join a game the "leader" of that party must join the queue for a gamemode'; Tower Defense Simulator's elevators likewise follow the leader who enters. A party has one queue-entry point, so a member staring at an identical Play button is being lied to.

18.rule: Build the roster to scroll and add a search box once the party can hold more than a screenful.
18.why: BedWars parties hold sixteen and its menu ships a search bar over the whole server's player list; PartyService Plus advertises a 'scrolling member list to support large parties without visual clipping' as a feature, which is a statement that fixed-height rosters clip at real sizes.

19.rule: Treat party state as cross-server state, and clean up three things on every disconnect.
19.why: PartyService Plus orchestrates parties over MemoryStoreService and MessagingService, and names what breaks when one member drops: lobby state must be cleaned up, LEADERSHIP TRANSFERRED, and the QUEUE ENTRY UPDATED. A roster rendered from the current server's player list is a different list from the party.

20.rule: Make the queue entry belong to the party, so disbanding withdraws it.
20.why: 'Matchmaking queue removal if a player leaves or the party disbands.' A queue entry that survives its party is a match about to be formed for people who are no longer together.

21.rule: Offer a room code alongside invites and the friends list.
21.why: PartyService Plus makes 'join via unique room codes' a first-class path. A code covers the case neither other path does: somebody who is not on your friends list and not in your server.

22.rule: Keep an unaccepted invite; do not let it expire into nothing.
22.why: Tower Defense Simulator moves an unaccepted lobby invite into the invites section of the party menu; BedWars shows invites bottom-right AND keeps them in an Invites tab. Both built the transient and the persistent form of one invite because a popup is missed while the player is doing something else.

23.rule: Let a stale invite delete itself when touched rather than erroring.
23.why: In BedWars, 'if a player selects a party that has already left the server it will disappear'. Cross-server rows go stale between render and click, and the honest response to a dead row is to remove it, not to explain it.

24.rule: Write invite copy as a set of variants that name the friend, not one string.
24.why: Tower Defense Simulator ships seven for invites 'during a match or on the Roblox sites' — 'Wave incoming! [Friend name] is inviting you to battle it out'. Its in-lobby invite is a third surface the page gives no copy for. An invitation is the one message a player receives repeatedly from the same source, and a single string reads as a system notice by the third time.

25.rule: Gate the skip button on everyone's readiness, and accept that this is a ready-check without a checklist.
25.why: In DOORS the glowing instant-start button works only once 'everyone must be spawned in and finished with the Pre-Run Shop'. It is the simplest working ready-check read anywhere here — and its weakness is that the only feedback for a blocked start is a button that does nothing, which is a cost worth taking deliberately rather than by accident.

26.rule: Make a full queue object single-use, and evict anyone who steps back in.
26.why: A DOORS elevator closes after its occupants leave and kicks a re-entrant out in 3–5 seconds. A queue object that merely stops accepting still looks available from across the lobby.

27.rule: Make private-server creation two decisions — capacity and audience — and let progression unlock fields inside that form.
27.why: A DOORS custom elevator is 'up to 50 players in their game, as well as a friends only option', while Modifiers require the 'Rock Bottom' achievement and a Backdoor elevator requires 'Detour'. Progression does not only unlock content; it unlocks controls on the host's setup screen.

28.rule: Derive the capacity control's maximum from the mode, and do not offer a maximum the design cannot carry.
28.why: DOORS caps a custom elevator at 50 normally, 8 in four listed modes and 4 in Daily Runs — and its own wiki says playing past FOUR is discouraged because hiding spaces run out. A configurable maximum reads as a recommendation, and this one offers 50 against an advised ceiling of four.

29.rule: Confirm an irreversible create, even when it is free — and never site it inside a scrollable list without one.
29.why: Roblox's redesigned server list dropped the confirmation modal its predecessor had, and creating a free private server adds it permanently to an inventory with no delete. The reported failure was a finger slipping while scrolling the list on a phone. Free is not the same as reversible, and a scroll gesture reaches every control in the thing being scrolled.

30.rule: Render an eligibility gate as the specific unmet condition, never as a disabled button.
30.why: RIVALS requires SIX things at once to reach ranked, one of which has to explain that email verification is excluded because of platform bugs; BedWars' gate is a disjunction whose other two branches are historical and unverifiable from the player's present state. Neither fits in a tooltip, and a greyed Play button tells a player nothing they can act on.

31.rule: Say what a penalty costs and when it ends, and put the current lockout where the queue is.
31.why: RIVALS: leaving an ongoing match is a 15-minute matchmaking lockout plus an automatic loss 'regardless of the reason'. BedWars escalates instead — a warning first, timeouts after repeats. Both are states the lobby has to render, because the player discovers them by trying to queue.

32.rule: Show a number that can change while the player is away as something that decays, not as a record.
32.why: RIVALS deducts 100 ELO per day from the eighth day of inactivity at Onyx I or above, down to a 3,000 floor. A rating that drops overnight is not a history of matches played, and a profile presenting it as one will be wrong the moment somebody takes a week off.

33.rule: Resolve a group decision in the open — show the tie being broken.
33.why: BedWars spins 'a fair wheel of RNG' when a team's kit ban vote is not unanimous; RIVALS chooses a map by elimination, banning two of three proposed maps so the last one stands. Neither game resolves the tie silently, because a group that did not see the resolution assumes it was rigged.

34.rule: Let a ban list shrink so that a player with little cannot be banned into nothing.
34.why: In RIVALS the default loadout 'cannot be banned unless every player in the match owns more than four weapons in the respective category'. A pick-and-ban phase that can strip a new player of everything they own is a paywall wearing a competitive mechanic's clothes.

35.rule: Put the player's own row at the bottom of a leaderboard nobody can top.
35.why: BedWars' monthly board shows the top 100 by wins and the top 200 by rank, 'and at the very bottom, it shows each individual player's position and wins per month'. A ranking that never mentions its reader is a poster.

36.rule: Teleport the party, not the toucher — check Player.PartyId or Player.Team first.
36.why: Roblox's own teleport guide says to check team or party after a Touched or ProximityPrompt event and use Team:GetPlayers() or SocialService:GetPlayersByPartyId() 'if you want to teleport the entire group rather than just the individual'. A pad that sends only whoever stepped on it splits every party that uses it.

37.rule: Order the player array deliberately, because its first element chooses the server.
37.why: 'If you don't specify a server, users are teleported into a public server; the information of the first user in the list is used for matchmaking.' Which member is element one is a matchmaking input that appears nowhere on screen, so it has to be chosen rather than inherited from iteration order.

38.rule: Start every teleport from the server; the queue control fires a remote, never a local teleport.
38.why: TeleportAsync is server-only and the client-side Teleport() is deprecated 'even if your place is configured as "Fully Open"'. The same server-authority rule the shop screen follows applies to the control that spends a player's session.

39.rule: Keep the lobby's queue state until the arrival is confirmed, and handle each teleport failure differently.
39.why: A teleport 'can still fail at the last moment without throwing an error and leave the user in the server', firing TeleportInitFailed. The documented handler waits 15 seconds on Flooded, 1 second on Failure, and refuses to retry anything else — three outcomes with three behaviours, across up to five attempts. A queue that clears itself on a successful call has already lost the player.

40.rule: Author the between-places screen with no logic in it.
40.why: A gui passed to SetTeleportGui runs no scripts: 'Any scripts within the ScreenGui do not run.' Whatever it shows must be a still frame, and the handoff on arrival is manual — GetArrivingTeleportGui, RemoveDefaultLoadingScreen, parent, destroy.

41.rule: Pass the roster forward, never the entitlements.
41.why: TeleportData 'is visible to the client and unencrypted' and the docs say not to put secure data in it. Names, avatars and loadout ids can ride along to the match screen; currency, ownership and rank cannot.

42.rule: Check the Access Control setting before blaming the lobby for friends landing in it.
42.why: Under anything other than 'Fully open', 'players who try to join their friends in non-start places will instead join your game's start place'. A friend who tried to join a match and arrived in the lobby looks like a lobby bug and is a dashboard setting — and 'Secure within universe only' is the documented choice for places that exclusively use reserved servers.

43.rule: Dismiss the lobby HUD with the transition that covers it.
43.why: The one defect a reviewer caught in a lobby-queue showcase was the interface failing to hide its own icons during the transition, six seconds in — 'Even though most players won't notice it, it still to be sure you should fix it'. A queue overlay that takes the screen while the lobby's buttons stay behind it shows the seam.

screens.label: The MAP screen, across genres — corner minimaps and their framing, rotation and its off switch, full-screen map overlays, legends and layer toggles, blips and marker vocabularies, player-placed and system-placed waypoints, off-screen arrows and distance readouts, fog and deliberately hidden regions, fast-travel selection from the map
demonstrates: THE PLAYER'S OWN MARKER IS A DIFFERENT SHAPE FROM EVERYONE ELSE'S, not a different colour. Other players are circles; the viewing player is an arrow. Shape carries 'this is you' and additionally carries heading, which a dot cannot; colour is left free to carry team.
Colour then carries team and only team: Criminals are a red circle, Police a blue circle. One channel, one meaning.

VISIBILITY IS PER-RELATIONSHIP, NOT A GLOBAL SETTING. Same-team players are shown wherever they are; opposite-team players only BLINK onto the minimap when they are near. The same marker type has two different existence rules depending on who is looking.
The corner is platform-dependent: bottom-left on desktop, top-right on mobile. The two platforms do not agree, and the page states both rather than one with an exception.
The minimap is dismissible by the player — a circle button on its frame closes it — so the minimap is chrome the player is allowed to refuse, not a fixed part of the HUD.
Mobile is given a SMALLER VIEWED AREA than a computer player gets, so the same widget shows less world on a smaller screen rather than shrinking the same world into fewer pixels.

A recorded fix worth designing against: after one update the minimap 'no longer covers your bounty'. A corner minimap sits on top of whatever HUD element already owned that corner, and shipping it is how you find out which one.

A recorded defect worth designing against: when the minimap 'was revamped in the Nukes Update, there was a glitch where the arrow of the player's location would point in the wrong direction than where they were facing', and it 'was patched in the Cargo Ship Update'. A LATER update — the page never says the NEXT one, and an earlier version of this row called it 'a full update cycle' on no evidence. A heading marker is the one piece of a minimap that can be confidently wrong without looking broken.

Map art drifts from the world and the page says so twice: the minimap image went unchanged for almost seven months while buildings were added, and two named locations did not appear on it at all until a later update. The map image is a separate artefact with its own release schedule, not a view of the place.
A gamemode can overlay the same minimap rather than replacing it — the battle-royale mode draws the closing storm on it. READ FROM A GALLERY CAPTION on that page, not from its body prose.

SYSTEM-PLACED WAYPOINTS SHIPPED FOURTEEN AND A HALF MONTHS BEFORE PLAYER-PLACED ONES. The update history dates the first waypoints to a robbery drop-off — 'arrows guiding the player to the drop off location', December 20, 2020 — and player-placeable waypoints to March 5, 2022. That is 14 months and 16 days; an earlier version of this row rounded it to fifteen. The game learned to point at one thing before it learned to let you point at anything.

PLACING A WAYPOINT AND EXPANDING THE MINIMAP SHIPPED IN THE SAME UPDATE, and that is causal rather than coincidental: the March 2022 entry reads 'Minimap is now able to be expanded, Waypoints are added'. You cannot click a destination on a corner widget, so the ability to place one required a full-size surface first.
Placement is a two-step mode, not a click: press an 'Add Waypoint' button, THEN click anywhere on the map. Removal is its own named button rather than a second click on the marker.
THE WAYPOINT'S REAL SURFACE IS THE WORLD, NOT THE MAP. Closing the map leaves arrows near the character leading to the destination — the map is where you set it and the world is where you follow it.
A waypoint deletes itself on arrival. Reaching the destination is the completion signal; there is no dismiss step and no stale marker.

Automatic waypoints are attached to STATE, not to place: they appear when the player picks up a crate, obtains a uranium rod, enters a particular vehicle with another officer, or steals from a named location, and they point at where that specific carried thing is turned in.

ONE AUTOMATIC WAYPOINT WAS DELIBERATELY DELAYED: the power-plant delivery point was changed 'to only appear once you exited the building'. A destination marker raised while the player is still inside points through walls and reads as noise, so it waits for the player to be somewhere it can be true.

A WAYPOINT-LED TUTORIAL WAS SHIPPED AND THEN WITHDRAWN. In March 2024 waypoints guided new joins to nearby robberies and gun shops, with 'new sub-text to waypoint guidance, providing more direction'; the update history then records the tutorial removed 'due to the experimental feature proving unsuccessful'. Guidance arrows are a plausible onboarding device that a large shipped game tried and took back out.
A waypoint can be a race fixture rather than navigation — the page names using one as a finish line to count laps, and a later entry toggles a waypoint to a track start line in private servers only.

ROTATION IS A PREFERENCE WITH AN OFF SWITCH. The page states that the minimap rotating with the direction the avatar faces 'can be turned off in the Options menu'. Rotate-with-heading versus fixed north is not a decision the designer gets to make once for everybody; a shipped game put it in settings.

The full map is a FILTERED VIEW WITH A CATEGORY PICKER, not one flat picture: six named categories — Players, Plots, Jobs, Points of Interest, Shops, Transport — reached from a selection menu the player can toggle on or off, so the legend and the filter are the same control.
Pin colour encodes SOCIAL RELATIONSHIP, not type: friends are green pins and other users are purple pins, inside the same Players category.

THE FULL MAP'S VIEW CONTROLS ARE THE FOUR THE PAGE ENUMERATES, not three: 'players can zoom in, zoom out, use the center button to return the view to their current location, and toggle the selection menu on or off.' A map you can pan needs a way back to yourself, and a map whose legend is a filter needs a way to put the filter away. AND THE SOURCE CONTRADICTS ITSELF ABOUT THE CENTRE BUTTON: its very next paragraph says 'Players can also pinpoint a location on the map by clicking the center button, which places a blue arrow pointing to the location', which is a second and different job for the same named control. One of the two sentences is wrong and this file cannot tell which, so nothing here should be built on that button doing exactly one thing.

A pinned location produces TWO artefacts at once — a blue arrow pointing to it, and a distance counter above it measured in studs. The page separately notes the waypoint system 'uses Roblox's standard unit of measurement, studs', so the number is engine units shown raw rather than a converted distance.

Hovering a marker reveals that location's NAME — READ FROM A GALLERY CAPTION, 'The name of a location appearing when hovering over it', because the body prose never mentions hover — so the map is drawn with icons and reads out words on demand rather than carrying labels at rest.

FAST TRAVEL IS A CATEGORY OF THE MAP. Clicking a bus-stop icon in the Transport category teleports the player, described by the page as 'an alternative to fast traveling at the bus stops themselves' — the same journey is purchasable from the world object and from the map, and the map did not replace the object.

The Transport category collects three different vehicle-rental systems — bus stops, e-scooter stands and bicycle stands — under one heading, so a category is named by what the player wants (to get somewhere) rather than by which subsystem owns the object.

THE MINIMAP'S CONTENTS CHANGE WITH THE ACTIVE JOB: while doing the delivery or taxi jobs, the minimap shows the customer's location. A task injects a transient marker into a widget that otherwise shows fixed geography.

THE MINIMAP IS DATED ON ITS OWN PAGE AND NOTHING MORE IS CLAIMED: it 'was added in Version 1.14.0', which the page's changelog link names as 'Version 1.14.0 - April 2026', and the article is filed under a Version 1.14.0 category. A game already at version 1.14 added a minimap in one of its versions. How long Bloxburg had shipped before that is NOT stated on this page — an earlier version of this row said 'years' and no source read here supports it.

WHO APPEARS ON THE ENEMY'S MAP IS DERIVED FROM SENSOR COVERAGE, NOT FROM A TOGGLE. The 2020 overhaul added 'anonymous markers for other players on the map for your team', and police 'are able to see map markers for all players near another police officer or traffic camera'. A civilian is on the police map because they drove past a camera. The map is a readout of a surveillance network the world actually contains, which makes concealment a route choice instead of a setting.
The markers for teammates are ANONYMOUS — a position without an identity. The map answers 'someone is there' and refuses 'who'.

THE FULL MAP WAS DELIBERATELY MADE SMALLER THAN THE SCREEN. The same overhaul 'changed the minimap GUI design into more of a modern tablet form so it doesn't cover the entire screen'. A full-screen map is the obvious shape and this game rejected it, so the player can keep driving while reading it.

The corner minimap doubles as the button that opens the full map — the page's caption on the current minimap image calls it one that 'also acts like a button to open the GUI'. THAT IS AN IMAGE CAPTION, not body prose, and it is the only place the page says it. The widget is its own affordance and needs no separate icon.

LETTERS WERE REPLACED BY ICONS, and the page dates it. Its trivia reads 'In older minimaps, letters were used to indicate major locations, such as gas stations and dealerships', and the 2020 entry reads 'All major locations that were marked with a letter were replaced with a mannered icon.' Both are quoted here as the page words them; an earlier version of this row reordered the first inside its quotation marks. A legend you have to consult was traded for glyphs you can read directly.

The marker set is an enumerated legend with a description per entry — spawn, gas station, police station, fire station, highway/DOT, trucker, transit, mail, hospital — so the icon vocabulary is a documented table rather than art added case by case.

SOME MARKERS ARE EVENTS, NOT PLACES: a structure-fire marker appears on any home currently on fire, and a mail marker on any home with mail to deliver or collect. The same legend carries permanent geography and live work.

A MARKER THE PLAYER CAN DISMISS: the icon showing the player's own parked vehicle can be removed from the map by selecting it. Your own belongings clutter a map faster than anything else, so the marker for them is disposable.

Navigation is a placed beacon that you then follow — 'pinpointing and following the green beacon you have made' — and a later phase added sharing your location with friends 'or to taunt police', so a position marker is a thing a player can publish on purpose.

The name of the road or city being driven through is shown as a banner, and only on PC and console — mobile does not get it. A text overlay that fits beside a minimap on a monitor is dropped rather than shrunk on a phone.

That road label became a ROUTE SHIELD rather than text: before one version the indicator spelled a route number as words, and after it displays the route's shield graphic. A sign the player already recognises beats the same characters set in the UI font.
