0.rule: Draw the player as a different SHAPE from everyone else — an arrow, not a coloured dot.
0.why: Jailbreak makes every other player a circle and the viewing player an arrow. Shape says 'you' and carries heading at the same time, which leaves colour entirely free to carry team; a game that distinguishes itself by colour has spent the one channel it needed for sides.

1.rule: Let rotation be a setting, and say which thing it follows.
1.why: Bloxburg's page states the rotate-with-facing behaviour 'can be turned off in the Options menu', so a shipped game refused to decide it for everyone. Plum's system rotates to the CAMERA and Bloxburg's to the AVATAR, and a third implementation leaves the map fixed and rotates the arrow instead — three shipped answers, which is the tell that this is a preference and not a fact.

2.rule: Pick a corner deliberately and expect to fight whatever already lives there.
2.why: Four sources give four placements — Jailbreak bottom-left on desktop and top-right on mobile, Bloxburg top-right, Ultimate Driving bottom-left, The Wild West bottom-right. There is no convention to inherit. Jailbreak separately records an update whose change was that the minimap 'no longer covers your bounty', which is what the corner question actually costs.

3.rule: Make the minimap itself the button that opens the full map.
3.why: Ultimate Driving describes its minimap as a thing that 'also acts like a button to open the GUI'; Jailbreak and ER:LC both list clicking the minimap alongside a key; and a user of Plum's system reported the full map as broken because clicking the minimap did nothing. Players try that gesture whether or not it was advertised.

4.rule: Give the full map a held-key peek as well as a pressed-key mode.
4.why: ER:LC opens the same map by 'holding Tab, M, or clicking on the minimap'. A hold closes itself when released, which is what a driver or a player under fire needs; a press is what a player planning a route needs. They are different interactions to the same surface, not two surfaces.

5.rule: Build the legend as toggleable layers, so the legend and the filter are one control.
5.why: Bloxburg's map has six categories reached from a selection menu; ER:LC toggles zip codes, street names, landmarks, jobs and ATMs; The Wild West toggles faction territory separately from icons and says most world markers 'can be disabled in Options'. Three unrelated games arrived at five or six switchable groups, which is also the size at which a static legend stops being readable.

6.rule: Treat labels as a layer too, not as part of the map art.
6.why: ER:LC lets the player switch street names and zip codes off, and Ultimate Driving's Chinese build ships with the legend table and the town and park labels removed entirely. If the words are baked into the image, neither of those is possible and the map cannot be localised or decluttered.

7.rule: Use shape for what a thing IS and colour for whose side it is on, and grade severity by adding to the glyph.
7.why: The Wild West runs three hostile tiers off one skull — bare, with a hat, with a hat and revolvers — while keeping red for hostility and blue and green for faction and self. Escalation costs no new colour, which matters because colour is already fully spent by the time a map has teams.

8.rule: Snap an off-radius marker to the border instead of culling it.
8.why: Plum's minimap sells border-snapping blips as a headline feature across both versions. A marker that disappears at the frame edge answers 'is it near?' and destroys 'which way?', and which way is the question a corner minimap exists to answer.

9.rule: Show a distance number only while the target is out of reach.
9.why: The Wild West's Mayor escort marker 'shows the distance to them, when not in range', with the range stated at roughly 50 metres — and the same page records that this feature 'no longer works and cannot be seen in-game' since quests were removed, so it is a construction that shipped rather than one running now. A counter that keeps ticking once the player can see the thing is a number they have stopped reading. Bloxburg's stud counter on a pinned location is the same instrument, but its page does NOT say the number is hidden on approach, so the out-of-range conditioning rests on this one withdrawn feature and nothing else read here.

10.rule: Set the waypoint on the map and follow it in the world.
10.why: Jailbreak's waypoints are placed on the expanded map and then, on closing it, appear as arrows near the character leading to the destination. The map is a planning surface and the world is a guidance surface; a waypoint that only exists inside the map makes the player keep the map open while driving.

11.rule: Place a waypoint in two steps — an explicit Add mode, then a click — and give Remove its own control.
11.why: Jailbreak names both buttons. A map that places a waypoint on any click cannot also be panned, zoomed or used to press a fast-travel icon, all of which the same surface has to support.

12.rule: Delete a waypoint when the player arrives.
12.why: Jailbreak's waypoints 'automatically remove themselves when you reach your destination'. Arrival is the completion signal the system already has; making the player dismiss it adds a step whose only outcome is stale markers when they forget.

13.rule: Attach system waypoints to STATE, and delay one that would point through a wall.
13.why: Jailbreak raises a delivery waypoint when the player picks up specific loot, and it changed the power-plant one 'to only appear once you exited the building'. A destination marker raised while the player is still inside the source building points at geometry and reads as noise, which is a bug the player experiences as the system being wrong rather than early.

14.rule: Ship system-placed guidance before player-placed waypoints, and do not assume guided onboarding will survive.
14.why: Jailbreak's first waypoints were robbery drop-off arrows in December 2020 and player-placeable ones arrived in March 2022 — pointing at one thing is a much smaller problem than accepting an arbitrary destination. The same history also records a waypoint-led tutorial added in 2024 and then removed 'due to the experimental feature proving unsuccessful', so the obvious use of guidance arrows is one a large game tried and withdrew.

15.rule: Ship the expandable map in the same change as the ability to place a waypoint.
15.why: Jailbreak's update history puts 'Minimap is now able to be expanded' and 'Waypoints are added' in one March 2022 entry. You cannot pick a destination on a corner widget the size of a thumbnail, so the placement feature is not shippable without the surface.

16.rule: Make markers a function of what the player is currently doing.
16.why: The Wild West shows drop-off points only while the player carries a stolen money bag; Bloxburg's minimap shows the customer while a delivery or taxi job is running; Ultimate Driving marks houses that are on fire and houses with mail waiting. A map that shows every possible destination at all times has the same information density as showing none.

17.rule: Derive who appears on an opponent's map from something in the world, not from a rule in the code.
17.why: Ultimate Driving shows police the markers of players near another police officer OR near a traffic camera, and Jailbreak blinks an opposing player onto the minimap only when they are close. Both make concealment a route decision the player can reason about, which a global visibility flag cannot be.

18.rule: An anonymous position marker is a legitimate design, not an incomplete one.
18.why: Ultimate Driving's 2020 overhaul added 'anonymous markers for other players on the map for your team'. The map answers 'someone is there' and refuses 'who'. NO SOURCE IN THIS FILE COVERS PHANTOM FORCES; the comparison this rule used to assert bare is recorded in the sibling packages/corpus/data/ui-references/fps_arena.json, where Phantom Forces 'showed the yes/no split on votekicks and changed it in 7.0.0 to show only the number who voted'. Same trade, read there and not here: less information, deliberately, because the extra field was usable against a person.

19.rule: Let the player dismiss markers for their own belongings.
19.why: Ultimate Driving lets a player remove their own parked-vehicle icon by selecting it. Self-generated clutter accumulates faster than authored clutter, and a marker the player placed by existing is the one they are most entitled to remove.

20.rule: Draw the same marker vocabulary in the world and on the map.
20.why: The Wild West lists its skull tiers, exclamation mark, money bag and faction star in one World Markers table, and the same glyphs reappear in the Legend of its Map page. The page says of the exclamation mark that it 'hovers over any criminal' and of the faction star that it 'can be seen through terrain and buildings', and describes the rest only as showing or revealing a location without naming a surface — so what this rule rests on is the shared vocabulary across the two surfaces, not a claim that every glyph hovers in the world. The player learns the alphabet once; a map with a private icon language has to be taught separately.

21.rule: Prefer a drawn glyph to a lettered key.
21.why: Ultimate Driving's 2020 pass records that 'All major locations that were marked with a letter were replaced with a mannered icon', and its trivia says 'In older minimaps, letters were used to indicate major locations, such as gas stations and dealerships.' A letter requires the legend to be open; a fuel pump does not.

22.rule: Use the sign the player already knows.
22.why: Ultimate Driving changed its road indicator from spelling out a route number to displaying that route's shield graphic. The characters were identical; the recognition was not.

23.rule: Consider not covering the whole screen with the full map.
23.why: Ultimate Driving's overhaul 'changed the minimap GUI design into more of a modern tablet form so it doesn't cover the entire screen', which for a driving game means the map can be read without stopping. Full-screen is the default shape and at least one shipped game rejected it on purpose.

24.rule: Let fast travel be selectable from the map without removing it from the world.
24.why: Bloxburg teleports the player when they click a bus-stop icon in the map's Transport category, and its own page calls this 'an alternative to fast traveling at the bus stops themselves'. The world object stays; the map is a second door to the same journey, which is what keeps the stops meaningful places.

25.rule: Give a pannable map a button that returns the view to the player.
25.why: Bloxburg's page lists a centre button that 'return[s] the view to their current location' among the four controls it enumerates for the full map — zoom in, zoom out, recentre, and toggle the selection menu. The moment a map can be dragged, 'where was I?' becomes a question the interface created and therefore has to answer. Read the caveat with it: the same page then says the centre button pinpoints a location and drops an arrow, so the source disagrees with itself about that control. The recentre reading is the one this rule takes and it is not certain.

26.rule: Put names behind hover rather than on the map at rest.
26.why: Bloxburg draws icons and reveals a location's name when the player hovers it. A map carrying every label permanently is a map that has to choose a font size for its densest district and live with it everywhere else.

27.rule: Correct for aspect ratio when projecting a world position onto a minimap frame, or every marker is wrong.
27.why: A 2026 Scripting Support thread reports icons placing correctly only while the minimap is a perfect square, because Camera:WorldToViewportPoint returns a point in the camera's aspect ratio and the code scaled it by the frame's size. The fix is to remap X about 0.5 by the ratio of the two aspects. This is geometry, not taste: the bug is invisible in a square prototype and appears when the widget is given its shipping shape.

28.rule: Know which minimap you are building: a pre-rendered image, a live ViewportFrame, or a per-frame raycast render.
28.why: The three appear in three separate sources with three separate costs. A pre-rendered image is nearly free and cannot show anything that moved since it was rendered — Jailbreak's page records its own image going unchanged for 'almost seven months (3/3/18 - 9/29/18)' while buildings were added. A ViewportFrame clones parts and, as written in the thread read here, explicitly excludes Terrain, Accessories and anything under a Humanoid, so it shows built geometry and nothing else. A raycast render updates live, and the one read here ran at 64x64 every frame — the author's own working figure on his own Ryzen 5 2400G, not a ceiling, since he names a way past it: 'You can still extract more performance by cheating and having the render be spread across several frames.' What he states as impossible is only the pixel-accurate end, which 'would fry your CPU with millions of raycasts per frame'.

29.rule: Author north as an object in the place, not as a world axis.
29.why: The working minimap read here measures the player's heading against the LookVector of a part placed for that purpose. A map image drawn at any rotation other than the world's can only agree with the world if the reference direction is authored beside it.

30.rule: Compute map fog from line of sight, not from a radius.
30.why: The MOBA fog system read here raycasts across the map against walls and barrier objects specifically so vision 'roughly matches what the player would actually be able to see in the game world rather than just revealing a basic circle around them'. A circle is wrong exactly where walls are, and in the genres that use fog, walls are where the game happens.

31.rule: Stop per-unit reveal from summing when a team groups up.
31.why: The same author lowers each unit's light brightness when several are close together, 'so that stacking several units in one place doesn't completely light up the map or blind everyone'. Additive reveal breaks precisely when a team does the most normal thing it does.

32.rule: Hiding a region from the map is a legitimate decision, and it is not the same as fog.
32.why: The Wild West keeps two named areas off the map permanently and previously hid everything north of a landmark 'on the Map but still accessible'. Fog fills in as you explore; this never does. A map that admits the existence of everything has given away the shape of the world before the player walks it.

33.rule: Encode height as darkness on a live map, and let it double as the edge of range.
33.why: The realtime raycast minimap darkens things below the player until they reach full black, which is also where the scan distance ends. One channel carries depth and the boundary of knowledge, and they are the same visual for an honest reason: both mean 'nothing reliable here'.

34.rule: Make an expensive high-resolution view a peek bounded by the gesture that holds it.
34.why: The same system renders at full resolution only while the cursor hovers the minimap, and its author says it is 'not really supposed to move around with it'. Tying an expensive mode to a hold rather than a toggle means the player cannot accidentally leave it running.

35.rule: Style the map image as a diagram with separated layers — buildings, roads, materials, water, zones, contours, outlines.
35.why: The generator read here names its predecessor's failure as producing 'similar-looking maps regardless of the game genre or style', so that 'racing games couldn't properly highlight their tracks' and 'RPGs couldn't distinguish between different zones'. A correct render of a place from above is not yet a map of the game played there.

36.rule: Tile a big world's map across several images.
36.why: Plum's system lists 'multiple images for larger maps' as a capability. Past some world size one texture cannot hold usable detail, and the resulting seams are an implementation problem that has to be planned rather than discovered.

37.rule: Attach the minimap system to a frame the designer authored, rather than letting it build its own.
37.why: A user of Plum's V2 reported nothing appearing until they tagged an existing Frame, which 'automatically turned that frame into a minimap'. Position, size, corner radius and stroke then come from the UI tree where every other element's do, instead of from a system's private defaults.

38.rule: A minimap the player cannot hide is a bug.
38.why: Jailbreak closes its minimap from a button on the frame; The Wild West hides it from a setting AND automatically in cinematic mode; The Wild West's marker page says most world markers can be disabled in Options. Screenshot modes and player preference are two independent reasons, and both need the same off switch.

screens.label: NOTIFICATIONS, TOASTS AND REWARD POPUPS, across genres — the toast stack and its lifetime, the banner, the coloured system line in chat, the actionable request card, the claim popup, the streak counter that outruns its own calendar, and what a shipped game does when one event has two different audiences
demonstrates: THE ENGINE HAS ALREADY CHOSEN THE CORNER. The documentation states the notification appears at the BOTTOM RIGHT of the screen. A game that draws its own toast top-right is not matching the platform, it is competing with it, and both will be on screen at once if anything ever calls SetCore.
TWO BUTTONS IS THE CEILING, stated outright: the notification may have up to two buttons. A three-choice notification is not a notification in this system; it is a dialog and belongs somewhere else.

Duration is a NUMBER OF SECONDS with a documented default of 5. That is the only hard lifetime figure found anywhere in this file, and it is the platform's, so a custom toast that lives noticeably longer or shorter than five seconds is making a choice against a known baseline rather than in a vacuum.

THE CALLBACK IS HANDED THE BUTTON'S TEXT, NOT AN INDEX OR AN ID. The BindableFunction 'should be invoked with the text of the button pressed'. That is a real trap: renaming a button label silently changes what the handler receives, so the label and the branch are coupled by string.

Title and Text are both REQUIRED; Icon, Duration, Callback, Button1 and Button2 are all optional. The minimum honest notification is therefore two lines of text, and everything else — including the icon — is decoration the platform does not insist on.

There is no field for priority, for a stack group, for a category, or for dismissal. The platform primitive has no concept of several notifications competing, which is why every kit below invents one.

THE TITLE IS NOT THE DEVELOPER'S TO WRITE. Notifications 'automatically use the title of your game as the notification title'. Everything the developer controls is body text, which means the body must never re-state the game's name — and the {experienceName} token exists precisely because you sometimes want it INSIDE the sentence instead.

The body is capped at 99 CHARACTERS and may carry unlimited custom parameters. A notification is therefore a TEMPLATE with holes — the documented examples fill in a quest count, an egg name, a race count and a friend's userId — not a string a script concatenates.

'There is no default game notification string, so this step is required.' The message must be authored on the Creator Dashboard and referenced by asset id. A notification's text is content with an id, versioned and moderated, not a literal in code.

THE THROTTLE IS ONE PER USER PER DAY, per experience, plus an aggregate daily cap across all experiences. That single slot is the whole design constraint: it forces a game to decide which one thing is worth a day, and it is why a generic 'come back and play' is not merely weak but actively spends the only slot there is.

DELIVERY IS NOT GUARANTEED, and the documentation LISTS SEVEN non-delivery cases: experience eligibility requirements not met, the recipient not opted in, the recipient's per-experience throttle reached, the recipient's aggregate daily throttle reached, missing or invalid request parameters, the notification string having been moderated, and — for notifications with user mentions — either the two players not being friends or the mentioned player having turned off 'Update friends about my activity?'. The last bullet splits in two, so it is eight outcomes on seven lines. They are not all silent: the same page says 'you receive transparent feedback when a user's throttle limit is reached.' Code that assumes a notification arrived is wrong on every path that does not report itself.

FALSE TIME PRESSURE IS BANNED BY NAME, and the example given is a notification telling a user to purchase within ten minutes or miss out. So is telling a user they will get something free when they will not, and disguising an advert as organic content. The countdown-and-scarcity vocabulary that reward popups reach for first is explicitly out of bounds on this channel.
'Games should not require users to turn on notifications in order to participate or advance in gameplay.' The notification channel may never be load-bearing for progression.

ONE EVENT, TWO TEXTS, CHOSEN BY AUDIENCE. When a bed is destroyed, the losing team is told their own bed is gone and that they will no longer respawn; every OTHER team is told which team colour lost its bed. Same event, two strings, and the second one names a team the first does not have to. Audience is a property of the notification, not of the recipient's filter.

EVERY NOTIFICATION IS MANUALLY DISMISSIBLE. The page says all of them can be made to disappear by clicking on PC or tapping on mobile. A timed lifetime and a tap-to-dismiss are both present; neither replaces the other.

THE PAGE'S OWN COUNT IS STALE AND THE LIST IS THE USEFUL PART. It reads 'There are currently ten types of notifications:' and then names TWELVE — beds, teleportation, team upgrades, party, the Vulcan kit, bed alarms, custom-match commands, lucky blocks, a Tesla coil trap, spirits, friends and sudden death. The discrepancy is recorded rather than resolved, because nothing on the page says which two were added after the sentence was written. What matters is the AXIS: the types are named after the SUBSYSTEM that raises them, not after severity or tone. There is no 'info / warning / error' taxonomy anywhere on the page.

A MESSAGE THAT DID NOT COME FROM YOUR OWN ACTION CARRIES A BRACKETED SOURCE PREFIX. The bed-alarm message and the host-announcement message both open with the subsystem name in square brackets. The prefix is how the player knows the line was not caused by the button they just pressed.

REFUSALS RIDE THE SAME CHANNEL AS CELEBRATIONS. Not enough diamonds to repair a table, a party already at maximum size, a queue that could not be joined, an invalid item, a kit name that does not exist — all of these are notifications, in the same stack that announces a teammate's purchase. The toast channel is the error channel.

AN ACTIONABLE SOCIAL NOTIFICATION IS A DIFFERENT SHAPE ENTIRELY. The party invite is the only notification on the page given as a TABLE rather than as a quoted line: a caption reading PARTY INVITE, an image cell, and the sender's display name. A notification that wants an answer stops being a sentence and becomes a titled card with a picture slot in it. WHAT THAT PICTURE SLOT RENDERS IS NOT RECORDED HERE — the wikitext holds a placeholder image file, and no image was looked at for this file.

A COUNTDOWN IS EXPRESSED AS DISCRETE NOTIFICATIONS AT DECREASING INTERVALS, not as a persistent timer. Sudden death announces at 59 seconds, again at 10 seconds, then announces the event itself. Three fires, no widget.

WHEN A CAP IS HIT, THE MESSAGE NAMES WHAT WAS DESTROYED TO MAKE ROOM. Placing a second trap reports that the oldest trap has been destroyed; placing a ninth spirit reports that an older one has been removed. The game does not merely refuse — it says which thing it evicted.
A NOTIFICATION CLASS CAN BE SWITCHED OFF INDEPENDENTLY: friend-join notifications have their own settings toggle. Opt-out granularity is per class, not one global mute.

THE CHANNEL IS THE CHAT BOX, NOT A FLOATING TOAST. The page describes boss and event announcements as appearing in the chat boxes. A server-wide announcement rides the chat the player is already reading, which is why it survives a busy screen and why it leaves a scrollback.

COLOUR IS APPLIED TWO DIFFERENT WAYS ON ONE PAGE, AND THE SPLIT IS BY AUDIENCE. Three of the four tables declare one colour for the whole section — 'All of the following messages appear red in the chat boxes' heads Boss, Event and Island Secrets — so a server-wide announcement is red because of the CHANNEL it arrives on, not because of what it says. Per-message colour exists only in the Player Messages table, where the player's own outcomes carry red, a bright green, a gold-yellow, magenta, a blue-violet and one plain yellow. The vocabulary there is a tendency rather than a mapping: gold carries items found AND 'The event shop has been restocked!' AND 'NEW SKILL AVAILABLE!', and magenta carries materials AND 'Stored <Sword>'. What the page supports is that colour separates kinds of message inside one channel — not that each colour means exactly one thing.

AN OUTLINE ACCOMPANIES MOST COLOURED MESSAGES, NOT ALL OF THEM. Of the 37 lines the wiki renders with its colour template, 24 also carry the text-outline template and 13 do not — 'Item drop: <Item>', 'NEW SKILL AVAILABLE!', 'FIGHT!', 'Enemy is immune to physical attacks!', 'Super Dash ready!' and the two bounty-penalty lines among them. Roughly two thirds: enough to call the stroke the default treatment for coloured chat text, not enough to call it universal. The reason to want it is a design argument rather than a citation — coloured text over a chat window sitting on top of arbitrary game world loses the legibility the colour was meant to add.

ONE NOTIFICATION CAN HOLD TWO COLOURS AND TWO MEANINGS. Finding a fruit is announced in green and immediately followed, in the same message, by a red warning that dying before eating it will lose it. The reward and its caveat are one line, coloured differently — not two notifications, and not a reward with the caveat dropped.

REWARDS ARE ANNOUNCED PER RESOURCE, ONE LINE EACH — money earned, experience earned (with the weapon it was credited to in parentheses), fragments earned, materials obtained with a quantity, an item drop with its own marker. There is no combined 'you earned 3 things' summary anywhere on the page.

THE SAME EVENT ESCALATES ITS COPY BY A NUMERIC BAND. A player joining with 5M–14.9M bounty triggers a warning-toned announcement; 15M–30M triggers a louder one declaring a god has arrived. One event, two strings, selected by a threshold — the notification's volume is a function of a stat.

AN ERROR MESSAGE CARRIES THE REMEDY AND THE HOTKEY. The message for hitting an immune enemy states the problem, names the ability that fixes it, and puts the key to press in square brackets at the end. A refusal that does not say what to do instead is a refusal the player has to leave the game to understand.

A NOTIFICATION IS USED AS A ROUTE. An unclaimed gift is announced as a line telling the player to check the shop — the message's job is not to deliver the thing but to point at the screen that holds it.

MANY ANNOUNCEMENTS DELIBERATELY DO NOT NAME THEIR SUBJECT. A boss spawning is announced in-fiction — tremors heard, a shiver down the spine, a barrier broken — and the wiki's Cause column exists precisely because players cannot tell from the message alone which boss it means. This is a shipped game choosing atmosphere over legibility on purpose, and the community building a decoder ring for it.

FAILURE BY EXPIRY IS ANNOUNCED TOO. When nobody kills the boss in time, the timeout gets its own message; when a timed puzzle's window closes, the closing gets its own message. An event that ends because nothing happened still fires.

THE STRONGEST RECORDED DECISION IN THIS FILE. In v1.75.2, on the same day the feature shipped, 'Claim pop-ups now display the item given instead of the name of the chest.' The popup originally named the CONTAINER the reward came out of. It was changed to name the thing the player actually received. A reward popup that says which box opened has told the player nothing they wanted to know.

In v1.75.3, playtime rewards began displaying HOW MANY chests they give, and reward pools became visible at all. A tier that hands out more than one thing has to say how many before the popup opens, or the popup is the first time the player learns the size of what they were waiting for.

In v1.76.0 the pool disclosure MOVED FROM AN EXPLICIT CONTROL TO HOVER: previously the reward pool list appeared on clicking a magnifying-glass icon, afterwards on hovering the chest. The odds went from something you had to go and find to something you fall over. That direction is worth arguing about on touch devices, where there is no hover.

Also in v1.76.0: 'Chest icons are now bigger' and 'Rewards are now displayed with an animation.' The claim moment acquired motion in a patch, after the data was already correct — the animation was the last thing added, not the first.
In v1.89.0 the consumable crate icons were REPLACED WITH GIFTBOXES. The icon vocabulary was changed so a reward tier reads as a gift rather than as an inventory item the player might already own.

A RECORDED DEFECT WORTH DESIGNING AGAINST, stated in the page's own bug line for v1.83.0: after one ad is played, every following ad is impossible to play 'even if the game makes it look like they are claimable', and it only resolves on rejoin. A control that renders in its claimable state while the thing behind it is exhausted is the specific failure a reward surface is most prone to.
The ladder is time-gated at 5, 15, 30, 60, 90 and 120 minutes, and v1.76.0 pushed every step after the first further out. The spacing of a playtime ladder is a tuned number, not a constant.
A watch-an-ad offer appears RANDOMLY rather than always, grants three extra boxes, and resets after 24 hours. The opportunity itself is an event that has to be announced when it appears.

0.rule: Pick the channel by AUDIENCE AND WEIGHT first, and only then design the thing: a toast for one player's own outcome, a banner for something happening to the whole server, a coloured chat line for an announcement that should leave a scrollback, a titled card carrying the sender's name for something that needs an answer.
0.why: The notification kit names toast, banner and chat message as three separate mechanisms with three scopes, Blox Fruits puts server-wide announcements in the chat box specifically so they survive a busy screen, and BedWars stops using a quoted line the moment the message needs an answer: its party invite is the one entry on that page rendered as a captioned card, with the sender's name and a picture slot beside it. Four sources, four channels, and the split is never about how important the message feels.

1.rule: The engine's own notification is bottom-right, at most two buttons, five seconds by default. Match that corner or knowingly take another one — and never take it by accident.
1.why: StarterGui's SendNotification documentation fixes all three. A custom stack in a different corner is fine until anything at all calls SetCore, at which point the player has two notification systems on screen; the decision has to be made rather than defaulted into.

2.rule: A notification that needs an answer gets AT MOST TWO ACTIONS, and if it needs three it is not a notification.
2.why: The platform primitive caps it at two buttons, and every actionable notification found in a shipped game is binary — accept or decline a trade, accept or decline a backpack request, accept or decline a suggested item. Nothing read here has a third branch.

3.rule: One event, several audiences, SEVERAL TEXTS. Write the message the losing side reads and the message everyone else reads as two separate strings.
3.why: BedWars tells the team that lost its bed that they will no longer respawn, and tells every other team which colour fell. Adopt Me warns the player giving too much that scamming is bannable, and warns the other one that they may be being scammed. Two independent games, same structure: a single templated string with the subject swapped would be wrong in both.

4.rule: Make every notification dismissible by tapping it, in addition to its timer.
4.why: BedWars states that all of its notifications can be cleared by clicking or tapping, and the author of the banner module lists 'not clickable' as a defect of his own product. A lifetime alone leaves a player who wants the screen back with nothing to do.

5.rule: Refusals go in the SAME channel as everything else, and the refusal names what to do instead.
5.why: BedWars sends 'not enough diamonds', 'party is full' and 'failed to join the queue' through the identical notification stack that announces a teammate's purchase. Blox Fruits goes one step further: its immune-enemy message names the ability that fixes it and puts the key to press in brackets. A refusal that only says no is a refusal the player has to leave the game to understand.

6.rule: Consider giving the refusal LESS chrome than the success, not more — and a different edge of the screen.
6.why: The notification kit's Alert template is red text at the bottom with no card behind it, reserved for what could not be done. That is deliberately the opposite of the instinct to make errors louder, and it is defensible: a 'not enough money' fires constantly during normal play and does not deserve the same panel as a level-up. Recorded as a decision to weigh, because only one source read here makes it.

7.rule: Cap the stack with a MAX-ON-SCREEN, and partition unrelated notifications into separate stack groups so a burst in one does not bury the other.
7.why: The notification kit carries both as attributes on the template frame, and they are the only explicit answer found anywhere in this research to what happens when several fire at once. The banner module that has neither ended up exposing a public 'how many are active' call, which pushes the same problem out to every call site.

8.rule: Anchor a stack by PLACING its template, and let direction, duration, sound and animation live on that frame as attributes.
8.why: 'Where you move it in Studio is where its notifications appear' — and because the behaviour is attributes rather than code, duplicating the frame yields a second stack that already works. A system where position is an argument and timing is in a script cannot be restyled without being rewritten.

9.rule: Let the CARD grow to fit the text. Never let the text shrink to fit the card — and check that no size constraint is quietly defeating AutomaticSize.
9.why: A banner module shipped with text that shrank, its author listed the distortion as a con, the thread proposed AutomaticSize, and the author answered that the UI uses a size constraint and will not scale even with automatic sizing on. THE THREAD DOES NOT END THERE: the fix shipped in Update 2.0 as a card that resizes, and the author later says it was done WITH automatic sizing, after converting Scale to Offset and splitting the card into smaller frames. So the constraint did not defeat AutomaticSize permanently — it defeated it until the card was restructured. That is the useful shape of the trap: the symptom looks like a font problem, the cause is a constraint, and the cure is surgery on the layout rather than one property.

10.rule: Give colour a small fixed vocabulary, decide deliberately whether a colour is carried by the CHANNEL or by the MESSAGE, and put a stroke behind coloured text.
10.why: Blox Fruits does both on one page: three of its four tables declare a single colour for the whole section ('All of the following messages appear red in the chat boxes') while the Player Messages table colours line by line — red for danger and refusal, green for a gain, gold for an item found, magenta for materials, a blue-violet for an ability unlocking, with gold and magenta each carrying a second meaning elsewhere on the same page. So the per-message vocabulary is real but loose, and it is not how the server-wide lines are coloured at all. The stroke is that wiki's majority treatment, on 24 of its 37 coloured lines rather than on all of them; the argument for putting it behind all of yours is that coloured text over an arbitrary game world costs more legibility than it adds without one, which is reasoning rather than citation.

11.rule: One notification may carry a gain AND its caveat, coloured differently, rather than splitting into two.
11.why: Blox Fruits announces finding a fruit in green and, in the same message, warns in red that dying before eating it will lose it. Splitting that would let the warning be dismissed separately from the thing it is about.

12.rule: A REWARD POPUP NAMES THE ITEM, NOT THE CONTAINER IT CAME OUT OF — and states how many things are coming before it opens.
12.why: Tower Defense Simulator shipped a playtime claim popup that displayed the chest's name and corrected it to display the item given in v1.75.2, then added a count of how many chests a tier awards in v1.75.3. A popup that names the box has told the player nothing they were waiting to learn.

13.rule: Announce each resource on its own line; never roll a multi-resource reward into one summary.
13.why: Blox Fruits has separate announcements for money earned, experience earned with the weapon it was credited to, fragments earned, and materials obtained with a quantity — and no combined line anywhere in the 174 messages the page transcribes. (The money, EXP and fragment icons in those rows are the WIKI'S own templates, not something the page says the game draws; the only glyph transcribed inside a message string is the coin on the item-drop line. The per-line split is the finding; the icon is not.) The same reasoning the shop file records for itemising a bundle applies here: a count is not comparable, a list is.

14.rule: Keep the displayed STREAK and the index into the reward calendar as two different numbers.
14.why: Tower Defense Simulator's login rewards repeat on a 28-day table while the streak counter carries on to 29 and beyond. A day tile bound to the streak count renders nothing at all on day 29, and a streak label bound to the table position tells a 200-day player they are on day 4.

15.rule: When a timed action can be confirmed, make the countdown BECOME the confirm control, and reset it whenever the thing being confirmed changes.
15.why: Adopt Me's trade counter counts from 5 and turns into the green accept button, resetting every time either player adds or removes an item — and the wiki states the reason outright: it stops a player accepting after the contents changed. A timer beside a live button is a race the player can lose.

16.rule: An unanswered actionable notification EXPIRES, and a blocked one notifies the sender instead.
16.why: Adopt Me expires a trade request left too long, and when the recipient has requests turned off the SENDER is prompted about it. Roblox's push-notification documentation lists seven non-delivery cases, the last of which splits in two — and it also says the throttle case comes back as 'transparent feedback', so some of those failures report themselves and some do not. Delivery is never to be assumed at either end.

17.rule: Give every notification CLASS its own off switch, and where a prompt exists only to ask permission, offer a third value that grants it standingly.
17.why: BedWars lets friend-join notifications be turned off by themselves; the notification kit ships an individual switch per announcement trigger; Adopt Me's backpack-viewing consent is always allow, always ask, or never allow, defaulting to ask. 'Always allow' is the interesting one — it does not mute the notification, it removes the interaction that would have raised one.

18.rule: Express a countdown to a scheduled event as discrete announcements at decreasing intervals, not as a persistent widget.
18.why: BedWars sudden death fires at 59 seconds, at 10 seconds, and then at the event. Blox Fruits does the same for its presents event, at ten minutes, at five or one, and then at 'starting' — its other timed events pre-announce at two minutes and one. Neither game spends permanent screen space on a clock for something that happens once.

19.rule: When a cap is reached, say WHAT WAS EVICTED to make room.
19.why: BedWars reports that placing a new trap destroyed the oldest one and that a ninth spirit removed an older one, rather than simply refusing. Applied to the notification stack itself this is the honest reading of a max-on-screen cap: a notification silently dropped because three others were already up is an outcome the player never learns, and that is the one case where 'nothing was shown' is indistinguishable from 'nothing happened'.

20.rule: Put the subsystem's name in brackets at the front of any message the player's own action did not cause.
20.why: BedWars prefixes its bed-alarm and host-announcement lines that way. The prefix is what tells a player the line is not feedback on the button they just pressed, which is otherwise indistinguishable in a shared stack.

21.rule: Compose a badge or award icon for a CIRCLE, at 512×512, before composing it for the card.
21.why: Roblox's badge upload trims and crops to a circular icon and the documentation shows the failure case of text cropped away. A custom badge notification that reuses the uploaded icon inherits that crop whatever shape the card is.

22.rule: On the OUT-OF-EXPERIENCE channel: the title is already the game's name, the body is 99 characters, it is a parameterised template with an asset id, and you get one per player per day.
22.why: All four are stated in Roblox's experience-notification documentation. The one-per-day throttle is the design constraint that matters — it makes 'which single thing is worth today's slot' the actual question, and a generic come-back-and-play does not merely underperform, it spends the only slot there is.

23.rule: Never build a notification around false scarcity, a promised free thing that is not free, or a deadline that does not exist.
23.why: Roblox's notification guidelines ban all three by name, with a ten-minutes-or-miss-out example given as the prohibited case. This is the vocabulary a reward popup reaches for first, and on the notification channel it is a policy violation rather than a style choice.

screens.label: The FIRST-RUN screen, across genres — forced tutorials, skippable tutorials, spotlight-and-arrow highlights, contextual just-in-time prompts, timed hints, checklist guides, gated controls, and what any of it does for a player who already knows
demonstrates: THE SPOTLIGHT IS THREE TREATMENTS AT ONCE, NOT ONE. The page's worked example — the _Hello Kitty Cafe_ highlight — is described as the desired button spotlighted while the rest of the screen is dimmed, a coloured outline on the button, AND an arrow pointing at it. Three simultaneous marks on one target, and the docs' claim for them is that there is then 'no mistaking what the player is expected to click next'.

The docs argue the highlight against the SENTENCE, not against nothing. They print the text version — open your inventory by clicking on the backpack button — and object that it makes the player interpret the word 'backpack' and then hunt the UI for it. The arrow removes the interpretation step, and that is the stated reason to prefer it.

A hint PERSISTS until the step is done rather than timing out: persistent visual elements 'stay on-screen until the player has completed a step of the tutorial', and the docs give wandering off as the case they are designed for — 'even if they choose to explore, the hints remain to guide them when they are ready to return'. A hint that expires punishes exactly the player it exists for.

Three named techniques, and they are three different mechanisms rather than three intensities of one: visual elements (arrows, particles, trails, in-world signs), contextual tutorials, and timed hints.

CONTEXTUAL TUTORIALS TRIGGER ON STATE, NOT ON PLACE. The example is _Squishmallows_: the combination-station tutorial fires when the player has two identical Squishmallows in their inventory. The stated reason to keep it out of the first-run sequence is that it 'would make it too long and irrelevant, and players may forget the information before they can use it'.

The same game uses a contextual tutorial for its MARKETPLACE deliberately, because the marketplace serves mid and late-game players — so a feature a new player cannot use yet is taught when they find it, not at minute one.

THE TIMED-HINT DELAY IS MEASURED, NOT CHOSEN. The worked example: playtesting finds most players press the button within 10 seconds, so the highlight is added at 11 seconds. The rule stated around it is that a timed hint should appear only AFTER the majority have already completed the objective, and that the balance to find is between firing so fast the player feels denied the chance to work it out and waiting so long they are frustrated.

Timed hints 'only appear the first time the task is presented' and should be 'sufficient to help struggling players after only being shown once'. One showing, first occurrence only, to the subset that needs it.

The hint system outlives the first session: the docs' own example of surfacing an overlooked feature is highlighting the trade button for a player who has not engaged with trading in their FIRST TWO SESSIONS.

A directional trail 'strongly suggests an action, but doesn't require it', and the docs claim the availability of choice is what makes the tutorial feel less forced. This is an argument for a non-blocking guide over a modal.

In _Color or Die_ a sign explaining the core survival mechanic is placed in the player's line of sight at the moment they collect their first paint bucket — described as impossible to miss, and as not preventing the player from starting the game. Prominence and non-blocking are treated as compatible.

The accessibility case is made in construction terms: arrows and particle effects 'communicate without words and don't require translation to be understood by a global audience', the docs count not having to 'worry about a text string getting longer after translation' as a benefit to the UI designer, and on mobile 'text can be too small to read comfortably'.

A feedback list is given for _Winds of Fortune_ — hit flashes, damage numbers flying off the enemy, a throbbing red low-health screen effect, both health meters updating, coins flying out on a kill, and the quest counter incrementing. What the docs claim for the combination is narrower than 'no tutorial': it 'ensures most players understand what's happening without a needing more explicit combat tutorial' (the missing word is the source's). Six feedback signals that make the lesson smaller, not a lesson deleted.

The closing warning is about the absence of feedback, not about teaching: without it players 'may not know that the action they took did anything, and wonder if they did something wrong, or wonder if the game is buggy'.

The FTUE is defined as 'the first few minutes of gameplay', and the docs say outright what it introduces, in this order: the game, the INTERFACE, and the mechanics. The interface is a first-class subject of onboarding rather than the container onboarding happens in.

Its success is defined by exactly two things — Day 1 retention and the onboarding goals — and D1 retention is defined as the share of players who make it through the FTUE. The tutorial is measured as a funnel that is 'widest at the top and narrowest at the bottom', and 'all games lose some amount of players along this path'.

The two designs Roblox names as the canonical A/B test against each other are 'a shorter dialogue sequence versus a guided arrow'. Those are treated as substitutes for the same job, which is the clearest signal in the docs that dialogue is one option and not the default.

Teaching the essentials is split into two obligations, not one: the player must grasp controls for navigation and interaction, AND the core loop. On the second the docs are explicit that the player must understand both what they are expected to do and WHY they should do it.

Complex, unfamiliar controls are to be DISPLAYED ON SCREEN, and the illustration named is a control readout from Super Striker League. A persistent control legend is a documented onboarding element, separate from any tutorial sequence.
Early XP thresholds should be kept low so the player levels up quickly, which makes the first level-up an onboarding beat rather than a progression one.

The docs prescribe ending onboarding with 'an intentionally designed moment of joy' — rewards, animation, celebratory effects at a milestone — and the stated purpose is the NEXT session, not this one.

By the end of onboarding the player should be aware of the full range of content available, with short, mid and long-term goals surfaced 'in highly visible places, either in the game-world or the UI'. The last thing onboarding does is point at things it did not teach.

THE ENGINE SHIPS A SEPARATE CALL FOR ONBOARDING. LogOnboardingFunnelStepEvent exists alongside the general LogFunnelStepEvent, and the difference is that the onboarding one is a ONE-TIME funnel: it takes no funnelSessionId, because the FTUE is defined as happening once per user. The engine has already decided that the first run is not repeatable.

A step is logged AFTER the player completes it, and the docs say the important thing is consistency about when the call is made and using 'easy-to-interpret names'. A step carries BOTH parts, not one: the call is LogOnboardingFunnelStepEvent(player, stepNumber, stepName), and the worked example passes `1, -- Step number` alongside `"In Farm" -- Step name`. The number orders the funnel; the name is what a human reads off the dashboard. The name is also droppable — the docs' own exploit-protection example logs (player, step) with the number alone.

A SKIP BUTTON SILENTLY FALSIFIES THE FUNNEL. The docs state that if you log step 3 without logging steps 1 or 2, the funnel considers 1 and 2 completed. A tutorial that jumps a skipping player to the end and logs it therefore reports that player as having finished every step.
Repeated steps are ignored — only the first instance of a step counts — which is why a player who disconnects and rejoins mid-tutorial needs no special handling in a one-time funnel.

Events can only be sent from the SERVER and only in published games; nothing can be logged from the client or from Studio. A tutorial that lives entirely in a LocalScript cannot report itself, and the docs' own example crosses that gap with a RemoteEvent.

That RemoteEvent is shown WITH its exploit: the client example deliberately fires step 10 on a three-step tutorial, and the server example rejects any step above maxStep before logging. Tutorial progress arriving from the client is untrusted input.

Filters apply ONLY to the first step of a funnel, so a player who starts the tutorial on mobile and finishes on desktop is attributed to mobile throughout. Device-specific onboarding cannot be read out of a mid-funnel breakdown.

Roblox's own reference project, Plant, is shown losing 70% of players between step 1 ('In Farm') and step 2 ('Plant Seed'). The published remedies are contextual indicators directing users to plant, or requiring a successful plant before the rest of the game opens.
A funnel step rename shows as a WARNING on the dashboard for any date range spanning the change, which is the engine admitting that a renamed step breaks comparability with its own history.

THE RETURNING-PLAYER CHECK IS A ROBLOX BADGE, NOT A SAVE FLAG. On first join an opening cutscene plays, and then: a player without the badge for beating the Tutorial is 'instantly sent to the Boot Camp mission which they have to complete', and a player who has it 'will be left in the Main Lobby'. Badge ownership is queryable from any server and survives a data-store failure; a profile flag does not.

The tutorial is FORCED and says so — the player "you are forced to complete at least the first mission". It is also replayable afterwards, from Settings: the update history records a bug where 'beating the Tutorial for the first time through settings does not reward the badge', which only makes sense if Settings carries a replay entry.

SKIPPING AND COMPLETING WERE CONFUSED FOR A YEAR. The 24 February 2024 entry records that skipping the tutorial still awarded the badge; it was fixed on 8 March 2024 and REGRESSED on 15 March 2024. Because the badge is also the gate, a skip that awards it is a skip that permanently turns the tutorial off.

THE HUD IS EDITED FOR THE LESSON. Base health is replaced by a progress bar, because losing by letting enemies reach the exit was made impossible on 25 June 2025. A number the game is built around is removed from the screen for the duration of teaching rather than left there showing a value that can no longer move.

The interface is progressively LOCKED, not progressively revealed, and each lock is a dated decision: consumables hotbar disabled (23 May 2024), only towers the narrator asks for are selectable (20 November 2024), access to Settings removed (30 April 2025), Skills disabled (28 May 2025). The tutorial narrows the interface to the one control being taught.

Loadout and cosmetics are overridden too: the player's chosen towers 'are replaced the moment the match starts', all skins are replaced with Default and golden perks are not applied. The tutorial refuses to run against player-authored state — and the one time a skin leaked through, it broke the lesson (31 July 2026: a non-default Sniper skin 'causes Wave 2 to break').

THE SOFTLOCK IS THE CHARACTERISTIC FAILURE OF A SCRIPTED TUTORIAL, and this page records four of them. Upgrading too fast could leave the player short of cash with no way forward; selecting the consumables hotbar could stop the requested action from registering; towers in the hotbar could become unselectable; opening the emote/sticker wheel could remove the inventory entirely, 'preventing progress until the player rejoins'. Every one is a step that waits on an exact state the player can leave.

One softlock survived a rejoin: a player who spent all their tutorial coins in a brief window where menus were not yet blocked could not buy the thing the next step required, 'and upon rejoining, also preventing finishing the Tutorial'. A tutorial that writes to persistent data mid-sequence can brick itself.

A BALANCE CHANGE BROKE THE TUTORIAL TWICE IN ONE DAY. On 11 March 2026 a tower price change made the Sniper unaffordable on Wave 2, 'making the Tutorial impossible to beat'; a hotfix raised the wave's cash the same day. A scripted tutorial is coupled to the live economy and has to be re-tested against every tuning pass.
