rules.note: Distilled from the references above. Numeric values come from the sources that stated them — chiefly Roblox's own interactive-ui tutorial, whose property values are exact — and are marked approximate where they were read from a fan recreation instead. Units are Roblox UI units. Colour is deliberately absent except where it is structural: a settings screen takes its palette from whichever genre theme wraps it.

panelShape.why: the official tutorial's settings menu is wider than tall and clamped in pixels at both ends; a settings screen is a row list and rows are horizontal, so the tall portrait sheet a shop uses is the wrong container. The clamp is what keeps it from becoming a 1600px strip on a monitor or a 250px sliver on a phone.

entryPoint.placement: an existing HUD launcher rail, beside the shop or inventory button
observedPositions: beside Crew/Ally in the HUD cluster (Blox Fruits)
entryPoint.never: a lone floating text button labelled SETTINGS
entryPoint.why: four independent shipped games put settings on the same rail as the other launchers and identify it by a gear; none of them give it its own bespoke corner

header.layout: single row, title flush left, close flush right
header.why: the DOORS recreation is a space-between flex row with a 300% title and a 45px close image; the official tutorial pins its close to the same corner. A settings screen does NOT get the overhanging plaque banner the simulator genre file mandates for shop panels — every settings reference keeps the title inside the panel.

closeButton.why: exact values from the official tutorial; it is an ImageButton with a 1:1 aspect constraint, so the close affordance is an icon in a square, never a text button in the footer

saveAffordance.rule: there is none — a change applies the instant the control moves, and the screen persists on close
saveAffordance.quote: item asylum: 'Options automatically save after leaving'
saveAffordance.theOnlyFooterButtonThatEarnsItsPlace: Reset to Default, and it is SCOPED to one section rather than the whole screen (BedWars scopes it to Controls)
saveAffordance.why: not one of the eight shipped references has a Save button. Save-and-Cancel is a desktop-application convention; on Roblox the control IS the commit, and a generator that emits a Save button has produced a screen no player will trust or press

grouping.headerStyle: all-caps text label, no box, no stroke, rows hanging directly beneath
grouping.why: DOORS runs two inline caps headers (VOLUME, MISC); 3008 crosses four groups and becomes four category tabs (Video, Audio, Gameplay, Controls); BedWars runs five named sections one of which holds a single row. The threshold sits between three and four. A flat twenty-row list appears nowhere.

sectionNaming.rule: name sections by DOMAIN, not by control type
sectionNaming.why: every shipped reference groups by what the setting affects; grouping by widget is a developer's mental model, not a player's

row.structure: label line, optional description line beneath it in quieter text, control flush right and vertically centred across both lines
row.controlColumn: right-aligned and ALIGNED ACROSS EVERY ROW in a section — one control column, not per-row positioning
row.descriptionLine: written in the game's own voice, one short sentence ('Toggles the damage indicators when you hit someone')
row.why: row size from the official tutorial (0.8 x 0.1 of the panel); the description line is item asylum's per-row in-game copy, and the two critique threads both name uneven spacing and mismatched text sizes as the first thing a viewer notices

rowLayout.mechanism: UIListLayout with FillDirection Horizontal, HorizontalFlex Fill, VerticalAlignment Center
rowLayout.why: exact from the official tutorial. The leading icon at 250% of the row height deliberately breaks the row's vertical band — the icon is bigger than its row, which is what stops a settings list reading as a spreadsheet

controlVocabulary.why: THE STRONGEST FINDING IN THIS FILE. Across Roblox's own settings tab and seven shipped games, a multi-option setting is always a CYCLE — the control shows the current value and advances to the next on click (Camera mode cycles four values; Movement mode three; Graphics mode two; item asylum's Shiftlock Angle three, with the arrow glyph itself as the value). Not one reference opens a list. A generator that reaches for a dropdown has produced a web form, and it will also have produced a control that needs a scrolling popup layer on a 375px phone screen.

cycleSelector.rule: the control displays the CURRENT value and advances on click; the glyph or word is the value
cycleSelector.why: Graphics mode is 2, Shiftlock Angle and Movement mode are 3, Camera mode is 4. Beyond roughly four a cycle stops being usable, and no reference went beyond four

toggle.rule: the control carries its own state; the row's default state is a known property of the row
toggle.why: every shipped wiki states a default per row ('It is on by default', 'This Option is Turned On By Default', a Default column in item asylum's table). A settings screen that cannot say what default means cannot offer Reset to Default either

slider.fillGrows: left to right from the track's left edge
slider.drag: UIDragDetector, DragStyle TranslateLine, ResponseStyle Scale, BoundingUI = the track
slider.why: all exact from the official tutorial. Three things a generator gets wrong without this: the track is CAPPED at 30px however big the panel gets, the knob is 120% of the track so it OVERHANGS it top and bottom, and the fill sits UNDER the knob (ZIndex 2 vs 3). A knob flush inside the track reads as a progress bar, not a control.

sliderValueReadout.rule: a slider always shows its value — as a count of discrete bars, as a number beside the track, or as an editable numeric field
sliderValueReadout.why: Roblox's own sliders are ten bars with 'no bars being mute'; the DevForum settings-slider tutorial pairs the bar with an editable 0-100 TextBox; BedWars states FOV as '80 as default. (70 - 100)'. A bare fill with no readout appears in none of the shipped references, and a volume slider that cannot reach silence is a bug in the control, not a choice

numericEntry.rule: a typed numeric value is COMMITTED by a separate control, not applied per keystroke
numericEntry.quote: 3008: 'Setting this to a value and clicking the check'
numericEntry.why: the only reference with free numeric entry gives it an explicit commit affordance and states each field's range and default (rotation 1-360, defaults 45 / 90 / 15). Roblox's own menu went the other way and REMOVED typed sensitivity entry in 2020 — so typed entry is the exception, earned by a value a slider cannot express

observed: Area / Death Sounds / Item Music / Emote (item asylum)
audioRows.why: unanimous across the shipped references and independently the documented accessibility recommendation. A single master volume is the single most common tell that a settings screen was invented rather than observed

reduceEffectsCluster.rule: a settings screen carries a reduce-effects group, and it is not the same thing as a graphics group
reduceEffectsCluster.why: appears in five independent shipped references. These rows are framed as comfort and competitive clarity, not as performance

performanceCluster.rule: a named preset that says what it REMOVES, not a quality number
observed: Fast Mode — 'removes all textures... especially for mobile'
Low Graphics Mode — 'Makes all objects a simple color'
performanceCluster.why: three shipped references ship a performance group aimed explicitly at mobile, and each names its mechanism. Roblox's own 1-10 graphics slider already exists in the Esc menu, so a game duplicating it adds nothing

dependentRows.greyOutWhen: the state is temporary and the player can change it — a parent row's value, a mode, a permission the developer toggles at runtime
dependentRows.removeWhen: the difference is permanent for this player or this device — wrong platform, unowned gamepass, absent role
dependentRows.why: Roblox greys camera/movement mode when the developer disabled them and keeps graphics quality visible-but-inert while the mode is Automatic; 3008 HIDES the watch row when the gamepass is not owned and BedWars HIDES Mobile Shift Lock on PC. The two behaviours are not interchangeable: a greyed row teaches the player what would unlock it, a hidden row would only confuse

platformVariance.rule: the screen declares that it varies by device and hides rows the device can never use
platformVariance.quote: BedWars: 'Some Options May Vary By Device'
hiddenOnDesktop: mobile-only movement aids (mobile shift lock, on-screen punch button, mobile crosshair)
platformVariance.contested: Ability Wars SHOWS its mobile rows on every device; BedWars, DOORS and 3008 hide platform-exclusive rows. Three of four hide, so hide — but the disagreement is real and is recorded rather than smoothed over
platformVariance.why: this is the rule most likely to be missing from an invented settings screen, because an inventing model has only ever seen one platform's screenshot

keybindSection.placement: inside the settings surface but as its OWN tab or page, never interleaved with toggle rows
keybindSection.platform: keyboard and gamepad only; absent on touch
keybindSection.row: action name left, a BUTTON showing the current binding right
states: listening (label replaced by a waiting marker)
rejected (the key is already bound to another action)
keybindSection.resetAffordance: Reset to Default, scoped to this section
keybindSection.why: 3008 keeps a separate 'Keybinds Menu (PC or Console Only)'; BedWars calls the section 'Controls (PC Only)' and gives it its own reset; Roblox moved its own Controls list into settings in 2022. The keybind row is the one row whose control is neither a toggle nor a slider, which is why it gets its own page

keybindGlyph.rule: the displayed key is read from the binding, never hardcoded
api: InputAction.PreferredBinding (read-only, updates as the device changes)
InputActionLabel to render it with no script
keybindGlyph.oneActionManyBindings: separate InputBinding children per device family (keyboard/mouse, gamepad, touch), so a controls list is per-device and the same action shows a different glyph on each
keybindGlyph.why: documented engine behaviour; a hardcoded 'E' is wrong the moment a controller is plugged in

aboutStrip.rule: reserve a corner or footer strip for the non-settings the settings panel is always asked to host — Codes, Update Log, Credits, server region and server age — visually separated so a tap there is not mistaken for a setting
observed: Blox Fruits: Codes and Update Log sit among the setting rows
Ability Wars: Update Log and Credits top-right, server age and region top-left
3008: Credits and Donations beside the categories
Roblox's own menu: version readouts behind an Advanced Settings category at the bottom
aboutStrip.why: four independent references put non-settings on this screen. Pretending they do not exist forces the generator to invent a second panel the player will never find

motion.open: Position tweens from (0.5, 0.4) to (0.5, 0.5) with bounce easing over 0.5s, Visible set true
motion.why: exact from the official tutorial: the panel rises a short distance with an overshoot and it does not animate out. The asymmetry is the point — an exit animation delays the player returning to play. The suppression rule is Roblox's documented accessibility signal, and it applies to exactly this tween

responsiveSizing.rule: Scale for position and size, AnchorPoint for origin, UISizeConstraint for the pixel clamp, layouts for the rows; branch on ViewportDisplaySize Small / Medium / Large via style queries
responsiveSizing.why: documented cross-platform guidance, and the official settings menu is built exactly this way

textSizing.rule: one text size for every row label on the screen, a second quieter size for description lines, and a UITextSizeConstraint rather than TextScaled
textSizing.why: both critique threads open with inconsistent text size as the first visible fault, and the accessibility documentation states that TextScaled BYPASSES the player's PreferredTextSize preference — so the settings screen, of all screens, must not use it

strokeAndRadius.why: read from the DOORS wiki's recreation, so approximate. Recorded because it CONTRADICTS the simulator genre file's 4px stroke and 20px radius: the settings screen is the least decorated panel in the game, and the critique threads confirm that stray strokes on small controls are the first thing a viewer spots. Where a genre theme mandates a heavier stroke, apply it to the panel edge only, not to every row and toggle

screens.label: The SHOP screen, across genres — tab rows, product grids, price pills, owned states, featured banners, currency headers, confirm dialogs
demonstrates: The Robux confirmation step is NOT the shop's to draw. PromptGamePassPurchase hands off to Roblox's own purchase dialog, and the shop only learns the outcome from the PromptGamePassPurchaseFinished event — a custom 'Are you sure?' in front of that puts two modals in a row.

A tile's name, price and description are read from GetProductInfo with Enum.InfoType.GamePass; the page's own framing for that call is displaying product information 'inside your game's marketplace', i.e. the shop screen is the documented consumer of that data.

Ownership is a QUERY, not a stored flag on the tile: UserOwnsGamePassAsync wrapped in pcall, and the docs say to run it on PlayerAdded so the state is already correct the first time the shop is opened.

Privileges are granted server-side from ServerScriptService, so the OWNED the tile renders is a mirror of server truth rather than the source of it — a client that flips its own tile to OWNED has changed nothing.

LOWER CONFIDENCE, recorded as such: the WebSearch result summary for this same docs page (2026-09-20) states that UserOwnsGamePassAsync can return false immediately after an in-experience purchase because of caching. That sentence was not in the fetched render, so it is noted rather than relied on — but it is the reason the finished-event payload, not a re-poll, should flip the tile.
PromptProductPurchase likewise raises Roblox's own confirmation dialog; the shop's job ends at the prompt call and resumes at ProcessReceipt.

Developer products are repurchasable without limit — they are consumables — so a product tile must NEVER acquire an owned state; the pass tile and the product tile are two different components that happen to sit in the same grid.

ProcessReceipt returns Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted or NotProcessedYet, and NotProcessedYet retries on the next join, so the tile's success feedback is owed to a server result and not to the prompt closing.

GetProductInfo with Enum.InfoType.Product returns Name, PriceInRobux, Description, IconImageAssetId and IsForSale — five fields that map one-to-one onto a tile's five slots, including an IsForSale that should remove the tile rather than grey it.
GetDeveloperProductsAsync returns all products at once, which is the documented way to populate a storefront — the grid is generated from data, not hand-placed.

The shop ships as seven named pieces, and the split IS the convention: a Main Background, a separate Shop Content sheet, a Tab Button, a Purchase Button, an Exit Button, an Open Shop Button and a Shine overlay.

'Main Background' and 'Shop Content' being two distinct pieces means the outer frame and the scrollable content area are never the same surface — the frame holds the chrome, the content sheet holds the grid.
The Tab Button is ONE reusable piece, so tabs are instances of a single template differing only by label and selected state, never hand-drawn per category.
A 'Shine' layer exists as its own element above the panel: the gloss is an overlay, not baked into the panel fill, and can therefore be removed or dimmed without redrawing the panel.

Currency icons are supplied per currency — gem, Robux, gold, and a separate gold-plus — rather than one generic coin, which says a price is an icon plus a number and the icon is selected by WHICH currency, not decorative.
The Open Shop Button is published as a piece of the set but is not part of the shop frame, which matches the tutorial row below: the opener lives outside the thing it toggles.

The first thing reviewers read off the screenshot was the ABSENCE of a layout object: inconsistent gaps between items told them the author was not using UIGridLayout. Uneven gutters are the tell that a shop was positioned by hand.
Second critique was stroke: outlines should be THICKER. This is the same finding simulator.json records — a shop that is otherwise right still reads wrong when the stroke is thin.
Third was padding: button contents felt cramped, meaning a card needs interior padding of its own and cannot rely on the grid's gutter to breathe.
Buttons expanded too far on hover, and selected items overflowed past the container edge — the hover scale must stay inside the cell.

The author's own note is the mechanical trap: the enlarged card sits in a ScrollingFrame and goes beyond its size, and UICorner does not solve that. A hover that grows a cell inside a scroller either gets clipped or spills.
Reviewers asked for UICorner on ALL buttons and on nested components — a single unrounded child inside a rounded card is visible.
The tab set was Coins, Levels and Rebirths — tabs named after WHAT IS SOLD, never after price band or vendor. Three tabs is an unremarkable count.

Reviewers said the category buttons 'seem a bit out of place being green': tab pills belong to the panel's own colour family, and green reads as the confirm/buy accent, so spending it on navigation misdirects the eye.
The same reviewer asked for the close button in a lighter colour so it sits in the theme rather than fighting it.
A flat panel drew the note that gradients would help — depth on the panel is expected, not optional decoration.

The author had put a background element in the bottom right and reviewers still proposed a fuller background frame treatment, i.e. a shop panel is expected to have a distinct interior surface behind the content, not bare panel colour.
Two tabs, Game Passes and Coin Packs — the minimum honest shop is one durable tab and one consumable tab, because the two have different states and cannot share a tile.
Four coin packs and three game passes: a tab holds three to four items, not twenty. The shop is a short curated list, and the grid is sized for that.
Each product carries an icon chip and a description line, so a tile is not icon-plus-price; the description is a first-class slot.
Exactly one 'BEST VALUE' badge across the coin packs — the tag is a singleton per ladder, and its job is to break the tie between tiers.
The buy button has two LIVE states, Buy and Owned, swapped at runtime rather than being two separate elements the author remembers to toggle.

Owned state is persisted on the player profile and the pass service only re-verifies passes the saved profile does not already have, so OWNED survives a MarketplaceService outage instead of flickering back to a sellable Buy.
Purchase feedback is a toast with a sound hook — the confirmation of success is in-shop and transient, not a second modal.
The whole catalogue lives in two config files, so tiles are generated from data; a shop with hand-placed tiles cannot be re-priced.
The default view is a HOME PAGE of featured products, distinct from category browsing — opening the shop does not land you on the first category, it lands you on a curated page.
Categories and subcategories are both supported and a product may appear in more than one category, so the tab row is a filter over one catalogue, not a set of separate shops.
Callout stickers are a named, enumerated set: 'Top Seller', 'Best Deal', 'New', 'Sale'. They are stickers ON a card, not a different card.

A product has title, subtitle AND description as three separate text slots, plus its own image, background and colour — the card template carries per-product colour rather than one shop-wide tile colour.
Multiple virtual currencies coexist with Robux developer products in the same store, and the player's currency is shown in the header.

rules.note: Distilled from the references above. This is a SCREEN, not a genre: the geometry tokens (stroke weight, radius, bevel, text stroke) come from the genre file the shop is being built in — simulator.json for a cartoony game. What is here is the shop's own construction: what parts it has, in what order, in what states, and which decisions the engine has already made for you.

shell.form: one centred modal sheet over a dimmed backdrop, opened and closed by a button that is NOT a descendant of the sheet
shell.backdropConfidence: the dim itself is attested only by a search summary; the centred modal and the outside opener are attested by fetched pages
shell.why: the tutorial series makes the outside opener its one emphasised structural rule, because an opener nested inside the frame it hides cannot reopen it — this is the single most common way a generated shop ships broken

surfaceSplit.rule: three surfaces, never two: an outer panel carrying the chrome, an inner content sheet in a different tint holding the scrollable grid, and the cards on top of it
surfaceSplit.why: the published graphics set ships 'Main Background' and 'Shop Content' as separate pieces, and a feedback thread still asked for a fuller interior background on a shop that had none — a flat panel loses its grid

contains: the player's balance for every currency this shop spends
header.balancePosition: opposite end of the header from the title
header.why: two independent sources put the balance in the header rather than in the world HUD, and a shop that does not show what you can afford forces the player to close it to check

currencyReadout.rule: icon then number, inside a pill, one pill per currency; the icon is chosen by which currency it is and is never a generic coin
currencyReadout.iconSizing: size the currency icon to the text beside it, not to the container it sits in
currencyReadout.why: the graphics set ships four distinct currency icons rather than one, and the loudest single critique in the tier-card thread was an oversized Robux icon

tabRow.position: directly under the header, above the content sheet
tabRow.naming: named by WHAT IS SOLD (Passes, Currency, Boosts, Cosmetics, Bundles) — never by price band, vendor or rarity
tabRow.template: one reusable tab component differing only by label and selected state
tabRow.colour: tabs stay in the panel's own colour family; the accent/confirm colour is reserved for buy actions
tabRow.why: three fetched sources give real tab sets and all three name them by merchandise, and reviewers specifically called green tab pills 'out of place' because green is the buy colour

tabSplitByState.rule: durable goods (passes) and consumables (developer products) go in DIFFERENT tabs, because their tiles have different states
tabSplitByState.minimumShop: one durable tab plus one consumable tab
tabSplitByState.why: a pass tile terminates in OWNED and a product tile never does; putting them in one grid forces one template to carry two incompatible end states

subCategories.rule: a tab may be subdivided inside itself (by region, level band, season); a subdivision never promotes itself to a top-level tab
subCategories.why: a shipped five-tab shop splits its currency tab by game region rather than adding three more tabs, which is what keeps the tab row under five

landingView.rule: the shop opens on a curated featured page, not on the first category
landingView.why: the store framework ships a home page of featured products distinct from category browsing, and a shop that opens on 'Category 1' has no way to promote anything

featuredBanner.form: full-width band at the top of the landing view, taller than a grid tile, its own background tint, larger art, its own price control
featuredBanner.why: the featured band is the only element that can carry an offer bigger than a tile, and more than one band turns the landing view into a second grid

grid.columnsBy: card content, not by taste — an icon-and-price square tile runs 4 across; a card carrying a description line runs 2 to 3 across; a row card with icon/text/price laid left-to-right runs 1 across
grid.itemsPerTab: 3 to 6 is normal; a shop tab is a short curated list
grid.layoutObject: UIGridLayout for tiles, UIListLayout for row cards — never hand-positioned
grid.why: the description slot is what forces the column count, and the very first thing reviewers read off a shop screenshot was uneven gutters telling them no layout object was used

gridSizing.canvas: ScrollingFrame.AutomaticCanvasSize = Y with CanvasSize reset to {0,0},{0,0}
gridSizing.responsive: recompute CellSize from the ScrollingFrame's AbsoluteSize on change, rather than expressing the cell as a fraction
gridSizing.why: scale-sized cells feed back into AbsoluteSize as the canvas grows and the grid inflates without bound, and AutomaticCanvasSize mis-measures Scale padding — this is a documented engine behaviour, not a style preference

cardAnatomy.textSlots: title, optional subtitle, optional description — three distinct slots, not one blob
cardAnatomy.perCardColour: the template carries a per-product colour and background, so tiles are allowed to differ from each other
cardAnatomy.padding: every card has interior UIPadding of its own and does not rely on the grid gutter
cardAnatomy.corners: UICorner on the card AND on every nested button and chip
cardAnatomy.why: the row anatomy is specified in that exact left/centre/right order by one source and the icon-chip-plus-description tile by another, and 'contents feel cramped' plus 'add UICorner to nested components' were both explicit critiques

priceDisplay.rule: currency icon then number, as one centred group INSIDE the buy button, or in a pill when the button is separate
priceDisplay.never: bare price text floating beside the button
priceDisplay.numberFormat: tight number with the prefix separated — a consumable states what you gain, written with a leading plus
priceDisplay.why: reviewers asked for the icon and price to be centred in the button as a single group, and criticised loose spacing inside the number while insisting the gap to the plus stay

priceSource.rule: read Name, PriceInRobux, Description and the icon from GetProductInfo / GetDeveloperProductsAsync at runtime; never hardcode a Robux price into the tile
priceSource.why: two independent fetched sources give the same reason: the price can be changed on the website and a hardcoded tile then lies about it

tierLadder.spread: multiplicative — a shipped ladder runs roughly 30x from cheapest to dearest across five steps
tierLadder.why: reviewers asked for progressively larger pack art matching rising price points, and a shipped five-tier ladder spans R$50 to R$1,499 — a linear ladder of near-equal steps gives the player nothing to compare

calloutTag.form: a sticker ON the card, not a different card
calloutTag.count: at most one per card, and at most one BEST-VALUE-class tag per ladder
calloutTag.why: the tag exists to break the tie between tiers, and a second one on the same ladder destroys the only job it has

ownedState.rule: swap the price control for an OWNED chip, mark it (a check glyph), and make the control non-interactive — all three at once
ownedState.never: leave the price visible and grey out the button
ownedState.implementation: an overlay child of the button toggled visible, so the card keeps its identity and position rather than being rebuilt
ownedState.thirdState: unknown — every ownership call is inside a pcall, so the tile needs a pending/unknown look and not just owned/unowned
ownedState.why: one source specifies checkmark + Owned label + disabled together, another shows the overlay-child mechanism, and simulator.json independently records that replacing the price beats greying it — a greyed price still reads as something to compare against your balance

ownedRefresh.singleFunction: one named refresh re-run from all three, so one place decides what OWNED looks like
ownedRefresh.flipFrom: the finished event's outcome, not an immediate re-query
ownedRefresh.persistence: cache ownership on the player's profile and re-verify only what the profile does not already have, so OWNED survives a MarketplaceService outage instead of flickering back to Buy
ownedRefresh.why: the three trigger points are specified in a working thread, and a shipped kit advertises outage-survival as a feature precisely because a re-query can come back false right after a purchase

consumableState.rule: a developer-product tile NEVER becomes owned; it shows the quantity the player already holds ('You have 340 coins') and stays buyable
consumableState.why: developer products are repurchasable without limit by design, so an owned state on one is a functional bug dressed as a style choice

confirmDialog.robux: do NOT draw one — PromptProductPurchase and PromptGamePassPurchase raise Roblox's own confirmation; a custom one in front of it stacks two modals
confirmDialog.softCurrency: DO draw one — a single dialog restating item and price with two buttons, confirm in the accent colour and cancel quiet
confirmDialog.why: Roblox's documentation makes the Robux dialog the engine's, while a shop article prescribes a confirmation for in-game spends specifically to prevent accidental transactions — the two paths look alike on the card and are completely different behind it

purchaseOutcome.success: a transient in-shop toast plus a sound; the card flips state in place and the shop does NOT close
purchaseOutcome.authority: success is owed to the server result (ProcessReceipt / the finished event), never to the prompt closing
purchaseOutcome.why: a shipped kit's feedback is a toast with a sound hook rather than a second modal, and the receipt callback can return NotProcessedYet, which means the prompt closing proves nothing

insufficientFunds.rule: the buy control becomes a route to the currency tab, not a dead grey button
insufficientFunds.why: the shop already knows the balance from its own header, and a dead button ends the session where a route continues it

serverAuthority.rule: every price check and every deduction happens on the server; the client's card is informational only
serverAuthority.why: stated outright by one source and demonstrated by another's RemoteEvent flow, where the server re-reads the balance before deducting — a client that spends its own currency is not a shop, it is a suggestion

closeControl.shape: circle in the danger colour, overhanging the top-right corner of the OUTER panel
closeControl.tone: keep it inside the theme rather than letting it be the loudest thing on screen
closeControl.why: simulator.json records the overhanging red circle across six references, and a shop feedback thread independently asked for the close button in a lighter colour so it stops fighting the panel

hoverState.scale: bounded — the grown card must stay inside its cell
hoverState.clipping: a card that grows past its cell inside a ScrollingFrame is clipped, and UICorner does not fix it; grow within the cell or animate something other than size
hoverState.why: an author hit exactly this and said so in the thread, and reviewers separately reported buttons expanding too large and selected items overflowing the container

depth.rule: gradient on the panel, symmetrical bevel on the buy button, a separate shine/gloss layer above the panel rather than baked into its fill
depth.why: the shine ships as its own piece in the graphics set so it can be dimmed without redrawing the panel, and both feedback threads asked for gradients and a symmetrical bevel on flat work

dataDriven.rule: the catalogue is config; tiles are generated from it and the grid is populated from GetDeveloperProductsAsync or an equivalent list
dataDriven.why: a shipped kit puts its whole catalogue in two config files, and Roblox documents fetching all products at once to populate a storefront — a shop with hand-placed tiles cannot be re-priced or re-ordered

responsive.rule: one layout that reflows: columns collapse toward 1 on phone, text scales, cells are constrained rather than free
responsive.why: the store framework targets PC, tablet and mobile from a single auto-sizing layout, and a shop article gives 2–3 columns desktop against 1 on mobile from the same markup

screens.label: The SOCIAL surfaces — friend lists with presence, party and guild/clan rosters, rank ladders, chat channels and tabs, chat tags, invite flows and the moderation controls that sit on all of them
demonstrates: A chat surface is FOUR configuration objects, not one: ChatWindowConfiguration, ChatInputBarConfiguration, ChannelTabsConfiguration and BubbleChatConfiguration. Each can be disabled independently, so 'hide the chat' is four different decisions — a game can keep bubbles over heads while removing the window entirely.

Two channels exist by default and they are not symmetric: RBXGeneral carries player messages and RBXSystem carries the game's own announcements. A system line is a MESSAGE IN A CHANNEL, not a separate toast layer.

A user in a channel is its own object — TextSource — and a user in three channels is THREE TextSources, each carrying that user's permissions in that channel. Whether someone can type is therefore a per-channel fact, so a muted-in-guild-chat state cannot be a flag on the player.

A chat command is a first-class instance (TextChatCommand with PrimaryAlias and SecondaryAlias) parented to the service, not a string compared inside a message handler. Commands and messages diverge at SendAsync: a command fires Triggered and STOPS — it never reaches the server's delivery path or any other client.

Every display callback must be NON-YIELDING. ShouldDeliverCallback, OnIncomingMessage, OnBubbleAdded and OnChatWindowAdded all block the whole chat system if they wait, which forbids the obvious implementation of a rank badge — look the rank up when the message arrives.

A sent message is drawn TWICE on the sender's own screen: once locally the moment SendAsync is called, and again when the server's processed copy comes back through MessageReceived. The local draw is optimistic and the second copy replaces it, so the message list is keyed and updated rather than appended to.

ShouldDeliverCallback runs on the server once PER TextSource in the channel, which is what makes proximity chat and permission-scoped delivery possible — the same message is a separate yes/no decision for every recipient.

THE CHANNEL TAB ROW IS OFF BY DEFAULT. Roblox ships the window and the input bar enabled and the tabs disabled, so the default shipped Roblox chat is a single undifferentiated stream and every multi-channel game has turned tabs on deliberately.

Tab names are assigned by the engine from a fixed table and two of the four are not what a designer would pick: RBXGeneral becomes 'General', RBXSystem is FOLDED INTO the General tab rather than getting its own, RBXTeam becomes 'Team', and RBXWhisper is titled with the USER NAME OF THE OTHER PLAYER. A whisper tab is named after a person; every other tab is named after a function.

A custom TextChannel's tab takes the channel's Instance.Name, and the overview page warns that two channels sharing a name causes unintended behaviour in the default window — so the channel name is an identity key, not a label.

THE SELECTED TAB DIFFERS FROM AN UNSELECTED ONE BY TEXT COLOUR ALONE. The full property list carries HoverBackgroundColor3 but NO selected-background property: the only selection-state property in the whole class is SelectedTabTextColor3, defaulting to pure white [255,255,255] against an unselected [175,175,175]. Hover gets a whole background ([125,125,125]); selection gets a lighter grey.

The tab strip is OPAQUE while the window it labels is translucent — ChannelTabsConfiguration.BackgroundTransparency defaults to 0 against the chat window's 0.3 and the input bar's 0.2. Chrome that names things is solid; the surface that carries the words is see-through.

Tab text is BOLDER than the messages under it — BuilderSansBold against BuilderSansMedium for the window and the input bar — and BOTH cited Roblox pages agree on that. WHETHER IT IS ALSO LARGER IS UNRESOLVED IN ROBLOX'S OWN DOCS AND THIS FILE DOES NOT SETTLE IT: the guide table on chat-window.md gives ChannelTabsConfiguration.TextSize a default of 18, while the class reference at reference/engine/classes/ChannelTabsConfiguration.md says verbatim 'Size of the text in channel tabs. Default value is `14`.' Both were re-fetched on 2026-09-20 and they still disagree; the window and the input bar are 14 on both pages, and every other tab property matches across the two. Do not use 18 as a measurement — the only way to settle it is to read the property in Studio, which nobody here did.

The tabs DROP the text stroke the messages keep — TextStrokeTransparency defaults to 1 on the tabs and 0.5 on the window and input bar. The stroke exists to hold legibility over an arbitrary 3D world; the tabs sit on an opaque strip and do not need it.

ChannelTabsConfiguration exposes AbsolutePosition and AbsoluteSize as read-only properties, so a custom social panel can measure where the default tab strip landed and lay itself out around it instead of guessing.

A user's name colour in chat defaults to their Player.TeamColor. Chat is team-coded before anyone writes a line of code, which is why a game that colours names by rank or clan is overriding a signal that is already there.

The message prefix is the sender's DisplayName, and prefix and body are separately styleable — PrefixTextProperties is its own properties object, so a tag, a colour or a UIGradient can be applied to the name without touching the message text.

THE PAGE DRAWS THE BOUNDARY EXPLICITLY, AND IT IS NOT WHERE A DESIGNER WOULD DRAW IT. Bubbles over an avatar's head, direct messages, the chat window and team messages are all chat. Menu text, status updates like 'Two minutes remaining!', admin-command announcements, moderation audit logs and — named outright — a user renaming their pet dog are NOT.

A comment box is not chat UNTIL IT GETS A REPLY BUTTON. The page says comments on posts are not chat, then adds that if the comments support replies those replies are a conversation and the policy applies. One affordance moves the whole surface across the line.

Any editable text one user can see from another must be rate-limited to AT LEAST ONE MINUTE — signs and bulletin boards are the named examples. A shared text field is not a text field; it is a chat surface with a cooldown.

Whether the local player may message another player is a SERVER QUERY, not something the game knows: CanUserChatAsync, CanUsersChatAsync and CanUsersDirectChatAsync exist because privacy settings, parental controls, the app store the player installed from and local law can each forbid it. A friend row's message button therefore needs an unavailable state driven by an answer the game has to ask for.
A channel built for direct messaging must be MARKED as one with TextChannel:SetDirectChatRequester(). A DM is not a two-person channel; it is a channel that has declared itself a DM.

Abuse reporting is not something the game builds. The page states TextChannels handle reportability automatically — so a custom chat frontend that bypasses TextChannel has silently removed the report path, and nothing on screen will say so.

With cross-server chat on, the window carries exactly TWO tabs and both are named after a PLACE rather than a function: 'Here' for this server and 'Global' for the rest. The tab row answers where, not what.

IT IS ON BY DEFAULT FOR ALL GAMES, and switched off from the Creator Dashboard under Audience → Communication Settings rather than in code. A game that has never thought about global chat already has it.

The Global tab is DISABLED IN PRIVATE SERVERS, stated as respecting users who only want to play with specific friends. The tab row is a different length depending on what kind of server you joined, so the count of tabs is not a constant the layout can assume.
Each global channel connects about 200 users, and the page gives readability and performance as the reason. A cap on who is in a room is a UI decision presented as an infrastructure one.
Under load the throttle applies to SENDERS AND RECEIVERS and messages DROP. A global channel is lossy by design, so a chat that guarantees delivery is describing a different feature.
The Global tab supports only a SUBSET of commands — /mute <username>, /unmute <username>, /help, /clear. The command vocabulary is per-channel, which means an autocomplete list is per-channel too.
Roblox groups servers for global chat by age, language and occupancy. Who is in the room is decided by the platform, not by the game, and the game cannot render a roster for it.

Replacing the chat is TWO separate ScreenGuis, not one panel: the input bar and the message list are built and parented independently, matching the two configuration objects that were disabled to make room for them.

The message list is a ScrollingFrame with a UIListLayout, and each message is a TextLabel NAMED AFTER ITS MessageId. The example looks the label up by that name on every arrival and edits it in place if it already exists — because MessageReceived fires once on send and once on receipt, and appending twice is the default failure.

THE PENDING STATE IS THE SAME ROW AT HALF OPACITY. An outgoing message — Status == Sending — is drawn with BackgroundTransparency 0.5 and settles to 0 when the server's copy lands. No spinner, no greyed-out duplicate, no separate 'sending' area.
The example's own comment states the expectation as a fact about users, not a preference: the input box is cleared after sending. It is cleared on FocusLost regardless of whether the send succeeded.
A failed send is reported INSIDE the transcript — the pcall's failure path calls DisplaySystemMessage('Failed to send message') into the same channel. The error lands where the message would have.

THE TAG EXAMPLE EXISTS TO WARN AGAINST THE OBVIOUS IMPLEMENTATION. Querying group membership inside OnIncomingMessage is called out as not recommended because the callback cannot yield and the chat system hangs. The prescribed shape is: resolve membership once on PlayerAdded, write it to a player ATTRIBUTE, and read the attribute in the callback.

The tag is applied by REBUILDING THE PREFIX — PrefixText becomes '[VIP] ' .. message.PrefixText — so a tag is a string prepended to the name, and a second tag from a second system would prepend again in whatever order the callbacks happened to run.

Returning nil from the callback means 'leave it alone'. The no-tag path is an absence of a properties object rather than a default one, so a tag system that always returns properties has opted every message into custom rendering.

THE FRIEND PICKER IS NOT THE GAME'S TO DRAW. PromptGameInvite raises Roblox's own prompt, which by default shows a menu of the player's friends each with an Invite button. The game's job ends at the call — the same hand-off shape the shop screen has with the Robux purchase dialog.

The ability to invite at all must be QUERIED FIRST with CanSendGameInviteAsync, wrapped in pcall, because the docs say it varies by platform and by player. An invite button that is always enabled is wrong on some devices and there is no way to find that out by looking.

0.rule: Ask whether the local player may contact this person before drawing a control that contacts them.
0.why: Roblox's chat guidelines page exists because privacy settings, parental controls, the installing app store and local law can each forbid a message, and it names CanUserChatAsync, CanUsersChatAsync and CanUsersDirectChatAsync as the way to find out. The invite path says the same thing for the same reason — CanSendGameInviteAsync must be checked first because the ability varies by platform and player. A message or invite button with no unavailable state is wrong on some devices and the screen cannot tell which.

1.rule: Do not draw the friend picker for an invite. Call the platform prompt and let it draw.
1.why: PromptGameInvite raises Roblox's own prompt, which already shows the player's friends each with an Invite button. This is the same hand-off screen-shop.json records for Robux purchases: a custom picker in front of the platform one stacks two choosers, and the custom one cannot see the friend list anyway.

2.rule: A friend row's action is present or absent, not enabled or disabled, when the action depends on where the friend is.
2.why: BedWars shows a Spectate button only when the friend is in a match and shows no button at all when they are in the lobby or in the studio's other game. A greyed button invites a click that can never succeed; the same wiki records that the one state where the button IS shown and cannot complete — a Custom Match — produces an error, which is the cost of getting this wrong.

3.rule: Scope the friends list to people the player is not already grouped with, or say why you did not.
3.why: BedWars excludes clan and party members from its friends list outright. It is a real decision with a real counter-argument — a player looking for a specific name will not find them — and it is the difference between a surface for starting contact and a directory. Whichever way a generator goes, it should go there on purpose.

4.rule: Do not re-query the friend list when the panel opens. Bootstrap it once and cache it.
4.why: Roblox's own GetFriendsWhoPlayed announcement gives this as rate-limit guidance in as many words: treat 'ever played' as an infrequent bootstrap, use since-timestamp calls to refresh, and avoid refreshing on every frame or every UI open. Opening a panel is the most natural place to refresh and it is the named anti-pattern.

5.rule: Every visible field on a friend row is a lookup the game performs itself.
5.why: GetFriendsWhoPlayedAsync returns an array of user ids and nothing else — the announcement states it does not store scores or rank players and that display is still yours. A row design with six fields is six fetch paths and six empty states, and the thread's own replies show developers asking for first- and last-played times the API does not return.

6.rule: Render a locator for a friend who is far away, and remove it when they are close.
6.why: Roblox's FriendsLocator module defaults thresholdDistance to 100 studs and shows NO icon for friends nearer than that, caps the screen at 10 icons, and draws them over world geometry. The indicator means distance, not presence — which is the inversion most implementations get backwards, and the cap is why a busy server does not turn into a wall of portraits.

7.rule: Make the presence indicator and the join action the same control.
7.why: FriendsLocator's icon teleports you to that friend on click by default. Splitting 'where are they' from 'take me there' adds a step to the only thing anybody wanted from the marker — and the module ships the split as an option (teleportToFriend = false) rather than as the default.

8.rule: Turn the channel tab row on deliberately, and expect its length to change at runtime.
8.why: ChannelTabsConfiguration ships DISABLED, so the default Roblox chat is one undifferentiated stream. And a tab row is not a fixed set once it is on: whisper tabs are titled with the other player's name and appear per conversation, and the cross-server Global tab is removed entirely in private servers.

9.rule: If you build the tab row yourself, give selection more than a text colour.
9.why: Roblox's own ChannelTabsConfiguration has HoverBackgroundColor3 and no selected-background property at all — the entire selected state is SelectedTabTextColor3 at white against [175,175,175]. Hover is louder than selection in the engine default, which is backwards. THE CROSS-FILE CITATION THIS REASON USED TO CARRY WAS FALSE AND IS DELETED: screen-shop.json records reviewers calling a tab row's pills 'a bit out of place being green' — a colour objection — not anyone misreading a selection state. That file is not evidence for this rule; the engine's own property list is.

10.rule: Key the message list by MessageId and update in place; never append on arrival.
10.why: MessageReceived fires twice for a message the local player sent — once optimistically at SendAsync and once when the server's processed copy returns. Roblox's own custom-frontend example names the label after the MessageId and edits it if it already exists, and the page carries an explicit warning about it.

11.rule: Draw a pending message as the same row at reduced opacity, in place.
11.why: The documented example uses BackgroundTransparency 0.5 while Status is Sending and 0 once it is confirmed. The message does not move, does not get a spinner, and does not get replaced by a different element — so a filtered message settling into its final text is a single visual change rather than a reflow.

12.rule: Resolve a sender's rank once when they join, store it as an attribute, and read the attribute in the message callback.
12.why: Every chat display callback must be non-yielding, and Roblox's own chat-tag example says querying group membership inside OnIncomingMessage is not recommended because it can hang the chat system. The tag on a message is cached state about a player, never a live lookup, which is also why a rank change mid-session will not repaint old messages.

13.rule: Give chat tags a small palette where the colour names the class of authority and the word disambiguates within it.
13.why: BedWars runs TEN chat tags in SIX colours, and seven of the ten share a colour with another tag: VIP and TRANSLATOR share a green — the wiki says TRANSLATOR uses the same light green as VIP — the two anti-cheat moderator tags share a purple, and three credit tags share a magenta, while DEV, MAP MAKER and PATRON each hold a colour alone. A reader learns the shared colours and reads the bracketed word only when the colour is ambiguous; ten unique colours would make every tag equally loud and none of them legible at a glance. The shipped instance is evidence for REUSING a colour across related tags, not for a clean colour-per-class scheme — half its colours carry a single tag.

14.rule: Treat a chat tag as a per-viewer decoration, not a property of the message.
14.why: BedWars records that as of 2026-01-07 players without Roblox face-age verification cannot see chat tags at all. The same message renders with and without its badge depending on who is reading, so anything that depends on the tag being visible — a rank a player is supposed to recognise, an authority signal before a moderation action — has to survive its absence.

15.rule: Reserve your own authority words everywhere a player can choose a string.
15.why: BedWars badges its developers [DEV] — formerly [ADMIN] — and its anti-cheat moderators [AC MOD] and [LEAD AC MOD] in chat, and its clan system blocks DEV, MOD and ADMIN as clan tags alongside named creators' tags such as TNQR and TANQR. The denylist is WIDER than the tag list: ADMIN is retired and MOD is never a tag by itself, only a stem inside [AC MOD]. Any game that shows a rank next to a name has created a vocabulary players will try to forge, and the denylist — old names and stems included — belongs on the creation form, not in moderation.

16.rule: Make the group's short tag the unique key and let the display name collide.
16.why: BedWars requires a clan TAG to be unique and explicitly allows two clans to share a NAME. The tag is what appears beside a player in chat, on the tablist and on their overhead nametag, so it is the thing that must identify; the name is read once on a roster screen where a collision costs nothing. Deepwoken makes the opposite call — a unique 1–26 character name — and pays for it with a character denylist and a paid, week-cooled rename.

17.rule: Build the rank ladder as a capability matrix, and cap promotion below the promoter's own rank.
17.why: Deepwoken publishes its ranks as a three-column table — invite/kick, promote, modify base — and a Lieutenant can promote only up to Officer. You cannot create your own peer, which is what stops a single compromised officer from replicating themselves through a roster. Every shipped group system read here grants INVITING first and keeps deletion and identity-editing for the top rung alone.

18.rule: Decide once whether a capability a player lacks is hidden or shown-unavailable, and apply it everywhere.
18.why: The two shipped games disagree in the open. BedWars hides the Invite tab below Officer and the Management tab below Admin, so the tab row is a different length per rank. Phantom Forces — recorded in fps_arena.json — leaves the votekick visible below Rank 25 and makes only the initiate action unavailable, which teaches what the rank is for. Mixing the two inside one product means a player cannot learn which absence means what.

19.rule: Do not hard-code rank labels. Treat them as data the group owns.
19.why: Arcane Odyssey ships leader, co-leader, admin, elite and member as DEFAULTS and lets a guild rename all five. A roster that hard-codes 'Officer' renders that game's guilds wrong, and a roster that derives the rank label from the permission set collapses Elite into Member — which is a distinct, purely honorific tier in the same list.

20.rule: Show the roster's member count against a denominator that can move.
20.why: Three shipped games give three different caps and two of them are purchased: BedWars starts at 10 and buys up to 80 in +5 steps, Blox Fruits starts at 15 and buys up to 30 one slot at a time, and Deepwoken has no cap at all. 'Members / cap' is a live pair, and a design that assumes a constant cap cannot render an unbounded roster or a growing one.

21.rule: State the roster's sort order, because there is no default and the shipped games do not agree.
21.why: Blox Fruits sorts crew members ASCENDING by bounty under a captain pinned above the sort; BedWars sorts its friends list alphabetically and does not float the one actionable row; Roblox's own GetPartyAsync returns members in the order they accepted the invite, with no rank field at all. Each order answers a different question, and picking one silently answers a question nobody asked.

22.rule: Give the group emblem a closed icon set when the emblem has to render in the world.
22.why: Deepwoken offers 89 icons and a single colour that drives both emblem and background, because the emblem appears above player names, in the player list, on ship sails and flags, on captured banners, on bases and beside War Mode counters. Blox Fruits instead accepts a free asset id and the wiki spends a whole section teaching players how to find one. The closed set is what makes the symbol legible at sail size; the open one is what makes it expressive on a roster screen. The right answer follows from where the thing is drawn.

23.rule: Rate-limit and price identity changes; do not rate-limit membership.
23.why: Deepwoken charges R$100 to rename a guild and imposes a week-long cooldown, applying that cooldown to newly created guilds too, while leaving membership uncapped. Arcane Odyssey charges the guild TREASURY 3,000 to change a name or logo and 1,000 for a colour. The thing other players have memorised is the expensive one to change.

24.rule: Make handing over ownership an explicit claim, not an automatic promotion.
24.why: In Deepwoken, when a guild leader is terminated, banned or leaves, leadership passes to the first person who speaks to a Guild Clerk — an NPC in the world — and the wiki is emphatic that it is not given out randomly. An automatic promotion means somebody logs in owning a group they did not ask for; a claim means the successor performed an act the roster can point to.

25.rule: Persistent group chat is not the same feature as server chat, and it is the hardest one on this screen.
25.why: The distinguishing property BedWars names for clan chat is that it saves even when the player leaves the game. That feature was added 2022-05-20, disabled 2022-05-21 — one day — and did not return until 2023-02-03. A generator asked for 'clan chat' should either build the persistent thing knowing that, or build a scoped channel and say that is what it built.

26.rule: If the channel selector is a prefix character rather than a tab, the input bar must say which channel it is in.
26.why: Deepwoken sends guild messages by prefixing '!' in public servers, and in instanced servers any message goes to everyone inside WITHOUT the prefix. The same keystrokes mean different audiences in different places, and nothing in the transcript distinguishes them before the message is sent.

27.rule: Scope a broadcast with a prefix that says how far it reached.
27.why: BedWars prefixes rare-drop announcements '[Server]:' or '[GLOBAL]:', and Roblox's cross-server chat names its two tabs 'Here' and 'Global'. A reader's first question about an announcement is who else saw it, and both a shipped game and the platform answer it in the first token.

28.rule: Scope the command vocabulary to the channel, and make the autocomplete follow it.
28.why: Roblox's Global tab supports only /mute, /unmute, /help and /clear, a strict subset of the standard set. BedWars splits its own commands between anyone-anywhere and Custom-Match-host-only in one list. ChatInputBarConfiguration.AutocompleteEnabled offers commands on '/' by default, so an autocomplete that does not know the channel offers commands that will be rejected.

29.rule: Build the invite picker from the population the invite can actually reach.
29.why: BedWars' party menu lists every player in the server with a search bar; Tower Defense Simulator lists friends first and then players in the server; Blox Fruits requires a typed username of somebody in your server who is not in a crew and is on the right faction. In all three the reachable set is narrower than 'your friends', and a picker drawn from the wrong population produces rows that fail on click.

30.rule: Let the row schema differ between candidate groups when different things are knowable about them.
30.why: Tower Defense Simulator's invite list shows friends with online status and NO level, and players in the server with their level. The same list carries two shapes because the game knows a server player's level and does not know an absent friend's. Forcing one schema means either an empty column or a fabricated one.

31.rule: Enumerate the invite failure messages, one per precondition.
31.why: Blox Fruits surfaces 'Player not found', 'Player is already in a Crew', 'Player is already in your Crew' and 'Member not found' at the top of the screen. A typed-name invite has at least four ways to fail and a single 'could not invite' leaves the captain retyping a name that was never the problem.

32.rule: Give an invite a transient notification AND a durable queue, and let stale entries disappear.
32.why: BedWars pops invites in the bottom-right corner and accumulates every one in an Invites tab, where selecting a party that has left the server makes the row disappear rather than error. Tower Defense Simulator does the same: an invite not answered immediately falls into an invites section with accept and deny. A pop-up alone loses invites that arrive mid-fight.

33.rule: Deliver invite copy as a pool of published notification strings, each interpolating the sender and the game.
33.why: Roblox requires the notification text to be a Notification asset created on the Creator Dashboard, containing the {experienceName} placeholder and optionally {displayName}. Tower Defense Simulator ships seven different invite lines built that way. One string repeated is the thing players learn to ignore, and the platform makes the plural version the documented path.

34.rule: Never assert 'you joined <friend>' on arrival. Treat it as a state the screen may upgrade into.
34.why: LaunchData is capped at 200 characters, arrives seconds late — Roblox's own sample retries ten times at one-second intervals — and a DevForum bug report open from 2023 through its last post in November 2025 says it is consistently blank in live experiences while working in test ones. The empty string is also the sentinel for 'not invited', so the failure is indistinguishable from the ordinary case.

35.rule: Let party size constrain the mode list, and say so before the player queues rather than after.
35.why: Three shipped games confirm the constraint independently — BedWars caps parties at 16 and restricts a full one to three modes, Tower Defense Simulator refuses to start when the party exceeds the selected squad size, and Rivals (in fps_arena.json) removes 1v1 from the list when two people are partied. Two of the three report it as an error after the attempt, which is the part worth improving rather than copying.

36.rule: Follow the platform's PartyId when assigning teams; do not invent your own grouping on top of it.
36.why: Player.PartyId is set by Roblox and its documented worked example is exactly team assignment: on join, find a party member already on a team and follow them, else balance. The party exists whether the game acknowledges it or not, and a game that splits one across teams has broken something it did not build.

37.rule: A party roster renders WHERE each member is, not just who they are.
37.why: GetPartyAsync returns PlaceId, JobId, PrivateServerId and ReservedServerAccessCode per member, because a party spans servers and places. The access code is there so 'join them' can work into a reserved server — which means the roster's join control has a different implementation per row depending on where that member is.

38.why: Roblox's sentinel for 'not in a party' is the empty string rather than nil, so a truthiness test passes for every player who has no party, and every party-aware branch runs for everybody.

39.rule: Anonymise a name into a stable token, not into a blank — and check what the token leaks.
39.why: BedWars' streamer mode replaces a tablist name with '<equipped kit>-###', keeping the row name-shaped, sortable and referable — that half is documented and it is the technique worth copying. The check is in the rule because this instance fails it on its face: the pseudonym still names the equipped kit, so a player hiding their identity is still broadcasting a gameplay attribute to everyone reading the roster. (The wiki also speculates — 'most likely' — that the tablist was once removed over players seeing others' kits. That motive is not documented and this rule does not rest on it.)

40.rule: Be willing to remove a field from a social screen when showing it invites pressure on a person.
40.why: One shipped precedent with a recorded reason, plus a community objection of the same shape. Phantom Forces changed its votekick popup to hide the yes/no split so a server could not see who to pressure (fps_arena.json). The community objection to GetFriendsWhoPlayed is that shape from the other direction — knowing which friends played lets a game choose whose name to put in front of you. BedWars did pull its whole tablist a week after shipping it and leave it out for fifteen months, but its wiki only guesses at why, so that case is evidence that a social screen CAN be withdrawn whole — not evidence about what triggers it.

41.rule: A social panel needs a matching switch on the settings screen.
41.why: BedWars lets players disable friends spectating them from settings, and Roblox's guidelines make communication access a function of privacy settings the player controls elsewhere. Every presence or contact surface implies an opt-out that lives on a different screen, and shipping the panel without the switch ships a feature the player cannot decline.

42.rule: Make a failure to load render as a failure, never as a plausible value.
42.why: Deepwoken's guilds fall back to displaying 'The Authority' — a real faction in the game — when a guild fails to load client-side. A player then reads a stranger as a member of a specific organisation on the strength of a network error, and no part of the screen distinguishes that from a correct render. The same shape appears in Blox Fruits, where a crew button silently does not appear after a faction change until the player rejoins.

43.rule: Give every roster stat an icon or leave the slot out; do not substitute a character.
43.why: Blox Fruits has no bounty icon and renders a currency sign in its place, so a bounty reads as money on a roster where money is a different thing. A missing asset that degrades into a wrong asset is worse than a missing column.

44.rule: If a custom chat replaces the default UI, it still has to go through TextChannel.
44.why: Roblox's guidelines state that TextChannels handle filtering, privacy settings and abuse reporting automatically, and that any user-to-user text must be filtered. The first reply a community chat replacement received on the DevForum was whether it bypasses moderation. A custom frontend that emits messages some other way has silently removed the report path, and nothing on screen will say so.

45.rule: Open the action menu from the username in the transcript.
45.why: A community chat replacement lists 'click on usernames for quick actions' among its headline features, and it is the cheapest bridge between the chat surface and the social one: the roster a player wants to act on is usually the list of people who have just spoken, and it is already on screen.

46.rule: Rate-limit any shared editable text to at least one minute, and treat it as a chat surface.
46.why: Roblox's guidelines require it outright for editable text one user can see from another, naming signs and bulletin boards. The same page draws the line in a place worth memorising: a comment box is not chat until it supports replies, at which point it is.

screens.label: The TRADE screen — two-sided offer windows, the add/remove timer, confirm-twice, value readouts and unbalanced refusals, escrowed listings, scam-prevention locks, and trade history
demonstrates: THE COUNTDOWN AND THE ACCEPT BUTTON ARE THE SAME CONTROL. A counter in the bottom-right of the trade menu counts down from 5, and when it ends it TURNS INTO the green accept button. There is no greyed-out accept to hammer at while you wait — the control does not exist until it is safe to press.

Every add AND every removal resets that counter, and the page states the reason outright: the cool-down 'prevents users from accidentally accepting a trade after items are removed, added, or replaced'. The reset is aimed at the removal, not at the addition.
Adding is a green '+' that opens a picker; REMOVING is clicking the item in the trade itself. Two different gestures, and the removal one is the same click that would inspect it.

THE UNFAIR-TRADE WARNING SAYS DIFFERENT THINGS TO THE TWO PLAYERS. When the game judges a trade unfair, the player on the winning side is warned that scamming is a bannable offence, and the other party is warned they might be getting scammed. If both proceed, the system grants 15 MORE SECONDS to accept or decline. It slows the trade down rather than refusing it.

Slot count is a shipped decision that moved twice: 4 items, raised to 9 in the November 2020 Trading Update, raised to 18 on 5 May 2023 — and the same 2023 change added trade CHAT NOTIFICATIONS so a player can keep track of changes made within a trade. The bigger the offer grew, the more the interface had to narrate its own changes.

Either player can request to view the other's BACKPACK from an icon in the trade chat menu; the other side gets an accept/decline prompt, and locked and untradable items are excluded from what is shown. The viewer can click an item to SUGGEST adding it, which posts to the trade chat with its own accept/decline — a suggestion is a message, not an action on the offer.
Suggesting a REMOVAL flashes a red 'x' over the item and posts to the trade chat. The suggestion is drawn on the thing it refers to as well as written down.

Backpack viewing has a three-way permission — always allow, always ask, never allow — defaulting to always ask, and the page names the reason it was built in January 2026: Roblox chat restrictions stopped players in different age groups from talking, so the negotiation had to move out of chat and into the interface.

Spectating is a first-class mode: a player already in a trade shows 'Spectate Trade' instead of 'Trade' on the interaction menu. Spectators react with a fixed emoji set that appears along the SIDE of the trading window, and a number in the bottom-right corner reports how many are watching.
A trade request that is left unanswered EXPIRES, and a player whose trades are off or set to friends-only never receives the request — the sender is told so rather than being left waiting.
The game turns OFF player interaction icons while a trade is open, which is how it killed 'fail trading'. The counter-measure was removing a control from the world, not adding one to the window.

THE WEAR BUTTON AND THE CONFIRM BUTTON SIT IN VERY SIMILAR SPACES, and the page says so in as many words as the reason a whole scam class works: a scammer gets the victim rapidly clicking Wear to change an outfit, and a click lands on Confirm. A destructive confirm placed where a harmless repeated action lives is a shipped, named, exploited layout defect.

THE ITEM PICKER COVERS THE OFFER. 'When the victim is adding items to the trade, the backpack covers most of their screen' — so the scammer swaps their side while the victim is choosing. The picker occluding the opposing offer is what makes a mid-add switch invisible, and Adopt Me's own later additions (trade chat change notifications, the flashing removal marker) are the fix arriving years after the hole.

THE LAST SLOT IS WHERE YOU GET ROBBED. A scammer fills the offer with low-value items so the high-value one lands in the final slot, then swaps it while the victim is still adding, 'as the victim would not pay as much attention to the bottom slot before accepting'. Position in a slot grid is not neutral — attention falls off toward the end of the list.

A VARIANT THAT CHANGES AN ITEM'S VALUE IS A LETTER BADGE ON THE CARD: a purple 'M' for Mega Neon, a green 'N' for Neon. The swap scam works precisely because the pet model is otherwise identical, so the badge IS the value — and a badge is a small mark to check under time pressure.

The window shows a LOADING state while an item is being added, and the page states that items always appear before either player can accept or decline. A side that has added nothing therefore shows nothing, never a spinner — which is why 'my trade menu is glitching' is diagnosable as a lie.

IDENTITY IS MARKED IN THE TRADE ITSELF: a smiley face beside the username means this is genuinely your friend, and the trade menu ALERTS you when you trade someone whose username is merely SIMILAR to one on your friends list. The near-miss is caught by the window, not left to the player's eyes.

A pop-up warning fires before a player's first trade AFTER JOINING A NEW SERVER — per session, not once per account. The warning is treated as something you need again in a new room, not a tutorial you dismiss forever.
The game intercepts the phrase 'trust trade' in chat and answers with a warning not to do it. The anti-scam surface extends outside the trade window into the text channel that sets the trade up.

THE GATE IS A TEST, NOT A LEVEL. Three scenarios are presented and the player must judge each as safe or a scam; the answer controls are a RED button for 'no, this is a scam' and a GREEN button for 'yes, this is safe'. All three must be right, and a failed test can be retaken without limit.
The licence gates a CAPABILITY, not the screen: without it a player still trades, just not ultra-rare or legendary pets. The trade window stays available and one class of item stays unmovable.
The licence is also the trade-history and report tool, and the history window is bounded — the LAST 30 DAYS, not all time.
History and reporting are reached by holding the licence and clicking or tapping the screen: the audit surface is an equipped object in the world rather than a tab inside the trade window.
The licence itself cannot be traded or given away, which is what stops the gate being purchasable from another player.

THE TWO SIDES OF A MARKETPLACE ARE TWO DIFFERENT NPCs. Robo-Todd is the sell desk — post a listing, view offers on it, modify it. Robo-Rob is the buy desk — search other players' listings, offer on them, review your own outstanding offers. The screen you are on tells you which side of the transaction you are.

SEARCH RUNS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: pick items from your own inventory to see what is being offered FOR them, or pick items you want to see what others are offering them for. The same search box answers 'what is mine worth' and 'what will this cost me'.

There is no empty-results state. Most relevant listings come first, and when there is no exact match — or the player has scrolled past every match — the screen falls back to listings for OTHER items that player owns.

LISTED ITEMS ARE ESCROWED. Anything placed in a listing or an offer cannot be equipped or used in another trade until the listing or offer is cancelled or completed. The item is visibly committed rather than merely promised.
Listing capacity is a priced scarcity stated on the screen: a listing costs 100 in-game Bucks, each player may hold two active listings, and a third slot is purchasable for 49 Robux.
Listings only display while their owner is IN A SERVER — an offline player's listings disappear rather than going stale, so what a buyer sees is always answerable.

AN UNBALANCED CHECK RUNS AT LISTING TIME TOO, AND THERE IT REFUSES: 'When posting a listing or offer, it will not go through if the trade is detected as too unbalanced.' The live window's answer to an unfair trade, on the Trade System page, is a WARNING plus 15 more seconds — so the asynchronous path blocks where the synchronous one only slows down. Neither page says the two checks are the same mechanism; only that both exist.

The companion phone READS EVERYWHERE AND WRITES IN ONE PLACE: trade history, active listings and active offers are viewable anywhere, but offers and listings cannot be created or modified unless the player is in the Hub.
The phone displays the player's LOCAL TIME in its top-left corner — a clock on a trading tool, because cross-server listings are the one part of the system that happens while you are not looking.

BOTH PARTIES ACCEPT TWICE, AND THE FAIRNESS CHECK COMES BEFORE THE WHOLE SEQUENCE: 'Once the trading system has decided that the trade is fair, both parties must accept two times to complete the trade.' The gate is in front of accepting at all, not specifically in front of the second press — the page says nothing about what happens between the two accepts. Fairness is a precondition of confirming, not a warning beside the button.
The system AUTO-DECLINES two shapes outright: items traded for nothing at all, and a high-value item traded for a low-value one. A refusal, not a nudge.

The unbalanced message is printed at the BOTTOM of the trade menu and it names the direction — 'Unbalanced: Your side is too low/high'. It is written from the reader's point of view, so the two players see different text about the same trade.
A trade request has a clock and the clock is SOLD: the other player has 1 minute to accept, or 90 seconds if the requester owns the Trading VIP pass. A gamepass buys patience from a stranger.
Eight items per side, and the inventory used to fill them gained a SEARCH function in a later update — a cap small enough to read alongside a picker too big to scroll.

ITEM CARDS ARE COLOUR-CODED BY TYPE, not by rarity: vehicles red, furniture yellow, weapon skins purple, vehicle customisations blue, consumables grey. The first thing the colour tells you is what KIND of thing you are being offered.
PROVENANCE IS A TINT, NOT A BADGE: if the current holder is the item's original owner, the whole card appears gold.
