This is one developer's own system rather than a shipped chart-topping game, and it is weighted below every wiki row above.

0.rule: Make the countdown BECOME the accept control, rather than greying an accept button out beside it.
0.why: Adopt Me's counter runs from 5 in the bottom-right of the trade menu and turns into the green accept button when it ends. A disabled button invites hammering, and a player hammering a button at the moment it becomes live is exactly the failure the cool-down exists to prevent.

1.rule: Reset the timer on every change to either side — and reset it hardest on a REMOVAL.
1.why: Adopt Me and Grow a Garden both reset their countdown when an item is removed, and both wikis name the same reason: the danger is accepting a trade whose contents changed after you read them. Adding something is visible; taking something away is what you miss.

2.rule: Confirm twice, and make the second confirm a DIFFERENT surface from the first.
2.why: Jailbreak requires both parties to accept twice once its trading system has judged the trade fair — the fairness check gates the sequence, not the second press in particular; Grow a Garden separates accept from confirm and states the confirm exists to make you check; the Roblox platform sends Accept to a whole separate screen that asks again. Three independent implementations, one shape: the second press must cost a glance, not a millisecond.

3.why: The Roblox platform routes Decline through its own are-you-sure and only then files the trade under Inactive. The decline is the cheap-looking control sitting beside the expensive one, and a misclick on it throws away a negotiation that took ten minutes to build.

4.rule: Never place the confirm where a harmless, repeatable action lives.
4.why: Adopt Me's own wiki records an entire scam class built on the Wear button and the Confirm button occupying 'very similar spaces': a scammer gets the victim clicking Wear rapidly and one click lands on Confirm. This is the clearest measured case in the library of adjacency itself being the defect.

5.rule: The item picker must not cover the opposing offer — and if it must, log every change to the offer in text.
5.why: Adopt Me's mega/neon switch scam works because 'the backpack covers most of their screen' while the victim is adding, so the other side can be swapped unseen. Adopt Me's answer, years later, was trade-chat notifications of changes and a red marker flashed over an item when its removal is suggested. The occlusion came first and the narration was the patch.

6.rule: Show a running total for EACH side, permanently, above the offers — and put per-item detail on hover.
6.why: Grow a Garden displays both players' full added value above the trading window and states its purpose as letting players judge fairness themselves; hovering an item adds its value and weight. A total that is present without being asked for is what makes a mid-trade swap arithmetically visible even when it is visually subtle.

7.rule: When refusing an unbalanced trade, say WHICH SIDE is wrong, from the reader's point of view.
7.why: Jailbreak prints 'Unbalanced: Your side is too low/high' at the bottom of the trade menu — the same trade produces different text for the two players. 'This trade is unfair' tells a player nothing they can act on.

8.rule: An automatic refusal and a human decline are DIFFERENT end screens.
8.why: Jailbreak's own gallery captions enumerate a trade 'denied automatically by the system due to being unbalanced' and a trade 'declined by the player' as separate states, alongside two distinct error dialogs for exploit-created items. Collapsing them teaches the player that the other person rejected them when the system did.

9.rule: Warn the two sides of a suspicious trade DIFFERENTLY, and extend the clock instead of blocking.
9.why: Adopt Me warns the advantaged player that scamming is bannable and the other that they may be being scammed, then grants 15 more seconds if both proceed. One message addressed to nobody in particular is the message neither player reads — and a hard block would also refuse every genuine gift.

10.rule: Pick ONE of: a hard fairness band, or a value readout — and know which you shipped.
10.why: Blox Fruits refuses any trade whose fruit values differ by more than 40% and widens the band toward 80–100% when Robux-bought products are involved; Jailbreak auto-declines the lopsided and was publicly pressured by its own players to make the balancing 'less restricting'; Grow a Garden shows totals and lets the player decide. A band protects the careless and blocks the generous; a readout does the reverse. A screen that shows a total AND silently refuses is the one combination that confuses everybody.

11.rule: Refuse the empty side, and refuse the empty inventory.
11.why: Jailbreak auto-declines items-for-nothing; Pet Simulator X raises a named pop-up when a player tries to trade away every pet they own. Both refusals cover the same moment — a player one click from having nothing — and neither is expressible as a fairness percentage.

12.rule: Cap the offer, and treat the cap as a layout decision: past about a dozen slots the offer scrolls, and a scrolling offer needs a change log.
12.why: The shipped caps are 4 then 9 then 18 (Adopt Me), 8 (Jailbreak), 4 unique with stacks (Murder Mystery 2), 4 (Blox Fruits), 13 (Grow a Garden) and 100 (Pet Simulator X). Both documented last-slot scams — Adopt Me's bottom-slot swap and Toilet Tower Defense's junk-spam — exist only because the offer grew taller than the screen.

13.rule: Make READY reversible and say for how long.
13.why: Toilet Tower Defense shows a timer after ready in which the player can unready. A commitment with a visible take-back window is a different promise from a delay you simply wait out, and it is the state a player reaches for the moment they notice something changed.

14.rule: Filter the partner list by who can actually be traded right now.
14.why: Pet Simulator X hides the trade option for a player already in a trade or who has disabled trading toward you, and lists only players with trading enabled. A request that can never arrive is a dead control that teaches the player the feature is broken.

15.rule: Privacy is a three-way choice — enabled, friends only, disabled — and it must exist on every platform you ship to.
15.why: Pet Simulator X and Pet Simulator 99 both ship exactly those three and almost the same words for them ('disable, enable, or set as friends only' / 'enable, disable, or set as only friends'); Toilet Tower Defense shipped four, two of which mean roughly the same thing and one of which its own wiki says most players cannot find. Adopt Me is NOT evidence for the third state — its page names only two, trades 'turned off' and the setting put to 'friends only'. Murder Mystery 2's toggle 'cannot be toggled on phones' — a consent control with no mobile path, recorded in the game's own reference.

16.rule: Mark identity inside the trade window, and alert on near-miss usernames.
16.why: Adopt Me shows a smiley beside a genuine friend's name in the trade and alerts the player when the partner's username is merely SIMILAR to one on their friends list. Impersonation by a lowercase L is invisible to a reader under time pressure and trivial for the window to catch.

17.rule: The mark that changes an item's value belongs ON the card, and the card's colour should encode TYPE.
17.why: Adopt Me distinguishes Mega Neon from Neon by a purple 'M' against a green 'N' — and a documented scam swaps one for the other precisely because the models are otherwise identical. Jailbreak colours cards by item type, tints a card gold when its holder is the original owner, and prints the season plus the level it required. In both, everything that determines worth is a mark you can check in one glance.

18.rule: Put provenance one tap behind the card, and prefer a rolling window to a lifetime total.
18.why: Jailbreak's cards carry a corner button opening original owner, creation date, monthly traded and monthly unique — and in July 2023 the lifetime 'times traded' figure was REMOVED the same week the monthly ones arrived. A total counts a decade of churn equally; a monthly figure answers whether this thing is moving NOW. It is arguable in both directions, which is why it is worth recording that a shipped game picked a side.

19.rule: State the fallback when provenance is unknown, rather than leaving the field blank.
19.why: Jailbreak shows items created before trading existed with their owner's join date, from May 2022 onward. A blank field looks like a bug; a stated default looks like history, and a player can reason about it.

20.rule: Escrow anything on offer, and show that it is locked.
20.why: Adopt Me's Trading Hub makes listed and offered items unequippable and unusable in any other trade until the listing is cancelled or completes, and an independent DevForum implementation of global trading names escrow as its first mechanic. Without it the same item is promised to three people, and two of them find out at the confirm.

21.rule: An asynchronous trade needs a fourth surface: an inbox where proceeds land.
21.why: The DevForum global-trading post delivers fulfilled items and currency to a player's inbox even while they are offline, backed by a dead-letter queue for failed hand-offs. Offer, history and listings cover the synchronous case; the moment a trade can complete while you are logged out, something has to hold the result.

22.rule: Trade history is its own screen, it is bounded, and it carries both relative and absolute time.
22.why: Toilet Tower Defense records how long ago each trade happened plus the date and time; Adopt Me's licence shows the last 30 days and is also the reporting tool; the Roblox platform files trades into completed and inactive buckets. Relative time is what a player reads; absolute time is what a report needs.

23.rule: Gate the CAPABILITY, not the screen — and gate it with a test when the risk is judgement rather than skill.
23.why: Adopt Me's licence is three safe-or-scam scenarios answered with a red and a green button, retakeable without limit, and it unlocks only ultra-rare and legendary trading; Murder Mystery 2 requires level 10 explicitly as an anti-dupe measure; Grow a Garden blocks accounts under 10 days from trading while still allowing them to GIFT. Hiding the whole window teaches nothing; leaving it open with one class of item immovable teaches exactly what the gate is for.

24.rule: Validate the free-text currency field, and document its ceiling.
24.why: Grow a Garden accepts abbreviated amounts like '5T' and silently refuses anything above 1QI; Toilet Tower Defense documents an exploit that puts a gem count of '-0' into the offer where every other screen shows '0' — its wiki calls that a visual glitch, and the 'infinite' part is what the scammer SAYS about the field rather than what the field prints. A number typed into a trade is an attack surface with a keyboard attached to it, and a field that will accept a negative zero is one a scammer can narrate.

25.rule: The cancel path must survive the trade window being unresponsive.
25.why: Blox Fruits documents a 'Freeze Trade' exploit that freezes the trade interface and prevents the victim from jumping so they cannot escape, and an 'Auto Accept' that presses the button for them. If the only way out is a control inside the frame that is stuck, there is no way out.

26.rule: Guarantee that what the other side's offer DISPLAYS is what will actually transfer.
26.why: Murder Mystery 2 records a mid-January 2022 exploit in which untradable effects, emotes, powers and radios could be put into a trade and then did not arrive — 'only the weapons or pets will be traded'. Its page states the missing delivery and not what the window showed, so what it proves is a gap between a trade's CONTENTS and its result. Toilet Tower Defense tells players to watch whether the green accept bar 'flicked' to detect a swapped offer. When the only evidence that an offer changed is a one-frame animation on another control, the window is not reporting its own state — the offer must be rendered from server truth and visibly reset when it changes.

27.rule: Make the trading place the game with things switched off.
27.why: Four independent games do the same thing: Jailbreak's island disables teams, arrests and damage; Toilet Tower Defense's plaza caps at 75 players, removes map teleporters, disables voice chat and drops WINS from the leaderboard so only coins and gems show; Grow a Garden's trade world strips every untradable item from the inventory on entry and makes the main currency unspendable; Blox Fruits confines trading to exactly two named places, a café in one sea and a mansion in another. The trading surface is defined as much by what it removes as by what it adds.

28.rule: Price the listing, not the handshake — and state the fee before the confirm, in the units the player will feel it.
28.why: Adopt Me charges 100 Bucks for EVERY Trading Hub listing and lets a player hold two active at once, with a third concurrent slot purchasable for 49 Robux — the first two slots are not free, they are the ones whose CAPACITY costs nothing; Grow a Garden caps its sale deduction at 10 tokens in ABSOLUTE terms rather than as a percentage; the Roblox platform takes a 30% fee from Robux moved and caps post-fee Robux at 50% of the RAP of the included items — RAP, not the community's 'value', which the same page defines separately as an unofficial appraisal built from submitted trade proofs. A flat cap stops mattering as the price rises and a percentage never does, and the player should be able to see which one they are living with.

29.rule: Put the negotiation inside the trade, because the platform may take the chat away.
29.why: Toilet Tower Defense ships a private chat button in the trade window. Adopt Me built backpack viewing with click-to-suggest in January 2026 for a stated reason: Roblox chat restrictions stopped players in different age groups from talking to each other, so the haggling had to become interface. A trade screen that assumes the players can type at each other is one policy change away from being unusable.

30.rule: Cap and clock the REQUEST separately from the trade.
30.why: Jailbreak gives the recipient 1 minute to answer, 90 seconds if the sender owns the VIP pass; Adopt Me expires unanswered requests; the Roblox platform caps an account at 100 trades SENT per day — its page's wording is 'a rate limit on trades', and it attributes the change only tentatively, to trade bots sending hundreds an hour. Sending is the spam surface, so it needs its own ceiling, and answering is the one that needs its own clock. Only the Jailbreak and Adopt Me clocks are stated to belong to the request rather than to the trade.
